SN2 nucleophilic substitution; converts a primary alkyl tosylate to the corresponding iodide using KI. Typically performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetone or DMF at reflux (50‑80 °C); KI is used in excess and potassium p‑toluenesulfonate precipitates out, driving the reaction forward.

Oxidative dissolution of technetium metal in concentrated nitric acid; Tc(0) is oxidized to pertechnetic acid (HTcO₄) while nitrate is reduced to NO₂ gas; typically refluxed in 6–12 M HNO₃, generating heat and effervescence of NO₂; no additional catalyst is required.

Oxidation (combustion) of phosphide. Solid sodium phosphide is heated in air or oxygen, where the P³⁻ ions are oxidised to phosphate, giving sodium phosphate (Na₃PO₄) as the product. Performed by direct ignition or heating to 300–500 °C in a furnace; the reaction is self‑sustaining once initiated. No solvent or catalyst.

Salt metathesis (anion exchange); replaces the iodide counter‑ion of 1‑ethylpyridinium with tetrafluoroborate by reacting sodium tetrafluoroborate with the pyridinium iodide salt. Usually carried out in aqueous or alcoholic solution at room temperature with stirring; NaI remains dissolved while the new pyridinium tetrafluoroborate can be isolated by solvent removal or precipitation.

Strong reduction of an ester (LiAlH₄ reduction). Lithium aluminium hydride delivers hydride to the carbonyl carbon of isopropyl formate, cleaving the C=O bond. The alkoxy fragment is as isopropanol, while the formyl carbon is reduced to methanol. Conducted in dry ether (THF or diethyl ether) at 0 °C to reflux under inert atmosphere; the reaction is quenched cautiously with water, then dilute acid to decompose excess LiAlH₄ and afford the two alcohol products.

Catalytic acyl transfer (transesterification of an anhydride); n‑Butanol attacks propionic anhydride in the presence of a copper‑based catalyst to give butyl propionate and propionic acid. Common conditions: copper(I) halide (e.g., CuCl) with a base (pyridine) in a high‑boiling solvent such as toluene or xylene, heated to 80‑120 °C under nitrogen. The copper catalyst accelerates the acyl‑oxygen cleavage and ester formation.

Eschweiler–Clarke reductive methylation of a secondary amine. Purpose: Convert the secondary amine to its N‑methyl analogue. Key transformation: Formaldehyde condenses with the amine to form an iminium ion; formic acid then reduces the iminium to the N‑methyl amine, releasing CO₂ and water. Typical conditions: aqueous or mixed aqueous/MeCN solvent, excess formaldehyde (as aqueous 37 % solution), excess formic acid (≈5 eq), reflux (≈100 °C) for several hours; reaction is tolerant of the thioether substituent.

Radical recombination/addition reaction: a hydrogen atom adds to nitrogen dioxide, converting NO₂ to nitrous acid (HNO₂). This gas‑phase process can be observed in low‑temperature radical environments such as atmospheric chemistry or flash‑photolysis experiments. The reaction is typically conducted in an inert carrier gas; the HNO₂ product is often trapped in an aqueous medium for analysis. No additional catalyst is required.

Acid‑catalyzed Markovnikov hydration of an alkene; cis‑2‑hexene is converted to 2‑hexanol by addition of water across the double bond. Typical conditions employ dilute sulfuric acid (≈5 %) or HgSO₄/H₂SO₄ (oxymercuration) at 25‑80 °C in aqueous media. The reaction proceeds via a carbocation intermediate, giving the more stable secondary alcohol.

LiAlH₄ reduction of a carboxylic acid; oleic acid is reduced to oleyl alcohol. Performed under anhydrous conditions in dry ether (THF or diethyl ether) at 0 °C to reflux, under nitrogen. After complete consumption of the acid, the reaction mixture is quenched with water and then acidified; aluminum hydroxide precipitates and is filtered off, leaving the primary alcohol as the product.

Acid‑catalyzed hydration (Markovnikov addition); concentrated H₂SO₄ adds across the double bond of 2-methylpent-1-ene to give 2-methylpentan-2-ol after aqueous work‑up. Conditions typically involve stirring the alkene with 60–98 % H₂SO₄ at 0–25 °C, followed by dilution with water and extraction. The reaction proceeds via protonation of the alkene, formation of a carbocation, and nucleophilic capture by water.

Salt metathesis / organometallic synthesis; used to prepare volatile trimethylgallium for semiconductor processes. Gallium trichloride reacts with methyllithium, exchanging chloride for methyl groups and forming lithium chloride as a by‑product. Typically performed under inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar) at 0 °C to –78 °C in anhydrous ether or THF; no additional catalyst required.

Acid‑base neutralization of a metal carbonate; employed to obtain terbium(III) acetate from the carbonate precursor. Glacial acetic acid protonates the carbonate, releasing carbon dioxide and water while the acetate anion coordinates terbium(III). Carried out by heating a suspension of terbium carbonate in excess glacial acetic acid (reflux, ca. 100 °C); the acid itself serves as solvent, no catalyst needed.

Hydrolysis / salt metathesis of a silicon halide; provides sodium silicate (water glass) from silicon tetrachloride. SiCl₄ is attacked by hydroxide ions, forming Si–O bonds, yielding Na₂SiO₃, water, and sodium chloride. Conducted in aqueous NaOH solution, often at 0–25 °C to control vigorous gas evolution; stirring is essential, and no catalyst is required.

Double‑displacement precipitation (metathesis); used to isolate sparingly soluble cerium(III) fluoride. Cerium(III) nitrate exchanges its nitrate anions for fluoride from potassium fluoride, precipitating CeF₃ while forming soluble KNO₃. Typically carried out in water at ambient or mildly elevated temperature (20–60 °C); the reaction proceeds without added catalyst and the solid is filtered and washed.

Redox reduction of a metal oxide by carbon monoxide; employed to regenerate metallic silver from silver oxide in catalytic cycles. CO reduces Ag₂O, being oxidized to CO₂ while Ag⁺ is reduced to elemental silver. Conducted in a flow of CO or CO‑containing gas at 200–300 °C in a furnace; solid‑state reaction, no solvent or catalyst is used.

Nucleophilic acyl‑transfer (anhydride exchange): sodium acetate attacks propionic anhydride, displacing the acetate side and yielding sodium propionate together with acetic acid as the by‑product. Usually performed in a polar solvent (e.g., water, methanol, or acetone) at ambient or gently heated temperature; no catalyst is required.

Nucleophilic ring‑opening addition of an epoxide to a urea derivative, yielding a cyclic urea (1,3‑dimethyl‑2‑imidazolidinone, a polar aprotic solvent). Dimethylurea attacks the electrophilic carbon of ethylene oxide, closing a five‑membered ring and eliminating the epoxy oxygen as part of the new carbonyl. Performed under sealed‑vessel conditions at 100–150 °C, often under slight excess of ethylene oxide; acid or basic catalysts such as zinc acetate or a tertiary amine can accelerate the reaction, but it may also proceed uncatalyzed.

Hydrolysis (acidic or basic cleavage) of the amide herbicide alachlor in water, breaking the N‑acyl bond to give 2‑chloroacetic acid, 2,6‑diethyl‑aniline and methoxyacetic acid; typically performed at elevated temperature (60‑100 °C) in aqueous solvent, often with a catalytic amount of acid or base to accelerate the cleavage.

This reaction is a metathesis (double displacement) reaction where cations and anions exchange partners. Thallium(I) chloride reacts with silver(I) hexafluorophosphate, causing precise formation of insoluble silver(I) chloride precipitate while thallium(I) hexafluorophosphate remains in solution. The reaction is performed in aqueous or non-aqueous solution and serves for selective anion exchange, commonly for isolation of less reactive or less soluble salts.

This is a nucleophilic substitution (SN2) reaction involving the alkylation of methylamine. The nitrogen in methylamine acts as a nucleophile, attacking the electrophilic carbon in cyclopentyl chloride, displacing chloride and producing a secondary amine, N-methylcyclopentanamine. A base, such as sodium carbonate or potassium carbonate, may be present to neutralize the hydrochloric acid generated, typically in an aqueous or alcoholic medium.

Acid–base neutralisation forming an organic sulfate salt; the strong acid (H₂SO₄) protonates and pairs with two equivalents of the basic amine mephentermine to afford mephentermine‑sulfate; carried out in water or aqueous ethanol at ambient temperature, with stirring until complete dissolution of the salt.

Metal insertion to form a Grignard reagent; purpose: generate 1‑phenylethylmagnesium bromide for subsequent nucleophilic addition reactions. Key transformation: magnesium inserts into the C–Br bond of 1‑bromo‑1‑phenylethane, producing the organomagnesium bromide. Typical conditions: anhydrous diethyl ether or THF, activated Mg (iodine, flame‑dry), reflux under dry nitrogen or argon; strict exclusion of moisture; no additional catalyst.

This is a nucleophilic substitution (SN2) allowing ethylamine to displace chloride in 4-(chloromethyl)pyridine, resulting in the formation of 4-(ethylaminomethyl)pyridine. The reaction requires a polar solvent like ethanol or dimethylformamide (DMF), often with mild heating or basic additive such as sodium hydroxide to scavenge hydrochloric acid, which enhances reaction completion.

Williamson‑type ether synthesis (SN2 substitution) in which the phenoxide anion of sodium 2,4,5‑trichlorophenolate attacks the electrophilic carbon of chloroacetic acid, displacing chloride and forming 2,4,5‑trichlorophenoxyacetic acid; usually performed in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., DMF or DMSO) or aqueous medium, heated to reflux, and then acidified to isolate the product, with NaCl as the by‑product.

Double displacement (metathesis) reaction; converts gold(I) chloride to gold(I) cyanide for increased solubility or further processing; KCN transfers cyanide to AuCl forming AuCN and KCl; typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; water is the solvent and no additional catalyst is required.

Double‑displacement precipitation: zinc acetate reacts with sodium carbonate in aqueous solution to form insoluble zinc carbonate and soluble sodium acetate; carried out at ambient temperature in water, stirring until complete precipitation.

Acid‑medi precipitation (metathesis) of tellurium dioxide from sodium tellurite by reaction with hydroiodic acid; the TeO₃²⁻ ion is protonated and precipitates as insoluble TeO₂ while Na⁺ pairs with I⁻ to give NaI and water is formed; conducted in aqueous solution, often under gentle heating (40‑80 °C) to improve crystal formation.

Oxidation with potassium permanganate; type: strong oxidative cleavage/oxidation of an aromatic side‑chain; purpose: convert the acetyl side chain to a carboxylic acid; key transformation: 1‑(4‑methylphenyl)ethanone → 4‑methylbenzoic acid (C=O → CO₂H); typical conditions: aqueous alkaline KMnO₄ (often 0.5–2 M), heating under reflux, followed by acidification (HCl) to precipitate the acid; excess MnO₂ filtered off.

Selective reduction of the benzimidazole C=N bond with sodium borohydride, yielding 2,3‑dihydro‑1H‑benzimidazole; performed in protic solvents (e.g., methanol, ethanol) at 0 °C to room temperature; NaBH₄ acts as hydride donor, no metal catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) aided by phase‑transfer catalysis; cyanide ion displaces bromide on benzyl bromide to form phenylacetonitrile, with KBr as by‑product; performed in a biphasic system (aqueous KCN and an organic solvent such as dichloromethane or toluene) with tetrabutylammonium bromide as the phase‑transfer catalyst; reaction is typically run at room temperature to gentle reflux.

High‑temperature solid‑gas redox/decomposition reaction; elemental carbon reduces potassium cyanate, producing carbon monoxide gas and potassium cyanide; carried out in a furnace at several hundred °C under dry conditions; no solvent or catalyst is used, only heat.

Catalytic dehydrogenation (or oxidative dehydrogenation); converts a saturated alkylbenzene to an alkene. Key transformation: ethylbenzene → styrene + H₂. Typical conditions: high temperature (500–650 °C) over heterogeneous metal oxide catalysts (e.g., Fe₂O₃/Cr₂O₃, CuCl‑based, or Pt‑Sn/Al₂O₃). Often carried out in the gas phase with an inert carrier gas; no solvent.

Acid‑catalyzed acetal formation (acetalization); formaldehyde reacts with methanol in the presence of hydrochloric acid to give dimethoxymethane (methylal) and water; the reaction proceeds under reflux in excess methanol, with removal of water (e.g., azeotropic distillation) to drive equilibrium; hydrochloric acid is the catalyst and methanol serves as both reactant and solvent.

Type: Nucleophilic substitution (alcohol to alkyl chloride, SN2). Purpose: Convert allyl alcohol into the corresponding chloride for further functionalization. Key transformation: Protonation of the hydroxyl group by HCl followed by attack of chloride ion, displacing water. Typical conditions: Excess gaseous or aqueous HCl, often in a non‑aqueous solvent such as diethyl ether or THF; reflux may be applied. Common solvents/catalysts: Ether or dichloromethane; sometimes ZnCl₂ (Lucas reagent) to accelerate the reaction.

Strong reduction of a ketone with lithium aluminium hydride; converts 2‑chloroacetophenone to 1‑(2‑chlorophenyl)ethanol; LiAlH₄ provides hydride in dry ether or THF under inert atmosphere, often with reflux or gentle heating; the C‑Cl bond is generally retained under controlled work‑up.

Halogen exchange (halide substitution) converting disulfur dibromide to disulfur dichloride while liberating bromine; used to prepare S₂Cl₂. Typically carried out in a dry, inert solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or chloroform at 0–25 °C; no catalyst required.

Electrophilic silylation of vinyllithium with trimethylsilyl chloride; Si–Cl bond is cleaved, LiCl precipitates and the vinyl group is transferred to Si(Me)3, giving vinyltrimethylsilane. Carried out in dry THF or diethyl ether at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen; no additional catalyst.

Acid–metal (or acid–intermetallic) reaction where aqueous hydrochloric acid dissolves zinc antimonide, releasing hydrogen gas and forming zinc chloride and antimony trichloride; a method to generate the metal chlorides and collect H₂. Conducted in aqueous HCl, usually with gentle heating (reflux) to accelerate gas evolution; no special catalyst.

Williamson ether synthesis (SN2 alkylation) that forms 4‑chloro‑2‑methylphenoxyacetic acid by deprotonating the phenol with NaOH to give the phenoxide, which attacks monochloroacetic acid. Performed in aqueous or alcoholic NaOH at 0–50 °C; simple base, no catalyst.

Organozinc preparation; oxidative insertion of zinc into the C–Cl bond afford ethylzinc chloride, a milder nucleophile used in cross‑coupling; carried out in dry ether or THF with activated Zn dust, often at 0 °C to reflux, under nitrogen.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation; exchanges anions to precipitate insoluble silver iodide; PrI3 + 3 AgNO3 → Pr(NO3)3 + 3 AgI↓; performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with water as solvent; no catalyst required.

Mitsunobu esterification converting gallic acid to its n‑propyl ester (propyl gallate) using triphenylphosphine and diethyl azodicarboxylate as the activating system; produces triphenylphosphine oxide and diethyl hydrazinedicarboxylate as by‑products. Conducted under inert atmosphere in anhydrous THF or dioxane, typically 0 °C to room temperature; reagents act as catalyst/system.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction in which sodium sulfide reacts with lead(II) sulfate to produce insoluble lead(II) sulfide precipitate and soluble sodium sulfate; used for qualitative Pb²⁺ detection or sulfide precipitation. Conducted in aqueous solution at room temperature, stirring; no catalyst.

Esterification (acylation) of 2‑phenylethanol with acetic anhydride to give phenethyl acetate; the hydroxyl group is replaced by an acetyl group, releasing acetic acid. Typically performed at 0–25 °C up to reflux, often neat or in a non‑nucleophilic solvent; catalytic amounts of pyridine, DMAP or triethylamine are used to neutralize the generated acid.

Lucas halogenation (SN1 substitution): 1‑pentanol is converted to 1‑pentyl chloride by treating the alcohol with concentrated HCl in the presence of catalytic ZnCl₂ (Lucas reagent). The alcohol is protonated, loses water to form a carbocation, and chloride ion attacks to give the alkyl chloride. Typical conditions are 0‑50 °C in aqueous HCl; ZnCl₂ acts as a Lewis‑acid catalyst.

Esterification of allyl alcohol with acetic anhydride to afford allyl acetate; the alcohol oxygen attacks the anhydride, forming an ester and releasing acetic acid. Conducted under mild heating (room temperature to reflux) either neat or in a solvent such as dichloromethane; catalytic pyridine or DMAP may be added to scavenge acid.

Conversion of acetic acid to acetyl chloride using phosphorus pentachloride (PCl₅); the carboxyl OH is replaced by Cl, yielding acetyl chloride, HCl, and POCl₃ as by‑product. Performed under anhydrous conditions, typically in a dry inert solvent (e.g., CH₂Cl₂, CCl₄) at 0 °C to reflux; no additional catalyst is required.

Copper(I)-catalyzed O‑alkylation of phenol with epichlorohydrin to produce phenyl glycidyl ether; phenoxide generated by Na₂CO₃ attacks the primary carbon of epichlorohydrin, displacing chloride and forming the epoxy ether, with NaCl and water as side products. Reaction is carried out in a polar aprotic solvent (DMF or DMSO) at 80–120 °C, using CuBr as catalyst and 1,10‑phenanthroline as ligand; Na₂CO₃ serves as base.

Metathesis/precipitation reaction of manganese carbonate with sodium hydroxide in aqueous solution, yielding soluble sodium carbonate and insoluble manganese(II) hydroxide precipitate. Conducted at ambient temperature in water; no catalyst required.

Double displacement (metathesis) ion‑exchange; used to prepare tetrabutylammonium fluoride as a soluble source of fluoride for organic reactions; NaF and tetrabutylammonium hexafluorophosphate are mixed in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., acetonitrile, DMF) at room temperature or mild heating, and the resulting salts TBAF and NaPF₆ precipitate or remain in solution; no additional catalyst required.

Chlorination of a primary alcohol with sulfuryl chloride; converts isobutanol to isobutyl chloride while generating HCl and SO₂; typically performed under inert atmosphere in anhydrous dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride at 0 °C to room temperature, sometimes with a base such as pyridine to trap HCl; proceeds via radical or SN1 pathway; no external catalyst.

Catalytic hydrogenation (H2/Pd‑C) of a ketone; hydrogen gas in the presence of palladium on carbon reduces the carbonyl of 4‑phenyl‑2‑butanone to give 4‑phenyl‑2‑butanol; common conditions are 1–5 atm H2, solvent such as ethanol, methanol or ethyl acetate, room temperature to 50 °C, with 5–10 wt % Pd‑C and reaction time of several hours.

O‑Methylation (phenol alkylation) of vanillin using dimethyl carbonate and sodium hydride; the phenolic OH is deprotonated by NaH and then methylated to give veratraldehyde (3,4‑dimethoxy‑benzaldehyde); carried out in dry THF or DMF under nitrogen, 0 °C to reflux, with stoichiometric NaH and excess dimethyl carbonate; no metal catalyst required.

N‑Alkylation (quaternization) of 4‑methyl‑5‑(2‑hydroxyethyl)thiazole with 1,12‑dibromododecane to form a bis‑thiazolium dibromide dication; the thiazole nitrogen attacks the primary bromide in an SN2 reaction, giving the 1,12‑bis(4‑methyl‑5‑(2‑hydroxyethyl)thiazol‑3‑ium‑3‑yl) dodecane dibromide; conducted in refluxing acetonitrile or DMF, often with a mild base (e.g., K₂CO₃) to neutralize HBr; no metal catalyst.

Hydrolysis and thermal decarboxylation of phenylurea; purpose is to break down the urea derivative into aniline and gaseous by‑products; key transformation is cleavage of the C–N bond of the urea moiety with loss of CO2 and NH3; typically performed by heating phenylurea with excess water at 150‑200 °C, often under acidic or basic catalysis; water is the solvent and the reaction may be carried out in a sealed tube or reflux apparatus.

Copper‑catalyzed Ullmann‑type C–N coupling (amination) of 2‑iodopyridine with ammonia to afford 2‑aminopyridine; 1,10‑phenanthroline ligates CuI, K₂CO₃ acts as base, and the reaction is heated in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMSO or DMF (100–150 °C); yields the aryl amine after displacement of iodide; catalyst is CuI/phenanthroline.

Aminolysis of an ester with ammonia – conversion of an ester into an amide. Ammonia attacks the carbonyl of 2-(dimethylamino)ethyl benzoate, displacing the 2-(dimethylamino)ethanol and forming benzamide. Usually performed in excess gaseous NH3 or aqueous NH3 (10–30 % aq.) at elevated temperature (50–100 °C) in a polar solvent such as methanol or ethanol; pressure may be applied for gaseous NH3.

Double displacement (metathesis) ion‑exchange; used to convert sodium metaborate into the more easily crystallized ammonium metaborate; Na⁺ is swapped for NH₄⁺ while the metaborate anion remains unchanged; carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; water is the solvent, no catalyst required.

Formation of an acyl chloride from 2‑chloropropionic acid using oxalyl chloride (Vilsmeier reagent); oxalyl chloride converts the carboxylic acid to 2‑chloropropanoyl chloride while releasing CO, CO₂ and HCl; typically performed at 0 °C to room temperature in dry dichloromethane, with catalytic DMF to enhance activation; no additional catalyst beyond oxalyl chloride.

Catalytic redox decomposition of H₂O₂ in acidic medium; MnO₂ acts as a catalyst (and is partially reduced) converting H₂O₂ to O₂ while MnO₂ is reduced to Mn²⁺ forming MnSO₄; overall: MnO₂ + H₂O₂ + H₂SO₄ → MnSO₄ + 2 H₂O + O₂; carried out in aqueous solution, dilute H₂SO₄, at room temperature; MnO₂ is the solid catalyst, water solvent.

Oxidation of a sulfide to a sulfoxide; peracetic acid acts as a mild peracid oxidant converting diphenyl sulfide to benzenesulfinylbenzene while being reduced to acetic acid. Performed at 0 °C to room temperature in an inert organic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform; no additional catalyst required.

Ester hydrolysis (saponification) of ethyl 3,4-dihydroxybenzoate to give 3,4-dihydroxybenzoic acid and ethanol. Purpose: convert the ester to the free acid. Key transformation: cleavage of the C–O bond of the ethyl ester, producing the carboxylic acid and ethanol. Typical conditions: aqueous acid (e.g., 1 M HCl) or base (NaOH) reflux for 1–4 h, followed by acidification if a base is used. Common solvent: water or water/ethanol mixture.

Redox (disproportionation) of bromine in alkaline medium; sodium carbonate provides carbonate that reacts with Br2, yielding sodium bromide, sodium bromate and carbon dioxide. Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; vigorous stirring, no catalyst needed.

Transesterification (ester exchange). The tert‑butyl 2,2,2‑trifluoroacetate reacts with methanol to give methyl 2,2,2‑trifluoroacetate and tert‑butanol. Typically catalysed by a Brønsted acid (e.g., p‑toluenesulfonic acid) or a base (e.g., NaOMe) under reflux in excess methanol; the volatile tert‑butanol is removed to drive the equilibrium.

Gem‑dichlorination of an aldehyde; phosphorus pentachloride converts butanal into 1,1‑dichlorobutane while generating HCl and POCl₃ as by‑products. Carried out under anhydrous conditions in a dry halogenated solvent (e.g., CH₂Cl₂) at 0 °C to reflux; the reaction is exothermic and does not require a catalyst.

Nef reaction (base‑promoted conversion of a primary nitroalkane to an aldehyde): 1‑nitropropane is deprotonated with NaOH to give a nitronate ion; upon acidic work‑up with acetic acid the nitro group is transformed into a carbonyl, affording propionaldehyde while NaNO₂ is produced as the nitrogen by‑product. Conducted in aqueous NaOH at 0‑25 °C followed by addition of excess AcOH; water is the common solvent.

Esterification (condensation) of 2‑diethylaminoethanol with 2‑chloro‑4‑aminobenzoic acid to form chloroprocaine and water. Typically carried out with a coupling reagent (e.g., DCC or EDC) or by heating the acid and alcohol with a catalytic amount of acid (e.g., DMAP) in a polar aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF; the reaction proceeds at 0 °C to rt.

Direct fluorination of elemental antimony; forms antimony trifluoride (SbF3) by reaction of Sb(0) with F2; key transformation is oxidation of antimony to +3 state with three fluorine atoms; typically carried out by passing F2 over heated antimony (200‑300 °C) in a fluorination furnace; no solvent or catalyst needed.

Acid‑base salt formation; hydrogen fluoride reacts with ammonium chloride to give hydrogen chloride gas and ammonium bifluoride (NH₄HF₂). Performed in aqueous solution at low temperature; no catalyst required.

Oxidation of a tertiary amine to its N‑oxide; hydrogen peroxide serves as oxidant and sodium tungstate (Na2WO4) acts as a homogeneous peroxidase‑type catalyst. The nitrogen atom gains an O‑atom, generating the N‑oxide surfactant and reducing H2O2 to water. Typical conditions are aqueous or biphasic media at 25–60 °C, pH neutral to slightly alkaline, often with a small amount of organic co‑solvent (e.g., methanol) to dissolve the long‑chain amine.

Alcoholysis of phenylacetyl chloride with ethanol to give ethyl phenylacetate; similar acyl‑substitution esterification. Performed in dry ethanol at 0 °C to rt; addition of a base (e.g., pyridine) helps neutralize the generated HCl.

Mixed‑anhydride exchange (acyl transfer) whereby acetic anhydride donates one acetyl group to hexanoic acid, forming hexanoic anhydride and liberating acetic acid. No external catalyst is required; the reaction is driven by excess acetic anhydride and removal of volatile acetic acid. Conducted under reflux (80–120 °C) in an inert solvent such as toluene directly neat, sometimes with azeotropic distillation of acetic acid.

Ester hydrolysis (saponification or acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis) of pentan‑3‑yl acetate to give pentan‑3‑ol and acetic acid. Under acidic conditions the reaction is performed by refluxing the ester in aqueous H2SO4 or HCl; under basic conditions it uses aqueous NaOH at room‑temperature to 60 °C followed by acid work‑up to liberate the alcohol. A miscible organic solvent (e.g., THF or acetone) is often added to improve phase contact.

Acid–base metathesis between iron(II) phosphate and excess glacial acetic acid, producing ferrous acetate and phosphoric acid. The solid phosphate is suspended in acetic acid and heated under reflux (80–110 °C) until dissolution; the mixture is then cooled and the ferrous acetate is isolated, while phosphoric acid remains in solution. No additional catalyst is needed; the reaction proceeds stoichiically.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis of an ether (2‑ethoxybutane) over Raney nickel, cleaving the C–O bond to afford ethanol and 2‑butanol. Performed under H2 pressure (1–5 atm) at 50–150 °C with Raney Ni as the heterogeneous catalyst; a solvent such as ethanol, isopropanol, or THF is used tose the substrate. The reaction proceeds via surface hydrogen addition followed by C–O bond scission.

O‑methylation of phenol with methyl fluorosulfate; nucleophilic substitution of the phenolic oxygen yielding anisole and fluorosulfonic acid; usually conducted in an inert aprotic solvent (dichloromethane, chloroform) at 0 °C to rt; addition of a weak base (pyridine or triethylamine) is common to capture the acid and improve yield.

Reaction type: diazotization followed by intramolecular cyclization (formation of a benzothiazole‑1,1‑dioxide). Purpose: construct the heterocyclic 1,1‑dioxo‑1,2‑benzothiazol‑3‑one core. Key transformation: the primary amine of anthranilic acid is converted to a diazonium salt with NaNO₂/HCl, which then undergoes nucleophilic attack by a sulfuroyl species generated from chlorosulfonic acid, expelling N₂ and H₂O and closing the thiazine ring. Typical conditions: aqueous HCl at 0‑5 °C for diazotization, slow addition of chlorosulfonic acid (often neat or in CH₂Cl₂) while maintaining low temperature, then gentle warming to 50‑80 °C to complete cyclization. Common solvent/catalyst: water/CH₂Cl₂; no metal catalyst required.

Esterification (Fischer esterification); purpose is to convert salicylic acid into the more lipophilic isopropyl salicylate ester used in fragrances or pharmaceuticals. Key transformation: condensation of the carboxylic acid with isopropanol forming the ester and water. Typical conditions: reflux of salicylic acid in excess isopropanol with catalytic p‑toluenesulfonic acid, removal of water (Dean‑Stark trap) or azeotropic distillation; solvent is the alcohol itself.

Acid‑base neutralisation forming an ammonium salt; generates ammonium glycolate from glycolic acid and ammonia; key transformation HOCH₂COOH + NH₃ → HOCH₂COO⁻ NH₄⁺; typically done in aqueous solution at room temperature by adding aqueous or gaseous NH₃ to glycolic acid; solvent water; no catalyst

Acylation (acetylation) of a phosphoramidothioate; purpose is synthesis of the organophosphate insecticide acephate. Key transformation: acetyl chloride transfers an acetyl group to the phosphorus‑bound nitrogen or oxygen, producing O‑acetyl‑dimethyl‑phosphoramidothioate (acephate) and releasing HCl. Typical conditions: low temperature (0 °C to room temp) in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or tetrahydrofuran, with a non‑nucleophilic base (e.g., pyridine or triethylamine) to scavenge HCl.

Base‑catalyzed amidic hydrolysis (saponification); purpose is to generate the acrylic acid salt and liberate ammonia. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of hydroxide on the carbonyl of acrylamide, leading to cleavage of the C–NH2 bond and formation of potassium acrylate plus NH3. Typical conditions: aqueous KOH, heating under reflux (e.g., 80–100 °C) for several hours; reaction performed in water or water/ethanol mixture.

Selective reduction of an aldehyde to a primary alcohol. Sodium borohydride reduces furfural to furfuryl alcohol. Conducted at 0 °C to room temperature in methanol or ethanol, using 1.1–1.5 equivalents of NaBH₄; reaction completes within 30 min to 1 h and is quenched with water.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction; purpose is to exchange anions and precipitate insoluble barium sulfate Key transformation: Zn²⁺ pairs with I⁻ to give soluble zinc iodide, while Ba²⁺ pairs with SO₄²⁻ to form insoluble BaSO₄ solid. Typical conditions: aqueous solutions of the two salts mixed at ambient temperature; stirring until precipitation of BaSO₄ is complete; filtration to isolate the solid.

Type: nucleophilic substitution (SN2). Purpose: replace bromide on a primary alkyl halide with an acetate group to give the acetate ester 2‑ethoxyethyl acetate. Key transformation: acetate anion attacks the carbon bearing bromine, displacing Br−. Typical conditions: sodium acetate (1–2 equiv) in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetone or ethanol, reflux for several hours. The reaction proceeds with inversion of configuration (irrelevant for a primary carbon) and generates NaBr as a by‑product.

Nucleophilic aromatic substitution (SNAr) on a pyrimidine ring; purpose is to replace chlorine atoms with amino groups, forming 2,4‑diaminopyrimidine. Key transformation: NaNH₂ (as NH₂⁻) attacks the electron‑deficient carbon atoms bearing chlorine, displacing Cl⁻ and forming C–NH₂ bonds while producing NaCl. Typical conditions: excess NaNH₂ dissolved in liquid ammonia, temperatures around –33 °C to –78 °C, reaction time of several hours; the mixture is subsequently warmed, quenched, and the product isolated.

Peracid‑mediated epoxidation; purpose is to convert the alkene of acrylamide into the oxirane (glycidamide). The C=C double bond is oxidized by m‑chloroperbenzoic acid, delivering an oxygen atom to give the epoxide while the peracid is reduced to m‑chlorobenzoic acid. Typically performed in an anhydrous chlorinated solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) at 0 °C to ambient temperature under inert atmosphere.

Aqueous double‑displacement/precipitation metathesis; the reaction swaps the oxalate anion oxalic acid with the nitrate of praseodymium(III) nitrate, forming soluble nitric acid and insoluble praseodymium oxalate precipitate. Conducted in water, often with gentle heating to improve dissolution and precipitation, no special catalyst required.

Peracid oxidation of a thioether to a sulfoxide; m‑chloroperbenzoic acid transfers an oxygen atom to the sulfur of thiepane, generating thiepane‑1‑oxide (the sulfoxide) while the peracid is reduced to m‑chlorobenzoic acid. Carried out in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature, typically under nitrogen.

Hydrolytic cleavage of an O‑alkyl phosphorothioate ester; water attacks the phosphorus center, breaking the P–OCH₃ bonds to give two equivalents of methanol and thiophoric acid. Reaction proceeds in aqueous medium, often mildly heated; can be acid‑ or base‑catalyzed but proceeds appreciably at neutral pH.

Acid‑induced decomposition/metathesis of silver oxalate with hydrofluoric acid; HF protonates the oxalate, leading to decarboxylation and release of CO₂, while silver ions exchange with fluoride to give soluble silver fluoride and water. Performed in aqueous HF, typically at low to moderate temperature; no additional catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of cyanogen bromide with sodium azide, analogous to reaction 2, affording cyanogen azide and sodium bromide. Conducted in dry acetonitrile or DMF at low temperature (0 °C to ‑20 °C) under inert gas, the azide ion replaces bromide. The product N3CN is thermally sensitive and must be handled with care.

Hydride reduction of a disulfide to the corresponding thiol; sodium borohydride donates hydride to the S–S bond of diisopropyl disulfide, cleaving it to yield two equivalents of 2‑propanethiol and forming sodium borate as the oxidized by‑product. Conducted in a protic solvent such as methanol or ethanol at 0 °C to reflux, under inert atmosphere; NaBH₄ acts as the reducing agent.

General type: nucleophilic acyl substitution forming a chloroformate ester. Purpose: preparation of propyl chloroformate as an activated carbonate for further synthesis. Key transformation: the hydroxyl oxygen of n‑propyl alcohol attacks the carbonyl carbon of phosgene, displacing chloride and generating HCl. Typical conditions: anhydrous, low temperature (0 °C to rt), inert atmosphere; solvent often dichloromethane or chloroform; a base such as pyridine or triethylamine is added to trap the liberated HCl.

Lithium aluminium hydride reduction; strong hydride reduction of veratraldehyde to veratryl alcohol using LiAlH4; performed under anhydrous conditions (dry ether such as THF or diethyl ether) at 0 °C to reflux, followed by careful aqueous work‑up to destroy excess reagent and isolate the alcohol.

Fischer esterification of methacrylic acid with 2‑ethoxyethanol to afford 2‑ethoxyethyl methacrylate; typically acid‑catalyzed (e.g., H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH) under reflux in an aprotic solvent such as toluene with removal of water (Dean‑Stark) to drive the equilibrium.

Type: nucleophilic substitution (S_N2) of an alcohol with thionyl chloride. Purpose: convert 2‑ethylhexanol into the corresponding alkyl chloride. Key transformation: –OH is replaced by –Cl while SOCl₂ is reduced to SO₂ and HCl. Typical conditions: anhydrous environment, 0 °C to room temperature, often in dry dichloromethane or chloroform; pyridine or triethylamine is added to trap the HCl. No metal catalyst required.

Type: acyl‑substitution (esterification) using an acid chloride. Purpose: synthesis of tert‑butyl benzoate. Key transformation: the hydroxyl of tert‑butanol attacks the carbonyl of benzoyl chloride, displacing chloride to form an ester and generating HCl. Typical conditions: 0 °C to rt in anhydrous dichloromethane or chloroform; a base such as pyridine, triethylamine, or DMAP is used to neutralize HCl. No metal catalyst needed.

Type: solid‑state metathesis / high‑temperature sulfide‑oxide exchange. Purpose: preparation of zinc telluride (ZnTe) and release of sulfur dioxide. Key transformation: TeO₂ oxidizes sulfide to SO₂ while Zn²⁺ combines with Te²⁻ to give ZnTe. Typical conditions: intimate powder mixture heated under inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar) at 500–800 °C for several hours. No solvent; occasionally a slight excess of ZnS is used to drive the reaction.

Type: Grignard carboxylation. Purpose: synthesis of 2‑naphthoic acid from 2‑bromonaphthalene. Key transformation: Mg inserts into the C–Br bond to give 2‑naphthyl‑MgBr, which then adds to CO₂ (dry ice) to form the magnesium carboxylate; acidic work‑up yields the carboxylic acid. Typical conditions: dry ether or THF, reflux under nitrogen; CO₂ gas bubbled or dry ice added at low temperature; aqueous NH₄Cl or dilute HCl used for quench. No additional catalyst.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) with precipitation; calcium succinate reacts with ammonium carbonate to form soluble ammonium succinate and insoluble calcium carbonate which precipitates; performed in water at room temperature; solid CaCO₃ is removed by filtration; no catalyst needed.

Type: acid‑base double displacement (metathesis) in aqueous solution. Purpose: generation of nitric acid and cobalt(II) sulfate. Key transformation: H₂SO₄ protonates nitrate ion, releasing HNO₃ while Co²⁺ pairs with sulfate to give CoSO₄·7H₂O. Typical conditions: aqueous solutions mixed at ambient temperature; the mixture is heated and HNO₃ is distilled off (boiling point ≈ 83 °C). No catalyst required.

Acidic substitution of secondary alcohol with HBr: 2‑Heptanol reacts with aqueous or concentrated HBr to give 2‑bromoheptane and water. The mechanism involves protonation of the hydroxyl group, loss of water to form a secondary carbocation, and capture by bromide (SN1). Typical conditions are reflux in 48 % HBr at 60‑80 °C, often with a catalytic amount of sulfuric acid to maintain acidity.

Reaction type: redox dissolution (oxidative acid digestion). Purpose: convert metallic gold into soluble chloroauric species. Key transformation: gold metal is oxidized by nitrate to Au³⁺ while chloride complexes it to AuCl₃; nitrogen dioxide is generated as the oxidant is reduced, and water forms from the acids. Typical conditions: concentrate nitric acid mixed with excess concentrated hydrochloric acid (aqua regia) at ambient to modestly elevated temperature, no added solvent; reaction is usually performed in a glass vessel under fume hood due to toxic gases.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) with a strong base; purpose is to exchange the cations, producing a more soluble sodium malate and calcium hydroxide. Key transformation: CaC₄H₄O₅ + 2 NaOH → Na₂C₄H₄O₅ + Ca(OH)₂↓. Carried out in water at ambient temperature with stirring; calcium hydroxide may precipitate, and the reaction proceeds without additional catalysts.

Single‑displacement/acid‑metal reaction; tin metal is oxidized by hydrochloric acid giving tin(II) chloride and hydrogen gas; used to prepare SnCl2 solution; key transformation: Sn → Sn2+ + 2e−, 2 H+ + 2e− → H2; performed in aqueous concentrated HCl, often with gentle heating to accelerate dissolution; no special catalyst.

Reaction type: double‑replacement (metathesis) acid‑base exchange. Purpose: prepare indium(III) sulfate from ind(III) acetate. Key transformation: acetate anions are protonated by sulfuric acid to give acetic acid, while sulfate anions replace acetate on indium, yielding In₂(SO₄)₃. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, stoichiometric excess of conc. H₂SO₄, heating to reflux for 1–2 h to drive off acetic acid; no special catalyst required. Common solvent: water (or a water‑acetone mixture to aid removal of acetic acid).

SN2 nucleophilic substitution; acetate ion attacks the primary alkyl sulfonate (butyl methanesulfonate), displacing methanesulfonate to give butyl acetate and sodium methanesulfonate. Typical conditions: polar aprotic solvent (DMF, DMSO) at reflux or 50–80 °C; inert atmosphere not required.

Reaction type: palladium‑catalyzed Buchwald‑Hartwig C–N cross‑coupling (aryl amination). Purpose: synthesize 2‑methoxyaniline from 2‑chloroanisole. Key transformation: palladium inserts into the aryl‑chloride bond, then transfers the aryl group to ammonia, forming the C–N bond and releasing HCl. Typical conditions: Pd(OAc)₂ or Pd₂(dba)₃ (2–5 mol %), a bulky phosphine ligand (e.g., Xantphos or BINAP), a strong base such as NaOtBu or Cs₂CO₃, ammonia supplied as a gas or aqueous NH₃ solution, solvent like toluene, dioxane or 1,4‑dioxane, temperature 80–120 °C under nitrogen, reaction time 12–24 h.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of pentan‑3‑yl methanesulfonate with sodium azide to afford 3‑azidopentane; purpose is introduction of the azide functionality; key transformation is displacement of the mesylate leaving group by N₃⁻, producing sodium methanesulfonate; conditions: polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO, 50‑80 °C, stoichiometric NaN₃, reaction time 2‑12 h.

Reaction type: acid‑catalyzed ether redistribution (trans‑etherification/etherification). Purpose: convert a symmetrical dipropoxy diol and ethanol into propanol and ethyl propyl ether. Key transformation: one propoxy fragment is protonated and eliminated as 1‑propanol, while the remaining alkoxy group attacks ethanol to form ethoxypropane (ethyl propyl ether). Typical conditions: catalytic amount of strong acid (e.g., 5–10 % H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH), reflux in a non‑nucleophilic solvent such as toluene or xylene, removal of water by azeotropic distillation (Dean‑Stark trap) to drive equilibrium, reaction time 2–6 h.

Reaction type: strong oxidation (benzylic oxidation). Purpose: oxidize diphenylmethane to the corresponding ketone, benzophenone. Key transformation: KMnO₄ oxidizes the benzylic –CH₂– group to a carbonyl, converting Ph‑CH₂‑Ph into Ph‑CO‑Ph while Mn⁷⁺ is reduced to Mn²⁺. Typical conditions: aqueous alkaline medium (e.g., NaOH or K₂CO₃) with excess KMnO₄, heating at 80–100 °C; after completion the mixture is acidified (HCl) to precipitate the product, which is extracted with an organic solvent such as ether or dichloromethane. No special catalyst beyond the permanganate oxidant.

Reaction type: thermal dehydration (condensation) of a strong base. Purpose: generate caesium oxide from caesium hydroxide. Key transformation: two CsOH molecules lose water upon heating to give Cs₂O and H₂O. Typical conditions: heating solid CsOH under dry, inert atmosphere (e.g., N₂) to temperatures around 350–400 °C; no solvent or catalyst is required.

Wurtz coupling; forms a new C‑C bond between two cyclohexyl groups to give bicyohexyl. Sodium metal reduces cyclohexyl chloride in a dry ether solvent (dry diethyl ether or THF) under reflux, producing NaCl as a by‑product. Reaction is generally performed under anhydrous, inert atmosphere to avoid side reactions such as elimination.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) and acid‑base neutralisation; zinc stearate reacts with aqueous sodium hydroxide to exchange the metal cations, yielding soluble sodium stearate (soap) and insoluble zinc hydroxide precipitate. Conducted in water at ambient or mildly heated temperatures; stirring is sufficient, no special catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of an alkyl halide with silver nitrite. The chloride ion is displaced by the nitrite anion, yielding ethyl nitrite and insoluble silver chloride that precipitates, shifting the equilibrium. Usually performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetone or ethyl acetate, often refluxed. Provides alkyl nitrite esters.

Acid‑base neutralisation forming a persulfate salt; peroxydisulfuric acid is neutralised by potassium hydroxide to afford potassium persulfate and water. The reaction is carried out in aqueous solution, often with cooling (ice bath) because the neutralisation is exothermic. No catalyst is needed; the pH is adjusted to around neutral.

Acid dissolution of a metal tungstate; concentrated hydrochloric acid protonates magnesium tungstate (MgWO4) to generate tungstic acid (H2WO4) which precipitates, while magnesium chloride stays in solution. Reaction is performed in aqueous HCl, typically with gentle heating to accelerate dissolution. No catalyst is required; the solid tungstic acid can be filtered off.

Direct amidation of a carboxylic acid with ammonia; purpose is formation of pentanamide from pentanoic acid. Typical conditions: excess gaseous NH₃ or concentrated aqueous NH₃ (10–20 %); reaction heated under reflux (≈150 °C) in a sealed vessel or with a Dean‑Stark trap to remove water, often 4–8 h. The equilibrium is driven to the amide by continuous removal of water.

Fischer esterification (acid‑catalysed ester formation); hexan‑1‑ol reacts with acetic acid in the presence of sulfuric acid to produce hexyl acetate and water. The mixture is refluxed in a suitable solvent (often excess alcohol or toluene) and sulfuric acid acts as both catalyst and dehydrating agent. Removal of water (e.g., Dean‑Stark trap) drives the equilibrium toward ester formation.

Oxidation‑acid‑base reaction; arsenic trioxide (As2O3) is oxidised by hydrogen peroxide in ammoniacal solution, converting As(III) to As(V) and forming tri‑ammonium arsenate ((NH4)3AsO4). The reaction proceeds in aqueous ammonia at room temperature to mild heating; the peroxide provides the oxidising power, and excess ammonia buffers the solution and supplies the ammonium counter‑ion. No additional catalyst is required.

Acid‑catalyzed nitrile hydrolysis; converts 3‑methoxypropanenitrile to 3‑methoxypropionic acid while forming ammonium chloride; typically performed by refluxing the nitrile in aqueous HCl (1–6 M) at 80–120 °C; water serves as solvent and proton source.

Hydrogen reduction of palladium(II) acetate; produces metallic Pd(0) (active catalyst) and acetic acid; carried out under H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) in glacial acetic acid or ethanol solvent at room temperature to reflux; no additional catalyst required.
Acid‑base salt metathesis; NaOH neutralizes ammonium sulfamate to give ammonium hydroxide in solution and sodium sulfamate; performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; water is the solvent.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution/barbiturate synthesis; phenylacetyl chloride acylates barbituric acid and NaOH neutralizes the product to give sodium phenobarbital; performed in aqueous NaOH or a water/ethanol mixture, often at 0 °C then warmed to 60–80 °C; NaOH serves as base and catalyst.

Oxidation of dimethyl sulfoxide to dimethyl sulfone; hydrogen peroxide oxidizes DMSO to the sulfone with water as by‑product; typically carried out in methanol or water at 0–25 °C under stirring; no metal catalyst is required, although a small amount of base can accelerate the reaction.

Alkali hydrolysis (SN2) of a primary alkyl chloride with aqueous sodium hydroxide; chloride is displaced by hydroxide to give 1‑nonanol and sodium chloride; reaction is performed by refluxing the alkyl chloride in aqueous NaOH (often 5–10 % w/w) or in a mixed ethanol/water medium; temperature 50–100 °C, excess NaOH ensures complete conversion.

Base‑ or acid‑catalyzed transesterification; methyl hexanoate reacts with ethanol to give ethyl hexanoate and methanol. Typical conditions: refluxing mixture of the ester with 2–3 equivalents of ethanol in the presence of a catalytic amount of NaOEt, K₂CO₃, or a few drops of concentrated H₂SO₄; methanol is distilled off to shift equilibrium. No inert solvent is necessary, though toluene can be used.

Redox decomposition: hydrogen peroxide acts as a reducing agent and calcium chlorate as an oxidizing agent, resulting in the formation of water, molecular oxygen and calcium chloride. Used as a chemical oxygen source or for waste‑oxidant destruction. Typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient or mildly elevated temperature (0–50 °C). No special catalyst required; reaction proceeds spontaneously once reagents are mixed.

Oxidation aldehyde to carboxylic acid: 4‑phenylbutanal is oxidized by aqueous potassium permanganate (KMnO₄) to give 4‑phenylbutyric acid. Serves to convert a terminal aldehyde into the corresponding acid. Conducted in water or a water‑miscible co‑solvent (e.g., acetone) under neutral to slightly basic pH, usually at 0–25 °C to avoid over‑oxidation, then acidified to isolate the product. No additional catalyst is needed; KMnO₄ is the oxidant.

Stille cross‑coupling: vinyltributylstannane couples with 2‑chlorofuran in the presence of tetrakis(triphenylphosphine)palladium(0) (Pd(PPh₃)₄) to furnish 2‑vinylfuran. Provides a reliable method for forming a C(sp²)–C(sp²) bond between a vinyl organostannane and an aryl/vinyl halide. Typical conditions involve an inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar), a polar aprotic solvent such as THF, DMF or toluene, heating to 80–110 °C for several hours. Pd(PPh₃)₄ acts as the catalytic system; no additional ligands are usually required.

Oxidative dehalogenation of 1‑(chloromethyl)‑2‑nitrobenzene to 2‑nitrobenzaldehyde using hydrogen peroxide in acetic acid. Reaction type: peroxyacid oxidation of a benzylic chloride to an aldehyde. Purpose: replace the –CH₂Cl group with a carbonyl functional group. Key transformation: conversion of the benzylic chloride to an aldehyde, generating HCl and water as by‑products. Typical conditions: mixture of glacial acetic acid and aqueous 30 % H₂O₂, temperature 30–60 °C, often with excess H₂O₂ to ensure complete oxidation. The acetic acid serves both as solvent and as a precursor to peracetic acid, the active oxidant.

Redox reduction ofrosyl bromide by copper metal: elemental copper reacts with nitrosyl bromide (NOBr) to yield copper(II) bromide (CuBr₂) and nitric oxide (NO). Serves to generate NO gas and to consume NOBr safely. Carried out in a dry, inert atmosphere (often in a sealed tube) at low to moderate temperature (–20 to 25 °C) to control the exotherm. No additional catalyst is required; the metal itself provides the reducing equivalents.

Oxidation of a silane (Si–H) by hydrogen peroxide; converts the Si–H bond of dimethylsilane into a Si–OH group yielding dimethylsilanol and water. Typically performed at 0 °C to room temperature in a mixed aqueous/organic solvent (e.g., THF/H₂O) possibly with a mild acid or transition‑metal catalyst to accelerate the peroxide oxidation.

Fischer esterification of phthalic anhydride with n‑butanol catalyzed by sulfuric acid; both anhydride carbonyls react to form two ester linkages, producing dibutyl phthalate and water. Conducted under reflux in excess 1‑butanol (or a suitable high‑boiling solvent) with catalytic H₂SO₄, and water is removed (e.g., by azeotropic distillation) to drive the equilibrium toward product.

Strong reduction of an aldehyde with lithium aluminium hydride. LAH supplies a hydride to the carbonyl of 2‑methoxyacetaldehyde, affording 2‑methoxyethanol after careful quench with water and dilute acid. Performed in anhydrous ether (diethyl ether or THF) under inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar) at reflux or room temperature; the reagent is highly reactive and must be handled dry. No additional catalyst.

Peracid synthesis (perpropionic acid) by reaction of propionic acid hydrogen peroxide; acid‑catalyzed equilibrium converts the carboxylic acid into its peroxy derivative, releasing water. Usually carried out at 0–5 °C in an organic solvent such as dichloromethane, with a strong acid catalyst (e.g., H₂SO₄ or HCl) to promote peracid formation while minimizing decomposition.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) in aqueous solution; nickel(II) acetate reacts with potassium cyanide to give nickel(II) cyanide (often as a precipitate) and potassium acetate; carried out in water at low to moderate temperature under strict cyanide‑safety protocols; no additional catalyst is employed.

Chemical reduction of Au(III) tetrachloroaurate to elemental gold using sodium borohydride; NaBH₄ reduces AuCl₄⁻ to Au⁰, producing hydrogen gas, NaCl, and sodium borate as by‑products. Performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature (often ice‑cold to control gas evolution) under inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst is required.

N‑methylation (alkylation) of N‑methylaniline with dimethyl sulfate to give N,N‑dimethylaniline; an example of nitrogen alkylation via SN2. The secondary aniline is deprotonated with a base (NaOH, Na2CO3, pyridine) and attacks a methyl group of dimethyl sulfate, producing N,N‑dimethylaniline and methyl hydrogen sulfate. Conditions: 0 °C to 50 °C in acetone, DMF, or dichloromethane; often under nitrogen; base present to neutralize the released acid.

Formation of a chloroformate (phenoxyethyl carbonochloridate) by reacting 2‑phenoxyethanol with phosgene (carbonyl chloride). Conducted at 0‑5 °C in an aprotic organic solvent such as dry dichloromethane or chloroform, with a base (triethylamine or pyridine) to trap the liberated HCl. The reaction yields the chloroformate and HCl (captured by the base).

Reaction type: acid–base salt formation (neutralization). Purpose: preparation of the pharmaceutical salt metoprolol succinate, which improves stability and handling. Key transformation: the two carboxyl groups of succinic acid are deprotonated by the basic secondary amine of metoprolol, yielding a dicationic metoprolol paired with a succinate dianion (1 succinate : 2 metoprolol). Typical conditions: dissolve succinic acid and metoprolol in a polar protic solvent (ethanol, isopropanol, or aqueous ethanol) at 40‑60 °C, stir until complete dissolution, then cool to induce crystallization of the salt. No catalyst is required.

Acid‑catalyzed cleavage of cumene hydroperoxide with phosphoric acid (Hock rearrangement variant); same overall transformation to phenol, acetone and water; phosphoric acid protonates the hydroperoxide and facilitates the phenyl migration and bond scission; usually performed with 10‑20 % H₃PO₄ at 30‑60 °C in water or a water‑organic mixed solvent.

double displacement (precipitation) reaction; conversion of soluble scandium chloride to insoluble scandium hydroxide; metathesis of Sc^3+ and OH^- to form gelatinous hydroxide precipitate while Na+ and Cl- remain in solution; aqueous phase at room temperature; no catalyst involved.

Transmetallation (metathesis) between dimethylzinc and mercury(II) fluoride; the methyl groups transfer from zinc to mercury, affording toxic dimethylmercury and zinc fluoride. Conducted under rigorously dry, inert conditions (e.g., N₂ or Ar) at low temperature (0 °C to –78 °C) in anhydrous ether or THF to prevent hydrolysis and oxidation.

Reaction type: SN2 alkylation of a carboxylate (nucleophilic substitution) to form an ester. Purpose: synthesis of methyl butyrate from sodium butyrate. Key transformation: the butyrate anion attacks methyl iodide, displacing iodide and forming the ester bond. Typical conditions: reflux in a polar aprotic solvent such as acet or DMF; sodium iodide precipitates and can be filtered off to drive the reaction forward. No additional catalyst required.

Reaction type: reduction. Purpose: regeneration of molybdenum metal. Key transformation: molybdenum trichloride reduced by hydrogen. Conditions: elevated temperature (400-1000°C), hydrogen atmosphere. Potential catalyst: transition metal (e.g., palladium). No solvent specified.

Reaction type: Nucleophilic ring opening of an epoxide (acid- or base-catalyzed). Purpose: preparation of a β‑alkoxy alcohol (1‑ethoxy‑2‑propanol). Key transformation: ethanol attacks the less‑substituted carbon of propylene oxide, opening the three‑membered ring and installing an ethoxy group while retaining the original hydroxyl on the adjacent carbon. Typical conditions: catalytic amount of acid (e.g., H₂SO₄) or base (e.g., NaOH) in a solvent such as ethanol or THF, temperature from 0 °C to reflux depending on catalyst strength.

Reaction type: Phosphorylation (formation of a phosphorochloridate) via substitution of chloride on POCl₃ with alkoxy groups. Purpose: synthesis of diethyl chlorophosphate, a useful phosphorylating reagent. Key transformation: two equivalents of ethanol replace two chloride ligands on POCl₃, generating diethyl chlorophosphate and releasing two equivalents of HCl, which are scavenged by pyridine to form pyridinium chloride. Typical conditions: anhydrous dichloromethane or THF, temperature maintained at 0 °C to 5 °C initially then allowed to warm to room temperature; pyridine acts as both base and solvent.

Reaction type: Salt metathesis / anion exchange (acid–base reaction). Purpose: preparation of copper(II) tetrafluoroborate, a non‑coordinating‑anion salt useful in catalysis. Key transformation: the sulfate anion of CuSO₄ exchanges with two tetrafluoroborate anions from HBF₄, yielding Cu(BF₄)₂ and free H₂SO₄. Typical conditions: aqueous solution at ambient temperature; the reaction proceeds spontaneously upon mixing equimolar solutions of CuSO₄ and excess HBF₄. No additional catalyst required.

Reaction type: precipitation/neutralization (double displacement). Purpose: isolate bismuth hydroxide as an insoluble precipitate from BiCl3. Key transformation: BiCl3 + 3 NaOH → Bi(OH)3 ↓ + 3 NaCl. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, addition of NaOH solution at 0–25 °C with stirring; excess NaOH avoided to prevent formation of soluble bismuthate. Common solvent/catalyst: water; no catalyst needed.

Oxidation of a primary alcohol to an aldehyde using pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC); purpose is to obtain the aldehyde without over‑oxidation to the acid; key transformation is conversion of the –CH2OH group to –CHO with loss of water; typically carried out in anhydrous dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature; no additional catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN1) of a tertiary alkyl bromide with cyanide; NaCN provides cyanide ion which attacks the tert‑butyl carbocation formed after ionization of tert‑butyl bromide, yielding tert‑butyl cyanide (tert‑butyl acetonitrile) and NaBr; typically performed in polar aprotic solvents such as DMF or DMSO, under reflux temperature (80–100 °C) with excess NaCN.

Base‑promoted dehydhalogenation (E2) tertiary alkyl chloride; 2‑chloro‑2,3,4‑trimethylpentane with aqueous or alcoholic NaOH yields the alkene 2,3,4‑trimethyl‑2‑pentene, NaCl and water; strong base abstracts a β‑hydrogen while chloride leaves, giving more substituted alkene; reflux in ethanol or isopropanol with NaOH (OH) is common; reaction is typically fast at 60‑100 °C.

Reaction type: Catalytic dehydrogenation (oxidative dehydrogenation) of a primary alcohol. Purpose: conversion of ethanol to acetaldehyde with concomitant generation of hydrogen gas. Key transformation: removal of two hydrogen atoms from ethanol (one from the α‑carbon and one from the hydroxyl group) to give the carbonyl compound acetaldehyde and H₂. Typical conditions: heterogeneous metal catalyst such as copper‑chromium oxide, copper‑zinc alloy, or palladium on carbon; temperature 300–350 °C; flow of inert carrier gas (e.g., nitrogen) often employed to sweep away H₂.

Reaction type: Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction. Purpose: isolation of calcium carbonate as an insoluble product and formation of soluble ammonium nitrate. Key transformation: calcium cations pair with carbonate anions to form solid CaCO₃, while ammonium cations pair with nitrate anions to remain in solution as NH₄NO₃. Typical conditions: aqueous solution at room temperature; stirring facilitates complete precipitation; the solid CaCO₃ is filtered and washed. No catalyst required.

Alkylation (N‑methylation) of a lactam; dimethyl sulfate transfers a methyl group to the nitrogen of 2‑pyrrolidone to give N‑methyl‑2‑pyrrolidone. Purpose is to generate the commercially important polar aprotic solvent NMP. Typically performed at 0–25 °C in an aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile or DMF, often with a mild base (e.g., K2CO3) to neutralize the formed sulfate acid.

Quaternization (methylation) of a tertiary amine; methyl trifluoromethanesulfonate methylates 1methylpyrrolidine to afford the N,N‑dimethylpyrrolidinium cation, which pairs with tetrafluoroborate from HBF4 to give 1‑methylpyrrolidin‑1‑ium tetrafluoroborate while CF3SO3H is released. Used to prepare stable ammonium salts. Conducted at 0 °C to rt in dry dichloromethane or acetonitrile under an inert atmosphere; HBF4 provides the BF4⁻ counter‑ion.

Reduction of an aldehyde to a primary alcohol; sodium borohride reduces 4‑pyridinecarboxaldehyde to 4‑(hydroxymethyl)pyridine, generating sodium borate as a by‑product. A straightforward method to obtain a pyridyl alcohol. Typically carried out in methanol, ethanol, or THF at 0 °C to room temperature, with careful quenching of excess NaBH4.

Reaction type: oxidative chlorination (halogenation) of a metal sulfide. Purpose: conversion of nickel sulfide to soluble nickel(II) chloride and generation of sulfur dichloride, a useful chlorinating reagent. Key transformation: chlorine gas oxidizes NiS, breaking the Ni–S bond; nickel is oxidized to Ni²⁺ forming NiCl₂, while sulfur is chlorinated to SCl₂. Typical conditions: pass dry Cl₂ gas over solid NiS at 200‑400 °C in a flow reactor; excess chlorine drives the reaction to completion. No solvent; the reaction is performed in the gas phase or in a closed tube.

Carbonylation of a vicinal diol to a cyclic carbonate; diphosgene (a phosgene equivalent) reacts with two equivalents of 1,2‑butanediol to afford two molecules of butylene carbonate and releases four equivalents of HCl. Provides an efficient route to cyclic carbonates used as solvents or monomers. Conducted at 0 °C to 25 °C in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or toluene, with a base (e.g., pyridine or triethylamine) to trap the generated HCl.

O‑Methylation of a phenol; methyl iodide alkylates the phenolic OH of 5‑hydroxytryptamine (serotonin) to give 5‑methoxytryptamine, with hydrogen iodide as a by‑product. Used to prepare the methoxy analogue of serotonin for pharmacological studies. Performed in a polar aprotic solvent (DMF or acetone) with a mild inorganic base (K2CO3 or NaHCO3) at room temperature under nitrogen.

Oxidative hydroxylation (C‑H activation) of kaempferol to morin using copper(II) acetate as a catalytic oxidant and hydrogen peroxide as the stoichiometric oxidant; introduces an additional phenolic OH at the 2′‑position. Typically performed in a polar organic solvent (e.g., methanol or acetonitrile) with a catalytic amount of Cu(OAc)₂ (5–10 mol %) and 1–2 equiv H₂O₂ at 25–60 °C under air; water and acetic acid are generated as by‑products.

Permanganate oxidation of 3‑ethylpyridine to pyridine‑3‑carboxylic acid (nicotinic acid) with cleavage of the terminal carbon to CO₂. This is a strong oxidative degradation of a benzylic alkyl side chain. Conducted in aqueous medium (often alkaline or slightly acidic) with excess KMnO₄, heated reflux (80–100 °C) until the purple MnO₄⁻ is reduced to brown MnO₂ precipitate; manganese dioxide remains as solid waste.

Acid‑ or base‑catalyzed hydrolysis of 5‑chloropentanenitrile to 5‑chloropentanoic acid with release of ammonia. Nitrile is converted to the corresponding carboxylic acid via an amide intermediate. Typical conditions: aqueous HCl (2–6 M) or NaOH (1–2 M), reflux 2–6 h; after completion, the reaction mixture is neutralized and the acid is isolated. Water is consumed and ammonia is liberated as NH₄⁺ (acidic work‑up) or NH₃ gas (basic work‑up).

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of allyl bromide by the formate anion from sodium formate; forms prop‑2‑enyl formate and sodium bromide; carried out in a polar aprotic solvent (DMF, DMSO, or acetone) at 50–80 °C; no additional catalyst is required, though a phase‑transfer catalyst may be used to improve rate.

Acid‑base neutralization forming lithium tungstate. Lithium hydroxide reacts with solid tungsten trioxide to give lithium tungstate (Li₂WO₄) and water. Conducted in aqueous solution at room temperature or mildly heated (≤80 °C) to ensure dissolution of WO₃; no additional catalyst required. The product precipitates upon cooling or can be isolated by evaporation.

Oxidation of thiourea to thiourea dioxide using sodium perborate in sulfuric acid medium. Perborate releases hydrogen peroxide in situ, which oxidizes thiourea; the acidic environment converts the borate by‑product to boric acid and generates sodium bisulfate. Usually performed in aqueous solution 0–40 °C, with stoichiometric amounts of NaBO₃·4H₂O (perborate) and excess H₂SO₄; the reaction consumes water, produces boric acid, thiourea dioxide, and sodium bisulfate as salts.

Metathesis/acid‑base displacement of cerium(III) oxalate with sulfuric acid to form cerium(III) sulfate and liberate free oxalic acid. Typically carried out in aqueous solution, adding concentrated H₂SO₄ to a suspension of Ce₂(C₂O₄)₃·x₂O at ambient temperature or with gentle heating (≤60 °C) to promote dissolution; the resulting Ce₂(SO₄)₃ remains in solution and oxalic acid can be recovered by evaporation or crystallization.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution (halogenation) of quinoline at the 2‑position to give 2‑chloroquinoline and HCl. Purpose: introduce a chlorine substituent onto the heteroaromatic ring. Typical conditions: Cl2 gas passed through a solution of quinoline in an inert organic solvent (e.g., carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane) in the presence of a Lewis acid catalyst such as FeCl3 or AlCl3, at reflux temperature (≈80‑100 °C).

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction between lead(II) sulfate and mercury(II) nitrate, exchanging anions to form mercury(II) sulfate and lead(II) nitrate. Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; the insoluble sulfates may precipitate, driving the reaction. No catalyst required; stirring and filtration are typical work‑up steps.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis (reductive deoxygenation) of cyclopentadecanol to cyclopentadecane, with water as the by‑product. Performed under high‑pressure H₂ (30–50 bar) at 100–200 °C using a metal hydrogenation catalyst such as Raney nickel, Pd/C, or PtO₂. Common solvents include higher alkanes, decalin, or alcohols (e.g., ethanol).

Multiple electrophilic aromatic substitution (chlorination) of 1,2‑dichlorobenzene with excess Cl₂ to give hexachlorobenzene and HCl. Used for synthesis of the persistent pesticide hexachlorobenzene. Reaction is carried out at elevated temperature (150–200 °C) in the gas phase or in a high‑boiling solvent, with a Lewis acid promoter such as FeCl₃ or AlCl₃, and often under a flow of Cl₂ to ensure complete substitution.

Oxidation of naphthalene with potassium permanganate to produce 1,4‑naphthoquinone. Reaction type: KMnO₄ oxidative dearomatization (benzylic oxidation to quinone). Purpose: introduce two carbonyl groups at the 1‑ and 4‑positions, converting a hydrocarbon aromatic to a quinone. Key transformation: addition of oxygen atoms to the aromatic ring with concurrent reduction of Mn(VII) to Mn(II). Typical conditions: reflux naphthalene in an aqueous alkaline medium (e.g., 2 M NaOH or KOH) containing excess KMnO₄ at 80–100 °C; reaction proceeds until the characteristic brown MnO₂ precipitate forms, then the mixture is acidified to precipitate the quinone. Solvent: water, often with a co‑solvent such as ethanol to aid solubility.

Acid‑catalyzed nitrile hydrolysis; converts benzonitrile to benzoic acid. The C≡N triple bond is hydrated and oxidized to a carboxyl group while ammonia is protonated to NH4Cl. Typical conditions: excess aqueous HCl, reflux (≈100 °C) for several hours; water or water/ethanol as solvent; HCl provides the acid catalyst.

Catalytic hydrogenation of carbon dioxide in the presence of methanol to produce methyl formate and water. The overall process combines CO₂ reduction to formic acid (or formate) followed by esterification with methanol. Typical conditions: H₂ pressure of 20–50 bar, temperature 150–200 °C, using a homogeneous transition‑metal catalyst (e.g.,‑ or Ir‑based complex) or a heterogeneous Cu/ZnO/Al₂O₃ catalyst, often with a base (such as KOH or an amine) to facilitate formate formation. Solvent can be methanol itself, which also acts as the reactant.

Intramolecular lactamization (dehydrative cyclization) of 6‑aminohexanoic acid to ε‑caprolactam; purpose is to form a seven‑membered lactam ring; key transformation is nucleophilic attack of the amino group on the carboxyl carbon with loss of water; typically performed by heating the amino acid neat or in a high‑boiling solvent (e.g., xylene) at 150‑200 °C, often with a catalytic amount of strong acid (H₂SO₄) or a dehydrating agent such as acetic anhydride to drive water removal.

Chlorination of a sulfonic acid to the corresponding sulfonyl chloride using thionyl chloride. Thionyl chloride converts the –SO₃H group to –SO₂Cl, releasing gaseous SO₂ and HCl. Reaction is performed under anhydrous conditions, often in CH₂Cl₂ or pyridine as solvent and base, at reflux or 0 °C to rt. By‑products are removed by gas evolution.

Oxidative cleavage (ozonolysis) of isobutene in the presence of water; purpose is to convert the C=C bond into carbonyl compounds; key transformation is addition of ozone to the double bond forming a molozonide and then a stable ozonide that, upon aqueous work‑up yields acetone and formaldehyde; carried out at low temperature (‑78 °C to 0 °C) in an inert solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform, followed by reductive (Zn/AcOH) or oxidative (H₂O₂) work‑up; water acts as the hydrolytic medium for the ozonide.

N‑hydroxymethylation of urea (formation of methylol‑urea) using formaldehyde in a choline chloride deep eutectic solvent; purpose is to generate a monomeric intermediate for urea‑formaldehyde resin synthesis; key transformation is nucleophilic addition of a urea nitrogen to the electrophilic carbonyl of formaldehyde, giving N‑(hydroxymethyl)urea; typically performed at 50‑80 °C under neat or aqueous DES conditions; no additional catalyst is required, the DES provides both solvent and mild ionic environment.

General type: thermal decomposition (reverse of direct combination); purpose: recover elemental aluminum and antimony or study stability of AlSb; key transformation: AlSb dissociates into Al and Sb solids (or vapors at very high temperature); typical conditions: temperatures above ~1000 °C under high vacuum or inert gas; solvents/catalysts: none.

Halide metathesis (double‑displacement) between anhydrous AlBr₃ and KF to give AlF₃ and KBr; purpose is to exchange bromide for fluoride on aluminum; transformation is the exchange of Br⁻ and F⁻ ions; usually conducted under dry, inert atmosphere at elevated temperature (200‑400 °C) either in the melt or in a high‑boiling, non‑coordinating solvent such as SOCl₂; solid‑state grinding (mechanochemical) can also be employed.

Double‑displacement precipitation of calcium citrate from aqueous sodium citrate and calcium nitrate; purpose is to isolate calcium citrate (insoluble) while forming soluble sodium nitrate; key transformation involves exchange of Na⁺ and Ca²⁺ ions to give Ca₃(C₆H₅O₇)₂ precipitation and 6 NaNO₃ remaining in solution; performed by mixing aqueous solutions at ambient temperature or with gentle heating to ensure complete dissolution, followed by cooling or pH adjustment to promote crystallization; no catalyst required.

Acid–base neutralization; lead(II) oxide reacts with aqueous hydrochloric acid to form soluble lead(II) chloride and water; typically carried out at room temperature with stirring in aqueous solution, no catalyst required.

Catalytic oxidation of p‑cresol (4‑methylphenol) to 4‑methylcatechol using hydrogen peroxide; purpose is to introduce a second ortho‑hydroxy group; key transformation is metal‑mediated (e.g., Fe²⁺, Cu²⁺, Ti‑silicalite, or Mo‑based) hydroxylation of the aromatic ring with H₂O₂ as oxidant, producing water as the only by‑product; typically carried out in water or a water‑organic mixed solvent at 25‑50 °C, with 1–5 mol % metal catalyst and stoichiometric H₂O₂ (often 30 % aq.).

Ester hydrolysis (neutral or acid-catalyzed); used to cleave the ester bond of a 2-(dimethylamino)ethyl benzoate, yielding the corresponding alcohol (2-(dimethylamino)ethanol) and benzoic acid derivative (4-(butylamino)benzoic acid). Typically performed by heating the substrate in water (often with reflux) or in a water/organic solvent mixture; no special catalyst required, though mild acid (e.g., HCl) can accelerate the reaction.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a primary cyclopropyl chloride by cyanide ion; NaCN provides CN⁻ which attacks the carbon bearing chloride, displacing NaCl and yielding cyclopropyl cyanide. Conducted in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO, often at reflux (80–100 °C) under an inert atmosphere.

Suzuki–Miyaura cross‑coupling between 3‑bromophenol and 4‑methoxyphenylboronic acid; purpose is to form a biaryl C–C bond yielding 3‑(4‑methoxyphenyl)phenol. Key steps are oxidative addition of the aryl bromide to Pd(0), transmetalation with the boronic acid (activated by base K₂CO₃), and reductive elimination. Typical conditions: Pd(OAc)₂ (5–10 mol %), PPh₃ ligand (10–20 mol %), K₂CO₃ as base, in a mixed solvent such as dioxane/water or DMF/water, heated to 80–100 °C under nitrogen for several hours.

Amide reduction with lithium aluminium hydride; converts a pyridine carboxamide to the primary amine (2‑pyridinemethanamine). LiAlH4 acts as a strong hydride donor, reducing the carbonyl to CH2NH2. The reaction is carried out under anhydrous conditions in dry ether (diethyl ether or THF) at 0 °C to reflux, under inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar). No additional catalyst is needed.

Transesterification of a cyclic carbonate with a diol; exchanges the alkoxy groups of propylene carbonate and 1,2‑butanediol to give propylene glycol and a new cyclic carbonate (butylene carbonate). Typically catalyzed by a Lewis acid (e.g., Ti(OiPr)4) or a basic catalyst (e.g., NaOMe) at 80–150 °C. The reaction can be run neat or in a high‑boiling solvent such as diphenyl ether; removal of the volatile glycol drives the equilibrium.

Reaction type: Fischer esterification (acid‑catalyzed formation of an ethyl ester). Purpose: convert 4‑chlorobenzoic acid into ethyl 4‑chlorobenzoate, affording a more volatile ester useful for purification or further transformations. Key transformation: similar to the methyl case, the acid reacts with ethanol, losing water to form the ethyl ester. Typical conditions: excess ethanol as solvent, catalytic strong acid (conc. H₂SO₄, p‑TsOH, or HCl), reflux (≈78 °C) for several hours; water removal (e.g., Dean–Stark) improves yield. Common solvents/catalysts: ethanol serves as both reagent and solvent; acid catalyst as above; sometimes a Dean–Stark apparatus with toluene/ethanol mixture is employed.

Base‑catalyzed transesterification of dimethyl phthalate with benzyl alcohol and n‑butanol; produces the mixed diester butyl benzyl phthalate and methanol as by‑product. Sodium methoxide serves as the nucleophilic catalyst, promoting alkoxy exchange under reflux in an anhydrous alcohol solvent (often excess n‑butanol). Methanol is removed by distillation to shift the equilibrium toward product formation.

Acyl‑chloride esterification (Schotten‑Baumann reaction); salicyloyl chloride reacts with phenethyl alcohol to form phenethyl salicylate and HCl. The HCl is neutralized by a base such as pyridine or triethylamine. The reaction is performed in an aprotic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere. Purpose is synthesis of the ester as a fragrance or pharmaceutical intermediate.

Catalytic hydrogenation (hydrogenolysis) of a five‑membered disulfide ring; 1,2‑dithiolane is reduced over palladium on carbon under H2 to open the ring and yield 1,2‑ethanedithiol. Typical conditions: H2 pressure (1–5 atm), Pd/C (5–10 % wt), solvent such as ethanol or THF, temperature ambient to 50 °C. The reaction provides a linear dithiol useful for polymer or ligand synthesis.

Aerobic oxidation of aldehyde to carboxylic acid; converts decanal to decanoic acid using molecular oxygen as the oxidant. Typical catalytic systems employ a transition‑metal catalyst (e.g., TEMPO/NaBr, Co‑salen, Mn‑salen) under O₂ pressure (1– atm) at 25–80 °C. Common solvents are acetonitrile, methanol or a water‑organic mixture. The reaction proceeds via aldehyde oxidation to the corresponding acid with release of water.

Electrophilic nitrosation of phenol; 2‑naphthol reacts with nitrosonium tetrafluoroborate (NO⁺ BF₄⁻) to give 1‑nitroso‑2‑naphthol and tetrafluoroboric acid. The process is an electrophilic aromatic substitution where the NO⁺ electrophile adds to the activated aromatic ring. It is usually performed at 0 °C to room temperature in anhydrous dichloromethane or chloroform under inert atmosphere; the by‑product HBF₄ is removed by a base if needed.

Selective carbonyl reduction of a 1,2‑diketone; sodium borohydride reduces benzil to benzoin by converting one carbonyl group to a secondary alcohol, yielding an α‑hydroxy‑ketone. The reaction is carried out in protic solvents such as methanol or ethanol at 0  to ambient temperature, often under nitrogen. Excess NaBH₄ may be used to drive complete conversion, and the work‑up involves quenching with water and extracting the product.

Condensation amidation; methylamine reacts with 2‑nitroacetic acid to form N‑methyl‑2‑nitroacetamide via loss of water. This is a typical amide‑formation (carboxylic‑acid/amine coupling) reaction. In practice the acid is activated (e.g., conversion to the acid chloride with thionyl chloride or to a mixed anhydride) or a coupling reagent such as EDC/HOBt is employed. The reaction is performed in an aprotic solvent (dichloromethane, THF) at 0 °C to rt under inert gas, followed by aqueous work‑up to isolate the amide.

Reduction of an N‑hydroxy amide (hydroxamic acid) to a primary amine; lithium aluminium hydride reduces N‑hydroxybutanamide to butylamine. The reaction proceeds via LiAlH₄‑mediated cleavage of the N‑O bond and reduction of the carbonyl, delivering the amine and generating LiAl(OH)₄. It is carried out in dry ether (diethyl ether or THF) under nitrogen at 0 °C to reflux, with careful addition of LiAlH₄ to avoid excessive heat. The mixture is quenched with water or dilute acid before work‑up.

Metathesis precipitation (double displacement); used to isolate zinc carbonate; Zn²⁺ combines with CO₃²⁻ forming insoluble ZnCO₃ while K⁺ pairs with Cl⁻ to give KCl in solution; performed in aqueous solutions of ZnCl₂ and K₂CO₃ with stirring at ambient temperature; no catalyst needed.

Base‑induced fragmentation of N‑methyl‑N‑nitroso‑p‑toluenesulfonamide (Diazald) to generate diazomethane. Reaction type: in‑situ diazomethane generation via alkaline decomposition of a sulfonyl‑nitroso precursor. Purpose: provide a safe, controllable source of diazomethane for methylation or cyclopropanation reactions. Key transformation: KOH abstracts a proton, leading to cleavage of the N‑SO₂‑p‑tolyl bond and release of diazomethane, water, and potassium p‑toluenesulfonate. Typical conditions: dry ether or hexane solution of Diazald kept at 0–5 °C under nitrogen; solid KOH (or NaOH) is added portionwise; the generated diazomethane is distilled or trapped directly into the reaction vessel. Anhydrous conditions are essential; no additional catalyst is required.
