Reductive amination; converts indole‑3‑acetaldehyde to N‑ethyltryptamine by forming an imine with ethylamine followed by NaBH4 reduction; creates a new C–N bond and reduces the C=N to a secondary amine; typically performed in methanol or ethanol at 0 °C–room temperature with NaBH4 added after imine formation.

Redox oxidation of telluride by bromine; purpose: similar to the chlorine reaction, producing elemental tellurium and potassium bromide; key transformation: bromine reduced to bromide ions while Te²⁻ is oxidized to Te⁰; typically performed by adding bromine to an aqueous solution of potassium telluride with gentle heating if required; water is the solvent and no catalyst is employed.

Acid‑catalyzed intramolecular dehydration (cyclodehydration); 1,4‑butanediol loses water to form tetrahydrofuran; purpose is synthesis of the cyclic ether THF; carried out in concentrated phosphoric acid at 140–180 °C, the acid serves as both catalyst and solvent.

Hydrolysis of a trialkylborane; trimethylborane reacts with water to cleave B–C bonds, yielding boric acid and three equivalents of methane; used as a work‑up step to destroy organoborane intermediates; performed by stirring the organoborane with aqueous solution at 0 °C to room temperature, no additional catalyst required.

Catalytic hydrogenation of trifluoroethylene: an alkene reduction using H₂ gas over a metal catalyst (Pd/C, PtO₂, or Ni) in a solvent such as ethanol or methanol, typically at 1–5 atm and 25–100 °C, to saturate the C=C bond and afford trifluoroethane.

High‑temperature solid‑state oxidation (calcination); manganese(II) carbonate reacts with oxygen to give trimanganese tetraoxide (Mn3O4) and carbon dioxide; employed to prepare the mixed‑valent oxide Mn3O4; performed by heating a mixture of MnCO3 in air at 800–1000 °C; no solvent or catalyst needed.

Oxidative cleavage (ozonolysis) of bromoethene; ozone adds to the C=C bond forming an ozonide which, upon oxidative work‑up with hydrogen peroxide, is converted to formic acid (from the unsubstituted carbon) and bromoacetic acid (from the brominated carbon); purpose is to break the alkene into carboxylic acids; conducted at –78 °C to 0 °C in dichloromethane, followed by aqueous H2O2 treatment, no additional catalyst.

Acid‑catalyzed acetal formation (trans‑acetalization). Ethylene glycol reacts with 1,3,5‑trioxane in the presence of concentrated H₂SO₄ to generate the five‑membered cyclic acetal 1,3‑dioxolane while water is released. Typical conditions: reflux in an aprotic solvent such as toluene or benzene, often with a Dean‑Stark apparatus to remove water. The strong Brønsted acid serves as catalyst; no additional reagents are required.

Oxidation of chromium(III) to chromium(VI); aqueous hydrogen peroxide in the presence of sulfuric acid oxidizes chromium(III) chloride hexahydrate to chromium(VI) oxide (CrO3), generating hydrochloric acid and water as by‑products. Typical conditions: dilute H2O2, concentrated H2SO4, temperature 0–25 °C to avoid over‑oxidation; aqueous solution.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of benzyl chloride by cyanide. Tetraethylammonium cyanide provides the nucleophilic CN⁻ which displaces chloride on the benzylic carbon to afford benzyl cyanide, with tetraethylammonium chloride formed as the by‑product. Common conditions: polar aprotic solvents (DMF, DMSO, or acetone) at 0 °C to reflux; the reaction may be conducted under phase‑transfer conditions if an aqueous phase is used. No metal catalyst is needed.

Reductive amination of piperazine with 3‑chlorobenzaldehyde. The aldehyde condenses with one nitrogen of piperazine in the presence of acetic acid/HCl to give an iminium intermediate, which is reduced in situ by sodium triacetoxyborohydride to the secondary aryl‑piperazine. The product is isolated as the dihydrochloride salt. Typical protocol: DMF or MeCN as solvent, 0 °C → rt, mild acidic medium, stoichiometric Na(OAc)₃BH; reaction is complete within 1–3 h.

Selective reduction of a nitro group to an aniline using sodium bis(2‑methoxyethoxy)aluminum hydride (Red‑Al). The reagent delivers hydride to the nitro aromatic, converting –NO₂ to –NH₂ while stopping short of over‑reduction to hydroxylamine or azobenzene. Standard conditions: THF or Et₂O, 0 °C to rt, inert atmosphere; the reaction is usually complete in 30 min to 2 h. No additional catalyst is required.

Carboxylation of an organolithium reagent. Isopropyl lithium adds to carbon dioxide gas to give the lithium salt of 2‑methylpropanoic acid (lithium 2‑methylpropanoate). Conducted at low temperature (‑78 °C) in dry THF under nitrogen or argon, CO₂ is bubbled into the solution. After completion, the mixture may be quenched with water or dilute acid to liberate the free acid if desired.

Double acylation (amidation) of 1,6‑diaminodexane with acetic anhydride. Each primary amine is acetylated, affording N‑(6‑acetamidohexyl)acetamide (a di‑acetylated diamine) and two equivalents of acetic acid as by‑product. Typical conditions: excess acetic anhydride in pyridine or dichloromethane, 0 °C to reflux; catalytic DMAP can be added to accelerate acyl transfer. Reaction is usually complete within 1–2 h.

Acid‑base hydrolysis; water protonates the sulfide ion of potassium sulfide forming potassium hydroxide and potassium hydrosulfide. Usually performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no special solvent or catalyst required.

Base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification); purpose is to convert nonyl acetate into the sodium salt of acetic acid and 1‑nonanol; key steps are hydroxide attack on the carbonyl, formation of a tetrahedral intermediate, and cleavage to give acetate anion and alcohol; carried out at ambient or elevated temperature (25–80 °C) in aqueous NaOH solution, often with ethanol or water as solvent.

Swern oxidation (oxidation of a primary alcohol to an aldehyde); DMSO is activated by oxalyl chloride to generate a chlorodimethylsulfonium intermediate, which reacts with 1‑octanol to form the corresponding alkoxysulfonium salt. Triethylamine deprotonates to give octanal and dimethyl sulfide. Typical conditions: -78 °C to 0 °C, inert atmosphere, dichloromethane (or CH2Cl2) as solvent; reagents added sequentially under dry conditions.

Ester hydrolysis (neutral or acid/base‑catalyzed cleavage of methyl phenoxyacetate); water attacks the carbonyl carbon, yielding phenoxyacetic acid and methanol. Usually carried out in aqueous medium, often with a small amount of acid (e.g., HCl) or base (e.g., NaOH) and heating under reflux. Solvent can be a water‑organic mixture such as THF/H2O or ethanol/H2O.

N‑acyl substitution (amide formation) using an acid chloride; the nucleophilic amine (aniline) attacks 4‑methylbenzoyl chloride, displacing chloride to give 4‑methylbenzamide; HCl is generated and is typically scavenged by a base. Conducted in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to rt, with a stoichiometric base (e.g., triethylamine or pyridine) to neutralize HCl.

Copper‑catalyzed Ullmann C‑N coupling (aryl amination); ammonia gas serves as the nitrogen nucleophile, CuI acts as the catalyst, and DIPEA functions as a base to deprotonate ammonia and maintain a neutral medium. Reaction performed in a polar aprotic solvent (DMF, DMSO, or NMP) at elevated temperature (100‑150 °C) under inert atmosphere, giving 3‑aminobiphenyl.

Oxidation of a trialkylphosphine by hydrogen peroxide; the phosphine reduces H2O2, forming water and the corresponding phosphine oxide (trioctylphosphine oxide). Typically run at room temperature or mild heating in a non‑protic solvent such as toluene, THF, or dichloromethane; no catalyst required.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction; used to exchange anions and isolate lead(II) chloride as an insoluble solid. Aqueous solution of potassium chloride and lead(II) acetate is mixed, stirred at ambient temperature, and the lead(II) chloride precipitate is filtered. Water is the solvent; no additional catalyst required.

Base‑mediated alkylation (SN2) of phosphoramide to synthesize hexamethylphosphoramide (HMPA). Iodomethane provides methyl groups, potassium carbonate acts as the base to deprotonate phosphoramide, and CO₂ and H₂O are by‑products. Typically performed in an aprotic polar solvent such as DMF or acetone, refluxing under an inert atmosphere. No metal catalyst is needed.

Acid‑base neutralisation forming thorium(IV) iodide; purpose is to obtain a thorium iodide salt, often as a step toward synthesis of organothorium compounds; OH− groups are protonated by HI to water and Th4+ binds four iodide ions; typically carried out in aqueous hydroiodic acid at ambient temperature or mild reflux; water is the solvent, inert atmosphere may be used to limit oxidation, no catalyst needed.

This is a transacetalization reaction. The dimethoxy acetal exchanges methoxy groups with ethoxy groups via an acid-catalyzed mechanism. Conducted with excess ethanol in the presence of catalytic H2SO4 or HCl, often at reflux temperatures to drive methanol removal.

Suzuki‑Miyaura cross‑coupling to form a C‑C bond between an aryl bromide (1‑bromonaphthalene) and phenylboronic acid, yielding 1‑phenyl‑naphthalene. Requires a palladium catalyst (e.g., Pd(PPh₃)₄ or PdCl₂(dppf)), potassium carbonate as base, and a mixed organic/water solvent (toluene‑water or dioxane‑water). Reaction is heated to 80–100 °C under nitrogen.

Catalytic hydrogenation of the C=C bond of 2‑cyclohexen‑1‑one to afford cyclohexanone; performed with H2 gas (1–5 atm) over Pd/C, Pt or Raney Ni in ethanol or ethyl acetate at ambient to 50 °C; carbonyl remains unchanged.

Electrophilic aromatic halogenation of 4‑chlorophenol with chlorine gas to give 2,4‑dichlorophenol and HCl. Reaction proceeds via electrophilic aromatic substitution, often in aqueous medium with a Lewis acid catalyst (e.g., FeCl₃) or under mildly acidic conditions, at 0–25 °C to control over‑chlorination. Introduces a second chlorine ortho to the existing substituent.

Acid‑base double‑displacement precipitation; aqueous potassium hydroxide reacts with magnesium dihydrogen phosphate to give a precipitate of Mg(OH)₂ and soluble potassium dihydrogen phosphate, carried out in aqueous solution at room temperature.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis of an ester (ester hydrolysis) converting ethyl but‑3‑enoate to but‑3‑enoic acid and ethanol. Usually carried out with aqueous mineral acid (HCl or H₂SO₄) and refluxing water or a water‑organic solvent mixture. After completion, the mixture is neutralized and the products are separated. No metal catalyst required.

Oxidative cleavage of an alkene using potassium permanganate; strong oxidizing conditions break the C=C bond of (Z)-non-3-enoic acid to give two carboxylic acids: malonic acid (C1‑C3 fragment) and hexanoic acid (C4‑C9 fragment). Typical conditions: aqueous KMnO₄ (often in basic medium), heated to reflux (80‑100 °C) until the purple MnO₄⁻ is reduced to MnO₂ precipitate. Solvent: water or water/acetone mixture; no additional catalyst required.

Permanganate oxidation of acetone to acetic acid and CO₂; potassium permanganate in aqueous acidic or alkaline solution oxidatively cleaves the C–C bond of acetone, yielding acetic acid that can be further oxidised to CO₂ and H₂O; reaction is performed in heated aqueous KMnO₄ (60–80 °C), often in dilute H₂SO₄ to keep MnO₄⁻ in solution.

SN2 N‑alkylation of a secondary amine; purpose is to methylate piperidine nitrogen. The lone pair on nitrogen attacks methyl bromide, displacing bromide and forming N‑methylpiperidine while generating HBr. Typically performed under reflux in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile or DMF, often in the presence of a base (e.g., triethylamine, K2CO3) to neutralize the acid.

Copper‑mediated Chan‑Lam coupling (oxidative azidation) of 4‑chlorophenylboronic acid with sodium azide to give 1‑azido‑4‑chlorobenzene. Copper(II) acetate acts as the oxidant/catalyst, pyridine serves as base and ligand, and water provides the reaction medium. Conducted at room temperature to moderate heating (≈40–80 °C) under air; boric acid is formed from the boronic acid substrate. No additional metal catalyst beyond Cu(OAc)₂.

Acid–base neutralization; nickel(II) oxide reacts with hydrochloric acid to produce nickel(II) chloride and water; performed in aqueous HCl with heating to dissolve the oxide; water is the solvent, no catalyst needed.

Combustion (oxidation) of 2,3,4‑trimethylhexane with molecular oxygen, producing carbon dioxide and water as the principal combustion products. The reaction requires ignition and excess O₂, proceeds at high temperature in a flame, and releases energy. No solvent or catalyst is used.

Esterification (Fischer esterification) – condensation of p‑hydroxybenzoic acid with n‑heptanol using ZnCl₂ as a Lewis‑acid catalyst; water is eliminated to give heptyl p‑hydroxybenzoate (a paraben). Typical conditions: reflux in excess n‑heptanol, catalytic ZnCl₂ (10–20 mol %), removal of water (e.g., Dean‑Stark). No special solvent beyond the alcohol.

Ozonolysis with reductive work‑up – cyclopentene is cleaved by ozone to form a carbonyl ozonide, which is reduced by dimethyl sulfide (DMS) to give pentanedial (dialdehyde). DMS is oxidized to dimethyl sulfoxide. Typical procedure: O₃ passed through a solution of cyclopentene in CH₂Cl₂ at –78 °C to 0 °C, then addition of excess DMS at low temperature, followed by aqueous work‑up.

Oxidative coupling (halogen‑mediated synthesis of a pseudohalogen) – bromine oxidizes thiocyanate ion to form thiocyanogen (SCN)₂ while being reduced to bromide. Conducted in a non‑aqueous or mildly aqueous medium (e.g., CH₂Cl₂ or acetone) at 0 °C to room temperature, often with gradual addition of Br₂ to a suspension of KSCN.

Acid‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis; converts ethyl cyanoacetate into cyanoacetic acid and ethanol; involves protonation of the ester carbonyl, nucleophilic attack by water, and loss of ethanol; carried out in aqueous hydrochloric acid, usually heated to reflux; water serves as the reaction medium and HCl is the catalyst.

Reduction of a carboxylic acid – borane (BH₃·THF complex) reduces heptanoic acid to heptanol. The carboxyl group is first converted to a borate intermediate, which upon hydrolysis yields the primary alcohol. Conditions: excess BH₃·THF under inert atmosphere, typically 0 °C to reflux in THF, followed by careful aqueous work‑up to destroy excess borane.

Chemical reduction of an aromatic nitro group – 2‑nitrofluorene is reduced to 2‑aminofluorene by sodium dithionite (Na₂S₂O₄) in alkaline solution. The dithionite serves as a soluble reducing agent, converting the nitro group to an amine under basic conditions. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (0.5–1 M), Na₂S₂O₄ added gradually, temperature 25–60 °C, with monitoring until reduction is complete.

Acid‑base neutralization (proton transfer) in aqueous medium; sulfuric acid protonates the benzoate anion to yield free benzoic acid and potassium hydrogen sulfate; performed in water, often heated to 80‑100 °C to drive the reaction to completion; no catalyst required.

Oxidation of a secondary alcohol (Jones oxidation) – chromic acid (generated from CrO₃·H₂SO₄) oxidizes 2‑methyl‑4‑heptanol to the corresponding ketone, 2‑methyl‑4‑heptanone, with water as the side product. Standard conditions: dilute H₂SO₄/acetone mixture (Jones reagent) at 0 °C to room temperature, short reaction time (5–30 min), followed by quenching with isopropanol or a reducing agent to destroy excess oxidant.

Esterification (condensation) of oxamic acid with ethanol to form ethyl oxamate; acid‑catalyzed dehydration that removes water; typically carried out by refluxing ethanol with a catalytic amount of strong acid such as sulfuric acid or p‑toluenesulfonic acid, often using a Dean‑Stark apparatus to continuously remove water and drive the equilibrium toward the ester.

Oxidation (oxidative dearomatization); converts naphthalene to 1,2‑naphthoquinone, introducing two carbonyl groups at the 1,2‑positions. Typically performed with aqueous potassium permanganate (often in a neutral to mildly alkaline medium) under reflux; work‑up with acid to isolate the quinone. No additional catalyst required.

Double displacement precipitation; aqueous mixing of cobalt(II) nitrate and sodium sulfide precipitates insoluble cobalt(II) sulfide while forming soluble sodium nitrate; typically performed in water at ambient temperature with stirring, no catalyst required.

Acid‑base neutralization of chlorosulfonic acid with sodium hydroxide producing hydrogen chloride gas and sodium hydrogen sulfate; an aqueous reaction carried out at low to moderate temperature (0‑25 °C) to control HCl evolution; the mixture is typically kept cold and stirred, and the solid NaHSO4 remains in solution.

Metal‑halogen exchange using n‑butyllithium; conversion of 2‑bromothiophene to 2‑lithiothiophene with formation of n‑butyl bromide; carried out at –78 °C in THF or diethyl ether under an inert atmosphere.

Catalytic dehydrogenation/aromatization of cyclohexane to benzene with release of three equivalents of hydrogen; high‑temperature process (≈500‑600 °C) over a metal catalyst such as Pt, Pd, or Cr₂O₃; hydrogen gas is removed continuously, and the reaction is conducted under inert atmosphere or slight pressure to prevent oxidation.

Electrophilic aromatic nitration of fluorene to 2‑nitrofluorene using a mixture of concentrated nitric acid and sulfuric acid; the sulfuric acid acts as a protonating agent to generate the nitronium ion (NO₂⁺) which attacks the 2‑position of fluorene; reaction is carried out at 0‑5 °C initially, then warmed to 30‑50 °C, typically in the acid mixture itself as solvent, and water is produced as a by‑product.

Reduction; conversion of a nitrile to a primary amine; LiAlH4 supplies hydride to reduce pivalonitrile to tert‑butylamine; performed in dry ether solvent (THF or diethyl ether) under inert atmosphere, typically 0 °C to reflux; purpose is preparation of the amine.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution (halogenation); pyridinium tribromide generates Br⁺ which brominates anisole preferentially at the para position to give 4‑bromoanisole; carried out at 0–25 °C in a non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane or acetonitrile; pyridinium bromide is formed as the by‑product.

Acid‑catalyzed esterification of malonic acid with methanol: Fischer esterification using catalytic H₂SO₄ (1–5 %) in excess methanol, refluxing at 65 °C to convert one carboxyl group to a methyl ester, yielding methyl malonate and water.

Acid‑base metathesis (neutralization); mixing aqueous HCl with ammonium dihydrogen phosphate transfers a proton to the phosphate, yielding phosphoric acid and ammonium chloride; conducted at ambient temperature in water; no special catalyst required.

Oxidation of a primary alcohol to a carboxylic acid; potassium permanganate in alkaline aqueous solution oxidizes 3‑chloro‑2,2‑dimethylpropan‑1‑ol to 3‑chloro‑2,2‑dimethylpropanoic acid, with MnO₂ precipitating and water formed; typically heated to 80–100 °C; purpose is conversion of the alcohol to the acid.

Hydrolysis of a thiocarbonyl sulfide; water attacks the C=S bond of tetramethylthiuram monosulfide, cleaving the sulfur and forming tetramethylthiourea while releasing hydrogen sulfide. Typically carried out in aqueous medium (often slightly acidic) at reflux temperatures (≈80‑100 °C). No special catalyst required; the reaction proceeds by nucleophilic attack of water.

Direct combination (solid‑state synthesis); white phosphorus reacts with elemental sulfur upon heating (200–300 °C) in a sealed tube or under inert atmosphere to form phosphorus sesquisulfide (P₄S₃); no solvent or catalyst is required; product is used in pyrotechnic formulations.
Nucleophilic substitution; synthesis of 2-chloroethanol; one chlorine atom substituted by a hydroxyl group; cold aqueous potassium hydroxide (aq KOH) as reagent and solvent; no catalyst required.

Oxidative decarboxylation combined with esterification; potassium permanganate oxidizes phenylacetic acid to benzoic acid (or directly to CO₂), which then reacts with methanol to form methyl benzoate. Usually carried out in aqueous alkaline KMnO₄ solution at reflux, followed by acid work‑up; methanol serves as both solvent and esterification partner.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a secondary alkyl halide by sodium methanethiolate to afford the thioether isopropyl methyl sulfide and sodium chloride. Conducted in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO at room temperature to reflux; inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation of thiolate.

Reductive deoxygenation of anthracene‑9,10‑dione to anthracene using zinc metal and hydroiodic acid. Zinc reduces HI to generate nascent hydrogen and iodide, which remove the carbonyl oxygens as water, forming ZnI₂ as by‑product. Performed by refluxing the quinone in concentrated HI (≈57 % w/w) with excess Zn; aqueous work‑up isolates anthracene.

Dimerization [2+2] cycloaddition of thioformaldehyde (CH₂=S) to give 1,3‑dithietane, a four‑membered heterocycle. Occurs when thioformaldehyde is generated in the gas phase or trapped at low temperature (often in a cryogenic matrix); no catalyst required, but the reaction is typically performed under inert atmosphere to prevent polymerization.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis of the imine back to benzaldehyde and aniline; water attacks the C=N bond, regenerating the carbonyl and releasing the amine. Typically carried out in aqueous acidic medium (e.g., 1 M HCl) at 50–80 °C for 1–3 h. Provides a method to deprotect the imine or to recover the starting materials.

Acid‑base salt formation; ammonia dissolves in water and reacts with sulfur dioxide to give ammonium sulfite (NH₄)₂SO₃. Conducted by bubbling SO₂ gas into an aqueous NH₃ solution at ambient temperature; the reaction is exothermic and proceeds without additional reagents or solvents.

Type: electrophilic aromatic hydroxylation using peracetic acid generated in situ. Purpose: convert meta‑cresol to 3‑methylcatechol by installing a second hydroxyl ortho to the existing phenolic OH. Key transformation: phenol ring undergoes substitution of a hydrogen by a hydroxyl group at the ortho position; acetic acid and H2O2 form peracetic acid, the oxidant. Typical conditions: mix meta‑cresol with excess acetic acid, add 30 % H2O2 slowly at 0–25 °C, then stir 1–2 h at room temperature; reaction is usually performed in aqueous or aqueous‑acetone medium. No metal catalyst required; water is the only by‑product.

Type: solid‑state ammonolysis (nitride synthesis). Purpose: prepare tantalum nitride (TaN) from tantalum pentachloride. Key transformation: chloride ligands are displaced by nitride via reaction with ammonia, releasing HCl gas. Typical conditions: suspend or place TaCl5 in a quartz tube, flow dry NH3 gas at 600–900 °C for several hours under inert atmosphere; the generated HCl is removed continuously. No solvent; the reaction is conducted in the gas phase or in a sealed tube.

Buchwald‑Hartwig amination of 3‑bromopyridine with ammonia: palladium‑catalyzed C–N cross‑coupling employing Pd(OAc)₂ (1–5 mol %), tri‑tert‑butylphosphine ligand, a base such as NaOtBu, in a polar aprotic solvent (toluene or dioxane) at 80–120 °C under inert atmosphere, producing 3‑aminopyridine.

SN2 alkylation of a carboxylate salt; sodium 2‑methylpropanoate reacts with methyl iodide, displacing iodide to give methyl 2‑methylpropanoate (methyl isobutyrate) and sodium iodide. Purpose: synthesis of a methyl ester. Key transformation: nucleophilic substitution of the carboxylate on a primary alkyl halide. Typical conditions: polar aprotic solvent such as acetone or DMF, reflux; excess methyl iodide may be used. Common solvent/catalyst: acetone (NaI precipitates, driving reaction forward).

Type: free‑radical halogenation (photochemical chlorination). Purpose: introduce a chlorine atom at the α‑carbon of THF to give 2‑chlorotetrahydrofuran. Key transformation: homolytic cleavage of Cl2 under UV light generates Cl· radicals which abstract a hydrogen from the 2‑position of THF, followed by radical recombination to give the chlorinated product. Typical conditions: THF solution saturated with dilute Cl2, irradiated with UV light (λ ≈ 254 nm) at 0 °C to ambient temperature; reaction is usually performed in a quartz vessel under inert atmosphere. No catalyst; dilute conditions limit poly‑chlorination.

Type: Finkelstein halide exchange (SN2). Purpose: convert a primary bromoalkane to the corresponding iodoalkane. Key transformation: KI provides I⁻ nucleophile that displaces Br⁻ in a backside attack on 1‑bromohexane, forming 1‑iodohexane and KBr precipitate. Typical conditions: excess KI (often 3–5 equiv) in dry acetone (polar aprotic), reflux under nitrogen for 2–6 h; KBr precipitates and is filtered off. No additional catalyst needed.

Carbothermic reduction of zinc sulfate; a high‑temperature redox reaction where solid carbon reduces Zn²⁺ to metallic zinc while being oxidized to CO₂ and SO₂. Conducted in a furnace at >900 °C under inert or open atmosphere; no solvent, often in a graphite crucible.

Acid‑base neutralization; lithium hydroxide neutralizes iodic acid to give lithium iodate and water. Performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; water is the solvent and no special catalyst is required.

N‑chlorination (oxidative chlorination) of glycine with aqueous hypochlorous acid; the primary amine is converted to an N‑chloro derivative, producing 2‑(chloroamino)acetic acid and water; performed in water at 0–5 °C, neutral to slightly acidic pH, no catalyst required.

Complex‑anion formation (fluoro‑complexation); titanium tetrafluoride reacts with potassium fluoride (typically in molten KF or anhydrous HF) to produce dipotassium hexafluorotitanate (K₂TiF₆); carried out at elevated temperature (200–400 °C) in the absence of water; no additional catalyst.

Acid‑base neutralization/ion exchange reaction; calcium hydrogen phosphate reacts with aqueous hydrochloric acid to produce calcium chloride and phosphoric acid; performed at ambient temperature in water; reaction is exothermic; no catalyst needed.

Redox metathesis (halide exchange) between germanium(IV) bromide and tin(II) bromide, yielding tin(IV) bromide and germanium(II) bromide. Typical conditions involve anhydrous, inert solvents such as dry dichloromethane or THF, low to moderate heating (0 – 50 °C) under nitrogen; no catalyst needed.

Double‑displacement precipitation (metathesis) reaction: barium chloride reacts with cerium(III) sulfate to precipitate insoluble barium sulfate while forming soluble cerium(III) chloride. Carried out in aqueous solution at room temperature; stirring and water as solvent; filtration isolates the BaSO₄ precipitate.

Base‑induced metathesis between terbium(III) phosphate and sodium hydroxide. Goal is to precipitate terbium(III) hydroxide and recover sodium phosphate in solution. TbPO₄ + 3 NaOH → Tb(OH)₃↓ + Na₃PO₄. Performed in aqueous medium at room temperature or with mild heating (25‑60 °C) under stirring. No catalyst needed; water is the solvent.

Aqueous double‑replacement/precipitation reaction. Purpose: isolate the sparingly soluble barium hydrogen phosphate salt. Key transformation: exchange of Cl⁻ and HPO₄²⁻ ions, producing solid BaHPO₄ and soluble NaCl. Typical conditions: aqueous solutions of BaCl₂ and Na₂HPO₄ mixed at ambient temperature with stirring; the BaHPO₄ precipitate is filtered, washed and dried. No catalyst required.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt formation); dimethylamine (a weak base) reacts with formic acid (a weak acid) to give the ionic salt dimethylammonium formate. Usually carried out at room temperature in a miscible solvent (water, methanol, or ethanol); the reaction proceeds quantitatively without catalyst.

Aluminothermic reduction of tungsten(IV) chloride; aluminum metal reduces WCl₄ to elemental tungsten while being oxidized to AlCl₃. Requires high temperature (typically 600–900 °C) in a sealed crucible or furnace; often performed in the molten state or with a flux such as NaCl/KCl eutectic; no external catalyst.

Base‑catalyzed saponification of prop‑2‑enyl formate with sodium hydroxide; produces sodium formate and allyl alcohol; performed in aqueous NaOH (or NaOH/ethanol) at 60–80 °C; reaction proceeds to completion as the sodium formate remains soluble; water is the solvent.

Acyl chloride esterification; purpose is to generate propyl benzoate from benzoyl chloride and 1‑propanol. The reaction converts an acid chloride to an ester, releasing hydrogen chloride. Usually carried out at 0 °C to room temperature in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF, with a base (pyridine, triethylamine, or DMAP) to neutralize HCl and prevent side reactions.

Hydrohalogenation with HCl; purpose: add HCl across the double bond to give 2‑chlorobutanoic acid; key transformation: Markovnikov addition of Cl to the more substituted carbon (C‑2) and H to C‑3; typical conditions: gaseous or aqueous HCl at 0–25 °C, often in ether or aqueous medium, no additional catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution at silicon (S_N2) where the thiocyanate anion displaces bromide on trimethylsilyl bromide to give isothiocyanatotrimethylsilane. Purpose: preparation of a silyl isothiocyanate reagent. Typical conditions: aprotic polar solvent such as acetonitrile or THF,°C to room temperature, inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst required.

Aerobic microbial oxidation (biodegradation) of 3‑chlorotoluene by Pseudomonas putida; purpose is to convert the aromatic alkyl chloride into a more polar carboxylic acid for further mineralization. Key transformation: enzymatic hydroxylation of the methyl group to a primary alcohol, subsequent oxidation to the aldehyde and then to 3‑chlorobenzoic acid. Typical conditions: aerobic shake‑flask culture at 25–35 °C, mineral salts medium with appropriate carbon source, pH around 7. No organic solvent required; the reaction occurs in aqueous broth.

Acid‑base salt metathesis (proton transfer) between sulfuric acid and cesium formate; purpose is to generate free formic acid and the cesium hydrogen sulfate salt. Key transformation: transfer of a proton from H₂SO₄ to the formate anion, producing HCOOH and CsHSO₄. Usually performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no special catalyst needed. The reaction proceeds readily under stirring.

Solid‑state phase conversion; reacts manganese monosilicide (MnSi) with excess silicon to produce manganese disilicide (MnSi₂). Conducted by intimate mixing of MnSi and Si powders followed by annealing at 800–1000 °C in argon or vacuum. No solvent; the reaction proceeds via diffusion of Si into the MnSi lattice.

Oxidative N‑dealkylation (metabolic oxidation) of thioridazine to mesoridazine with release of formaldehyde; purpose is the biotransformation of the phenothiazine drug into a less lipophilic metabolite. Key transformation: cleavage of the N‑methyl (or N‑ethyl) side chain via a cytochrome P450‑mediated oxidation, forming a hemiaminal that collapses to formaldehyde and the demethylated product mesoridazine. Typically occurs in liver microsomes or cultured hepatocytes at 37 °C, in phosphate buffer, with NADPH as the reducing cofactor. In a chemical laboratory, strong oxidants such as KMnO₄ or NaOCl under controlled pH can achieve a similar cleavage.

Condensation polymerization (ification) of ethane‑1,2‑diol with benzene‑1,4‑dicarbonyl dichloride to give bis(2‑hydroxyethyl) terephthalate; purpose is to form a low‑molecular‑weight polyester di‑ester. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of each hydroxyl group on a carbonyl chloride, releasing HCl and forming ester linkages. Typical conditions: anhydrous dichloromethane or THF as solvent, addition of a base (e.g., triethylamine or pyridine) to scavenge generated HCl, temperature 0 °C to room temperature, under nitrogen atmosphere. Reaction is driven to completion by removal of HCl (often as a salt with the base).

The general type is a double displacement (metathesis) reaction. Purpose is to precipitate copper(II) sulfide. Key transformation involves sulfide ions from sodium sulfide reacting with copper ions to form an insoluble product. Conditions occur in aqueous solution at ambient temperature. Solvent is water, and no catalyst is required.

Redox (acid‑catalyzed disproportionation) of potassium chlorate by hydrochloric acid to generate chlorine dioxide gas. Purpose: laboratory preparation of ClO₂ as an oxidant or bleaching agent. Conducted in dilute aqueous HCl, temperature kept low (0–5 °C) to control gas evolution; vigorous stirring; sometimes a small amount of a reducing additive (e.g., sulfite) is used, but not essential.

Acid‑base neutralization of bismuth carbonate with acetic acid to form bismuth acetate; purpose is to prepare the soluble metal acetate for further reactions. Key transformation: protonation of the carbonate anion, release of CO₂, and formation of water alongside the bismuth acetate salt. Typical conditions: refluxing glacial acetic acid (or a mixture of AcOH and water) with solid Bi₂(CO₃)₃ at 60–80 °C until gas evolution ceases. The reaction proceeds without a catalyst; the product precipitates upon cooling and can be isolated by filtration.

Electrophilic α‑halogenation of an aldehyde. Bromine adds to the α‑carbon of butanal via the enol or enolate tautomer, producing 2‑bromobutanal and releasing HBr. Usually carried out in an inert, non‑nucleophilic solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or chloroform at 0 °C to room temperature, often with a catalytic amount of acid or base to generate the enol.

Double displacement (metathesis) reaction used industrially to produce sodium hydroxide (caustic soda) from sodium chloride and calcium hydroxide (lime); key transformation exchanges Na⁺ and Ca²⁺ forming NaOH and CaCl₂; performed in aqueous solution or slurry of solid NaCl with slaked lime at 100‑150 °C; water acts as solvent, no catalyst required.

Base‑induced hydrolysis/neutralization of boron trichloride with sodium hydroxide; converts BCl₃ (Lewis acid) into sodium metaborate while generating NaCl and water; typically carried out in aqueous solution with excess NaOH at ambient to modestly elevated temperature; water solvent, no additional catalyst.

Acid‑catalyzed peracid formation: benzoic acid reacts with hydrogen peroxide to give perbenzoic acid and water; O‑O bond insertion into the carboxyl group; performed with dilute H₂O₂ (30 %) in water or acetic acid, often with a catalytic amount of mineral acid (e.g., H₂SO₄) at 0–25 °C.

Selective reduction of an ester (methyl benzoate) to an aldehyde (benzaldehyde) using di‑isobutyl‑aluminum hydride (DIBAL‑H); key step is transfer of one hydride equivalent to the carbonyl, stopping at the aldehyde, with methanol released; conducted at –78 °C to 0 °C in anhydrous ether or THF under inert atmosphere; reaction quenched with aqueous work‑up; no catalyst beyond DIBAL‑H.

High‑temperature metallothermic reduction of molybdenum trioxide by magnesium; redox process reduces MoO₃ to metallic Mo while Mg is oxidized to MgO; carried out in a furnace at 800–1000 °C under inert gas or vacuum; solid‑state reaction, no solvent or catalyst, often mixed as powders and pressed into pellets.

Electrophilic aromatic chlorination (halogenation) of benzophenone, installing a chlorine atom at the para position of one phenyl ring to give 4‑chlorobenzophenone with concomitant formation of HCl; usually carried out with Cl2 gas in the presence of a Lewis acid catalyst such as FeCl3 or AlCl3, in a non‑polar solvent (e.g., CCl4 or CH2Cl2) at 0–25 °C; light or gentle heating may be applied.
Acid-carbonate neutralization reaction. The carboxylic acid reacts with sodium carbonate to form a sodium salt, releasing carbon dioxide and water. Proceeds in aqueous medium at moderate temperature.

Strong oxidative decomposition of silane by concentrated nitric acid; silane is oxidized to silicon dioxide, nitric acid is reduced to nitrogen dioxide, and water is formed; performed by adding SiH₄ to cold (0–5 °C) concentrated HNO₃, sometimes in aqueous medium; vigorous gas evolution; no catalyst, reaction controlled by temperature.

Hydrolysis of an alkyl nitrate (amyl nitrate) to nitric acid and the corresponding alcohol (pentanol); water attacks the nitrate ester, cleaving the N‑O bond; can be performed under mild heating (50–80 °C) in aqueous medium, optionally acid‑catalyzed; solvent water or mixed water‑alcohol; no special catalyst required.

Oxidation; conversion of phenol to 1,4‑benzoquinone using a strong oxidizing agent. The aromatic ring is oxidized, losing two electrons and two protons to form the quinone carbonyls. Typical conditions: aqueous acidic medium (often H₂SO₄) with Na₂Cr₂O₇·2H₂O, heated under reflux. Water is the usual solvent; the reaction is carried out under ambient pressure.

Thermal decarboxylation of a benzylic acid; heating 2‑(4‑methylphenyl)acetic acid (often with a metal oxide catalyst such as CuO or Ag2O) causes loss of CO2 and formation of p‑xylene. Purpose: remove a carboxyl group to generate a simple aromatic hydrocarbon. Typical conditions: 200–300 °C in a sealed tube or flow reactor, optionally on a solid catalyst; usually performed solvent‑free or in a high‑boiling inert solvent.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of an alkyl sulfonate with fluoride ion. Ethyl p‑toluenesulfonate acts as a good leaving group, allowing KF to attack the primary carbon to give fluoroethane and potassium p‑toluenesulfonate. Conducted in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO, often with a phase‑transfer catalyst (e.g., 18‑crown‑6) and heated (80–120 °C) to improve KF solubility.

Complete combustion; cyclopentane is fully oxidized by excess O₂ to carbon dioxide and water, releasing heat. The reaction proceeds via a high‑temperature flame (>1000 °C) in the presence of atmospheric oxygen; no solvent or catalyst is needed. It is a redox process in which cyclopentane is oxidized (carbon oxidation state from –2 to +4) and O₂ is reduced to H₂O and CO₂.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt hydrolysis). Pyridin‑4‑ylmethanamine·2HCl is treated with aqueous NaOH; the hydroxide deprotonates the ammonium groups, generating the free amine, water, and NaCl. The reaction is carried out at room temperature or with gentle heating (0–25 °C) in water. Stoichiometric amounts of NaOH (2 equiv) are used; no special catalyst is required.

N‑alkylation (SN2) of 3,7‑dimethylxanthine (theobromine) with butyl bromide. NaOH deprotonates the imide nitrogen of the xanthine, forming a nucleophilic anion that attacks the primary butyl bromide, yielding isbufylline (N‑butyl‑3,7‑dimethylxanthine) with NaBr as the by‑product (water is also formed from the deprotonation step). The reaction is normally performed in ethanol or a mixed ethanol/ water solvent, refluxed (≈80 °C) under nitrogen to avoid oxidation. A slight excess of base and alkyl halide improves yield; no additional catalyst is required.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2). Alkylation of pyrrole using an alkyl halide to form N-ethylpyrrole. Typically occurs in polar aprotic solvents (e.g., DMF, DMSO) under basic conditions to deprotonate pyrrole, generating a stronger nucleophile.

Acid-catalyzed epoxide ring-opening followed by nucleophilic substitution. Ethylene oxide reacts with hydrogen iodide to form 1,2-diiodoethane. Conditions include concentrated HI and heat, with water as a byproduct from the ring-opening.

Fischer esterification of tert‑butyl alcohol with acetic acid; produces tert‑butyl acetate. Acid catalysis protonates the alcohol, facilitating loss of water and nucleophilic attack by the acetate ion to give the ester. Standard conditions: reflux in excess acetic acid or in a non‑polar solvent (toluene, benzene) with a catalytic strong acid (H2SO4, p‑TsOH), and continuous removal of water (Dean‑Stark) to shift equilibrium toward product.

Jones oxidation (chromium(VI) oxidation of a primary alcohol to a carboxylic acid). Purpose: convert the 2‑(furan‑2‑yl)ethanol side chain into the corresponding acid. The CrO₃/H₂SO₄ reagent oxidizes the CH₂OH group first to an aldehyde then to the carboxylic acid, yielding 2‑(furan‑2‑yl)acetic acid. Typical conditions: 0 °C to room temperature, acetone as solvent, 1.5 equiv CrO₃ in aqueous H₂SO₄ (≈2.5 M). Reaction is quenched with isopropanol or methanol; no additional catalyst.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution. Phosgene (carbonyl bromide) reacts with aniline to form carbanilide via two successive substitutions. Common conditions use an inert solvent (e.g., benzene, chloroform) and a base (e.g., pyridine) to neutralize HBr.

Salt metathesis. Benzenediazonium chloride exchanges its chloride with tetrafluoroborate to form the corresponding tetrafluoroborate salt. Conducted in aqueous solution at low temperatures to prevent diazonium decomposition.

Single‑displacement/redox reaction of an alkali metal with water; potassium metal reacts violently with liquid water to give aqueous potassium hydroxide and hydrogen gas; performed at room temperature, often in a dry ice bath to control vigor; no catalyst, but reaction is highly exothermic and must be handled with care.
Nucleophilic substitution with intramolecular cyclization. Ammonia displaces bromide in 1,8-dibromooctane, leading to azocane formation. Typically uses polar solvents (e.g., ethanol, water) and heat.

Acid–base neutralization producing a metal fluoride; purpose is to obtain yttrium fluoride, a material used in optics or ceramics; key transformation is protonation of yttrium hydroxide by hydrofluoric acid yielding YF₃ and water; performed in aqueous HF solution, typically at low to moderate temperature with careful HF handling; no catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution at phosphorus. Sodium cyanide replaces chloride in phosphorus trichloride to yield tricyanophosphine. Reactions often occur in polar aprotic solvents (e.g., DMF) with NaCl as a byproduct. No catalyst required.

Aerobic oxidation of a primary alcohol to a carboxylic acid; glyceric acid is oxidized by molecular oxygen to tartronic acid while the secondary alcohol remains unchanged, producing water as the only by‑product. Typical conditions employ a catalytic amount of a transition‑metal oxide (e.g., Pt/C, Pd/C, or a Cu/TEMPO system) in aqueous or mixed aqueous‑organic solvent at 50–120 °C under an O₂ atmosphere; no stoichiometric reagents other than O₂ are required.

Oxidative conversion of 5‑hydroxymethylfurfural (HMF) to 2,5‑furandicarboxylic acid (FDCA) using concentrated nitric acid. The reaction is a strong oxidizing acid oxidation that cleaves the benzylic CH₂OH group to a carboxyl group while releasing water and nitrogen dioxide gas. It is usually carried out by refluxing HMF in excess HNO₃ (≈70 % aq.) at 80–120 °C; the mixture is cooled and the FDCA is isolated by filtration and washing. No additional catalyst is needed, but careful temperature control is required to avoid over‑oxidation.

Acid‑base protonolysis of lithium hydride with trifluoromethanesulfonic acid (TfOH). The strong Brønsted acid protonates the hydride ion, generating hydrogen gas and the lithium triflate salt. The reaction is typically performed in an aprotic, non‑nucleophilic solvent such as dry THF or diethyl ether at 0 °C to room temperature under an inert atmosphere to avoid moisture; the evolution of H₂ is observed as effervescence.

Salt metathesis (acid‑base) between barium oxalate and nitric acid. The strong acid displaces the oxalate anion from the insoluble Ba²⁺ salt, forming soluble barium nitrate and free oxalic acid in solution. The reaction is conducted in aqueous solution, often by adding solid BaC₂O₄ to dilute (≈1–2 M) HNO₃ at 20–40 °C with stirring; the resulting oxalic acid can be isolated by evaporation or crystallization.

Ligand substitution (coordination‑complex formation) of dipotassium tetrachloroplatinate(II) with ammonia. Two ammonia molecules replace two chloride ligands on the Pt(II) center, yielding cis‑[Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂] (the cis‑platin precursor) and potassium chloride as a by‑product. The reaction is carried out in aqueous solution, typically by mixing K₂PtCl₄ with excess NH₃ (or NH₄OH) at ambient temperature or mild heating (≈30–60 °C) under dark conditions to prevent photoreduction; the cis‑complex precipitates and is filtered off.

Double‑displacement precipitation (acid‑base neutralization) of indium(III) sulfate with sodium hydroxide. Hydroxide ions replace the sulfate ions around indium, forming insoluble indium(III) hydroxide precipitate and soluble sodium sulfate. The reaction proceeds in aqueous solution at room temperature; a stoichiometric excess of NaOH (6 mol per 1 mol In₂(SO₄)₃) ensures complete precipitation. The indium hydroxide is isolated by filtration and can be washed with water.

Nucleophilic substitution at silicon (Si–C bond cleavage) using hydrofluoric acid; purpose is to replace one ethyl group on tetraethylsil with fluorine, yielding ethane and triethylfluorosilane. Key transformation: Si–C bond broken, Si–F bond formed, ethane released. Typical conditions: excess HF (often aqueous or 48 % HF) at 0–25 °C, sometimes in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile; reactions are conducted in glass or PTFE equipment due to HF corrosion.
Esterification; produces diethyl selenate from selenic acid and ethanol; proceeds via condensation with water as a byproduct; no catalyst is required under standard heated conditions.

Acid‑base neutralization of zinc hydroxide with lactic acid; purpose is the same as #4—formation of zinc dilactate. Zn(OH)₂ reacts with two equivalents of lactic acid to afford Zn(Lac)₂ and water. The reaction is carried out in water or a water/ethanol mixture, usually under gentle heating (40–70 °C) to ensure complete conversion; no additional reagents are required.

Acid‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (hydrolysis of butacaine, an ethyl‑diethylamino‑ethyl ester of 4‑butoxybenzoic acid). Purpose is to cleave the ester linkage to regenerate the parent acid and alcohol. Key transformation: cleavage of the C(=O)–O bond, producing 4‑butoxybenzoic acid and 2‑(diethylamino)ethanol. Typical conditions: aqueous acidic medium (e.g., 1–2 M HCl or H₂SO₄) reflux for 2–6 h; solvent often a mixture of water and ethanol or methanol.

Alcoholysis (esterification) of a cyclic anhydride; oxepane‑2,7‑dione reacts with excess ethanol to afford the diethyl ester, diethyl heptanedioate. The reaction is run under reflux in absolute ethanol, often with a catalytic amount of acid (e.g., catalytic H2SO4 or p‑TsOH) or base (pyridine) to accelerate ring opening and formation. After reflux, excess ethanol is removed and the ester purified.

Fischer esterification between formic acid and hexanol to give hexyl formate. Purpose is synthesis of a short‑chain formate ester. Key transformation: condensation of the carboxylic acid and alcohol with loss of water, forming the hexyl ester. Typical conditions: excess formic acid or removal of water (Dean–Stark) at 80–100 °C, catalytic amount of strong acid (e.g., 0.1–1 % H₂SO₄); solvent can be the acid itself or a non‑reactive solvent such as toluene.

Neutralization (soap formation, saponification) of a fatty acid; palmitic acid reacts with aqueous sodium hydroxide to give sodium palmitate (soap) and water. The reaction proceeds at modest heating (50–80 °C) in an aqueous or mixed aqueous‑alcoholic medium; stirring ensures complete dissolution and conversion.

Copper(II)‑catalyzed oxidative bromination of 4‑aminobenzenesulfonamide. Purpose is to install bromine atoms at the 3‑ and 5‑positions of the aromatic ring. Key transformation: electrophilic aromatic substitution with in‑situ generated Br₂ from KBr oxidized by H₂O₂ in the presence of CuCl₂, yielding 4‑amino‑3,5‑dibromobenzenesulfonamide; CuCl₂ is reduced then re‑oxidized, ending as CuBr₂ (cupric bromide). Typical conditions: aqueous or mixed aqueous–organic medium (e.gCN/H₂O), 0–25 °C to 40 °C, with stoichiometric H₂O₂ (30 % aq.) and catalytic CuCl₂ (5–10 mol %), KBr as bromide source; pH often mildly acidic.

Reductive iodination of an aldehyde (HI reduction). Formaldehyde reacts with concentrated hydroiodic acid, where iodide acts as nucleophile and reducing agent, converting the carbonyl carbon into a gem‑diiodide (diiodomethane) while water is formed. The reaction exemplifies the HI‑mediated conversion of carbonyls to diiodides. Conducted by heating neat or aqueous HI (≈48 %) at 80–120 °C, often in the presence of red phosphorus to regenerate HI and suppress oxidation; no external catalyst.

S‑methylation of cysteine. The cysteine thiolate (generated under basic aqueous conditions) nucleophilically substitutes methyl iodide to afford S‑methyl‑L‑cysteine; HI is scavenged by the base. Typical: water/acetone, pH ≈ 9 (NaHCO₃ or NaOH), 0 °C to rt, 1 equiv MeI, 1–2 h.

Base‑catalyzed saponification of hexyl acetate. Purpose is to convert the acetate ester to the corresponding alcohol and acetate salt. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of OH⁻ on the carbonyl carbon, forming hexanol and potassium acetate. Typical conditions: aqueous KOH (1–2 equiv) at reflux (≈80–100 ) for 1–3 h; solvent may be water or a water‑alcohol mixture (e.g., methanol/water).

Acid‑base salt metathesis of bismuth subsalicylate with hydrochloric acid. Purpose is to liberate salicylic acid and generate soluble bismuth chloride. Key transformation: protonation of the salicylate anion releasing salicylic acid, while the bismuth cation forms BiCl₃or BiClₓ depending on stoichiometry). Typical conditions: aqueous HCl (1–3 M) at room temperature to gentle heating (30–50 °C); reaction is rapid and proceeds to completion with stirring.

Single displacement (metallothermic reduction) reaction; calcium metal reduces promethium trichloride to elemental promethium while forming calcium chloride; performed at high temperature in a sealed tube or molten salt under inert gas; no additional catalyst.

Double displacement (anion exchange) in aqueous solution; bismuth(III) chloride exchanges chloride for acetate with sodium acetate to give bismuth(III) acetate (poorly soluble) and sodium chloride. Reaction performed at room temperature in water or dilute ethanol; no catalyst required.

SN1 nucleophilic substitution of a tertiary alkyl chloride with acetate ion, producing tert‑butyl acetate; commonly carried out by heating tert‑butyl chloride with excess sodium acetate in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetone (50‑80 °C), allowing NaCl to precipitate and be removed.

SN2 substitution of methyl 2‑chloroacetate with sodium azide to afford methyl 2‑azidoacetate and sodium chloride; azide displacement. Typical conditions: NaN₃ (1.1–2 equiv) in DMF or DMSO, 0–50 °C, inert atmosphere; care taken because of azide safety hazards.

Acid‑catalyzed ether cleavage by hydrogen iodide, converting dimethyl ether into methanol and iodomethane; proceeds via protonation of the ether oxygen followed by SN2 attack of I⁻ on a methyl group; typically performed with excess HI under reflux, often in the absence of solvent or in a non‑polar solvent, with the volatile CH₃I distilled off.

Multicomponent condensation (acridine synthesis) of formaldehyde, dimethylaniline and m‑phenylenediamine to give acridine orange base with loss of three molecules of water; involves stepwise electrophilic aromatic substitution and cyclization under acidic or reflux conditions in ethanol or glacial acetic acid, providing the tricyclic dye scaffold.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a primary alkyl bromide with aqueous ammonia to afford the primary amine 2‑amino‑6‑methylheptane; carried out by refluxing 2‑bromo‑6‑methylheptane in concentrated NH₃ solution (or aqueous NH₃) often in ethanol or water, generating ammonium bromide as the by‑product.

Acid–base neutralization forming a salt. Methylamine reacts with hydrogen chloride gas (or aqueous HCl) to give methylammonium chloride (methylamine hydrochloride). Usually performed in anhydrous ether or chilled water to crystallize the salt; the reaction is exothermic and proceeds at low to ambient temperature.

Acid–base/fluoride exchange reaction between concentrated sulfuric acid and manganese difluoride, liberating hydrogen fluoride gas and forming manganese(II) sulfate; performed by heating the solid mixture of H₂SO₄ and MnF₂, typically in a sealed apparatus or with gas‑scrubbing to capture HF.

Catalytic hydrogenation of α‑ketoisocaproic acid to 2‑hydroxyisocaproic acid using palladium on carbon; the ketone is reduced to a secondary alcohol under H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) in a protic solvent such as ethanol or methanol at ambient to mild temperature, delivering the hydroxy acid (HICA) with high chemoselectivity.

Halide exchange/complex formation; generates potassium heptafluoroniobate and liberates hydrogen fluoride; NbF5 reacts with KHF2 to form K2NbF7 and HF; performed in anhydrous HF or dry non‑aqueous medium under inert atmosphere, typically at low temperature; no additional catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed condensation/cyclization (Prins‑type) to afford chroman heterocycle; formaldehyde adds to salicylaldehyde followed by intramolecular cyclization under p‑toluenesulfonic acid; generally carried out in refluxing toluene or dichloromethane with catalytic p‑TsOH for 1–6 h; solvent acts as reaction medium, no further catalyst needed.

Gas‑phase radical oxidation; a chlorine atom abstracts an oxygen from ozone, producing chlorine monoxide radical and molecular oxygen; key step in stratospheric chlorine activation; occurs in the gas phase under stratospheric pressures, initiated by thermal or photochemical energy, no solvent or catalyst.

Oxidative conversion (redox) of chloral hydrate to trichloroacetic acid by concentrated nitric acid; chloral hydrate is oxidized while nitric acid is reduced to nitrogen dioxide, releasing water; conducted by adding chloral hydrate to cold (0–5 °C) conc. HNO3 in aqueous solution with vigorous stirring; water is the solvent.

Enzymatic methyl transfer; SAM donates a methyl group to norisoboldine yielding isoboldine and S‑adenosyl‑L‑homocysteine; carried out in aqueous buffer (pH 7.5–8.5) with the appropriate O‑methyltransferase enzyme at 25–37 °C; enzyme acts as catalyst, no organic solvent required.

Acid‑metal redox dissolution; americium metal is oxidized by hydrochloric acid to americium(III) chloride while protons are reduced to hydrogen gas; performed in aqueous HCl (concentrated or 1 M) at ambient to moderate temperature, often under inert atmosphere due to radioactivity; water is the solvent.

Fischer esterification; citric acid reacts with ethanol in the presence of catalytic sulfuric acid to form triethyl citrate, with water as by‑product; the reaction is refluxed in excess ethanol (also solvent) with conc. H2SO4 for 2–4 h, often using a Dean‑Stark apparatus to remove water; ethanol serves as both reactant and solvent.

Oxidation of aldehyde to carboxylic acid; selenium dioxide acts as an oxidant converting phenylacetaldehyde into phenylacetic acid while being reduced to elemental selenium. Typically performed by heating the aldehyde with excess SeO2 in a polar protic solvent such as aqueous dioxane or ethanol under reflux; the reaction may be carried out under inert atmosphere to avoid over‑oxidation.

Iodine‑mediated oxidative cyclization; elemental iodine reacts with an (E)-α,β‑unsaturated hydroxy‑aryl ketone to promote electrophilic activation of the double bond, followed by intramolecular attack of the phenolic OH, forming the 5‑hydroxy‑2‑phenyl‑4H‑chromen‑4‑one (flavone) scaffold and generating hydrogen iodide. Usually carried out in a non‑nucleophilic solvent such as dichloromethane or acetonitrile at room temperature to 50 °C; a base (e.g., pyridine) is often added to scavenge HI.

Acid chloride formation and cyclization to an oxazolidinedione; thionyl chloride reacts with 2‑fluorophenylacetic acid to give the corresponding acid chloride, releasing SO2 and HCl. The acid chloride then condenses with 2‑oxazolidinone, forming an amide that cyclizes to the 2‑oxazolidine‑2,4‑dione (Felbamate) ring, with concomitant loss of HCl. Typical conditions involve refluxing the acid and thionyl chloride in anhydrous dichloromethane or toluene, followed by addition of 2‑oxazolidinone under nitrogen; the reaction is often performed in the presence of a base such as pyridine to trap HCl.

Alkylation of a primary amine (SN2) to give a secondary amine; ethylamine acts as nucleophile toward isopropyl chloride, displacing chloride and forming isopropylethylamine with generation of HCl. Performed in an aprotic solvent such as THF or ethanol, often with an excess of the amine to serve as both reagent and base; temperature may be kept at 0 °C to reflux depending on substrate reactivity.

Acid‑base neutralization; rubidium hydroxide deprotonates formic acid, yielding rubidium formate and water. Typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; stoichiometric amounts of base and acid are mixed, and the resulting salt can be isolated by evaporation or crystallization.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt formation); hydrogen cyanide (a weak acid) reacts with lithium oxide (a basic oxide) to give lithium cyanide and water; typically performed in aqueous solution or melt, heated to promote complete reaction; no special solvent beyond water, stoichiometry 2 HCN + Li2O → 2 LiCN + H2O.

Hydrolysis of phenyl‑ethyl chloroformate to regenerate 1‑phenylethanol; a cleavage of the chloroformate functional group releasing carbon dioxide and hydrogen chloride; water attacks the carbonyl, forming an unstable carbonate that decomposes to the alcohol, CO₂ and HCl; typically done by stirring the chloroformate in a mixture of water and an organic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) at 0–25 °C, sometimes with a mild base (pyridine) to neutralize HCl.

Double displacement (precipitation) reaction; aqueous ammonia (NH4OH) reacts with lead(II) chloride producing lead(II) hydroxide precipitate and ammonium chloride in solution; performed in water at room temperature, excess NH4OH may be used to ensure complete precipitation, solid filtered off.

Phenol acetylation (esterification) using acetic anhydride; 3,5‑dichlorophenol attacks the carbonyl of acetic anhydride forming 3,5‑dichlorophenyl acetate and liberating acetic acid; usually carried out at 0 °C to room temperature in an inert organic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) with a base such as pyridine or DMAP as catalyst to neutralize generated acid.

Chromic acid oxidation (Jones oxidation) of a primary alcohol; benzyl alcohol is oxidized by sodium dichromate in sulfuric acid to benzoic acid, with reduction of Cr(VI) to Cr(III) sulfate and production of water; reaction is performed in aqueous acetone or mixed water/acetone at 0–25 °C, then warmed gently; excess oxidant is quenched with a reducing agent or by addition of isopropanol.

Alkaline hydrolysis (saponification) of diethyl succinate; two equivalents of NaOH cleave the ester bonds, yielding sodium succinate and two equivalents of ethanol; carried out in aqueous NaOH solution under reflux (80–100 °C) for several hours; after completion, the mixture may be acidified to precipitate succinic acid if desired.

Nitridation of yttrium(III) oxide; purpose is preparation of yttrium nitride; Y2O3 reacts with ammonia gas, releasing water and forming YN; carried out at 900‑1100 °C under flowing NH3 (often with a small H2 co‑feed to aid reduction); solid‑state reaction, no solvent; furnace with gas‑tight seals.

Catalytic hydrogenation; Tanshinone I is reduced under hydrogen gas in the presence of platinum on carbon (Pt/C) to give dihydrotanshinone I by saturation of one or more double bonds; typical conditions are 1–5 atm H₂, Pt/C (5–10 % loading), solvent such as ethanol or ethyl acetate, at room temperature to 50 °C, with reaction monitored by TLC or HPLC.

Fischer esterification; thioglycolic acid reacts with ethanol in the presence of an acid catalyst (e.g., concentrated H₂SO₄ or p‑toluenesulfonic acid) to form ethyl thioglycolate and water; performed by refluxing the mixture in ethanol or toluene, often with a Dean‑Stark apparatus to remove water and drive equilibrium toward ester formation.

Acid‑catalyzed ring‑opening of β‑propiolactone by hydrogen chloride, converting the four‑membered lactone into 3‑chloropropionic acid; the carbonyl is hydrolyzed to a carboxylic acid and chloride adds at the β‑carbon. Typically performed in aqueous HCl (≈1 M) at 0 °C to reflux; water serves as solvent; no additional catalyst needed.

Thionation of benzophenone to thiobenzophenone using Lawesson’s reagent with catalytic 4‑dimethylaminopyridine (DMAP). The carbonyl C=O is replaced by a thiocarbonyl C=S. Commonly carried out under nitrogen in an aprotic solvent such as toluene or THF, refluxing 2–6 h; DMAP (5–10 mol %) accelerates sulfur transfer; no other catalyst required.

Acidification of sodium molybdate with hydrochloric acid, yielding molybdenum trioxide as a solid precipitate, water, and sodium chloride in solution. This is a straight acid‑base neutralization and precipitation. Conducted in aqueous medium at ambient temperature with 2 equiv HCl; no special solvent or catalyst beyond the acid.

Isocyanate hydrolysis (addition); water adds across the N=C=O of ethyl isocyanate, yielding ethylamine and carbon dioxide; usually carried out in aqueous medium at ambient or slightly elevated temperature, optionally acid‑ or base‑catalyzed, with vigorous stirring to evolve CO₂.

Reaction of zinc carbonate with aqueous sodium hydroxide, producing carbon dioxide, water, and sodium zincate (often written Na₂ZnO₂). It is a double‑replacement/neutralization where the carbonate is deprotonated and Zn²⁺ forms the zincate complex. Performed in water at room temperature or with mild heating; stoichiometric NaOH (2 eq) is used; no additional reagents.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a primary alkyl bromide with cyanide ion to afford the corresponding nitrile, hexadecanenitrile, and KBr; typically uses potassium cyanide in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO, heated to 50‑80 °C.

High‑temperature steam oxidation of indium metal: steam reduces to hydrogen gas while indium is oxidized to indium(III) oxide. This redox (metal‑steam) reaction is carried out in a furnace or flow reactor at ≥300 °C with a steady flow of superheated steam; no solvent or catalyst required.

Combination (synthesis) reaction; magnesium metal reacts with hydrogen sulfide gas to form magnesium sulfide solid and hydrogen gas. Typically performed by heating a mixture of Mg and H2S (dry, inert atmosphere) at temperatures above 300 °C; no solvent required.

Fischer esterification of p‑hydroxybenzoic acid with n‑heptanol in the presence of catalytic sulfuric acid, forming heptyl p‑hydroxybenzoate (a paraben) and water. The reaction proceeds by refluxing excess n‑heptanol (140–160 °C) with 1–5 % H₂SO₄; water is removed by azeotropic distillation or a Dean‑Stark trap; the solvent is the heptanol itself.

Oxidation of an aromatic aldehyde to the corresponding benzoic acid; the aldehyde carbonyl of o‑orsellinaldehyde is converted into a carboxylic acid to give o‑orsellinic acid. Typical reagents include Jones reagent (CrO₃/H₂SO₄), KMnO₄ in aqueous acidic medium, or NaClO₂ with NaH₂PO₄. Reaction is performed in water/acetone or methanol at 0 °C to reflux temperature.

Hydrazone formation – condensation of 2‑methylbenzaldehyde with phenylhydrazine yields the phenylhydrazone and water; typically carried out by refluxing the reactants in ethanol or glacial acetic acid with a catalytic amount of acid to promote water removal.

Direct oxidative chlorination (halogenation) of the intermetallic samarium antimonide (SmSb) with chlorine gas to afford antimony trichloride (SbCl₃) and samarium chloride (SmCl₂ or SmCl₃ depending on stoichiometry). Conducted in the gas phase at elevated temperature (≈200–400 °C) under a flow of Cl₂; no solvent is required.

Thermal decomposition (calcination) of zinc oxalate; heating solid ZnC₂O₄ yields ZnO plus gaseous CO and CO₂; carried out by heating to 300–400 °C in a furnace, either in air or under inert gas; no solvent or catalyst required.

Hydrolysis of the β‑glucan lichenan to monosaccharide glucose; purpose is saccharification of a polysaccharide; key transformation is cleavage of β‑1,3/1,4 glycosidic bonds; typically achieved by acid hydrolysis (e.g., 0.1 M HCl, 100 °C, 1–2 h) or enzymatic action of lichenase/β‑glucosidase in aqueous solution; water serves as the reaction medium.

Chlorination of technetium dioxide (TcO₂) with chlorine gas, a redox chlorination that yields technetium tetrachloride (TcCl₄) and releases oxygen gas. The solid‑state reaction is carried out at 300–400 °C in a chlorine atmosphere; it is performed without solvent.

Oxidative conversion of methylhydroquinone to 2,5‑dimethyl‑1,4‑benzoquinone using sodium periodate as the oxidant. The periodate oxidizes the hydroquinone diol to the quinone, typically in aqueous buffer or dilute acetic acid at 0 °C to room temperature. No metal catalyst is required.

Reaction of aqueous ammonium hydroxide with calcium hypochlorite producing nitrogen trichloride (NCl₃), calcium chloride and water. This is a chlorination/disproportionation of ammonia to NCl₃, performed in water at low temperature (0–5 °C) to control the highly reactive NCl₃; the reaction is usually carried out with careful pH control and slow addition of hypochlorite.

Grignard addition of ethylmagnesium bromide to pentanal, yielding the secondary alcohol 2‑heptanol. The aldehyde undergoes nucleophilic addition of the ethyl nucleophile under anhydrous conditions (dry diethyl ether or THF) at 0 °C to room temperature, under nitrogen or argon atmosphere. The alkoxide intermediate is subsequently protonated during aqueous work‑up.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2); sodium methanethiolate attacks ethyl bromide, replacing bromide to afford ethyl methyl sulfide and sodium bromide; conducted in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., DMF, DMSO, acetone) at ambient temperature; no catalyst required.

Acid- or base-catalyzed hydrolysis of a diamide; water cleaves both N‑acetyl groups of N‑(6‑acetamidohexyl)acetamide to give 1,6‑diaminohexane and two equivalents of acetic acid. Typically carried out by heating the substrate in excess aqueous mineral acid (e.g., 6 M HCl) or aqueous NaOH at reflux; solvent is water or water/ethanol mixture.

Metallothermic reduction (single‑displacement redox) of gadolinium chloride with lithium metal to afford elemental gadolinium and lithium chloride. Lithium reduces GdCl3, usually with three equivalents of Li per GdCl3, under dry, inert conditions (argon or vacuum) at high temperature (≈600 °C) in a sealed tube or molten salt bath. No solvent or external catalyst is employed.

Double displacement precipitation; reaction of aqueous lanthanum(III) chloride with silver nitrate precipitates silver chloride while generating lanthanum nitrate in solution; carried out in water at room temperature, often used to remove chloride ions, no catalyst needed.

Redox oxidation; hydrogen peroxide oxidizes nitrogen dioxide to nitric acid while being reduced to water. Conducted in aqueous solution, often under acidic conditions, at moderate temperatures; no external catalyst required, though metal ions may accelerate the reaction.

Nitration/esterification of triethylene glycol to give triethylene glycol dinitrate (a nitrate ester). Conducted with concentrated HNO₃ (often mixed with H₂SO₄ as a dehydrating/catalytic agent) at 0‑5 °C initially, then warmed to 20‑30 °C; the acid mixture itself serves as solvent and reaction medium.

Acid‑catalyzed imine formation (Schiff‑base synthesis). Acetone reacts with ammonium acetate, which supplies ammonia and acetate; condensation yields the imine 2‑propanimine while acetate protonates the carbonyl and is converted to acetic acid. Typical conditions: reflux in an aprotic solvent (e.g., ethanol or toluene) with removal of water (Dean‑Stark trap) or gentle heating; no external catalyst required beyond the acetate acting as a weak acid.

Hydrolysis of tungsten(IV) chloride; water attacks WCl₄, producing tungsten(IV) oxide (WO₂) and four equivalents of HCl gas. Typically carried out by stirring solid WCl₄ in excess water at reflux or under mild heating; reaction proceeds in aqueous medium without additional catalyst.

Halide‑acetate metathesis (ligand exchange) of phenylmercuric chloride with potassium acetate, forming phenylmercuric acetate and potassium chloride. Conducted in an aqueous or alcoholic solution (e.g., water/acetone) at ambient or mildly heated temperature; the reaction proceeds without catalyst, though gentle heating improves solubility.

Metal‑ligand complexation (chelation). Purpose: preparation of a zinc(II) catecholate complex. Zinc acetate reacts with benzene‑1,2‑diol; the two phenolic OH groups are deprotonated, forming the catecholate dianion that coordinates to Zn²⁺ while acetic acid is released. Conducted in ethanol or methanol under reflux, mixing stoichiometric Zn(OAc)₂ and catechol (1 : 1) under nitrogen if desired. No external catalyst.

Free radical halogenation; bromination of propyl acetate by Br₂ under UV light produces hydrogen bromide and bromopropyl acetate via radical substitution at the alkyl chain; typically carried out in an inert non‑polar solvent (e.g., CCl₄) with light irradiation, ambient temperature, no catalyst.

Redox (oxidation‑reduction) reaction; aqueous chlorine oxidizes Mn(II) chloride to insoluble manganese dioxide while being reduced to chloride, yielding hydrochloric acid; performed in water at room temperature, often with stirring; no special catalyst required.

Acidic hydrolysis/neutralization; concentrated sulfuric acid protonates and hydrolyzes zinc nitride, forming zinc sulfate and ammonium sulfate; reaction is heated gently under reflux in aqueous medium; stoichiometric acid in excess, no additional catalyst.

Rosenmund‑von Braun cyanation; purpose: replace aryl bromide with cyano group to give para‑dicyanobenzene; key transformation: aryl‑Br displaced by CN from CuCN, producing CuBr; typical conditions: CuCN (1– equiv) in dry pyridine or NMP, heated 150–200 °C under nitrogen for several hours; solvent: dry pyridine, NMP, or DMF; catalyst: copper(I) cyanide (stoichiometric reagent).

Valence tautomerization (electrocyclic rearrangement); benzene oxide interconverts to its ring‑opened isomer oxepin via a thermally allowed electrocyclic ring‑opening; usually conducted by heating the neat compound or in an inert solvent (e.g., benzene) without added reagents.

Reductive alkylation (reductive amination) of a ketone with ethyl hydrazinecarboxylate; condensation forms a hydrazone which is reduced by sodium triacetoxyborohydride to give ethyl 2-(1‑phenylethyl)hydrazinecarboxylate; typically run in dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to rt, with NaBH(OAc)₃ as the mild hydride source, often with a catalytic amount of acetic acid.

N‑acylation of benzimidazole; purpose is to protect the N‑H or introduce a benzoyl substituent; the N‑H of benzimidazole is converted to an N‑C(O)Ph group with release of HCl; typically carried out in a dry, non‑nucleophilic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform with a base (pyridine or triethylamine) to scavenge the HCl, often under reflux or at room temperature.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a primary benzyl sulfonate by potassium thioacetate; the thioacetate ion attacks the benzylic carbon displacing methanesulfonate to give benzyl thioacetate; carried out in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF, DMSO or acetone at 0 °C to ambient temperature, no catalyst needed.

Acid‑base (carbonate‑acid) reaction. Magnesium carbonate reacts with nitric acid to produce magnesium nitrate, carbon dioxide, and water; conducted in aqueous solution with dilute HNO3 at temperatures around 0–50 °C to moderate gas evolution; no catalyst required.

Alkoxylation of a primary amine: monoethanolamine undergoes nucleophilic ring‑opening of two equivalents of ethylene oxide to give the tertiary polyol triethanolamine; typically performed in a sealed reactor at 100‑150 °C under ethylene oxide pressure, often in water or an alcohol solvent, with base catalysis to deprotonate the amine.

Reaction type: Fischer esterification of a dicarboxylic acid; purpose: convert decanedioic acid to its dimethyl ester for increased volatility or further synthetic manipulation; key transformation: condensation of each carboxyl group with methanol, releasing water; typical conditions: reflux methanol (3–5 equiv) with catalytic mineral acid (e.g., H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH), removal of water by Dean‑Stark or azeotropic distillation, reaction time several hours.

Reduction reaction. This reaction involves lithium aluminium hydride acting as a strong reducing agent to reduce carbon tetrachloride. The key transformation is the replacement of a chlorine group in carbon tetrachloride by hydrogen. Reaction occurs under anhydrous conditions, typically in an inert solvent such as tetrahydrofuran (THF). Key byproducts include aluminium and lithium chlorides.

Nucleophilic substitution (hydrolysis) of an α‑chloro ketone; water attacks the carbon bearing chlorine, replacing Cl with OH to give 3‑hydroxybutan‑2‑one and HCl. Usually carried out in aqueous medium, often refluxed, sometimes with mild acid catalysis; common solvent is water or aqueous acetone.

Strong oxidative side‑chain oxidation: meta‑xylene is oxidized by hot aqueous potassium permanganate (often in alkaline medium) to cleave both benzylic methyl groups to carboxylic acids, affording benzene‑1,3‑dicarboxylic acid (m‑phthalic acid) and water; reaction refluxes for several hours followed by acid work‑up and filtration of MnO₂ precipitate.

Thionation of an amide: benzamide is treated with Lawesson’s reagent, which replaces the carbonyl oxygen with sulfur to give thiobenzamide; the reaction is run under inert atmosphere, refluxing in a non‑protic solvent such as toluene or THF for 2‑6 h.

Base‑catalyzed transesterification: triacetin (glycerol triacetate) reacts with ethanol, exchanging one acetate group to form ethyl acetate and diacetin (glycerol diacetate); typically catalyzed by sodium methoxide or a mineral acid (e.g., H₂SO₄) in excess ethanol at reflux, with removal of ethanol to drive equilibrium.

Catalytic hydrogenation of a fluorinated ketone: 1,1,1‑trifluoro‑2‑propanone is reduced over palladium on carbon under H₂ (1–5 atm) in a protic solvent such as methanol or ethanol at 25‑50 °C to yield 1,1,1‑trifluoro‑2‑propanol.

SN2 halide exchange (Finkelstein‑type). Purpose: convert benzyl chloride to the more reactive benzyl iodide. Iodide ion from tetraethylammonium iodide attacks the benzylic carbon, displacing chloride and forming tetraethylammonium chloride. Typical conditions: reflux in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetone, DMF or acetonitrile; the reaction is driven to completion by using excess iodide and removing the precipitated ammonium chloride.

Copper‑catalyzed thiolation (C–S cross‑coupling). Purpose: form a C‑S bond to produce thiophenol from iodobenzene. Sodium hydrosulfide provides the nucleophilic –SH group, which, under Cu(I) (e.g., CuI) with a suitable ligand (often N,N‑dimethylethylenediamine or L‑proline) and a base, undergoes oxidative addition/reductive elimination to replace iodine with –SH, yielding thiophenol and sodium iodide. Conditions: 100–150 °C in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO, under inert atmosphere.

Oxidation of a trivalent phosphine to the corresponding phosphine oxide; hydrogen peroxide oxidizes chlorodiphenylphosphine, converting P(III) to P=O while chloride is released as HCl. Performed in a mixture of water and an organic solvent (e.g., THF/water) at 0–25 °C; a base (NaOH or Na₂CO₃) is added to neutralize the generated HCl.

Reductive cleavage (hydrogenolysis) of a thioether. 1,5‑Bis(methylsulfanyl)pentane undergoes Pd/C‑catalyzed hydrogenolysis (or Raney Ni under H₂) to break the C‑S bonds, producing dimethyl sulfide as the organic sulfur fragment and pentane as the alkane fragment. Conditions: H₂ pressure (1–5 atm), Pd/C (5–10 wt %), solvent such as ethanol or ethyl acetate, temperature 25–80 °C.

Acid–base neutralization to form an aluminum carboxylate (aluminum sorbate); Al(OH)₃ deprotonates sorbic acid, yielding water and coordinating three sorbate anions to Al³⁺; purpose is preparation of a metal‑organic salt used as a stabilizer or additive; generally carried out in aqueous or aqueous‑alcoholic solution at 60‑80 °C with stirring; excess base may be used; no additional catalyst needed.

Acid-catalyzed nucleophilic ring-opening reaction of an epoxide. Hydrogen bromide opens the epoxide ring of 2-butyloxirane to form 2-bromo-1-butanol. This transformation involves the bromide ion attacking the more substituted carbon, consistent with acidic ring-opening. The reaction is conducted in polar protic solvents such as water or alcohol at ambient conditions.

Acid‑base proton transfer (deprotonation of alcohol). Purpose: generate sodium isopropoxide and ammonia by reacting isopropanol with the strong base sodium amide. The NaNH₂ abstracts the proton from the hydroxyl group, forming the alkoxide and releasing NH₃ gas. Conditions: typically performed in liquid ammonia or dry THF at –78 °C to 0 °C under inert atmosphere to avoid moisture, with stoichiometric NaNH₂.

Chromium(VI) oxidation of a primary propargylic alcohol (Jones oxidation). Purpose: oxidize propargyl alcohol to propiolic acid (carboxylic acid oxidation of a primary alcohol adjacent to an alkyne). Chromium trioxide is dissolved in aqueous sulfuric acid (Jones reagent) and added to the substrate in acetone at 0 °C to room temperature. The reaction proceeds through a chromate ester intermediate, yielding propiolic acid, chromium(III) sulfate, and water.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation; exchanges cations and anions to precipitate zinc hydroxide; performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; water is the solvent and no catalyst is required.

Acid‑catalyzed electrophilic addition (hydration) of water to 2‑methylhex‑2‑ene to give the tertiary alcohol 2‑methylhexan‑2‑ol; follows Markovnikov rule; typical conditions use dilute mineral acid such as H₂SO₄ or HgSO₄/H₂SO₄, aqueous medium, often refluxed; water (or water/organic mixture) serves as solvent, acid acts as catalyst.

Williamson ether synthesis (SN2 alkylation) of the hydroxymethyl group of 5‑hydroxymethylfurfural with methyl iodide under basic conditions; converts –CH₂OH to –CH₂OCH₃ producing 5‑methoxymethyl‑2‑furaldehyde; carried out in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., DMF or acetone) with potassium carbonate as base at room temperature to reflux; potassium iodide is formed as by‑product.

Acid–base neutralization (salt metathesis) between acetic acid and sodium methylparaben; proton transfer yields free methylparaben and sodium acetate; performed in aqueous solution at room temperature; no catalyst needed.

Acidbase neutralization of a strong base (strontium hydroxide) with lactic acid; purpose is synthesis of strontium lactate. The hydroxide is protonated, giving strontium lactate and water. Reaction proceeds in water or mixed solvent at room temperature or mild heating; stoichiometry is 1 : 2 (Sr(OH)₂ : 2 HOCH(CH₃)CO₂H).

Reaction type: oxidative dehalogenation/oxidation of a primary alcohol to a carboxylic acid. Purpose: obtain glycolic acid while removing the bromine atom.
