Key transformation: KMnO₄ oxidizes the primary alcohol of 2‑bromoethanol to the corresponding carboxylic acid and reduces the C–Br bond, generating bromide ion; MnO₂ precipitates as a brown solid. Typical conditions: aqueous alkaline KMnO₄ (often 0.1–0.5 M KOH), temperature 20–60 °C, reaction monitored until purple color disappears. Common work‑up: filtration to remove MnO₂, acidification to isolate glycolic acid; potassium bromide remains in solution.

Formation of a Grignard reagent by oxidative insertion of magnesium into the C–I bond of 1‑iodopropane; purpose is to generate propylmagnesium iodide for carbon–carbon bond formation; key transformation is metal insertion forming R‑Mg‑I; conducted under dry, inert atmosphere in anhydrous ether (diethyl ether or THF) at 0 °C to reflux; no external catalyst.

Acid–base reaction; purpose is to dissolve manganese carbonate and generate a soluble nitrate salt; carbonate is protonated by nitric acid forming carbonic acid which decomposes to CO₂ and H₂O while Mn²⁺ forms Mn(NO₃)₂; generally performed in aqueous solution at ambient to mild heating with stirring; water is the solvent, no catalyst required.

Acid‑base (salt hydrolysis) reaction; concentrated sulfuric acid reacts with iron(II) cyanide in aqueous medium, often cooled to limit HCN loss; yields iron(II) sulfate in solution and hydrogen cyanide gas; purpose is generation of HCN; water as solvent, temperature control, performed in fume‑hood, no catalyst.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis (ring‑opening hydrogenation); converts a cycloalkane into a linear alkane. Performed under high H₂ pressure (50–100 atm) at 150–250 °C with a heterogeneous metal catalyst such as Pt, Raney Ni, or Ru on carbon. No solvent is essential; the substrate may be used neat or in a high‑boiling hydrocarbon. Key transformation: cleavage of C–C bonds in the ring, yielding n‑hexane.

Oxidation reaction with a peroxyacid. m-Chloroperbenzoic acid specifically oxidizes the amine nitrogen in 3,4-methylenedioxy-N-methylamphetamine to produce the corresponding hydroxylamine derivative. This selective oxidation typically proceeds under mild conditions in non-reactive solvents such as dichloromethane. Reaction type is oxidative N-hydroxylation.

Nucleophilic addition of benzylamine to carbon disulfide in basic medium forms a dithiocarbamate which is oxidatively dehydrohalogenated by bromine to give benzyl isothiocyanate; water is produced and sodium bromide precipitates. Reaction type: base‑promoted condensation followed by oxidative desulfurization. Typical conditions: NaOH (1–2 eq) in aqueous/acetone mixture at 0 °C to room temperature, slow addition of Br₂ under stirring, work‑up with water and extraction. No special catalyst required.

Hydrolysis (ester cleavage) of pentyl nitrite to the corresponding alcohol and nitrous acid. Reaction type: nucleophilic substitution (water acting as nucleophile). Usually carried out in aqueous solution, often mildly acidic or neutral, at ambient or slightly elevated temperature (20–50 °C). No catalyst is required; excess water drives the reaction to completion.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2); alkyl halide displacement by guanidine to form guanethidine (2‑chloromethylpyridine + guanidine → guanethidine + HCl); purpose is synthesis of the antihypertensive agent guanethidine; key transformation is C–Cl bond cleavage and formation of a new C–N bond; typical conditions use excess free‑base guanidine in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO, heated to 80‑120 °C, with a base (e.g., NaHCO3) to neutralize released HCl; no metal catalyst required.

Electrophilic demethylation of aryl methyl ethers using boron tribromide; 2,6‑dimethoxypyridine is converted to 2,6‑dihydroxypyridine with formation of methyl bromide; usually carried out in anhydrous dichloromethane at –78 °C to 0 °C, then warmed to ambient temperature; BBr₃ serves as both Lewis acid and methyl‑halide source.

Decarboxylation of an α‑keto acid (2‑oxovaleric acid) to give the aldehyde butyraldehyde and CO₂; a classic α‑keto acid decarboxylation (often enzymatic or metal‑catalyzed). Key transformation: cleavage of the C–C bond between the carbonyl carbon and the carboxyl group, forming an aldehyde and releasing carbon dioxide. Typical conditions: heating (80–150 °C) in the presence of a base (e.g., NaHCO₃) or a catalytic amount of thiamine‑pyrophosphate or a transition‑metal salt (e.g., Ag⁺, Cu²⁺) in aqueous or polar protic solvent; sometimes performed in a sealed tube under inert atmosphere.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction; employed to precipitate silver sulfide from silver acetate and sodium sulfide. Silver ion reacts with sulfide ion to give black Ag2S solid while sodium acetate remains in solution. Carried out in water at room temperature; no catalyst required.

Metathesis/synthesis of antimony(III) selenide by reaction of gaseous hydrogen selenide with antimony(III) bromide. Reaction type: precipitation/solid‑state synthesis of a metal chalcogenide with concomitant formation of hydrogen bromide gas. Conducted under an inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar) in a dry, aprotic solvent such as THF or ethanol, at low to moderate temperature (0–25 °C) to control H₂Se evolution. No additional catalyst needed.

Partial hydrolysis of 1,3‑dichlorobutane to give 4‑chlorobutan‑1‑ol and hydrochloric acid. Reaction type: SN2 nucleophilic substitution of a primary alkyl chloride by water. Typically performed in aqueous NaOH or simply refluxing water, 80–100 °C, for several hours; the reaction mixture is then acidified to liberate HCl. No catalyst required.

Grignard addition of octylmagnesium bromide to acetaldehyde followed by aqueous work‑up to afford 2‑nonanol; purpose is carbon‑carbon bond formation extending the carbon chain and producing a secondary alcohol; key transformation is nucleophilic attack of the Grignard reagent on the aldehyde carbonyl, forming an alkoxide which is protonated; typical conditions involve anhydrous ether solvent (diethyl ether or THF), addition at –78 °C to 0 °C, then quench with dilute acid; the Grignard reagent itself serves as the nucleophilic catalyst.

Alkaline hydrolysis (saponification) of dimethyl suberate with NaOH to produce suberic (octanedioic) acid and methanol. Reaction type: base‑catalyzed ester cleavage. Conducted in aqueous NaOH (excess, 1–2 eq per ester) with heating under reflux (80–100 °C) for several hours. After reaction, the mixture is acidified (e.g., with HCl) to precipitate suberic acid; methanol remains in the aqueous layer. No special catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration (ether formation). Two molecules of tert‑butanol condense to give di‑tert‑butyl ether and water. Typically performed neat or in excess t‑BuOH with a strong acid such as H₂SO₄, p‑TsOH or HCl at 50‑80 °C; water is removed to drive equilibrium.

Base‑mediated sulfonamide synthesis. n‑Butylamine attacks benzenesulfonyl chloride, displacing chloride; sodium carbonate neutralises the generated HCl. Conducted in anhydrous dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to rt, often with a slight excess of amine; no additional catalyst required.

Base‑catalyzed transesterification. Sodium methoxide deprotonates ethanol, which then exchanges the alkoxy group of methyl salicylate to give ethyl salicylate and methanol. Typically refluxed in a mixture of ethanol/methanol (solvent is the alcohol) with 5–10 % NaOMe; removal of methanol shifts equilibrium.

Catalytic hydrogenation of pyrazine to piperazine. Under H₂ pressure (≈3 atm) with a metal catalyst (Pd/C, PtO₂, Raney Ni) the aromatic N‑heterocycle is fully reduced to the saturated diamine. Reaction carried out in ethanol or methanol at 25‑80 °C.

Exhaustive N‑methylation (SN2 alkylation) of p‑phenylenediamine. Potassium carbonate deprotonates the amine groups, which then react with excess methyl iodide to give N,N,N′,N′‑tetramethyl‑p‑phenylenediamine; KI and water are formed as by‑products. Performed in DMF or DMSO at reflux (80‑120 °C).

Thermal decomposition of lead(II) formate; heating solid lead(II) formate results in breakdown to lead(II) oxide, carbon dioxide gas, and hydrogen gas; carried out under inert atmosphere or air at 200–300 °C; solid‑phase reaction, no solvent or catalyst needed.

Full reduction of an ester to a primary alcohol using lithium aluminium hydride; purpose is to obtain 3‑methyl‑1‑butanol; key transformation: methyl 3‑methylbutanoate + LiAlH4 → 3‑methyl‑1‑butanol + methanol (released during work‑up); conducted in dry ether (diethyl ether or THF) under inert atmosphere, typically 0 °C to reflux; quench with aqueous acid after reaction.

Hydrolysis of an acyl bromide; water attacks the carbonyl carbon, displacing bromide and forming acetic acid while releasing HBr. Usually carried out at 0 °C to rt in aqueous medium; exothermic, often with cooling; no catalyst required.

SN2 alkylation of potassium 2‑fluoroacetate to form methyl 2‑fluoroacetate. Methyl iodide reacts with the carboxylate anion, displacing iodide and yielding the ester; potassium iodide is the only by‑product. Conducted in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or acetone at 50‑80 °C, often under inert atmosphere.

Redox / reduction‑fluorination. Hydrogen reduces molybdenum(VI) fluoride to molybdenum(IV) fluoride while being oxidized to HF. Typically performed in the gas phase at 300–500 °C in a quartz or steel reactor under inert atmosphere; no solvent used.

Metathesis/acid‑base neutralization: sodium chloride reacts with chloroplatinic acid to exchange ions, forming sodium hexachloroplatinate and liberating hydrochloric acid. Typically performed in aqueous solution with stirring, often at mild heating (40‑60 °C) to drive off HCl gas; water is the solvent and no catalyst is required.

Alcoholysis of chloroacetyl chloride with methanol to give methyl 2‑chloroacetate and hydrogen chloride; a nucleophilic acyl substitution of an acid chloride. Performed in methanol at 0–25 °C, often with a base such as pyridine or triethylamine to scavenge the generated HCl.

Base‑catalyzed hydrolysis of a gem‑dihalide to a ketone; alkaline aqueous NaOH attacks the carbon bearing both halides, displacing bromide and chloride and forming acetone; carried out with aqueous NaOH under reflux; water is the solvent, no additional catalyst required.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction): 2,3‑butanedione is reduced by hydrogen in the presence of palladium on carbon to give 2,3‑butanediol, converting two carbonyl groups to secondary alcohols. Conducted under H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) at 25‑60 °C in a protic solvent such as ethanol or methanol; Pd/C (5‑10 wt %) serves as the catalyst.

Metal‑hydride reduction of a nitrile; LiAlH₄ reduces hexanenitrile to the corresponding primary amine (hexan-1-amine) via an imine intermediate. Conducted in dry ether (e.g., THF or diethyl ether) under inert atmosphere, 0 °C to reflux; work‑up with water and dilute acid.

Oxidation with hypochlorite: 3,4‑dihydroxybenzyl alcohol is oxidized by sodium hypochlorite to the corresponding aldehyde, 3,4‑dihydroxybenzaldehyde, with formation of water and sodium chloride. Reaction is usually carried out in aqueous buffer (pH ≈ 9) at 0‑5 °C to limit over‑oxidation; NaOCl is the oxidant and no additional catalyst is needed.

Acid‑base salt formation: Betazole (a weak base) is protonated by two equivalents of hydrochloric acid to give the betazole dihydrochloride salt. The process is done by dissolving betazole in aqueous HCl (often 1 M) at ambient temperature, followed by evaporation or crystallization; water is the solvent and no catalyst is required.

Acid‑base reaction with gas evolution: Sodium bicarbonate reacts with fluorosilicic acid to generate carbon dioxide and water while forming sodium hexafluorosilicate as the solid salt. Performed in aqueous solution at room temperature with vigorous stirring; CO₂ evolution drives the reaction forward; no catalyst is needed.

Acid digestion of a metal nitride: Holmium nitride reacts with hydrochloric acid to yield holmium(III) chloride and ammonia gas. Typically carried out by adding solid HoN to aqueous HCl (conc. 1‑6 M) and heating gently (50‑80 °C) to promote gas release; water is the reaction medium and no catalyst is required.

Fischer esterification; purpose is to form an ester (hexyl acetate) from a carboxylic acid and an alcohol. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of hexanol on the protonated carbonyl of acetic acid followed by loss of water. Typical conditions: reflux with a catalytic amount of strong acid (e.g., sulfuric acid or p‑toluenesulfonic acid) and removal of water (azeotropic distillation). Common solvent: toluene or benzene; sometimes a Dean–Stark trap is used.

Nucleophilic aromatic substitution (SNAr) of a chloro substituent by ammonia on a quinoline ring; purpose is to replace chlorine with an amino group to afford 4‑aminoquinoline and HCl. Key transformation is replacement of C–Cl by C–NH2. Typical conditions: excess gaseous or aqueous NH3, polar aprotic solvent (e.g., DMF or DMSO), heating at 150–200 °C in a sealed tube or autoclave, often with a base (e.g., NaHCO3) to neutralize the liberated HCl.

Acyl chloride amidation (acetylation of an amine); purpose is to protect or modify the hydrazide group of isoniazid. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of the isoniazid nitrogen on acetyl chloride, generating N‑acetyl isoniazid and releasing HCl. Typical conditions: 0 °C to rt in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane, with a base (pyridine, triethylamine, or TEA) to scavenge HCl. Reaction is rapid and exothermic.

Nitro reduction; converts the para‑nitro group of N,N‑diethyl‑4‑nitroaniline to an amine (N,N‑diethyl‑p‑phenylenediamine) using tin(II) chloride in aqueous hydrochloric acid; SnCl2 is oxidized to SnCl4 and water is formed; typically carried out under reflux in water or aqueous ethanol with excess HCl as acid medium.

Halogen exchange (metathesis) between chlorine and bismuth(III) bromide; purpose is to convert BiBr₃ to BiCl₃ while liberating bromine. Key transformation: chlorine oxidizes bromide ions to bromine and is reduced to chloride, which coordinates to bismuth. Typical conditions: dry, inert atmosphere; gaseous reagents mixed at elevated temperature (≈100–150 °C) in a sealed vessel. No solvent is required; the reaction is often carried out in the gas phase or in a non‑coordinating liquid like carbon tetrachloride.

Jones oxidation; purpose is to oxidize a secondary alcohol to the corresponding ketone (cyclopentanone). Key transformation: chromium(VI) species (CrO₃·H₂SO₄) oxidizes the alcohol, reducing to Cr³⁺ while the alcohol is converted to a carbonyl. Typical conditions: 0 °C to rt, reagent prepared by dissolving CrO₃ in dilute sulfuric acid and adding to a solution of cyclopentanol in acetone. Solvent: acetone (dry); reaction is quenched with isopropanol or methanol to destroy excess oxidant.

Electrophilic addition of hydrogen chloride (Markovnikov addition) to an alkene. Key transformation: trans‑2‑pentene + HCl → 2‑chloropentane. Typical conditions: gaseous HCl or concentrated aqueous HCl, often in anhydrous ether or dichloromethane, at 0–25 °C. Lewis acid catalysts such as ZnCl₂, FeCl₃, or AlCl₃ can be employed to accelerate the reaction; the process proceeds via protonation of the double bond followed by capture of the carbocation by chloride ion.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (esterification) of formyl chloride with methanol yielding methyl formate and HCl; conducted in a dry aprotic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) at low temperature, usually in the presence of a base or pyridine to neutralize HCl.

Acid‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (esterification reverse); tert‑butyl pentanoate is treated with aqueous acid (e.g., 1 M HCl) under reflux to cleave the ester, regenerating pentanoic acid and tert‑butyl alcohol. Typical solvent: mixture of water and a water‑immiscible organic solvent (e.g., THF or dioxane).

Eschweiler–Clarke methylation; purpose is to N‑methylate the amine of 2,5‑dimethoxy‑amphetamine. Key transformation: formaldehyde reacts with the amine to form an iminium intermediate, which is reduced by formic acid (hydrogen donor) to give the N‑methyl product, generating CO₂ and water. Typical conditions: aqueous or alcoholic solution of formic acid and formaldehyde, heated to reflux (≈80–100 °C) for several hours. Solvent: methanol or water; reaction is mild and tolerates many functional groups.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution of a primary alkyl chloride with ammonia; purpose is to replace the chloro group with an amino group, forming 1‑(2‑aminoethyl)pyrrolidine. Key transformation: ammonia attacks the electrophilic carbon bearing chlorine, displacing chloride as ammonium chloride. Typical conditions: excess gaseous or aqueous NH₃, reflux in ethanol or water, often in a sealed pressure tube to maintain ammonia pressure. Common solvent: ethanol; product isolated after basification and extraction.

Alkylation of a secondary amine via SN2 nucleophilic substitution; 1‑bromobutane reacts with di‑n‑butylamine to give tributylamine and HBr. Typically performed under reflux in anhydrous solvent (e.g., ethanol or THF) with the amine in excess to capture the generated HBr, sometimes using a base such as triethylamine to neutralize the acid.

Acid‑base (neutralization) reaction; hydroxide deprotonates ammonium ion to generate ammonia gas and water, while iodide remains as NaI; overall: NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ → NH₃↑ + H₂O; performed in aqueous solution, usually with excess NaOH; gentle heating may be applied to liberate NH₃; no catalyst required.

Base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification); purpose is to convert propyl benzoate to the sodium salt of benzoic acid and 1‑propanol. The ester is treated with aqueous NaOH (often 1–2 M) and heated under reflux in a mixture of water and an organic cosolvent (e.g., ethanol or THF). The reaction proceeds via nucleophilic attack of hydroxide, giving sodium benzoate and propanol after acidification of the aqueous layer.

Acid‑base salt formation by treating the free tertiary amine with gaseous or aqueous HCl; typically done in cold aqueous solution to give the stable hydrochloride salt of 2‑methylpropan‑2‑amine; no special catalyst needed.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis (reductive deoxygenation) of a primary alcohol; hydrogen reduces 1‑propanol to propane with formation of water. Requires high‑pressure H₂ (30–100 atm), elevated temperature (150–250 °C), and a metal catalyst such as Raney Ni, Cu‑Cr₂O₃, or Pd‑Cu alloy, usually in a high‑boiling solvent like diphenyl ether or in the gas‑phase over the catalyst.

Formation of a Grignard reagent (organomagnesium halide); insertion of magnesium into the C–Cl bond of chlorobenzene to give phenylmagnesium chloride. Requires anhydrous conditions, dry ether (diethyl ether or THF) as solvent, activation of magnesium (e.g., iodine or a crystal of Mg) and inert atmosphere; usually performed at reflux or gentle heating.

Grignard addition to an epoxide (nucleophilic ring opening); isobutylmagnesium bromide attacks ethylene oxide at the less hindered carbon, yielding 4‑methyl‑1‑pentanol after aqueous work‑up, with MgBr₂ as by‑product. Conducted in dry ether (diethyl ether or THF) at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere, followed by protonation with dilute acid or water.

Nitrosation of a secondary amine; diethylamine reacts with nitrosonium tetrafluoroborate (NO⁺ BF₄⁻) to form N‑nitrosodiethylamine and tetrafluoroboric acid. Performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile or dichloromethane at 0 °C to ambient temperature, often under anhydrous conditions and inert atmosphere to avoid side reactions.

Reductive amination (hydrogenation) of phenylacetone with methylamine to give DL‑methamphetamine; hydrogen and Pd/C catalyze the condensation of phenylacetone and methylamine followed by in‑situ reduction of the imine intermediate. Typical conditions: 30–50 bar H₂, 50–80 °C, solvent methanol or ethanol, catalyst loading 5–10 % Pd on carbon, reaction time 4–12 h.

Base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification) of ethyl trifluoroacetate. Aqueous NaOH attacks the carbonyl, yielding the trifluoroacetate anion which complexes with Na⁺ to give sodium trifluoroacetate; ethanol is released as the alcohol side‑product. Conditions: aqueous NaOH (1–2 M), reflux (≈80 °C), water/ethanol solvent system. Common method to prepare trifluoroacetate salts.

Enzymatic oxidation (dehydrogenation); 2,3‑dihydroxypropyl dihydrogen phosphate (glycerol‑1‑phosphate) is oxidized by NAD⁺ to dihydroxyacetone phosphate (DHAP) with reduction of NAD⁺ to NADH (and release of H⁺). Purpose: generate DHAP for glycolytic flux. Catalyzed by glycerol‑3‑phosphate dehydrogenase in aqueous buffer (pH 7–8), requires Mg²⁺, proceeds at 25–37 °C under aerobic conditions.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a primary benzylic bromide with hydroxide; aqueous NaOH attacks the bromomethyl group of 1‑(bromomethyl)naphthalene to give 1‑(hydroxymethyl)naphthalene and NaBr; the reaction is carried out in water or a water/ethanol mixture at reflux or 50–80 °C; after cooling, the product is extracted into an organic solvent.

Salt metathesis (double displacement) ion exchange; lithium nitrate reacts with potassium hexafluoroantimonate to exchange cations, yielding potassium nitrate and lithium hexafluoroantimonate. Conducted in aqueous solution at room temperature with stirring; products remain in solution and can be isolated by evaporation or crystallization.

Acid–base neutralization; formation of a metal acetate salt. Neodymium(III) hydroxide reacts with acetic acid in aqueous solution, releasing water and yielding neodymium triacetate. Typically performed at ambient temperature or with gentle heating; water is the solvent and no catalyst is required.

Direct combination (synthesis) reaction of mercury with iodine; produces mercury(II) iodide (HgI₂) as a red crystalline solid; elemental iodine is sublimed onto heated mercury (≈150–200 °C) in a sealed tube or under inert atmosphere; no catalyst needed.

Redox (oxidation–reduction) reaction; conversion of nitrous oxide to nitrogen gas with simultaneous oxidation of copper metal to copper(II) oxide. Solid copper is heated in the presence of N₂O gas, often in a flow reactor at temperatures above 300 °C. No solvent or catalyst is needed.

Fischer esterification: 2‑fluoroacetic acid condenses with phenol to form phenyl 2‑fluoroacetate and water; requires a strong acid catalyst (conc. H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH), removal of water (Dean–Stark trap), and reflux in a high‑boiling solvent such as toluene or benzene.

Palladium‑catalyzed Stille cross‑coupling; purpose is to install a phenyl group onto the tetrazole ring. The aryl‑tributylstannane transfers a phenyl moiety to 5‑iodo‑2H‑tetrazole under the action of Pd(II) (often reduced in situ to Pd(0)) with triethylamine as base. Typical conditions: inert atmosphere, reflux in polar aprotic solvent such as DMF, THF or dioxane, catalytic amount of phosphine ligand may be used; reaction is run at 80‑120 °C until completion.

Hydrolysis of an organoarsenic cyanide; water attacks cacodyl cyanide to generate hydrogen cyanide gas and cacodylic acid (dimethylarsinic acid). The reaction proceeds in aqueous solution at room temperature or mild heating; no additional catalyst is required, though acidic or neutral pH aids cyanide release.

Solid‑state metathesis (double displacement) exchange; magnesium stearate reacts with zinc oxide to form zinc stearate and magnesium oxide. Usually carried out by thoroughly mixing the powders and heating to 200–300 °C to promote diffusion; no solvent or catalyst is employed.

Acid‑carbonate neutralization; sulfuric acid reacts with sodium sesquicarbonate (a mixture of sodium carbonate and bicarbonate) to produce carbon dioxide gas, water, and sodium sulfate. Performed in aqueous solution with stirring; mild heating accelerates CO₂ evolution. No catalyst is needed.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation; used to convert insoluble carbonate and silicate salts; potassium carbonate reacts with calcium silicate forming soluble dipotassium silicate in water while calcium carbonate precipitates; typically carried out in aqueous solution with stirring and mild heating (50‑80 °C); water is the solvent, no catalyst required.

Base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification). Aqueous NaOH hydrolyzes 2‑hydroxyethyl acetate, converting the acyl group to sodium acetate while releasing ethylene glycol. Typical conditions: excess NaOH solution, reflux (60‑80 °C) for 1–2 h, followed by acidification if the free acid is desired.

Acidic (or basic) hydrolysis of phenyl hexanoate; purpose is to cleave the ester back to hexanoic acid and phenol. Key transformation: water attacks the carbonyl carbon, leading to carboxylic acid and phenol release. Typical conditions (acidic): reflux phenyl hexanoate in aqueous 1 M HCl or dilute sulfuric acid (5–10 % v/v) for 2 h; alternatively, basic hydrolysis with aqueous NaOH (1 M) at reflux followed by acidification to precipitate the acid.

Halogenation/acid dissolution of a metal oxide; hydroiodic acid reduces zirconium dioxide to zirconium tetraiodide with formation of water; performed with excess anhydrous HI under reflux (100‑150 °C) in a sealed tube or under nitrogen to avoid moisture; no additional catalyst; solvent is liquid HI (often azeotropic with water).

Alkaline hydrolysis of an amide; aqueous NaOH cleaves the acetamide bond of N‑(2‑phenylethyl)acetamide to give 2‑phenylethylamine and sodium acetate; reflux in aqueous NaOH for several hours, followed by acidification to liberate the free amine.

Oxidation (redox) of a metal sulfide; hydrogen peroxide oxidizes zinc sulfide to zinc sulfate while being reduced to water; usually carried out in aqueous solution, often acidic (pH 2‑4) to promote oxidation, at ambient or slightly elevated temperature (20‑60 °C); may be assisted by a small amount of Fe²⁺ as a catalyst; water is the solvent.

Acid‑base neutralization; cerium(IV) hydroxide is protonated by sulfuric acid producing cerium(IV) sulfate and water; conducted in aqueous medium at room temperature with vigorous stirring; water is the solvent, no catalyst needed.

Redox/acid dissolution of a metal; iron metal is oxidized by citric acid to ferrous citrate with simultaneous evolution of hydrogen gas; performed in aqueous citric acid solution, often heated gently (30‑60 °C) to increase rate; water is the solvent, no catalyst required.

Thermal decomposition of nickel(II) cyanide; heat induces breakdown of Ni(CN)2 to elemental nickel metal and cyanogen gas (C₂N₂). Conducted at high temperature (≈600 °C or higher) under an inert atmosphere to prevent oxidation; no solvents or catalysts are used.

O‑alkylation (SN2) of phenol by methyl perchlorate to give anisole; purpose is to convert phenol into a methyl ether (protecting group or synthesis step); phenoxide attacks the methyl group of methyl perchlorate, forming anisole and releasing perchloric acid; typically performed in anhydrous aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature, often with a base like pyridine or triethylamine to capture the acid.

Ion‑exchange (metathesis) reaction; aqueous sodium hydroxide exchanges its sodium ion for the iodide of benzyltrimethylammonium iodide, yielding sodium iodide and benzyltrimethylammonium hydroxide; carried out in water at ambient temperature with stirring; water is the solvent, no catalyst needed.

Thermal decomposition / disproportionation reaction; purpose is to generate sulfur dichloride and chlorine gas from sulfur tetrachloride; key transformation: sulfur tetrachloride cleaves to give sulfur dichloride and elemental chlorine; typically carried out by heating SCl₄ above about 100 °C, often under an inert atmosphere; can be performed in the gas phase or in a non‑reactive solvent such as carbon tetrachloride; no catalyst required.

Reductive amination followed by catalytic hydrogenation; used to synthesize 3‑methoxymethamphetamine. The carbonyl of 3‑methoxyphenylacetone condenses with methylamine to form an imine, which is then reduced by H₂ over a metal catalyst (Pd/C, Raney Ni or PtO₂) to give the secondary amine, releasing water. Typical conditions: H₂ pressure 10–50 atm, catalyst 5–10 % wt, ethanol or methanol solvent, 25–80 °C, inert atmosphere.

Acid‑base neutralization forming an ammonium salt. Aqueous ammonia neutralizes salicylic acid, producing ammonium salicylate and water. Reaction proceeds readily at ambient temperature in water; no catalyst required. The ammonium salicylate remains soluble; it can be isolated by evaporation or cooling.

Reductive dehalogenation (metal‑acid reduction); purpose is to remove the bromine from an α‑bromo‑ketone while leaving the carbonyl intact. Zinc dust donates electrons and acetic acid supplies protons, reducing the C–Br bond to C–H and forming zinc bromide and water. Typical conditions: reflux in glacial acetic acid with excess Zn dust, stirring under inert atmosphere; aqueous work‑up removes ZnBr₂.

Halogen‑lithium exchange; generates a vinyllithium reagent for further organometallic chemistry. tert‑Butyllithium swaps lithium for bromine on bromoethene, yielding CH₂=CHLi and tert‑butyl bromide. Conducted in dry THF at –78 °C under nitrogen or argon, using stoichiometric t‑BuLi, no additional catalyst.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation; prepares cobalt(II) sulfide. Sulide ions from Na₂S replace sulfate on CoSO₄, forming insoluble CoS precipitate and soluble Na₂SO₄. Carried out in aqueous solution with vigorous stirring, often at room temperature or with gentle heating; filtration isolates the CoS solid.

Ester hydrolysis (neutral or acid‑catalyzed); converts ethyl iodoacetate to iodoacetic acid. Water attacks the carbonyl carbon, cleaving the ethyl ester to give iodoacetic acid and ethanol. Typical conditions: reflux in water (or water/ethanol) at 80–100 °C, optionally with a catalytic amount of HCl or NaOH to accelerate the reaction; reaction time 1–4 h.

Double displacement precipitation; employed to test for bromide ions or to produce soluble strontium nitrate; bromide anion swaps with nitrate producing insoluble AgBr precipitate and Sr(NO₃)₂ in solution; reaction is performed in water at room temperature; no catalyst needed, water as solvent.

Direct combination (solid‑state synthesis) of a Group II metal with silicon to form an intermetallic silicide; purpose is to prepare barium silicide (BaSi2) as a semiconductor or battery material; key transformation is metal‑silicon bond formation; typically carried out by mixing powdered Ba and Si and heating under inert atmosphere (argon) at 800–1000 °C, often by arc‑melting or high‑temperature furnace; no solvent, inert gas protection required.

Selective ketone reduction; NaBH₄ reduces the carbonyl of acetovanillone to the corresponding benzylic alcohol, giving 4‑hydroxy‑3‑methoxybenzyl alcohol; carried out in protic solvents such as methanol or ethanol at 0 °C to room temperature; reaction is rapid and inexpensive, and the alkoxy groups remain untouched.

Carbothermic reduction of praseodymium(III) oxide to metallic praseodymium. Pr₂O₃ is mixed with carbon (graphite or coke) and heated to 1500‑1800 °C under an inert or reducing atmosphere, reducing the oxide to Pr metal while carbon is oxidized to CO₂. This solid‑state high‑temperature reduction requires no solvents; the carbon acts as the reductant.

Friedel‑Crafts acylation (electrophilic aromatic substitution) of N,N‑dimethylaniline with acetyl chloride using aluminum chloride as Lewis‑acid catalyst; purpose is to introduce an acetyl group para to the dimethylamino substituent giving 4‑acetyl‑N,N‑dimethylaniline; by‑product is hydrogen chloride; key steps are generation of the acylium ion (CH3CO⁺) by AlCl3 and its attack on the aromatic ring; performed in anhydrous, non‑nucleophilic solvent such as dry dichloromethane or carbon disulfide at 0 °C to reflux under nitrogen; AlCl3 is used in stoichiometric excess, and the mixture is quenched with ice‑water to neutralize HCl.

Metathesis/acid‑base double displacement reaction between aqueous hydrofluoric acid and palladium(II) nitrate; purpose is to convert soluble Pd(NO3)2 into insoluble palladium(II) fluoride while generating nitric acid; key transformation is exchange of nitrate for fluoride ligands; typically carried out in dilute aqueous solution at room temperature or slightly cooled to avoid HF volatilization; the precipitated PdF2 is filtered off, and the filtrate contains HNO3; safety measures for handling HF are essential.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt formation) of manganese(II) oxide with acetic acid producing manganese(II) acetate and water; purpose is to obtain the soluble acetate salt for use as a precursor or catalyst; key transformation is protonation of the oxide surface and formation of Mn(OAc)2; performed by suspending MnO in excess glacial acetic acid and heating to reflux (≈118 °C) for several hours; water generated is removed by azeotropic distillation with acetic acid; no additional catalyst required.

Neutralization (salt hydrolysis). Guanidine hydrochloride reacts with aqueous sodium hydroxide, liberating free guanidine, forming sodium chloride and water. Usually carried out in water at room temperature to gentle reflux; no catalyst.

Fluorination‑driven metathesis of strontium tungstate (SrWO4) with hydrofluoric acid; purpose is to liberate tungstic acid (H2WO4) and precipitate strontium fluoride (SrF2); key transformation is replacement of strontium by hydrogen and formation of insoluble SrF2; typically performed in aqueous HF solution at low to moderate temperature (0–50 °C) with stirring; the SrF2 precipitate is filtered, and the filtrate contains tungstic acid which can be isolated by evaporation; careful handling of HF is mandatory.

Acid‑base reaction of cadmium carbonate with tetrafluoroboric acid (HBF4); purpose is to generate cadmium tetrafluoroborate, a non‑coordinating anion salt, while releasing CO2 and water; key transformation is protonation of carbonate leading to decarboxylation (CO2 evolution) and formation of Cd(BF4)2; carried out in aqueous solution of HBF4, often at room temperature with gentle heating to accelerate CO2 release; the resulting Cd(BF4)2 remains in solution and can be isolated by evaporation or precipitation; no additional catalyst required.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) ion‑exchange in aqueous solution; tetramethylammonium tetrafluoroborate reacts with sodium hydroxide to give tetramethylammonium hydroxide and sodium tetrafluoroborate. The process is carried out in water at ambient temperature, often with stirring to ensure complete exchange. No catalyst is needed; the reaction is driven by the solubility differences of the salts.

Ester acetylation (acylation of an alcohol). Primary hydroxyl of ethyl 6‑hydroxyhexanoate reacts with acetic anhydride to give the acetate ester (ethyl 6‑acetoxyhexanoate) and one equivalent of acetic acid. Typical conditions: 0 °C to room temperature in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or pyridine; a base (pyridine or DMAP) is added to scavenge the generated acid. Reaction proceeds quickly and is driven to completion by removal of acetic acid or by using excess anhydride.

Lithium aluminium hydride reduction of an amide; reduces N‑(3‑methoxyphenyl)acetamide to the corresponding secondary amine, N‑ethyl‑3‑methoxyaniline, by replacing the carbonyl carbon with two hydrogen atoms and retaining the ethyl fragment from the acetamide; carried out in anhydrous ether (THF or diethyl ether) under nitrogen at 0 °C to reflux, followed by careful acidic work‑up to quench excess LiAlH₄ and isolate the amine.

Fischer esterification (acid‑catalyzed esterification) of terephthalic acid with methanol; produces dimethyl terephthalate, a key monomer for PET polymer, and water as by‑product; the reaction uses concentrated H₂SO₄ as catalyst, refluxing excess methanol (often 60–80 °C) and removing water azeotropically or by continuous distillation to drive the equilibrium toward ester formation.

Direct fluorination/oxidation (redox) of calcium phosphide with elemental fluorine; phosphorus is oxidized from –III to +V yielding volatile phosphorus pentafluoride (PF₅) and calcium fluoride solid precipitate; conducted in a fluorine‑compatible reactor (often nickel or Monel) at to moderate temperatures (‑78 °C to 0 °C) under anhydrous, inert conditions; no solvent is used, and the exotherm is controlled by diluting F₂ with an inert gas.

SuFEx click condensation of phenol with sulfamoyl fluoride to give phenyl sulfamate and HF; nucleophilic attack of phenoxide on the sulfur(VI) center displaces fluoride; typically performed at room temperature in an aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile or dichloromethane with a mild base (e.g., triethylamine or pyridine) to trap the released HF.

This is a single displacement (redox) reaction where bromine replaces iodine. Purpose is to produce cobalt(II) bromide and liberate iodine. Key transformation involves oxidation of iodide ions by elemental bromine. Typically occurs in aqueous or polar solvent at ambient temperature.

Oxidative dissolution of tellurium in alkaline medium (base‑promoted oxidation); elemental tellurium is oxidized by molecular oxygen in the presence of potassium hydroxide to give potassium tellurite (K₂TeO₃) and water; typically performed in aqueous KOH solution at room temperature or mild heating with continuous bubbling of air or O₂; the reaction proceeds without additional catalysts, and the tellurite product remains soluble in the basic solution.

Friedel‑Crafts acylation; electrophilic aromatic substitution that installs an acetyl group para to the isobutyl substituent, giving 4‑isobutylacetophenone. Conducted with acetyl chloride and a stoichiometric amount of AlCl3 as Lewis‑acid catalyst under anhydrous conditions, typically in dry dichloromethane or carbon disulfide, cooled to 0 °C then allowed to warm to reflux; hydrogen chloride gas is evolved as by‑product.

Fischer esterification; acid‑catalyzed conversion of vanillic acid (4‑hydroxy‑3‑methoxybenzoic acid) to its methyl ester, methyl vanillate. Reflux vanillic acid in excess methanol with a catalytic amount of concentrated H2SO4; water is removed by azeotropic distillation or excess methanol drives the equilibrium toward ester formation. Methanol serves as both reactant and solvent.

Selective aldehyde reduction; NaBH4 reduces the aldehyde function of 3‑hydroxy‑2‑methylpropanal to a primary alcohol while leaving the existing hydroxyl untouched, producing 2‑methyl‑1,3‑propanediol. Reaction performed at 0 °C to room temperature in a protic solvent such methanol or ethanol; aqueous work‑up quenches excess borohydride.

NaBH4 reduction of aldehyde; 3‑pyridinecarboxaldehyde is converted to 3‑pyridinemethanol by nucleophilic hydride attack on the carbonyl carbon. Usually carried out in methanol, ethanol, or a MeOH/THF mixture at 0 °C to rt; the by‑product is sodium borate after aqueous work‑up.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction; two equivalents of nitric acid react with calcium tetrafluoroborate to exchange anions, yielding calcium nitrate and two equivalents of tetrafluoroboric (hexafluoroboric) acid. Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no special catalyst required, and the reaction proceeds to completion upon mixing of stoichiometric amounts.

Halide exchange (Finkelstein‑type SN2); silver fluoride provides fluoride ion that displaces bromide in 1‑bromoheptane to give 1‑fluoroheptane, with precipitation of insoluble AgBr driving the equilibrium. Performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetone, DMF, or acetonitrile, often under mild heating; the reaction is typically run under inert atmosphere to avoid moisture.

Oxidation‑reduction (redox) reaction; hydrogen peroxide oxidizes arsenite (AsIII) to arsenate (AsV). Key transformation: As(III) → As(V) with concomitant reduction of H2O2 to water. Typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no special catalyst required, mild acidic or neutral pH is common; water is the solvent.

Reductive amination; acetaldehyde reacts with ethylamine and molecular hydrogen to give diethylamine and water. Key steps: condensation of aldehyde with amine to form an imine, followed by catalytic hydrogenation of the imine to the secondary amine. Conducted under hydrogen pressure (1–50 atm) with a metal catalyst such as Raney nickel, Pd/C, or PtO2, in an alcohol or ether solvent at 25–80 °C.

High‑temperature reduction/decomposition of silicon carbide by hydrogen. The Si–C bond is cleaved; hydrogen reduces the carbon to methane while silicon is liberated as elemental Si. Reaction is performed in the gas phase at very high temperatures (≈1300–1500 °C) often in a flowing H2 atmosphere; no solvent, sometimes a graphite or SiC crucible is used.
Hydrolysis of a secondary alkyl bromide; 3‑bromopentane reacts with water to afford 3‑pentanol and HBr; similar conditions to reaction 3—reflux in aqueous solvent, may be acid‑catalyzed.

LiAlH₄ reduction of an ester; reduces 2‑phenoxyethyl acetate to the primary alcohol phenoxyethanol and releases ethanol from the acetate moiety. Reaction performed in anhydrous ether or THF at 0 °C to reflux under nitrogen, using stoichiometric LiAlH₄; work‑up with aqueous acid quenches excess hydride.

Acid‑peroxide reaction; produces hydrogen peroxide and potassium chloride. KO2 reacts with HCl, the peroxide ion is protonated to H2O2, and K⁺ combines with Cl⁻ to form KCl. Conducted in aqueous hydrochloric acid, typically cold (0‑10 °C) to preserve H2O2; water is the solvent, no catalyst needed.

Ester reduction with LiAlH4; phenyl 2,2‑dichloroacetate is reduced to phenol and 2,2‑dichloroethanol. LiAlH4 delivers hydride to both the carbonyl carbon and the phenoxy oxygen, yielding the two alcohols. Carried out in an aprotic ether solvent (dry diethyl ether or THF) at 0 °C to, under inert atmosphere; reaction quenched cautiously with water or dilute acid.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt formation); sulfuric acid reacts with cobalt(II) oxide to give cobalt(II) sulfate and water. The oxide behaves as a base, accepting protons from the diprotic acid. Usually performed by stirring solid CoO in aqueous H2SO4, heating gently (≤100 °C) to ensure dissolution; water is the reaction medium.

Deprotonation (acid‑base) of the imide NH of phenytoin by sodium hydride, producing the sodium salt of phenytoin and hydrogen gas. Sodium hydride abstracts the acidic hydrogen, forming H2. Conducted in dry, aprotic solvents such as THF or DMF under nitrogen or argon; the mixture is stirred at room temperature or slightly elevated temperature.

Oxidation (combustion) of vanadium nitride; V₄N₄ reacts with O₂ at high temperature (~600‑800 °C) in the gas phase, converting the nitride to vanadium(V) oxide (V₂O₅) while nitrogen is released as N₂; no solvent or catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a primary alkyl halide with silver nitrite; nitrite anion displaces chloride to give benzyl nitrite (alkyl nitrite) and insoluble AgCl precipitates. Typically carried out in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetone or acetonitrile at 0 °C to reflux; silver nitrite is used in excess and the reaction is driven to completion by removal of AgCl.

Acid-catalyzed substitution (hydrohalogenation) of a secondary alcohol with hydrogen chloride; the hydroxyl group is protonated, water leaves to form a carbocation, then chloride attacks to afford 2‑chloro‑4‑methylpentane. Commonly performed with concentrated aqueous HCl (or gaseous HCl) at reflux; sometimes ZnCl₂ (Lucas reagent) is added to accelerate the reaction. No special solvent required beyond the aqueous HCl medium.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction in aqueous solution; potassium hydroxide neutralizes magnesium nitrate, forming potassium nitrate and insoluble magnesium hydroxide which precipitates. Usually carried out at room temperature in water with vigorous stirring; no catalyst is needed.

Halogen exchange (nucleophilic substitution at phosphorus) between phosphorus trichloride and hydrogen iodide; the three chloride ligands are replaced by iodide to give phosphorus triiodide and hydrogen chloride gas. Conducted in anhydrous non‑protic solvent such as dry ether or carbon tetrachloride, often under reflux with an excess of HI; inert atmosphere is used to avoid oxidation.

Free‑radical chlorination of the methyl group attached to silicon; chlorine gas abstracts a hydrogen from the CH₃ group of methyltrichlorosilane, forming trichloro(chloromethyl)silane (Cl₃Si‑CH₂Cl) and hydrogen chloride. Initiated by UV light or a radical initiator (e.g., peroxide) in an inert solvent like carbon tetrachloride or chloroform; reaction performed at ambient or slightly elevated temperature with continuous removal of HCl.

Reduction of an aromatic aldehyde to a primary alcohol using lithium aluminium hydride; LiAlH₄ delivers hydride to the carbonyl carbon of salicylaldehyde, forming the alkoxide which upon work‑up gives salicyl alcohol (2‑hydroxybenzyl alcohol). Reaction is carried out in dry ether (diethyl ether or THF) under nitrogen or argon, typically at 0 °C to reflux, and quenched carefully with water or dilute acid after completion.

Direct combination (synthesis) reaction; elemental chromium is oxidized by chlorine gas to give chromium(III) chloride, used as a pigment, catalyst precursor, or laboratory reagent; performed by passing dry Cl₂ over powdered Cr at 200‑400 °C; product collected as a green solid; gas‑phase, no solvent.

Hydroformylation (oxo process) of a terminal alkene. Purpose: introduce a formyl group and extend the carbon chain by one carbon to afford an aldehyde. Key transformation: 5‑methyl‑1‑hexene reacts with syngas (CO/H₂) to give 6‑methylheptanal via addition of an H–C=O fragment across the terminal double bond. Typical conditions: 80–120 °C, 5–30 atm CO/H₂ (1:1), rhodium catalyst (e.g., HRh(CO)(PPh₃)₃) or cobalt carbonyl with phosphine ligands, in a polar aprotic solvent such as toluene or dioxane. Reaction is usually conducted in a sealed autoclave.

Type: radical bromination (free‑radical substitution). Purpose: halogenate neopentane at a primary carbon. Key transformation: bromine radicals abstract a hydrogen atom from neopentane, forming a carbon radical that recombines with Br· to give 1‑bromo‑2,2‑dimethylpropane and HBr. Typical conditions: UV light or heat, often in an inert solvent such as CCl₄ or carbon tetrachloride; no catalyst needed aside from light.

Acid‑base precipitation and ligand exchange; converts Europium(III) acetylacetonate to insoluble Europium(III) phosphate while freeing acetylacetone; phosphoric acid protonates the acetylacetonate ligands releasing 2,4‑pentanedione and Eu³⁺ complexes with PO₄³⁻ to precipitate EuPO₄; performed in aqueous medium with ammon hydroxide to adjust pH to mildly basic (≈8–9), often refluxed; water is the solvent, no catalyst required.

Demethylation of an aryl methyl ether with boron tribromide (BBr3); purpose is to deprotect the methoxy group to a phenol. Key transformation: cleavage of the C–O bond, delivering catechol (1,2‑dihydroxybenzene) and methyl bromide (CH3Br). Typical conditions: 1–2 equiv BBr3 in dry CH2Cl2, added at –78 °C to 0 °C, then warmed to rt; reaction performed under inert atmosphere (N2) and anhydrous conditions.

Combustion reaction; oxidation of the alkane to carbon dioxide and water; purpose is energy release; occurs via radical chain oxidation when 2,4‑dimethylpentane is exposed to excess oxygen at high temperature (typically >300 °C) with an ignition source; usually carried out in open flame or furnace, no solvent, in air.

Catalytic transesterification; swaps the alkoxy groups of 2‑methylpropyl acetate with methanol to give acetate and 2‑methyl‑1‑propanol; methanol attacks the carbonyl of the ester under acid (e.g., H₂SO₄) or base (e.g., NaOH, KOH) catalysis, displacing the propyl group; carried out with excess methanol at reflux (~65 °C) for several hours; methanol serves as both reactant and solvent; no additional reagents needed.

Dimerization (association) of borane; monomeric BH₃ combines to give diborane (B₂H₆). Occurs spontaneously when BH₃ is generated (e.g., from NaBH₄ + BF₃) in the gas phase or in inert solvents at low temperature (‑78 °C to 0 °C) under anhydrous, inert atmosphere; no catalyst.

Transesterification; purpose is to exchange the alkoxy group of a fluorinated ester. The butyl ester is cleaved and a methyl ester formed while n‑butanol is released. Typically performed under acid catalysis (e.g., catalytic p‑toluenesulfonic acid) at reflux in a high‑boiling solvent such as toluene or with excess methanol; removal of butanol drives the equilibrium.

Oxidation‑reduction (redox) of nitrite by ozone; ozone oxidizes nitrite ion to nitrate ion, releasing molecular oxygen; NO₂⁻ + O₃ → NO₃⁻ + O₂; typically carried out in aqueous solution, often acidic (pH 2–4) and at low temperature (0–5 °C) to control ozone decomposition; water is the solvent, no additional catalyst required.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution (nitration) of phenol; purpose is to introduce a nitro group onto the aromatic ring producing nitrophenol (ortho/para mixture) with loss of water; usually performed with concentrated nitric acid, often mixed with concentrated sulfuric acid as a catalyst, at 0–50 °C in aqueous or mixed solvent; temperature control is essential to avoid over‑nitration.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt metathesis); sodium hydroxide deprotonates spermidine·HCl to liberate free spermidine, forming sodium chloride and water; NaOH + HCl·spermidine → spermidine + NaCl + H₂O; performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stoichiometric NaOH; water is the solvent, no catalyst needed.

Oxidation of a primary alcohol using pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC); purpose is selective conversion of 3‑nitrobenzyl alcohol to the aldehyde without over‑oxidation; key transformation is oxidation of the benzylic CH₂OH to CHO; reaction is carried out in dry CH₂Cl₂ at room temperature under inert atmosphere, often with a stoichiometric amount of PCC; water is the only by‑product.

SN2 alkylation of a primary amine; methyl iodide alkylates 2,2,2‑trifluoroethylamine hydrochloride in the presence of sodium carbonate, which neutralizes the HCl and generates CO₂ and H₂O; the nitrogen attacks CH₃I, displacing I⁻ to give N‑methyl‑2,2,2‑trifluoroethylamine; reaction is run in a mixed solvent (e.g., acetone, ethanol, or water) at room temperature to reflux; by‑products are sodium iodide, carbon dioxide and water; no additional catalyst required.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an alkene; purpose is to reduce the C=C bond to a saturated C–C bond; key transformation is addition of H₂ across the double bond of 1,2‑dichloroethene to give 1,2‑dichloroethane; typical conditions use a heterogeneous metal catalyst (Pd/C, PtO₂, Raney Ni) under H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) at room temperature to 80 °C in a solvent such as ethanol, methanol or ethyl acetate.

Acid‑base reaction (carbonate neutralization). Boric acid protonates the carbonate of barium carbonate, releasing CO₂ and forming barium metaborate and water; usually performed in aqueous solution with gentle heating to drive off CO₂, no catalyst required.

Nucleophilic addition/reduction; NaBH4 reduces the ketone carbonyl of 3‑methyl‑2‑butanone to the secondary alcohol 3‑methyl‑2‑butanol. Typical conditions: protic polar solvent such as methanol or ethanol (or THF), 0 °C to room temperature, aqueous work‑up to quench excess borohydride.

Acid–base neutralization/precipitation; phosphoric acid reacts with FeO (iron(II) oxide) to form iron(II) phosphate and water. Usually carried out in aqueous solution with stirring and gentle heating; the insoluble Fe(II) phosphate precipitates and is isolated by filtration. No special catalyst required.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (acid‑chloride esterification). Ethanol attacks the carbonyl of but‑2‑ynoyl chloride, displacing chloride to give ethyl but‑2‑ynoate; HCl is generated and typically trapped by a base such as pyridine or triethylamine. Common conditions: anhydrous dichloromethane, 0 °C to room temperature, inert atmosphere.

Acid‑catalyzed acetal formation (protecting‑group synthesis); ethylene glycol condenses with acetaldehyde in the presence of the acidic clay Montmorillonite K10 to give 2‑methyl‑1,3‑dioxolane and water. Typical conditions: reflux in an inert organic solvent (toluene or dichloromethane) with removal of water (e.g., Dean–Stark trap) or azeotropic distillation; catalytic amount of the clay, dry atmosphere.

Radical oxidative coupling (disulfide formation) via chlorination; 2‑butyl mercaptan reacts with Cl₂ to generate dibutyl disulfide and two equivalents of HCl. Conducted in an aprotic solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; Cl₂ is added slowly to control radical formation. No additional catalyst required.

Double displacement/precipitation reaction in aqueous solution. Mercurous chloride reacts with potassium iodide to exchange halide ions, forming insoluble mercurous iodide precipitate and soluble potassium chloride. Typically carried out at room temperature in water; no catalyst required.

Oxidation of phenol to quinone; catechol is oxidized by potassium dichromate in concentrated H₂SO₄, yielding o‑benzoquinone, water, and Cr³⁺ as chromium(III) sulfate. Conditions: aqueous sulfuric acid medium, temperature 60–100 °C, stoichiometric dichromate, vigorous stirring. The reaction proceeds via reduction of Cr(VI) to Cr(III).

Jones oxidation (chromic acid oxidation) of primary alcohol to carboxylic acid; tetrahydropyran‑2‑methanol is oxidized by chromic acid (generated from Na₂Cr₂O₇/H₂SO₄) to tetrahydropyran‑2‑carboxylic acid. Typical procedure: Jones reagent in acetone, added at 0 °C then warmed to room temperature; aqueous work‑up quenches excess oxidant.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an aromatic ring; purpose is to saturate the benzene core while retaining bromine substituents; key transformation is reduction of three C=C bonds of 1,4‑dibromobenzene to give 1,4‑dibromocyclohexane; typically performed under elevated H₂ pressure (50–100 atm) with Pd/C as catalyst in a protic solvent such as ethanol or methanol at 25–80 °C.

Metathesis/precipitation double‑replacement reaction; purpose is to prepare cobalt(II) stearate (a metal soap) and soluble sodium sulfate; key transformation is exchange of cations between CoSO₄ and Na‑stearate yielding insoluble cobalt stearate precipitate; carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with vigorous stirring; no special solvent beyond water is required.

SN2 alkylation (nucleophilic substitution); piperidine displaces bromide of 4‑bromo‑2‑butanone to afford 4‑piperidin‑1‑ylbutan‑2‑one; the reaction proceeds in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or acetonitrile at reflux, often with a mild inorganic base (e.g., K₂CO₃) to capture the generated HBr.

Palladium‑catalyzed allylic substitution (Tsuji–Trost allylation); purpose is carbon‑carbon bond formation to give dimethyl 2‑allylmalonate; key transformation is attack of the dimethyl malonate enolate on the π‑allyl‑Pd complex generated from allyl acetate, releasing acetate which is protonated to acetic acid; typical conditions use 5 mol % Pd(0) (e.g., Pd(PPh₃)₄), a base such as NaH or NaOEt, THF or DMF as solvent, and temperature from 0 °C to reflux under inert atmosphere.

Nitrosation of a secondary urea; purpose is synthesis of the N‑nitroso‑N‑propylurea class of nitrosoureas; key transformation is conversion of the N‑H of N‑propylurea to an N‑N=O group by electrophilic attack of nitrous acid; performed in aqueous acidic medium generated in situ from NaNO₂ and HCl at 0–5 °C to control side reactions; product is isolated after work‑up; no additional catalyst is required.

Conversion of a carboxylic acid to an acyl bromide using phosphorus pentabromide; purpose is to generate acetyl bromide for subsequent acylation steps; key transformation is substitution of the hydroxyl of acetic acid by bromine, producing acetyl bromide, hydrogen bromide, and phosphorus oxybromide as by‑products; typically carried out by adding PBr₅ to acetic acid in anhydrous dichloromethane or pyridine at 0 °C to reflux, under nitrogen; the reaction mixture is often quenched with a base to absorb released HBr.

Thermal decomposition (redox) of calcium bromate; purpose is to obtain calcium bromide and release oxygen gas; key transformation is reduction of bromate (BrO₃⁻) to bromide (Br⁻) with concomitant evolution of O₂; accomplished by heating the solid calcium bromate strongly (generally >300 °C) in a furnace or tube; no solvent or catalyst is required.

Hydrolysis (deprotection) of a trimethylsilyl ester; water cleaves the Si‑O bond to regenerate benzoic acid and produce trimethylsilanol. Usually performed at ambient temperature in a mixture of water with a miscible organic solvent (THF, acetone, or MeCN); may be buffered to neutral pH to avoid side reactions.

Base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification); purpose is to cleave methyl trifluoroacetate into methanol and the trifluoroacetate anion. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of OH⁻ on the carbonyl carbon, producing sodium trifluoroacetate and methanol. Usually performed in aqueous NaOH, often heated to reflux; water is the solvent and excess NaOH drives the reaction.

Gas‑phase synthesis of boron nitride; a high‑temperature nitridation/dehydrogenation where diborane reacts with ammonia to form solid BN and release H₂. Typically carried out at 800–1000 °C in an inert or flow reactor; no solvent, no catalyst required.

Acid‑ or base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis; methyl levulinate is cleaved by water to give levulinic acid and methanol. Performed in aqueous medium (often with excess H₂SO₄ or NaOH) under reflux (≈80–120 °C). Reaction is homogeneous; water is the solvent.

Formation of a hydrazide by nucleophilic addition of hydrazine to maleic anhydride; produces maleic hydrazide with concomitant release of water and sulfuric acid from the hydrazine sulfate salt. Conducted in aqueous solution at reflux temperature (≈80–100 °C); no additional catalyst needed.

Jones oxidation of a secondary alcohol; potassium dichromate in dilute sulfuric acid oxidizes 4‑heptanol to 4‑heptanone, reducing Cr(VI) to Cr(III) sulfate and generating water. Usually run in a mixture of water and acetone (or acetic acid) at 0–25 °C then warmed; the dichromate/H₂SO₄ mixture acts as the oxidant.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation; aqueous sodium carbonate reacts with lead selenate, precipitating sparingly soluble lead carbonate and forming soluble sodium selenate. Performed at ambient temperature in water with stirring; no catalyst required.

Halogen exchange (SN2) fluorination; benzyl chloride reacts with hydrogen fluoride to substitute Cl with F, yielding benzyl fluoride and HCl. Conducted in anhydrous HF or HF‑pyridine complex, often at 0–25 °C in aprotic solvents such as acetonitrile; superacid additives (e.g., SbF₅) can be used to enhance reactivity.

Acid‑base deprotonation (metalation). n‑Butyllithium abstracts the acidic proton of tert‑butanol, generating lithium tert‑butoxide as a strong, non‑nucleophilic base and releasing butane gas as the conjugate acid of the butyl anion. Typical conditions are anhydrous, inert atmosphere (argon or nitrogen) at –78 °C to 0 °C in a dry ethereal solvent such as tetrahydrofuran (THF) or diethyl ether. No additional catalyst is required.

O‑methylation (Williamson‑type ether synthesis). Dimethyl sulfate acts as a methylating agent; in the presence of solid potassium carbonate as a base, the phenolic hydrogen of 4‑allylphenol is removed, allowing the phenoxide to attack a methyl group of dimethyl sulfate, forming estragole (4‑allyl anisole). The reaction is usually carried out under reflux in polar aprotic solvents such as acetone or dimethylformamide (DMF) with vigorous stirring; the by‑product is potassium hydrogen sulfate (KHSO₄). No transition‑metal catalyst is needed.

Hydrolysis of a silyl fluoride; purpose is to convert a trimethylfluorosilane into the corresponding silanol while liberating HF; the Si‑F bond is cleaved by water to give trimethylsilanol and hydrofluoric acid; typically carried out at ambient temperature or mild heating in aqueous medium; no special catalyst required, water itself is the solvent.

Oxidation of potassium hydrogen selenite (Se(IV)) by hydrogen peroxide in aqueous medium (neutral to slightly acidic) at 0‑25 °C, converting it to potassium selenate (Se(VI)) with water as the only by‑product.

Carbamate formation (urethanation). The phenolic oxygen of 2‑isopropylphenol adds to the electrophilic carbon of methyl isocyanate, producing the O‑aryl carbamate known as Isoprocarb (methyl N‑(2‑isopropylphenyl)carbamate). The reaction proceeds under mild conditions (0 °C to ambient temperature) in anhydrous organic solvents such as dichloromethane or toluene, often in the presence of a weak base or catalyst (e.g., pyridine) to neutralize the formed acid. No metal catalyst is required.

Dehydrative condensation of trimethylsilanol to form hexamethyldisiloxane and water. A silanol self‑condensation reaction, usually driven by removal of water (azeotropic distillation) and may be accelerated by acid or base catalysts. Conducted in an inert solvent like toluene at reflux.

Oxymercuration‑hydration (Markovnikov addition of water). Mercuric acetate (Hg(OAc)₂) adds across the C=C bond of tridec‑1‑ene to give an organomercury intermediate; subsequent hydrolysis with water installs a hydroxyl group at the more substituted carbon, yielding 2‑hydroxytridecane. The reaction is typically performed in a mixture of TH acetone and water at 0 °C to room temperature, followed by reduction or aqueous work‑up to remove mercuric residues (often with NaBH₄ or Na₂S). No additional catalyst is needed beyond Hg(OAc)₂.

Oxidation of 2‑methylbenzaldehyde to 2‑methylbenzoic acid – potassium permanganate in aqueous alkaline solution (pH ≈ 13) oxidizes the aldehyde to the corresponding carboxylic acid; reaction performed at reflux in water, followed by acidification to isolate the acid.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration of a β‑hydroxy ketone; 4‑hydroxy‑4‑methyl‑2‑pentanone loses water under heating with a mineral acid (e.g., H₂SO₄) or solid acid catalyst to form the α,β‑unsaturated ketone 4‑methyl‑3‑penten‑2‑one (mesityl oxide). Typical conditions: 80–120 °C, dilute acid, often in toluene or a non‑polar solvent to remove water azeotropically.

Double‑displacement precipitation (metathesis). Sodium carbonate reacts with strontium iodide in aqueous solution, exchanging anions and cations to form soluble sodium iodide and insoluble strontium carbonate, which precipitates out. The reaction is carried out at ambient temperature with stirring in water; the solid SrCO₃ is collected by filtration. No catalyst is required.

Redox oxidation‑reduction solid‑state reaction; elemental oxygen oxidizes cobalt(II) iodide to cobalt(II) oxide while iodine is liberated; typically carried out by heating a mixture of CoI2 and O2 at elevated temperature (200–400 °C) in a furnace, often in the gas phase or in a sealed tube; no solvent, sometimes a catalyst such as a small amount of metal oxide is used to promote oxygen transfer.

Oxidation; converts a thioether to a sulfoxide using Oxone (potassium peroxymonosulfate) as the oxidant; adds one oxygen atom to sulfur, forming di‑n‑propyl sulfoxide and water, with potassium bisulfate as by‑product; typically performed in a mixed aqueous/organic medium (e.g., water/acetone) at 0 °C to room temperature, no additional catalyst required.

Carboxylation of a Grignard reagent (CO₂ addition); purpose is to synthesize 3‑phenylpropionic acid; key transformation is nucleophilic attack of the organomagnesium on CO₂ forming a magnesium carboxylate, which upon acidic work‑up yields the free acid and MgBr₂; typical conditions involve bubbling CO₂ through the dry THF solution of the Grignard at 0 °C to –20 °C, followed by quench with dilute HCl or NH₄Cl; no catalyst.

Ammonolysis of scandium chloride; gaseous NH3 reacts with ScCl3 at high temperature (≈800–1000 °C) in a flow reactor, replacing chloride with nitride to form scandium nitride (ScN) and evolving hydrogen chloride gas; solid‑state metathesis, no solvent, purpose is synthesis of ScN from the chloride precursor.

Steam hydrolysis (oxidative hydrolysis) of tantalum nitride; yields tantalum pentoxide and ammonia. Nitride is oxidized by water vapor, forming Ta–O bonds and liberating NH₃. Performed at 800‑1000 °C in a flowing steam atmosphere; solid‑state reaction, no solvent or catalyst required.

Aqueous double‑displacement/precipitation reaction forming basic lead carbonate (white‑lead) from lead nitrate, sodium carbonate and ammonium hydroxide; solutions are mixed at ambient to 50 °C, pH adjusted with NH₄OH to keep lead species alkaline, causing precipitation of PbCO₃·Pb(OH)₂ while NaNO₃ and NH₄NO₃ remain in solution; water is the solvent; no catalyst; used for pigment preparation.

Salt metathesis (acid–base double displacement); reacts phosphoric acid with scandium trichloride to precipitate scandium phosphate while generating three equivalents of hydrochloric acid; carried out in aqueous solution, often with gentle heating to promote HCl evolution and precipitation of ScPO₄.

Decarboxylation of an α‑keto acid to an aldehyde; indole‑3‑pyruvic acid loses CO₂ to give indole‑3‑acetaldehyde; commonly achieved enzymatically by indole‑3‑pyruvate decarboxylase (pyridoxal‑phosphate cofactor) in aqueous buffer (pH 6‑7) at 30‑40 °C, or chemically with mild oxidants/mediators under an inert atmosphere.

Salt metathesis (acid–base precipitation); phosphoric acid reacts with yttrium(III) acetate hydrate to form solid yttrium(III) phosphate and release three equivalents of acetic acid and one molecule of water; performed in aqueous medium, often with heating to concentrate and isolate the insoluble YPO₄ precipitate.

Transesterification; replaces the butyl alkoxy group with an ethyl group to give the ethyl 2,2‑difluoroacetate. Conducted under acid (or sometimes base) catalysis, refluxing with excess ethanol in a solvent like toluene or directly under solvent‑free conditions; the reaction is driven to completion by removal of n‑butanol.

Base hydrolysis of a carbamoyl chloride; a nucleophilic substitution that converts N‑methylcarbamoyl chloride to methyl isocyanate. Sodium hydroxide aqueous solution (0‑5 °C, then allowed to warm) replaces the chloride with hydroxide, which eliminates HCl and gives the isocyanate, with NaCl and water as by‑products. No catalyst required; water or a water‑mixed organic solvent (e.g., THF) is used.

Acid‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis; aqueous hydrochloric acid hydrolyzes the ethyl ester of 2‑amino‑5‑carbamimidamidopentanoate to afford L‑arginine (as its HCl salt) and ethanol; typically refluxed in dilute HCl (1–3 M) for several hours at 80‑100 °C, followed by neutralization or crystallization of the amino acid.

Electrophilic addition (Markovnikov) of hydrogen chloride to isobutylene, forming tert‑butyl chloride; proceeds in anhydrous ether or dichloromethane at 0‑25 °C, often catalyzed by ZnCl₂ (Lucas reagent); key step is formation of a tertiary carbocation that captures Cl⁻.

Nucleophilic aromatic substitution (SNAr); sodium phenoxide displaces chlorine on the 3‑position of 3‑chloropyridine to give 3‑phenoxypyridine and sodium chloride; carried out in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO at 80‑120 °C, often with excess phenoxide to drive the reaction.

Acid–base neutralization; purpose is to convert picric acid into its water‑soluble potassium salt; key transformation is transfer of the phenolic proton to acetate, producing acetic acid and potassium 2,4,6‑trinitrophenolate; typically performed in aqueous or mixed water/ethanol at ambient temperature; no catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (acidic saponification); butyl formate is hydrolyzed with water and sulfuric acid to regenerate formic acid and n‑butanol; reflux in aqueous acid, often with excess water, furnishes the products.

Quaternization (SN2 alkylation) of a tertiary amine; purpose is to prepare a benzyl‑triethylammonium salt; key transformation is nucleophilic attack of triethylamine on benzyl chloride forming N‑benzyltriethylammonium chloride; usually carried out in an aprotic solvent such as acetone or dichloromethane at room temperature or gentle reflux; triethylamine acts as nucleophile and base, no external catalyst.

Base‑catalyzed ester saponification; purpose is to generate the sodium salt of p‑hydroxybenzoic acid; key transformation is nucleophilic attack of ethoxide on the ethylparaben carbonyl, yielding ethanol and sodium p‑hydroxybenzoate; performed by heating ethylparaben with sodium ethoxide in ethanol (or methanol) under reflux; no additional catalyst needed.

Acid–base metathesis (halide exchange); purpose is to produce hydrobromic acid and a quaternary‑ammonium hydrogen sulfate; key transformation is proton transfer from sulfuric acid to tetrabutylammonium bromide forming HBr and tetrabutylammonium hydrogen sulfate; typically done in aqueous solution at 0–25 °C to avoid decomposition; no catalyst required.

Type: redox displacement (metallothermic reduction). Purpose: reduce vanadium trichloride to metallic vanadium, producing sodium chloride as by‑product. Key transformation: Na⁰ reduces VCl₃ to V⁰, forming NaCl. Typical conditions: high temperature (≈500–700 °C) in a sealed vessel, inert atmosphere; often performed in a molten NaCl flux.

Double‑displacement precipitation; purpose is to isolate nickel(II) chromate; key transformation is exchange anions producing insoluble nickel(II) chromate and soluble potassium chloride; conducted in aqueous solution with both salts dissolved, often at room temperature; stirring aids precipitation; no catalyst.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction); benzaldehyde is reduced to benzyl alcohol by addition of H2 across the C=O bond. Conducted with palladium on carbon (5–10 % Pd) under H2 gas (1–3 atm) in an aprotic solvent such as ethanol, methanol or ethyl acetate at ambient or slightly elevated temperature (25–50 °C). No other reagents required.

Double‑displacement precipitation; purpose is to obtain insoluble barium sulfate and soluble ammonium acetate; key transformation is exchange of acetate and sulfate ions yielding barium sulfate precipitate and ammonium acetate in solution; performed in aqueous medium at ambient temperature; filtration isolates BaSO₄; no catalyst.

SN2 alkylation of ethanolamine with n‑butyl iodide; the amine nitrogen attacks the primary alkyl halide to give N‑butylethanolamine and HI; typically run in a polar aprotic solvent (DMF or DMSO) at 0–80 °C with a base such as K₂CO₃ to scavenge the acid.

Hydrolysis (reverse of amide formation): N‑hydroxyformamide is treated with water, often with mild heating, to cleave the N‑formyl bond, regenerating formic acid and hydroxylamine; illustrates hydrolytic cleavage of an N‑acylhydroxylamine.

Oxidative over‑oxidation of a disulfide to a sulfone. Diphenyl disulfide reacts with excess hydrogen peroxide (often in the presence of a base such as NaOH or Na₂CO₃) to afford diphenyl sulfone (PhSO₂Ph) and water. Typical conditions are aqueous or mixed aqueous‑organic solvent (e.g., MeOH/H₂O) at 40–80 °C; the reaction may be accelerated by a catalytic amount of transition‑metal ions (e.g., Mo or W catalysts) but proceed uncatalyzed with strong peroxide excess.

Acid‑base neutralization; the strong acid protonates the citrate anion of potassium citrate, converting it to citric acid while exchanging potassium for chloride to give potassium chloride. Usually performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; water serves as the solvent.

Hydrolysis/neutralization; boron tribromide reacts with hydroxide ions, where bromide is displaced and water adds to generate boric acid (B(OH)3) and sodium bromide. Conducted in aqueous or water‑alcohol medium, with the addition of BBr3 done slowly and often under cooling because it reacts vigorously with water.

Acid‑base carbonation; selenic acid (H2SeO4) neutralizes potassium carbonate, producing potassium selenate (K2SeO4), water and carbon dioxide gas. Performed in aqueous solution; gentle heating may be applied to release CO2.

Catalytic dehydrogenation; cycloundecane is converted to cycloundecene with liberation of hydrogen gas, an oxidative dehydrogenation. Requires high temperature (300–500 °C) and a metal catalyst such as Pt, Pd, or Ni on a support, under an inert or slight hydrogen‑acceptor atmosphere; the substrate is typically introduced as a liquid or vapor.

Nucleophilic substitution (amine alkylation); methylamine attacks the allylic carbon of cinnamyl bromide, displacing bromide to form the secondary amine (cinnamedrine) and hydrogen bromide. Carried out in an aprotic solvent such as ethanol or THF at 0–25 °C; a base (e.g., NaHCO3) is often added to neutralize the generated HBr.

Metathesis/complexation; chloride ligands from gold(III) chloride exchange with sodium ions from NaCl, yielding the soluble tetrachloroaurate(III) anion paired with Na+ (Na[AuCl4]). Conducted in aqueous HCl or concentrated HCl solution to maintain AuCl4⁻ stability, typically at room temperature with stirring.

Acid‑base protonation (salt metathesis) of sodium 2‑aminoacetate: treatment with aqueous hydrochloric acid protonates both the amino and carboxylate groups, regenerating glycine (NH₂CH₂COOH) and generating NaCl as a by‑product. Performed in water at 0 – 25 °C, often with excess HCl to drive the reaction to completion.

Acid‑catalyzed redox reaction; hydrogen peroxide reduces perchlorate derived from potassium perchlorate in sulfuric acid, producing water, molecular oxygen, and chloride ion (as potassium chloride); conducted in aqueous solution under acidic conditions, usually at 0–25 °C to control vigorous gas evolution; dilute or concentrated H2SO4 can be used, with water as the solvent; no additional catalyst required.

N‑methylation of p‑chloroamphetamine by methyl iodide (SN2 alkylation) in the presence of sodium carbonate as base; yields p‑chloromethamphetamine and NaI as by‑product. Conducted in an aprotic polar solvent such as DMF or acetonitrile, with Na₂CO₃ (2 equiv) and MeI (1.2 equiv) at 0 °C to 50 °C for several hours; the mixture is then worked up and purified, often by extraction and chromatography.

Oxidation (dehydrogenation) of allyl alcohol to the α,β‑unsaturated aldehyde acrolein using cerium(IV) sulfate as the oxidant; performed in aqueous acidic medium (often dilute sulfuric acid), temperatures 0‑25 °C to minimize polymerization, water as solvent, cerium(IV) acts as the oxidizing catalyst.

Kumada‑type cross‑coupling (alkyl‑alkyl coupling) between methylmagnesium bromide and ethyl iodoacetate catalyzed by copper(I) iodide, yielding ethyl propionate and magnesium bromide; conducted in anhydrous ether solvent (THF or diethyl ether) under inert atmosphere, typically 0‑25 °C, CuI serves as the catalytic mediator.

Base‑induced hydrolysis/decomposition of sodium borohydride by sodium hydroxide, producing hydrogen gas and sodium metaborate; carried out in aqueous solution at room temperature or with mild heating, no special catalyst required.
NaBH₄ reduction of a ketone; 3‑phenylbutan‑2‑one is treated with NaBH₄ in methanol or ethanol at 0 °C to rt, affording the secondary alcohol 3‑phenylbutan‑2‑ol.

Condensation of benzaldehyde with phenylhydrazine to form a phenylhydrazone followed by oxidative dimerization with sodium hypochlorite, giving 1,5‑diphenylcarbazone; performed in aqueous (often buffered) medium containing bleach, pH mildly basic, temperature 0‑25 °C, water/ethanol as solvent, NaOCl acts as the oxidant.

Nucleophilic substitution (alkylation) of ethylenediamine by 2‑chloroethylamine hydrochloride to afford diethylenetriamine with release of two equivalents of hydrogen chloride; typically heated in an excess of ethylenediamine or in an alcoholic solvent, optionally with a base to scavenge HCl, temperatures 50‑100 °C.

Free‑radical halogenation (photochemical substitution). UV light activates Br₂ to generate bromine radicals that abstract a hydrogen from the α‑carbon of diethyl ether, followed by radical recombination to give 2‑bromo‑ethyl ethyl ether and HBr. Typically performed in an inert, non‑protic solvent (e.g., carbon tetrachloride or chloroform) under UV irradiation; no additional catalyst is required.

Enzymatic aromatization (biotransformation). Androstenedione is converted to estrone by the cytochrome P450 aromatase (CYP19) which oxidatively aromatizes the A‑ring and removes the C‑19 methyl as formic acid, yielding the phenolic estrone. The reaction occurs under physiological pH (≈7.4) at 37 °C in the presence of NADPH and molecular oxygen; no synthetic reagents are needed.

Lewis‑acid‑catalyzed intramolecular electrophilic aromatic cyclization (Friedel‑Crafts‑type). Aluminum chloride coordinates to the ether oxygen of diphenyl ether, increasing its electrophilicity and promoting attack of one phenyl ring onto the ortho‑position of the other. This cyclization forms the heterocyclic dibenzofuran framework with loss of HCl. Conducted in dry dichloromethane or carbon disulfide at 0 °C to reflux; stoichiometric AlCl₃ is used as the catalyst.

Nucleophilic alkylation of a nucleobase (SN2). The O⁶ atom of guanine acts as a nucleophile toward methyl iodide, displacing iodide to afford O⁶‑methylguanine and H⁺ (which combines with I⁻ to give HI). The reaction is usually carried out in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO, at room temperature or mild heating, often under inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of an alkyl halide. Sodium methanesulfonate provides the methanesulfonate anion, which attacks ethyl bromide to produce ethyl methanesulfonate and NaBr. The transformation is performed in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., DMF, DMSO, or acetonitrile) at 50–80 °C to ensure complete conversion; no additional catalyst is required.

Hydrolysis (ring opening) of a cyclic anhydride to the corresponding dicarboxylic acid; purpose is to revert maleic anhydride to maleic acid. Key transformation: addition of water across the anhydride carbonyls, yielding two carboxyl groups. Typical conditions: aqueous medium (often with a small amount of acid or base to catalyze), mild heating (50–80 °C); solvent can be water alone or water/acetone.

Carbodiimide‑mediated esterification (condensation coupling). N,N‑Diisopropylcarbodiimide activates the carboxyl group of cinnamic acid to form an O‑acylisourea intermediate, which is converted to a more reactive ester by 1‑hydroxybenzotriazole (HOBt). Benzyl alcohol then attacks, yielding benzyl cinnamate and releasing urea by‑product. Conducted in anhydrous dichloromethane or DMF at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen; stoichiometric DIC and catalytic HOBt are employed.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) hydrolysis of an alkyl triflate. Water attacks the electrophilic carbon of ethyl trifluoromethanesulfonate, displacing the triflate anion to give ethanol and trifluoromethanesulfonic acid. Typically performed in a biphasic water/acetone mixture at ambient or mild heating; no catalyst required.
