Oxidation of an aldehyde to a carboxylic acid using sodium hypochlorite (bleach). The aldehyde carbon is converted to a carboxyl group while NaOCl is reduced to chloride. Conducted in aqueous NaOCl solution, often buffered to pH ≈ 8–9, at 0 °C to room temperature; no metal catalyst needed.

Partial oxidation (combustion) of acetylene to carbon monoxide and water. Three equivalents of O₂ react with two equivalents of acetylene under high‑temperature flame conditions, producing CO and H₂O as the major gaseous products. Requires a combustion torch or furnace; no solvent or catalyst is employed.

Catalytic dehydrogenation of tetrahydrofuran. THF loses molecular hydrogen to form 2,5‑dihydrofuran. Typically carried out at 300–400 °C over a metal catalyst such as palladium, platinum, or Raney nickel on an inert support, under an inert gas flow; hydrogen is collected as a by‑product.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis of a phenylhydrazone. Aqueous hydrochloric acid protonates the C=N bond of benzaldehyde phenylhydrazone, enabling water to attack and cleave the C‑N bond, regenerating benzaldehyde and releasing phenylhydrazine. Reaction performed under reflux in dilute HCl solution; no additional catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed transesterification; similar to reaction 0 but using ethanol, producing phenethyl alcohol and ethyl acetate; performed in excess ethanol with a catalytic amount of a mineral or organic acid (H₂SO₄, HCl, p‑TsOH) under reflux; ethanol serves as both reagent and solvent.
Acid‑base neutralization; proton transfer from valeric acid to aqueous ammonia forms ammonium valerate and water; performed at ambient temperature in water; no catalyst required.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt formation). Hydrochloric acid protonates the hydroxide of choline, yielding water and the ionic salt choline chloride. Conducted in aqueous solution at room temperature; straightforward stoichiometric neutralization.

Acid‑base neutralization (protonation of an organolithium). Used to quench a lithium 2‑pyridylide and regenerate neutral pyridine while forming LiOH. Key transformation: Li‑C bond is protonated, yielding pyridine and lithium hydroxide. Typically performed as an aqueous work‑up after lithiation, often in THF or ether; water is added at 0 °C to –20 °C to avoid side reactions. No catalyst required.

Nitrite ester formation (in‑situ generation of nitrous acid). HCl protonates NaNO₂ to give HNO₂, which reacts with tert‑butanol to produce tert‑butyl nitrite (R‑ONO) and water; NaCl is a by‑product. Conducted at 0–5 °C in a mixed aqueous/organic medium (e.g., water/acetone) to control acid strength and minimize decomposition. No additional catalyst.

Metathesis/precipitation (acid‑base double displacement). Strong sulfuric acid displaces the weaker sulfurous acid from lead(II) sulfite, yielding soluble lead(II) sulfate (often precipitates) and sulfurous acid in solution. Carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring. No catalyst; the reaction proceeds spontaneously.

Double‑replacement precipitation (metathesis). Copper(II) sulfate exchanges anions with sodium molybdate to give insoluble copper(II) molybdate (CuMoO₄) as a precipitate and soluble sodium sulfate. Performed in water at room temperature or with gentle heating to improve solubility. No catalyst needed.

Oxidative acid digestion of a mixed metal oxide; concentrated nitric acid oxidizes zinc chromite (ZnCr2O4) to soluble zinc nitrate and chromium(III) nitrate while generating water; performed by refluxing the solid with hot, concentrated HNO3 (≈ 68 %) for several hours; typically carried out in glassware with stirring; no extra solvent beyond the acid, and the reaction is driven by the strong oxidizing power of nitrate.

Fischer esterification (acid‑catalyzed ester formation). Acetic acid reacts with dodecanol to form dodecyl acetate and water. Typically catalyzed by a strong acid such as sulfuric acid or p‑toluenesulfonic acid, refluxed in an inert solvent (toluene, xylene) or the alcohol itself; removal of water (e.g., azeotropic distillation) drives the equilibrium to the ester. No special reagents beyond the acid catalyst.

Redox halogen exchange (direct fluorination) reaction; elemental fluorine oxidizes chloride in mercury(II) chloride to chlorine gas while forming mercury(II) fluoride; conducted in a fluorination apparatus using fluorine gas, usually at low temperature (−78 °C to 0 °C) in an inert fluorinated solvent such as perfluorohexane or in the gas phase; no additional catalyst.

Esterification of an acid chloride with methanol; nucleophilic acyl substitution producing methyl 4‑bromobutyrate and HCl. Typically carried out in an aprotic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) at 0 °C to room temperature with a base such as pyridine or triethylamine to trap the liberated HCl.

Acid‑catalyzed ether cleavage to generate chloromethyl methyl ether; dimethoxymethane reacts with dry HCl gas, producing ClCH₂OCH₃ and methanol; performed in dry ether or dichloromethane at 0–25 °C, often with a Lewis acid (e.g., ZnCl₂) to enhance rate.

Reductive deoxygenation of N,N‑diethylhydroxylamine to N,N‑diethylamine using zinc metal and hydrochloric acid; purpose is preparation of the secondary amine from its hydroxylamine; key transformation is reduction of the N–O bond with concomitant formation of ZnCl₂ and water; typical conditions: zinc dust added to a cold 1–3 M HCl solution of the hydroxylamine, then the mixture is warmed to reflux; solvent is aqueous HCl.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (amide formation); trichloroacetyl chloride reacts with dimethylamine to afford 2,2,2‑trichloro‑N,N‑dimethylacetamide and HCl; carried out at 0 °C to rt in a non‑protic solvent such as CH₂Cl₂ or THF, using a base (pyridine or triethylamine) to scavenge the generated HCl.

Aqueous co‑precipitation/redox reaction forming magnetite (Fe3O4). Fe(III) is partially reduced by Fe(II) in alkaline solution, yielding Fe3O4 solid, NaCl and Na2SO4. Conducted in water with excess NaOH, heated to 80–90 °C, pH around 10, often under inert atmosphere; product is collected by magnetic separation.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution (ammonolysis); purpose: synthesize primary amine from alkyl iodide; key transformation: C–I replaced by C–NH2; typical conditions: excess aqueous NH3, heat (reflux); common solvent: water/ethanol.

Double‑displacement metathesis in water; silver nitrate reacts with calcium chromate to precipitate insoluble red silver chromate (Ag2CrO4) and form soluble calcium nitrate. Performed at ambient temperature in aqueous solution; the precipitate is filtered and washed.

nucleophilic substitution (sn2), purpose alkyl amine synthesis, transformation bromide replaced by ammonia-derived amine group. occurs in presence of excess ammonia, typically in ethanol or water under heat with sealed tube conditions to prevent ammonia evaporation.

Molten‑salt double‑displacement (metathesis); CuCl₂ reacts with NaNO₃ in the molten state to exchange anions, yielding Cu(NO₃)₂ and NaCl; performed at temperatures sufficient to melt the nitrate (≈250–300 °C) in a dry inert atmosphere, no additional solvent is required.

Catalytic reductive amination to synthesize trimetazidine. Piperazine condenses with 2,3,4‑trimethoxybenzaldehyde forming an imine, which is hydrogenated over Raney nickel under H2 pressure (1–5 atm) in an alcoholic solvent (e.g., ethanol) at 50–80 °C, yielding trimetazidine and water.

Electrophilic sulfonation of camphor using fuming sulfuric acid and sulfur trioxide. The reaction introduces a sulfonic acid group at the 10‑position, producing dl‑10‑camphorsulfonic acid with water as by‑product. Conducted at 0–25 °C in the concentrated acid mixture, often under nitrogen; the product is isolated by crystallization from the reaction mixture.

Redox (oxygen transfer) reaction: m‑chloroperbenzoic acid oxidizes trimethylphosphine sulfide to trimethylphosphine oxide while being reduced to m‑chlorobenzoic acid; elemental sulfur precipitates. Typically carried out in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; no catalyst required.

Base‑catalyzed ring‑opening etherification; ethylene oxide opens at the terminal alkoxy oxygen of diethylene glycol dimethyl ether, extending the chain to give triethylene glycol dimethyl ether; common conditions employ a mild base such as KOH or NaOH (0.1–1 mol % relative to substrate) at 80–120 °C, the product often serves as both reactant and solvent.

Acid–base metathesis (double displacement): sulfuric acid protonates the phosphate in tin(II) phosphate, exchanging anions to afford phosphoric acid and tin(II) sulfate. Performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; stirring until complete dissolution; no special catalyst needed.

Fischer esterification: gallic acid reacts with 1‑octanol in the presence of catalytic sulfuric acid to form octyl gallate (the octyl ester) and water. Carried out under reflux (≈120 °C) with excess octanol acting as solvent; water is removed azeotropically (e.g., Dean–Stark) to drive equilibrium toward ester formation.

High‑temperature redox (metal displacement): metallic calcium reduces nickel(II) fluoride, producing elemental nickel and calcium fluoride. Conducted as a solid‑state reaction in a sealed tube or furnace at 600–800 °C under inert atmosphere (argon); no solvent or catalyst required.

Gas‑solid redox synthesis of a chalcogenide: hydrogen selenide gas reduces tin(IV) oxide to tin(IV) selenide, generating water as the by‑product. Typically performed in a quartz tube at 300–600 °C under flowing H₂Se (or in sealed ampoule) with an inert carrier gas; no additional catalyst needed.

Thermal or reductive decomposition of tetramethylstibonium iodide back to trimethylstibine and methyl iodide; the quaternary stibonium salt dissociates upon heating, releasing MeI and regenerating the trivalent antimony species. Performed by gentle reflux in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., acetonitrile) or under vacuum; no catalyst required.

Reduction of a sulfonyl chloride to a thiol using lithium aluminium hydride; converts the S(VI) sulfonyl chloride functional group to an S(II) thiol, cleaving the S–Cl bond and forming a S–H bond. Typically performed in dry ether or THF under inert atmosphere at 0 °C to reflux; LiAlH₄ is the reagent, no additional catalyst needed.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a primary alkyl bromide by hydrosulfide ion; replaces the bromide with a thiolate to give a primary thiol and sodium bromide. Usually carried out in aqueous or ethanolic NaSH solution, heated under reflux; no catalyst required.

Thermal decomposition (acid‑base salt dissociation) of ethylammonium acetate; the ammonium cation donates a proton to the acetate anion, liberating volatile ethylamine and acetic acid. Conducted by gentle heating or vacuum distillation; no catalyst or solvent is essential.

Palladium(II)-catalyzed oxidative dehydrogenation of allyl alcohol to acrolein; O₂ serves as the terminal oxidant while Pd(OAc)₂ mediates the removal of two hydrogen atoms to form the α,β‑unsaturated aldehyde. Typically run in acetic acid or a polar solvent at 150–200 °C under a flow of oxygen; Pd(OAc)₂ is the catalyst.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis (ester cleavage) of cyclodecyl acetate to cyclodecanol and acetic acid; water attacks the carbonyl carbon, leading to formation of the corresponding alcohol and acid. Performed in aqueous acidic medium (e.g., dilute H₂SO₄) with heating/reflux; no additional catalyst beyond the acid.

Acid- or base‑catalyzed amide hydrolysis; purpose is to convert an amide into the corresponding carboxylic acid and release ammonia; key transformation is cleavage of the C–N bond of benzamide to give benzoic acid and NH3; typically performed in aqueous HCl (reflux, 1–2 M) or aqueous NaOH (heated, then acidified); common solvent is water (often with a co‑solvent such as ethanol for solubility).

Chromium(VI) oxidation of abietic acid to dehydroabietic acid in concentrated sulfuric acid; CrO₃ oxidizes the terpene, reducing to Cr(III) sulfate while generating water. Conducted by refluxing the mixture of abietic acid, H₂SO₄ and CrO₃ at elevated temperature (≈150 °C); chromium(VI) species acts as the oxidant, sulfuric acid provides the acidic medium.

Preparation of a phosphine‑stabilized copper(I) hydride complex; metal‑hydride synthesis by reduction of CuCl with phenylsilane in the presence of KOtBu, which activates the silane and generates Cu‑H; typically performed under inert atmosphere in THF or toluene at 0 °C to rt, yielding the hexameric [CuH(PPh3)]6 used as a catalyst for hydrosilylation or conjugate reductions.

Neutralization/acid‑base reaction; aqueous ammonium fluoride is treated with sodium hydroxide, yielding sodium fluoride, ammonia gas and water; conducted at ambient temperature with excess NaOH to drive off NH₃; no catalyst, water as solvent.

Formation of a cyanoacetohydrazide via condensation of hydrazine with cyanoacetic acid; nucleophilic acyl substitution (hydrazide synthesis); water is eliminated; usually carried out in refluxing ethanol or aqueous ethanol, sometimes with a catalytic amount of acid, to afford the hydrazide precursor for heterocycle construction.

Fischer esterification of acrylic acid with 1‑propanol to afford propyl acrylate. Purpose: synthesis of an alkyl acrylate monomer. Key transformation: the carboxyl –OH of acrylic acid is replaced by O‑propyl, producing water. Typical conditions: reflux in a solvent such as toluene or xylene with excess 1‑propanol, catalytic 1–5 % H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH, and removal of water (Dean–Stark or azeotropic distillation). Solvent: toluene; catalyst: strong acid.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis (ring‑opening) of a strained oxabicyclic ether to a vicinal diol; produces trans‑1,2‑cyclooctanediol. Water attacks the electrophilic carbon of the bicyclic ether under acidic conditions (e.g., dilute H2SO4 or AcOH) leading to cleavage of the C–O bond and formation of two hydroxyl groups in a trans arrangement. The reaction is performed in aqueous acidic medium at room temperature to moderate heating (20‑50 °C); no additional catalyst beyond the acid is required.

Acid‑catalyzed cycloacetal formation of 1,3‑dioxolane from ethylene glycol and formaldehyde (generated from paraformaldehyde); classic acetalization (formation of a five‑membered cyclic acetal); methanesulfonic acid serves as the proton donor; reaction is run at reflux in a Dean‑Stark apparatus (toluene or benzene) to continuously remove water and drive the equilibrium to the dioxolane product.

Salt metathesis (anion exchange) to produce zinc tetrafluoroborate, a non‑coordinating Lewis acid; ZnCl2 reacts with two equivalents of NaBF4, precipitating NaCl; performed in polar aprotic solvents such as acetonitrile or aqueous solution at ambient temperature, followed by filtration to remove NaCl and isolation of Zn(BF4)2.

Nucleophilic substitution (azide‑iodine exchange) generating iodine azide (IN3) from sodium azide and iodine monobromide; the azide anion attacks the electrophilic iodine, displacing bromide; carried out at low temperature (0 °C to –78 °C) in an aprotic solvent like dichloromethane or acetonitrile under inert atmosphere because IN3 is thermally unstable; NaBr is the by‑product.

Acid–base neutralization to form diethyldithiocarbamate; deprotonation of N,N‑diethylcarbamodithioic acid by NaOH, producing water and the sodium dithiocarbamate salt; typically performed in aqueous solution at room temperature, giving a water‑soluble dithiocarbamate used as a metal‑chelating agent or antioxidant.

General type: oxidative cleavage (ozonolysis) of an alkene. Purpose: convert the C=C double bond of (E)-4-hexen-1-ol into carbonyl fragments. Key transformation: O3 adds across the double bond forming a molozonide that rearranges to ozonide; reductive work‑up (e.g., Zn/AcOH or dimethyl sulfide) splits the ozonide giving acetaldehyde from the terminal carbon and 4‑hydroxybutanal from the internal carbon. Typical conditions: solution of substrate in an inert, aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform at –78 °C to 0 °C under an O3 atmosphere, followed by immediate addition of the reductive work‑up reagent at low temperature, then warming to rt and aqueous work‑up.

Acid‑catalyzed nitrosation of phenylhydroxylamine; nitrous acid (generated from NaNO₂/HCl) adds a nitroso group to the nitrogen, yielding N‑nitroso‑N‑phenylhydroxylamine and water; carried out at 0–5 °C in aqueous acid to avoid over‑reaction.

General type: electrophilic aromatic substitution (nitration) of an aromatic polycyclic hydrocarbon. Purpose: introduce a nitro group onto acephenanthrylene. Key transformation: nitronium ion (NO2⁺) generated from nitronium tetrafluoroborate attacks the electron‑rich aromatic ring, forming nitroacephenanthrylene; BF3 and HF are generated as stoichiometric by‑products from the BF4⁻ counter‑ion. Typical conditions: dry, non‑nucleophilic solvent such as dichloromethane or nitromethane, temperature 0 °C to rt, inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst is required because BF4⁻ serves as the nitronium source.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt formation); conversion of cinnamic acid to its ammonium salt; key transformation: cinnamic acid + NH₃ → ammonium cinnamate; usually carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; solvents: water or ethanol/water mixture; no catalyst required.

General type: catalytic hydrosilylation (addition) of an alkyne. Purpose: synthesize a vinylsilane functional group. Key transformation: the Si–H bond of triethoxysilane adds across the C≡C triple bond of acetylene, delivering vinyltriethoxysilane with retention of the Si–OEt groups. Typical conditions: palladium on carbon (5–10 wt %) as catalyst, inert atmosphere (N2 or Ar), solvent such as THF or toluene, temperature 25–80 °C, sometimes mild pressure of acetylene (1–5 atm); reaction proceeds without external hydrogen.

General type: oxidation of an aldehyde to a carboxylic acid. Purpose: convert acetaldehyde into acetic acid. Key transformation: hydrogen peroxide oxidizes the aldehydic carbonyl to a carboxyl group, releasing water. Typical conditions: aqueous H2O2 (30 % w/w) under mildly basic or neutral pH, often with a catalytic amount of a transition‑metal catalyst (e.g., Na2WO4, MoO5·2H2O, or Fe‑TA) at 25–60 °C; reaction is exothermic and monitored to avoid over‑oxidation.

General type: acid‑catalyzed transacetalization (acetal exchange). Purpose: convert trioxane into the simpler dimethoxymethane acetal. Key transformation: methanol attacks the cyclic acetal trioxane, opening the ring and forming dimethoxymethane (CH(OCH3)2) while releasing water; three equivalents of dimethoxymethane and three equivalents of water are generated per trioxane. Typical conditions: excess dry methanol as solvent, catalytic amount of a Brønsted acid (e.g., p‑toluenesulfonic acid or HCl), reflux temperature (~65 °C) for several hours; removal of water (e.g., by azeotropic distillation) drives the equilibrium toward product.

General type: acid‑base neutralization/precipitation reaction between a strong acid and a carbonate salt. Purpose: generate hydrogen bromide salt and evolve CO2. Key transformation: two equivalents of HBr protonate carbonate (CO3²⁻) to produce CO2 and H2O; simultaneously silver ions precipitate as insoluble AgBr. Typical conditions: aqueous solution at ambient temperature, vigorous stirring; reaction proceeds spontaneously without need for heating or additional reagents.
Redox synthesis of hypochlorous acid; H2O2 oxidizes Cl2 to give 2 HOCl, used to generate a disinfecting acid; performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, neutral pH, no catalyst required.

Free radical benzylic chlorination; converts the methyl group of 4‑nitrotoluene to a chloromethyl group. Typically performed with chlorine gas (Cl₂) under UV light or thermal conditions (≈80 °C) in an inert solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or CCl₄; hydrogen chloride is generated as a by‑product.

Oxidative cleavage of 1,4‑cyclohexadiene with potassium permanganate to produce adipic acid; both double bonds are oxidized to carboxyl groups, yielding hexanedioic acid; carried out in hot alkaline aqueous KMnO4 (often NaOH or KOH) under reflux; water is the solvent and excess KMnO4 is used.

Acid‑ or base‑catalyzed hydrolysis (saponification) of pentyl dodecanoate to dodecanoic acid and pentan‑1‑ol; water adds across the ester bond; conducted by refluxing the ester in aqueous acid (e.g., dilute H2SO4) or base (NaOH) followed by acid work‑up; solvent is water or aqueous ethanol.

Acid‑base neutralization of strontium carbonate with formic acid to give strontium formate, CO2, and water; two molecules of HCOOH react with SrCO3 forming Sr(HCOO)2 + CO2 + H2O; carried out in aqueous solution at room temperature; water is the medium.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of primary bromides by cyanide to give a dinitrile (adiponitrile); 1,4‑dibromobutane is treated with NaCN in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO, or in molten NaCN, at 200–250 °C, affording adiponitrile and NaBr. This is an industrial route to nylon‑6,6 monomer.

Double‑displacement precipitation between sodium sulfite and barium nitrate forming insoluble barium sulfite and sodium nitrate; Na2SO3 + Ba(NO3)2 → BaSO3↓ + 2 NaNO3; performed in aqueous solution with stirring at ambient temperature; BaSO3 precipitates out.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution using phosgene; produces benzyl chloroformate, a protecting group for amines; key transformation is conversion of the alcohol to a chloroformate with loss of HCl; typically carried out in anhydrous dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride at 0 °C to rt with a base such as pyridine or triethylamine to trap the generated HCl.

Electrophilic aromatic chlorination via in‑situ electrochemical generation of chlorine from aqueous HCl; converts isophthalonitrile to tetrachloro‑isophthalonitrile (chlorothalonil), a fungicide; reaction proceeds in aqueous hydrochloric acid under constant current, temperature 0–25 °C; no organic solvent needed, chlorine is produced at the anode and reacts immediately with the aromatic ring.

High‑temperature solid‑state synthesis (calcination) of lead titanate (PbTiO₃); sodium hydroxide hydrolyzes lead nitrate to lead hydroxide, which reacts with TiO₂ to give the perovskite oxide and water; performed by grinding the solid reactants and heating to 700–800 °C in air; no solvent; product isolated after cooling and washing to remove NaNO₃.

Carbodiimide‑mediatedide coupling (condensation) to form niflumic acid from anthranilic acid and 3‑(trifluoromethyl)aniline; DCC activates the carboxyl group, producing dicyclohexylurea as a by‑product; carried out in dry dichloromethane or DMF at 0 °C to rt under inert atmosphere; precipitated dicyclohexylurea is filtered off and the amide product purified.

Condensation of o‑phenylenediamine with benzaldehyde to give 2‑phenylbenzimidazole and water; aromatic aldehyde cyclization. Conducted in ethanol, acetic acid, or toluene under reflux (80‑120 °C) with a Brønsted acid catalyst (HCl, p‑TsOH) or polyphosphoric acid. In toluene, a Dean‑Stark trap may be used to remove water and drive the equilibrium toward product formation.

Aqueous hydrolysis of europium tribromide to europium hydroxide with release of hydrobromic acid; water abstracts bromide ligands forming Eu(OH)₃ precipitate; conducted in dilute aqueous solution at ambient temperature, often with gentle heating to aid precipitation; the resulting Eu(OH)₃ is filtered and washed, and the HBr remains in solution.

Acid‑catalyzed acetal hydrolysis: 3,3‑dimethoxyprop‑1‑ene is treated with water and dilute HCl, cleaving the dimethoxyacetal to produce acrolein and methanol. Typically carried out at 0–25 °C in aqueous HCl; HCl acts as catalyst.

Base‑induced E2 elimination of 2‑chloropropane with potassium tert‑butoxide; bulky strong base abstracts a β‑hydrogen to give propene and potassium chloride; reaction is run in an aprotic polar solvent such as THF or DMSO at 0 °C to rt under inert atmosphere; the alkene evolves from the reaction mixture and can be isolated by distillation.

Double displacement reaction; used to precipitate ytterbium(III) phosphate. Ytterbium(III) ions react with phosphate ions to form insoluble ytterbium(III) phosphate, while sodium and chloride ions remain in solution. No catalyst required. Typically performed in aqueous solution.

SN2 substitution of a primary alcohol with phosphorus tribromide; purpose is to convert 1‑pentanol into the corresponding alkyl bromide. The alcohol oxygen attacks PBr₃, forming a phosphite intermediate that is displaced by bromide to give 1‑bromopentane and phosphorous acid. Typically performed at 0 °C to reflux in anhydrous ether or pyridine under inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed transesterification. An ester (propyl acetate) reacts with a diol (diethylene glycol) under acidic conditions (e.g., H₂SO₄, p‑TsOH) to exchange the alkoxy groups, producing propyl alcohol (the leaving group) and a mono‑acetylated glycol. Typical conditions: reflux, removal of the volatile alcohol to drive equilibrium; can be run neat or in a high‑boiling solvent such as toluene or xylene.

Fischer esterification (acid‑catalyzed ester formation). Methacrylic reacts with the tri‑hydroxy compound trimethylolpropane to give the tri‑ester trimethylolpropane trimethacrylate and water. Conditions: excess acid or removal of water, catalytic amount of strong acid (H₂SO₄, p‑TsOH), reflux in a solvent such as toluene, xylene, or directly under solvent‑free conditions with azeotropic removal of water.

Epoxidation (Prilezhaev reaction) of 1‑hexene with peroxyacetic acid, converting the C=C double bond into a three‑membered oxirane ring to give 1,2‑epoxyhexane; the peracid is reduced to acetic acid; typically carried out at 0–25 °C in a non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform, often with a mild base (e.g., NaHCO₃) to neutralize acid, no catalyst required.

Strong chemical reduction with lithium aluminium hydride; LiAlH₄ reduces the N=N bond of azobenzene to N–N, yielding hydrazobenzene; conducted under inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar) in dry ether (THF or diethyl ether) at 0 °C to reflux; work‑up involves careful quenching with water and dilute acid.

Thermal decomposition of ammonium chloride yielding ammonia and hydrogen chloride gases; used for generating dry NH3 or HCl. Key transformation: dissociation of NH4Cl into NH3 and HCl. Achieved by heating the solid to ~340 °C under reduced pressure or by heating an aqueous solution to drive off the gases; no catalyst required.

Double displacement (metathesis) acid‑base reaction; used to exchange anions and generate a metal acetate salt; acetic acid donates acetate to cadmium while nitrate pairs with proton to form nitric acid; typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient or mildly heated temperatures; no special catalyst required.

Oxidation of a secondary alcohol to a ketone using hydrogen peroxide. Cyclohexanol is oxidized by H₂O₂ in the presence of a catalyst (e.g., tungstate, molybdate, or a transition‑metal complex) under mildly acidic or neutral conditions to give cyclohexanone and water. Common conditions: 0 °C to 50 °C, aqueous or mixed organic–aqueous solvent (acetone, MeCN), catalytic amount of acid (H₂SO₄) or base (Na₂WO₄·2H₂O) to activate H₂O₂.

Sodium dithionite (Na₂S₂O₄) reduction of a nitro compound; purpose is a mild, aqueous reduction to the amine; key transformation: 2‑nitrofuran is reduced to 2‑aminofuran, with dithionite oxidized to sulfite; typical conditions: aqueous solution, pH adjusted to mildly acidic or neutral, temperature 20–30 °C, stoichiometric or slight excess of Na₂S₂O₄ (1.2–1. equiv); reaction proceeds under inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation.

Double displacement (metathesis) acid‑base reaction; employed to prepare gallium(III) chloride from the nitrate; gallium nitrate exchanges its nitrate ions for chloride from hydrochloric acid, producing GaCl₃ and nitric acid; performed in aqueous medium, often cooled to avoid hydrolysis; no catalyst needed.

Type: Acid‑catalyzed amide hydrolysis (cleavage). Purpose: deprotect amide to regenerate ethanolamine. Key transformation: water attacks the carbonyl of the amide, yielding acetic acid and 2‑aminoethanol. Conditions: reflux in aqueous 6 M HCl (or 1 M NaOH for basic hydrolysis) for several hours; solvent water or water/MeOH mixture.

Silicon + oxygen → silicon dioxide: Oxidation (combustion) reaction. Forms SiO₂, the major component of glass and ceramics. Overall: Si(s) + O₂(g) → SiO₂(s). Usually performed by heating powdered silicon in air or pure O₂ at temperatures above 800 °C; can be done in a furnace or torch flame. No solvent; solid‑gas reaction.

Double‑displacement precipitation (metathesis). Praseodymium acetate reacts with potassium phosphate in aqueous solution; the insoluble praseodymium phosphate precipitates out, while potassium acetate remains in solution. Reaction is carried out at ambient temperature; the solid product is collected by filtration, washed, and dried. No catalyst required.

Isomerization of a branched alkane; a skeletal rearrangement moving a methyl group from carbon‑4 to carbon‑5 to give 2,5‑dimethyloctane. Typically performed at elevated temperatures (250‑350 °C) over solid acidic catalysts such as HZSM‑5 zeolite or amberlyst‑15; reactions are conducted in the gas phase or in acarbon solvent under pressure. The process realigns C–C bonds without changing molecular formula, useful for optimizing fuel properties.

Transesterification between 1‑butanol and ethyl propionate giving butyl propionate and ethanol. Classified as an ester interchange reaction; equilibrium is driven toward products by using an excess of the alcohol or by continuously removing ethanol. Common catalysts are acid (e.g., H₂SO₄, p‑toluenesulfonic acid) or base (e.g., NaOMe, K₂CO₃) and the reaction is run under reflux in a solvent‑free system or in toluene/methanol. Typical temperature 60‑120 °C for several hours.

Selective reduction of pyrrole‑2,5‑dicarboxaldehyde to the corresponding diol using lithium aluminium hydride (LAH). This is a strong hydride reduction converting aldehyde groups to primary alcohols while leaving the heterocyclic ring intact. Conducted under inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar) in anhydrous THF or diethyl ether at 0 °C to room temperature; quench with aqueous ammonium chloride. Provides 1H‑pyrrole‑2,5‑dimethanol in high yield.

Hydrogen reduction (hydrogenation) of tantalum nitride; produces metallic tantalum and ammonia. Hydrogen reduces the Ta–N bond, abstracting nitrogen as NH₃ while depositing Ta metal. Carried out at 800‑1000 °C under a flow of H₂ gas (often mixed with inert carrier); no solvent; sometimes a small amount of catalyst (e.g., Ni) is used to promote reduction.

Acid‑base neutralization of sodium 2,4‑dichlorophenoxyacetate with hydrochloric acid to liberate 2,4‑dichlorophenoxyacetic acid and form NaCl. Performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; stirring until pH reaches ~1‑2. No special catalyst needed; the reaction proceeds to completion upon full acid addition, and the product acid can be extracted with an organic solvent (e.g., ethyl acetate).

Acyl‑chloride esterification of prop‑2‑ynoyl chloride with phenol in the presence of triethylamine. Triethylamine neutralizes the generated HCl, giving phenyl propiolate (phenyl 2‑propynoate). Typical procedure: dissolve reagents in CH₂Cl₂, add TEA at 0 °C, stir to rt, filter off triethylammonium chloride.

Metathesis/neutralization double displacement; converts strontium bromide to strontium hydroxide while forming sodium bromide; hydroxide anion displaces bromide; reaction performed in aqueous solution, typically at room temperature; no catalyst; water serves as solvent.

Halide‑silyl metathesis (salt exchange) between copper(I) bromide and trimethylsilyl isothiocyanate yielding copper(I) thiocyanate and trimethylsilyl bromide. Executed in anhydrous, non‑coordinating solvent such as CH₂Cl₂ or CH₃CN under nitrogen at 0 °C to rt. The reaction proceeds without additional catalyst; the volatile TMS‑Br can be removed under reduced pressure, leaving CuSCN as a solid precipitate.

Double‑displacement (precipitation) reaction between barium sulfamate and ammonium sulfate forming insoluble barium sulfate and soluble ammonium sulfamate. Carried out in aqueous medium with vigorous stirring at room temperature; the BaSO₄ precipitate is filtered and washed, while the filtrate contains 2 equivalents of NH₄⁺ + HSO₄⁻. No catalyst required.

Esterification via acyl chloride: methanol acts as nucleophile attacking but‑2‑ynoyl chloride, displacing chloride to give methyl but‑2‑ynoate and HCl. Performed at 0 °C to rt in an aprotic solvent (e.g., CH₂Cl₂) with a base such as pyridine or triethylamine to scavenge HCl.

Salt formation (acid–base neutralization): protriptyline (a tertiary amine) is protonated by aqueous HCl, producing the water‑soluble protriptyline hydrochloride salt. Conducted by dissolving protriptyline in a minimal amount of organic solvent, adding dilute HCl at rt, and isolating the precipitated salt.

Williamson ether synthesis with epibromohydrin: phenol is deprotonated to phenoxide (by NaOH, K₂CO₃, or NaH) which attacks the bromomethylene carbon of epibromohydrin, displacing Br⁻ and forming phenylglycidyl ether while releasing HBr. Typical conditions: DMF or acetone solvent, 0 °C to rt, inert atmosphere.

Selective aldehyde reduction: 3‑pyridinecarboxaldehyde is reduced by sodium borohydride to the corresponding primary alcohol, 3‑(hydroxymethyl)pyridine. Reaction is carried out in methanol or ethanol at 0 °C to rt, quenching with water after completion.

Single‑displacement redox (metal displacement): manganese metal reduces Cu(II) chloride to metallic copper while being oxidized to Mn(II) chloride. Usually performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature or with gentle heating; no catalyst required.

Alkaline dissolution of germanium: elemental germanium reacts with hot aqueous NaOH, being oxidized to sodium germanate (Na₂GeO₃) and liberating hydrogen gas. Conducted under reflux with excess NaOH; the reaction proceeds only at elevated temperature.

Halogen exchange (fluorination) of uranium tetrabromide with elemental fluorine; purpose is to convert UBr4 to the more thermally stable UF4 while releasing bromine gas; key transformation is substitution of Br ligands by F atoms, uranium remains in the +4 oxidation state; typically carried out in a sealed fluorination reactor at 200‑400 °C under an inert atmosphere, no solvent, using excess F2.

Fluorination; generates uranium hexafluoride, the volatile feedstock for isotope enrichment. Uranium metal reacts with F2 gas at 200‑400 °C in a moisture‑free reactor; no solvent or catalyst required.

Reduction of a primary amide to a primary amine using lithium aluminium hydride; LiAlH4 converts the carbonyl group of cyclopentanecarboxamide into a methylene, yielding cyclopentylamine; typically carried out in dry ether or THF under inert atmosphere at 0 °C to reflux, followed by acidic work‑up.

Redox reaction of sodium metal with hydrogen peroxide; purpose is to generate hydrogen gas and sodium peroxide; key transformation is oxidation of Na^0 to Na^+ forming Na2O2 and reduction of H2O2 to water‑derived hydrogen; performed under dry, oxygen‑free conditions, often at 0‑25 °C to control vigorous evolution of H2, without solvent or in a non‑reactive inert liquid such as dry THF.

Base‑catalyzed saponification – NaOH hydrolyses 2-(diethylamino)ethyl acetate to give 2-(diethylamino)ethanol and sodium acetate; OH⁻ attacks the carbonyl, forming acetate anion and alcohol; carried out in aqueous NaOH (often with methanol) at reflux; water/methanol serve as solvent.

Carbonyl reduction of 3‑octanone to 3‑octanol using lithium aluminium hydride followed by aqueous work‑up; purpose is to convert a ketone to a secondary alcohol; key transformation is hydride transfer from LiAlH4 to the carbonyl carbon, forming an alkoxide that is hydrolyzed to the alcohol while generating LiOH (and Al(OH)3) as by‑products; conducted in anhydrous ether (diethyl ether or THF) under nitrogen at 0‑25 °C during addition, then quenched with water or dilute acid at 0‑25 °C.

Halogen exchange (Finkelstein‑type substitution) – silver fluoride replaces the chloride in 1‑chloro‑1‑fluoroethane to give 1,1‑difluoroethane, precipitating insoluble AgCl. Used for selective fluorination of gem‑dihalides. Usually performed in dry polar aprotic solvent such as acetone or acetonitrile, ambient mildly reflux temperatures; AgCl precipitation drives the reaction forward.

Ligand substitution/coordination complex formation of ruthenium(III) chloride with acetylacetone (pentane‑2,4‑dione) to give tris(acetylacetonato)ruthenium(III) and release HCl; purpose is to prepare a stable Ru(III) chelate; key transformation is replacement of three chloride ligands by bidentate β‑diketonate ligands, producing Ru(acac)3 and three equivalents of HCl; refluxed in ethanol or methanol (≈70‑80 °C) for several hours under nitrogen, using excess acetylacetone as both ligand and solvent.

Gas‑solid tellurization. Tungsten dioxide is exposed to hydrogen telluride gas at 300–500 °C, converting to tungsten telluride with release of water. Performed in a flow tube or sealed ampoule under inert carrier gas; H₂Te is the reagent, no catalyst.

Direct combination (heterocumulene formation): carbon monoxide and elemental selenium combine at high temperature (≈400‑500 °C) or on a metal catalyst surface to give carbonyl selenide (COSe). Gas‑phase synthesis; no solvent.

Catalytic hydrogenation of 3‑(methylamino)propionitrile to 3‑(methylamino)propylamine; purpose is to reduce the nitrile functional group to a primary amine; key transformation is addition of two equivalents of H2 across the C≡N bond to give the corresponding primary amine; carried out with Raney nickel as heterogeneous catalyst under H2 pressure (1–5 atm) at 50‑150 °C in a protic solvent such as ethanol or methanol, with continuous stirring.

Solid‑state metathesis (double displacement) between BeCl2 and CuO to produce BeO and CuCl2; requires high temperature (often 400–600 °C) in a furnace; reaction performed in the solid state, no solvent, sometimes mixed thoroughly as powders; no catalyst needed.

Double‑displacement precipitation (metathesis) between silver nitrate and ammonium selenite; purpose is to isolate insoluble silver selenite; key transformation is exchange of nitrate and selenite ions, forming solid Ag2SeO3 (silver selenite) and soluble ammonium nitrate; performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, with vigorous stirring; the precipitate is filtered and washed, no special catalysts required.

Formation of ammonium triiodide by comproportionation of elemental iodine with potassium iodide and ammonium iodide; synthesis of a polyiodide salt where I2 reacts with I⁻ to give I₃⁻ which pairs with NH₄⁺ to give NH₄I₃; typically performed in aqueous or alcoholic solution at ambient temperature, no catalyst required.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction converting lutetium(III) iodide to lutetium(III) acetate using ammonium acetate; key transformation is exchange of I⁻ for CH₃COO⁻, producing ammonium iodide as by‑product; carried out in water or dilute aqueous solution with gentle heating to dissolve the salts; no catalyst needed.

Ligand‑exchange synthesis of (1,1′‑bis(diphenylphosphino)ferrocene) dichloropalladium(II) from palladium(II) nitrate in concentrated hydrochloric acid; nitrate ligands are displaced by chloride ions, generating nitric acid and the PdCl₂(dppf) complex; performed in aqueous HCl (often refluxed) sometimes with a polar organic co‑solvent such as methanol; no additional catalyst.

Acid–salt metathesis; barium acetate and hydrochloric acid exchange partners to give soluble barium chloride and acetic acid; usually conducted in aqueous medium, mild heating may be applied to ensure complete reaction; no catalyst required.

Redox reaction in which bromine oxidizes hydrogen selenide to elemental selenium while being reduced to hydrogen bromide; overall conversion H₂Se + Br₂ → Se↓ + 2 HBr; usually carried out in an ice‑bath or at 0 °C in aqueous medium to control gas evolution; no catalyst required.

Oxidation of 5‑aminopentan‑1‑ol to 5‑aminopentanoic acid using sodium dichromate in sulfuric acid (Jones oxidation); primary alcohol is oxidized to a carboxylic acid while Cr(VI) is reduced to Cr(III); reaction conducted in aqueous H₂SO₄/acetone mixture at 0–25 °C; stoichiometric oxidant, no extra catalyst.

Hydrolysis of 2‑chloroethyl chloroformate with water to give 2‑chloroethanol, carbon dioxide and hydrogen chloride; cleavage of the chloroformate ester releasing CO₂ and HCl; performed in aqueous solution, often with mild heating (room temperature to reflux); no catalyst needed.

Double displacement/acid–base precipitation; weak acid HCN neutralizes basic Ag2O forming insoluble silver cyanide and water; typically performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, no catalyst required.

Nitrosation of a secondary amine; NaNO2 and HCl generate nitrous acid in situ which nitrosates diethanolamine to give N‑nitrosodiethanolamine, with NaCl and water as by‑products; carried out in cold (0‑5 °C) aqueous medium, often under stirring; no additional catalyst.

Ester aminolysis (amide formation); ammonia attacks methyl pivalate, displacing methanol and yielding pivalamide; usually conducted with excess aqueous or gaseous NH3 under reflux (80‑120 °C) in a solvent such as ethanol or toluene; no catalyst needed.

Hydrolysis (neutral/acidic) of an acetate ester; water cleaves 2‑phenoxyethyl acetate to produce phenoxyethanol and acetic acid; commonly performed by refluxing the ester in water or dilute acid (e.g., H₂SO₄) for several hours; no special catalyst beyond the acid if used.

Base‑catalyzed aldol condensation; acetaldehyde enolizes under NaOH (or other base) and adds to 2‑nitrobenzaldehyde, followed by dehydration to give 2‑nitrocamaldehyde; reaction typically run in ethanol or methanol at 0 °C to room temperature, then warmed to promote elimination; base serves as catalyst.

General type: oxidation of an aldehyde to a carboxylic acid using a peracid. Purpose: convert veratraldehyde (3,4‑dimethoxybenzaldehyde) into veratric acid (3,4‑dimethoxybenzoic acid). Key transformation: peroxyacetic acid transfers an oxygen atom to the aldehyde carbon, generating the corresponding carboxylic acid and acetic acid as by‑product. Typical conditions: peracetic acid (generated in situ from H₂O₂ and Ac₂O or used as commercial solution) added to a solution of veratraldehyde in a solvent such as dichloromethane or acetone, temperature 0 °C to rt; the reaction may be acid‑catalyzed; after completion the mixture is washed, extracted and the acid purified.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation; aqueous solution of lead(II) perchlorate mixed with potassium bromide results in insoluble lead(II) bromide precipitating while potassium perchlorate remains dissolved; typically carried out at ambient temperature with stirring, no catalyst required.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution; cyanide ion replaces bromide on the α‑bromo ketone to give 3‑cyanobutan‑2‑one. Typically performed with potassium cyanide in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO at moderate temperature (50‑80 °C). The by‑product is potassium bromide precipitated out.

Double‑displacement precipitation (metathesis); aqueous calcium phosphate reacts with praseodymium nitrate exchanging cations to precipitate praseodymium phosphate while calcium nitrate remains soluble; performed in water with vigorous stirring at room temperature; no catalyst required.

Reaction type: double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation. Purpose: qualitative test for iodide ions and preparation of soluble zinc nitrate. Key transformation: Ag⁺ exchanges with Zn²⁺, forming insoluble AgI as a pale‑yellow precipitate while Zn²⁺ pairs with NO₃⁻ to remain in solution as Zn(NO₃)₂. Conditions: both reagents dissolved in water, mixed at room temperature; no additional solvent or catalyst required.

N‑Acylation (acetylation) of an amine; used to protect or modify the amino group of N‑phenylglycine. The carbonyl oxygen of acetic anhydride transfers an acetyl group to the nitrogen, releasing one equivalent of acetic acid. Typically carried out in an aprotic solvent (e.g., pyridine, dichloromethane) at 0 °C to room temperature; catalytic DMAP or pyridine often serves as base/solvent.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of an α‑halo amide by ammonia; converts 2‑iodopropanamide to 2‑aminopropanamide while generating hydrogen iodide. Reaction proceeds in excess gaseous or aqueous ammonia, usually under reflux in a polar protic solvent such as ethanol or water. The HI formed is neutralized by the ammonia or removed as gas.

Amide formation via Schotten‑Baumann acylation; the amine of 4‑aminosalicylic acid attacks benzoyl chloride, giving the benzoylamide product and liberating HCl, which is scavenged by DIPEA. Conducted at 0 °C to rt in anhydrous dichloromethane or THF under inert atmosphere; stoichiometric DIPEA (or other tertiary amine) prevents acid buildup.

Carboxylation of a Grignard reagent; phenethylmagnesium bromide adds to CO₂ to form the magnesium carboxylate, which after acidic work‑up yields phenylpropionic acid and MgBr₂; performed in dry ether or THF at low temperature under a CO₂ atmosphere, then quenched with dilute HCl; no catalyst.

Thermal decarboxylation of a strained cyclopropene carboxylic acid; produces cyclopropene gas and CO₂. Key transformation: loss of CO₂ from the carboxyl group, generating the highly strained cyclopropene ring. Typical conditions: neat heating to 150–200 °C under inert atmosphere; sometimes CuO or other metal oxides are added to facilitate decarboxylation. Solvent: none (neat) or high‑boiling inert solvent (e.g., toluene) if needed.

Halogen exchange (metathesis) redox reaction; elemental fluorine oxidizes uranium(IV) chloride, replacing chloride ligands with fluoride to afford uranium tetrafluoride while liberating chlorine gas. Performed in a sealed, corrosion‑resistant vessel at elevated temperature (often 200–400 °C) under an inert gas blanket; no solvent is used due to the reactivity of F₂.

Metal‑boride formation via borohydride reduction; sodium borohydride reduces nickel(II) acetate, generating nickel(II) boride (Ni₂B) as a solid catalyst and releasing hydrogen gas and sodium acetate. Usually carried out in aqueous or alcoholic media (e.g., ethanol/water) at 0 °C to reflux under nitrogen or argon to avoid oxidation.

Base‑catalyzed hydrolysis of hexanenitrile to sodium hexanoate; the nitrile is converted to the carboxylate ion with liberation of NH3. Carried out with aqueous NaOH (excess) under reflux (≈100 °C) for several hours, often in water or water/ethanol mixture; yields the sodium salt of the acid.

Acid‑catalyzed nitrile hydrolysis; 4‑chlorophenoxyacetonitrile is converted to 4‑chlorophenoxyacetic acid with concomitant formation of ammonium chloride from the released ammonia. Conducted by refluxing the nitrile in concentrated aqueous HCl (often 6 M) for several hours; after cooling, the acid is isolated and the ammonium chloride remains in solution.

Elimination (E2) of 1‑bromohexadecane to give 1‑hexadecene and hydrogen bromide; typically performed with a strong base such as KOH or sodium ethoxide in ethanol or THF at reflux, where the base abstracts a β‑hydrogen and the C‑Br bond departs to afford the terminal alkene.

Strong acid–base neutralization; nitric acid reacts with potassium hydroxide to form water and potassium nitrate; carried out in aqueous medium at ambient temperature; stoichiometric 1:1 molar ratio; no special solvent beyond water needed.

Base‑promoted elimination (E2) of a gem‑dichloride; converts 2,2‑dichloropropane to the alkene 2‑chloro‑1‑propene while forming water and sodium chloride; uses aqueous or alcoholic NaOH as strong base, heated to reflux; reaction proceeds via concerted dehydrohalogenation, no additional catalyst.

Fischer esterification of phthalic anhydride with n‑butanol and isobutanol to afford the mixed diester butyl isobutyl phthalate and water; performed under strong acid catalysis (conc. H₂SO₄ or p‑toluenesulfonic acid) at 150‑180 °C, often in toluene or xylene with azeotropic removal of water to drive the equilibrium toward ester formation.

Oxidative coupling of benzeneselenol with iodine to produce diphenyl diselenide and hydrogen iodide; proceeds at room temperature in a non‑nucleophilic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform, where iodine oxidizes two PhSeH molecules to the diselenide, releasing HI; no additional catalyst is required.

Acidic substitution of diazomethane with hydrobromic acid to generate methyl bromide and nitrogen gas; carried out at 0‑5 °C in an ether solvent (diethyl ether or THF) to control the reactive diazomethane, HBr protonates the diazo compound causing loss of N₂ and formation of CH₃Br.

Redox dissolution of thulium metal in nitric acid; purpose is to generate thulium(III) nitrate pentahydrate and nitrogen dioxide gas. Thulium is oxidized to Tm³⁺, nitrate is reduced to NO₂, and water is formed. Reaction is carried out in dilute aqueous nitric acid, temperature controlled (0–30 °C) to moderate gas evolution; performed in water with no extra catalyst.

Double‑displacement precipitation reaction; common method to exchange anions and isolate silver chloride; aqueous MnCl2 solution mixed with AgNO3 solution yields white AgCl precipitate and Mn(NO3)2 remaining in solution; carried out at room temperature in water; no catalyst.

Catalytic hydrogenation of 2‑(cyanomethyl)pyridine over palladium on carbon to reduce the nitrile to the primary amine 2‑pyridinemethanamine; conducted under hydrogen pressure (1‑5 atm) in ethanol or methanol at room temperature to ~50 °C, where Pd/C facilitates transfer of hydrogen to the C≡N bond, yielding the corresponding amine.

Suzuki‑Miyaura cross‑coupling; palladium‑catalyzed aryl‑alkyl C–C bond formation to install two methyl groups onto 1,4‑dibromonaphthalene, yielding 1,4‑dimethylnaphthalene. Uses PdCl2(PPh3)2 (or Pd(PPh3)4) as catalyst, K2CO3 as base, mixed THF/H2O or dioxane solvent, heated to 80‑100 °C under inert atmosphere.

Complete aerobic oxidation (combustion) of acetaldehyde to carbon dioxide and water. Typically occurs in excess O2 at elevated temperature (flame or furnace); may be catalyzed by metal oxides in industrial settings.

Acid‑catalyzed transesterification (Fischer esterification) converting methyl 4‑methylbenzoate to ethyl 4‑methylbenzoate while releasing methanol. Conducted with catalytic H2SO4 in excess ethanol, refluxing (≈78 °C) in ethanol as both solvent and reactant; removal of methanol drives equilibrium to products.

Double‑displacement precipitation: lead(II) bromide mixed with copper(II) sulfate forms insoluble lead(II) sulfate precipitate and soluble copper(II) bromide; conducted in water at room temperature, no catalyst.

Halogen exchange (nucleophilic substitution, SN2) of 1‑hexyl bromide with silver fluoride to give 1‑fluorohexane. Performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetone or DMF at mild heat; AgBr precipitates, driving the reaction forward.

Nitrosation of methylamine with nitrous acid to form N‑nitrosomethylamine and water. Generated in situ from NaNO2 and HCl (or other acid) at 0‑5 °C in aqueous solution; low temperature limits side reactions and over‑oxidation.

Finkelstein halide exchange (SN2) of phenethyl bromide with sodium iodide to afford phenethyl iodide and sodium bromide. Carried out in dry acetone (or another polar aprotic solvent) under reflux; NaBr precipitates, shifting equilibrium toward the iodide product.

Double displacement/acid dissolution; nitric acid protonates cadmium tellurite, converting the insoluble CdTeO₃ into soluble cadmium nitrate and releasing tellurous acid (H₂TeO₃); performed in aqueous solution, often with gentle heating and stirring.

Hydrolysis of a metal fluoride; CrF3 is treated with, leading to cleavage of Cr–F bonds and formation of insoluble Cr(OH)3 solid while releasing HF into solution. Conducted in aqueous medium at ambient or mildly elevated temperature (≈60 °C) with stirring; no catalyst needed.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis (reductive dehalogenation). Hydrogen gas in the presence of palladium on carbon reduces all four C–Br bonds of 1,2,4,5‑tetrabromopentane, yielding pentane and generating hydrogen bromide as a by‑product. Usually carried out under 1–5 atm H₂ at room temperature or slight heating in a solvent such as ethanol, methanol, or ethyl acetate; the Pd/C catalyst facilitates the cleavage.

Acid‑base/oxide dissolution; Al2O3 (amphoteric oxide) is protonated by H3PO4 to form AlPO4 and H2O; carried out in aqueous phosphoric acid, often with reflux to improve conversion; no catalyst needed.

Acid- or base‑catalyzed epoxide hydrolysis; purpose is to synthesize phenylglycol, a vicinal diol used as a chiral building block; water attacks the less‑substituted carbon of styrene oxide opening the three‑membered ring to give 2‑phenyl‑1,2‑ethanediol; typical conditions are reflux in aqueous acid (e.g., 5 % H₂SO₄) or aqueous base (NaOH) often in a water/acetone mixture; common solvent is water or aqueous methanol, catalyst is a Brønsted acid or base.

Hydrolysis (decomposition) of isothiocyanic acid; purpose is breakdown of HNCS to simple gases; key transformation: HNCS + H₂O → OCS + NH₃; typical conditions: aqueous solution at ambient or mildly elevated temperature (often 25–60 °C); no catalyst required, reaction proceeds spontaneously in water.

Transacetalization (acetal protection); benzaldehyde reacts with 1,1‑dimethoxypropane under catalytic acid (e.g., p‑TsOH) to form the benzaldehyde dimethyl acetal while acetone is liberated; carried out in dry aprotic solvents such as dichloromethane or toluene, typically at room temperature and with removal of acetone to drive equilibrium.

Carbothermic reduction (high‑temperature redox) of arsenic(III) oxide; carbon reduces As₂O₃ to elemental arsenic, being oxidized to carbon monoxide; conducted in a furnace at 900–1100 °C under inert or reducing atmosphere; solid‑state reactants, no solvent or catalyst.

Ester reduction (LiAlH4); reduces 2‑(acetoxymethyl)pyridine (an acetate ester) to pyridin‑2‑ylmethanol with concomitant formation of ethanol; performed in dry ether (THF or Et2O) at 0 °C then reflux under nitrogen; work‑up with aqueous acid quenches excess hydride.

Nickel‑catalyzed Ullmann ether synthesis (cross‑coupling); phenol and iodobenzene are coupled in the presence of zinc dust, NiCl₂ and the bidentate phosphine ligand dpppe to afford diphenyl ether; the reaction is run in polar aprotic solvents such as DMF or NMP at 100–150 °C under nitrogen or argon.

Lewis‑acid promoted skeletal rearrangement; alpha‑pinene undergoes BF₃·OEt₂‑catalyzed isomerization to 3‑carene via a cationic intermediate; typically performed in dry diethyl ether (or another ether) at 0 °C to room temperature, using catalytic amounts of the boron trifluoride etherate.

Alpha‑halogenation of an ester (radical/electrophilic substitution); chlorine attacks the α‑position of ethyl acetate, yielding ethyl chloroacetate and hydrogen chloride; the transformation is carried out under UV light or with a mild acid/base catalyst in an inert solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or chloroform.

Intramolecular cyclization (acid‑catalyzed Friedel‑Crafts acylation); converts 2‑phenylpropionic acid to 1‑indanone by dehydration and ring closure; performed by heating the substrate in concentrated H₂SO₄ (≈150–200 °C) which acts as both solvent and catalyst; purpose is synthesis of the ketone scaffold.

Type: Grignard addition to an aldehyde. Purpose: Form a primary alcohol with one‑carbon chain extension. Key transformation: Octylmagnesium bromide attacks formaldehyde, giving a magnesium alkoxide that after acidic work‑up furnishes 1‑nonanol. Typical conditions: Anhydrous ether or THF, formaldehyde source (paraformaldehyde solution) at 0 °C to rt, then dilute HCl or NH₄Cl work‑up. No catalyst.

Hydrolysis of an organobismuth compound; trimethylbismuth reacts with water to give bismuth oxide (Bi₂O₃) and methane gas; typical conditions are ambient temperature in aqueous medium, often followed by gentle heating to drive off CH₄ and to decompose any Bi(OH)₃ intermediate to Bi₂O₃; purpose is disposal or conversion of the organometallic reagent.

Metathesis/precipitation reaction; ferric chloride reacts with phosphoric acid to form solid iron(III) phosphate (FePO₄) and liberates hydrochloric acid; carried out in aqueous solution at room temperature with stirring; the insoluble FePO₄ precipitates and is filtered; used to prepare the phosphate salt.

Acid‑catalyzed condensation (dimerization) of indole‑3‑carbinol; two molecules combine with loss of water to give 3,3′‑diindolylmethane (DIM). Key transformation: electrophilic aromatic substitution between the benzylic carbon of one indole‑3‑carbinol and the 3‑position of another, followed by dehydration. Conducted in mildly acidic aqueous solution (pH 4‑5) at room temperature or slightly elevated temperature (20‑40 °C). No special catalyst beyond the acid medium.

Acid‑base salt formation; the basic amine Pargyline is protonated by hydrogen chloride to give Pargyline·HCl (pargyline hydrochloride); usually performed by dissolving Pargyline in an ether or ethanol solution and bubbling HCl gas or adding aqueous HCl, then isolating the crystalline salt; purpose is to obtain a more water‑soluble, stable pharmaceutical salt.

Prilezhaev epoxidation of cyclohexene with meta‑chloroperbenzoic acid (m‑CPBA) to give cyclohexene oxide; purpose is formation of an epoxide; key transformation C=C → epoxide ring; conditions: m‑CPBA (1.1–1.5 eq) in dry dichloromethane at 0 °C to rt, inert atmosphere; by‑product is m‑chlorobenzoic acid; no additional catalyst needed.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) in aqueous solution; sodium phosphate reacts with thallium(I) sulfate to exchange anions, yielding insoluble thallium(I) phosphate precipitate and soluble sodium sulfate; performed at ambient temperature with stirring; the precipitated Tl₃PO₄ is filtered off; used for isolation of thallium phosphate.

Acid–salt reaction; conversion of magnesium phosphate to soluble phosphates. In aqueous solution the strong acid protonates the phosphate anion, releasing phosphoric acid while forming magnesium chloride. Typically performed at ambient temperature in water with excess 6 M HCl; no special catalyst required.
Acid‑base metathesis; nitric acid protonates acetate to give acetic acid and forms soluble praseodymium(III) nitrate. Executed in aqueous solution, usually at room temperature; no catalyst.

Proton transfer (acid–base neutralization) to generate an ionic salt. p‑Toluenesulfonic acid protonates 2,4,6‑trimethylpyridine (collidine) forming collidinium p‑toluenesulfonate, a protic ionic liquid. Reaction proceeds at room temperature, usually in a non‑nucleophilic solvent such as acetonitrile or dichloromethane, and may be isolated by evaporation of the solvent.

Metal‑acid redox (single‑displacement) reaction; sodium metal reacts with hydrochloric acid to generate sodium chloride and hydrogen gas; Na is oxidized to Na⁺ while H⁺ is reduced to H₂; occurs rapidly at room temperature in aqueous HCl; no catalyst needed, but the reaction is vigorous and must be controlled.

Acid‑base protonation of cyanate (generation of cyanic acid). Sodium cyanate is treated with hydrochloric acid to produce cyanic acid (HNCO) and sodium chloride. Performed in dilute aqueous solution, at 0–25 °C to avoid decomposition of HNCO. No catalyst needed.

Halide exchange (fluorination) similar to #3; replaces bromide ligands of titanium(III) bromide with fluoride using HF, generating hydrogen bromide; TiBr3 + 3 HF → TiF3 + 3 HBr; conducted in aqueous HF, temperature 0–100 °C; excess HF ensures complete conversion; no catalyst required.

Hydrolysis of oxolan‑3‑yl acetate with water (acidic or neutral conditions) to regenerate tetrahydrofuran‑3‑ol and produce acetic acid. Purpose: deprotect the acetate. Key transformation: acetate cleavage to alcohol + acetic acid. Typically heated in aqueous acid (e.g., dilute HCl) or under reflux in water/THF mixture.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction) of nitrogen trichloride. Hydrogen gas reduces NCl₃, converting nitrogen to ammonia while chlorine is transferred to hydrogen to form HCl. Typically performed in the gas phase over a Pd or Pt catalyst at elevated temperature (150–250 °C) and moderate pressure; the products are collected after cooling and condensation.

Redox reduction of Pd(II) by carbon monoxide (CO reduction). Palladium(II) chloride is reduced by CO in the presence of water, producing metallic palladium, carbon dioxide (oxidation product of CO) and hydrogen chloride. Employed for palladium metal recovery or catalyst preparation. Reaction carried out under a CO atmosphere (often 1–5 atm) in aqueous acidic medium at 50–100 °C; continuous CO bubbling provides the reductant, no additional catalyst.

Salt formation (acid–base neutralization) to afford norepinephrine bitartrate. Tartaric acid protonates the amine of norepinephrine, producing the stable bitartrate salt. The reaction is carried out in aqueous or aqueous‑ethanol solution, often at 0–5 °C to control crystallization, followed by evaporation or cooling to isolate the crystalline norepinephrine bitartrate.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) alkylation of a primary amine; purpose is to install a methyl group on butylamine forming N‑methylbutylamine. The methyl bromide acts as electrophile, butylamine as nucleophile, releasing hydrogen bromide. Typically performed under anhydrous conditions, often using excess amine as solvent or a tertiary amine base (e.g., triethylamine) to trap HBr; temperatures range from 0 °C to reflux in solvents such as dichloromethane or ethanol.

Williamson ether synthesis (SN2) between methyl chloride and sodium methoxide; purpose is to generate dimethyl ether and sodium chloride. The methoxide ion attacks the methyl carbon, displacing chloride. Conducted in anhydrous methanol or a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., DMF) under reflux; pressure may be applied to keep methyl chloride in solution. Often performed at 50‑80 °C with inert atmosphere.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation in aqueous solution; purpose is to exchange cations and precipitate aluminium molybdate, a sparingly soluble salt, while forming soluble sodium nitrate. Mix aqueous solutions of aluminium nitrate and sodium molybdate, typically at room temperature or slight warming; stirring leads to a precipitate of Al₂(MoO₄)₃ which is filtered and washed. No special catalyst required; water is the solvent.

Acid–metal redox reaction; purpose is to convert hydrogen cyanide into lithium cyanide while liberating hydrogen gas. Metallic lithium reduces the acidic N–H bond of HCN, forming LiCN and H₂. Conducted under inert atmosphere (argon or nitrogen) at low temperature (0‑25 °C) in dry aprotic solvents such as THF or liquid ammonia to dissolve lithium; vigorous stirring needed. No additional catalyst.

Lewis‑acid/base salt formation: fluoride ion from potassium fluoride coordinates to boron trifluoride, generating the stable tetrafluoroborate anion as potassium tetrafluoroborate. Usually carried out in an aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile or dichloromethane at 0 °C to ambient temperature; the reaction is fast and quantitative.

Halogen exchange (redox displacement) reaction; chlorine gas oxidizes bromide in arsenic tribromide, producing arsenic trichloride and bromine vapor; performed in a dry, inert solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane under reflux or gentle heating; no additional catalyst needed.

Reductive transformation of a nitro group to an amino group using sodium dithionite; purpose is to obtain the 5‑amino derivative of the imidazole scaffold. Sodium dithionite (Na₂S₂O₄) reduces the nitro substituent under aqueous, mildly alkaline or neutral conditions (pH ≈ 7‑9) at ambient temperature. Reaction mixture typically contains water or a water‑methanol blend; the process is carried out under nitrogen to avoid oxidation. No metal catalyst is required.

Pinnick oxidation of an aldehyde to a carboxylic acid using sodium chlorite; purpose is to convert 4‑chlorophenoxyacetaldehyde into 4‑chlorophenoxyacetic acid. Sodium chlorite (NaClO₂) oxidizes the aldehyde in aqueous buffer (often phosphate, pH 3‑5) at 0‑25 °C. A scavenger such as 2‑methyl‑2‑butene may be added to consume hypochlorous acid by‑product, though not shown. Reaction proceeds without metal catalysts; water is the solvent.

Oxidation (Pinnick oxidation). Converts perillyl aldehyde to perillic acid by selective oxidation of the aldehyde functional group using sodium chlorite. Typically performed in aqueous buffer (phosphate or acetate) at ambient temperature, often with a scavenger such as 2‑methyl‑2‑butene to trap chlorine dioxide. Common solvent mixture is water/tert‑butanol; no metal catalyst required.

N‑alkylation (SN2) of a primary amine. 2‑Heptanamine is deprotonated by triethylamine, then methyl iodide alkylates the nitrogen to give N‑methyl‑2‑heptanamine; triethylammonium iodide is formed as the by‑product. Typical solvent is an aprotic polar solvent such as acetonitrile or dichloromethane, reaction run at 0 °C to rt.

Oxidation (Pinnick–type oxidation with hydrogen peroxide). Transforms pyrrole‑2‑carboxaldehyde into pyrrole‑2‑carboxylic acid using sodium chlorite in the presence of hydrogen peroxide as the oxidant. Conducted in a buffered aqueous medium (phosphate buffer, pH ≈ 5–6) at room temperature; a halogen‑scavenger (e.g., 2‑methyl‑2‑butene) may be added. Solvent is typically water/t‑butanol; no additional catalyst is needed.

Acidic dichromate oxidation of a secondary alcohol to a ketone; purpose is oxidation of 2‑propanol to acetone. Same reagents as above (K₂Cr₂O₇/H₂SO₄) in water, heated gently with stirring. Chromium(VI) is reduced to Cr(III) (chromium(III) sulfate) and water is formed.

Ion‑exchange (acid‑base exchange). Sodium chloride is passed through a cation‑exchange resin in the hydrogen form loaded with L‑glutamic acid releasing hydrochloric acid and forming sodium L‑glutamate on the resin. Reaction occurs in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; the resin acts as the solid phase, no external catalysts required.

Oxidation/synthesis; phosphorus trichloride is oxidized by molecular oxygen to give phosphoryl chloride (POCl₃), raising phosphorus from +3 to +5; usually performed in the gas phase under controlled O₂ flow at 200–300 °C; sometimes a small amount of catalyst such as copper or activated carbon is employed; no solvent.

Oxidative combustion of a germanium hydride. Dichlorogermane (GeH₂Cl₂) reacts with molecular oxygen under high‑temperature conditions (e.g., flame or heated furnace) to give germanium dioxide (GeO₂) and hydrogen chloride gas. The transformation is an overall oxidation of Ge(II) to Ge(IV). No solvent; performed in the gas phase or in sealed high‑temperature reactors.

Sandmeyer cyanation (diazotization followed by nucleophilic substitution). 4‑Chloroaniline is diazotized with sodium nitrite in hydrochloric acid at 0‑5 °C to form the corresponding diazonium chloride, which then reacts with copper(I) cyanide to produce 4‑chlorobenzonitrile, liberating nitrogen gas, water, sodium chloride, and copper(I) chloride. Reaction is carried out in aqueous acidic medium, typically with ice‑bath temperature control; CuCN serves as the cyanide source and catalyst.

Oxidative decomposition of sodium formaldehyde sulfoxylate. Hydrogen peroxide oxidizes sodium formaldehyde sulfoxylate (HOCH₂SO₂Na) in aqueous solution, yielding formaldehyde, water, and sodium. Reaction proceeds at ambient temperature in water; excess H₂O₂ may be used to drive the oxidation to completion. No additional catalyst is required.

N‑alkylation of a primary amine via nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of ethylamine on 2‑bromopropane to give the secondary amine isopropylethylamine and HBr; typically performed in an aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile or dichloromethane, often with a base (e.g., triethylamine) or excess amine to neutralize the HBr, under reflux.

Alkaline hydrolysis of diselenium dichloride to sodium selenite: Same transformation as above but with NaOH, yielding sodium selenite (Na₂SeO₃), sodium chloride and water. Reaction conditions identical: aqueous NaOH, room temperature, stoichiometric excess to drive to completion. No catalyst required.

Hydrolysis (acid‑base neutralization) of aluminum phenoxide to regenerate phenol and precipitate aluminum hydroxide; carried out simply by adding water to the metal phenoxide, usually with gentle heating, no catalyst required.

N‑acylation using carbonyldiimidazole (CDI); acetic acid is activated by CDI to an imidazolide which is attacked by indoline nitrogen, yielding N‑acetylindoline, imidazole and CO₂; performed in dry THF or DMF at room temperature under nitrogen; CDI acts as coupling reagent, no external catalyst.

Acid‑base neutralization of silver carbonate with trifluoroacetic acid, producing silver trifluoroacetate, carbon dioxide, and water; usually conducted in an organic solvent such as dichloromethane or acetonitrile at room temperature with gentle stirring, allowing CO₂ evolution.

Double‑displacement/metathesis reaction in aqueous solution where sodium hydroxide neutralizes zinc iodate, precipitating zinc hydroxide and forming sodium iodate; performed at room temperature or with mild heating, aqueous medium, no special catalyst.

Catalytic transfer hydrogenation (reduction) of nitrobenzene to aniline using ammonium formate as hydrogen source; purpose: reduction of nitro group to primary amine; key transformations: nitrobenzene → aniline, oxidation of formate to CO₂, NH₃, and H₂O; typical conditions: palladium on carbon (5‑10 % Pd) catalyst, ethanol or methanol solvent, 80‑100 °C, excess ammonium formate (3‑5 equiv), inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar); catalyst: Pd/C.

Acyl‑chloride esterification (nucleophilic acyl substitution) of acetyl chloride with 2‑butoxyethanol to produce 2‑butoxyethyl and HCl; conducted in an inert aprotic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) at 0 °C to rt, using a base such as pyridine or triethylamine to scavenge the generated HCl.

Redox/halogenation reaction in which iodine oxidizes aluminum nitride, liberating nitrogen gas and forming aluminum triiodide; generally carried out in a sealed tube at elevated temperature (150–200 °C) under an inert atmosphere, no catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed esterification of succinic anhydride with 1‑butanol to give dibutyl succinate and water; Montmorillonite K10 (solid acid clay) serves as the catalyst, reaction run under reflux (≈120 °C) either solvent‑free or in a high‑boiling solvent such as toluene.

Reaction type: synthesis/halogenation (direct fluorination). Purpose: preparation of anhydrous aluminum fluoride, used as a catalyst and in ceramics. Key transformation: Al → Al³⁺, F₂ → F⁻, yielding AlF₃. Typical conditions: anhydrous F₂ gas introduced to heated Al (150‑300 °C) in a nickel or steel vessel; the reaction is highly exothermic and must be controlled, often performed at low temperature with excess F₂. No solvent; inert gas (N₂ or Ar) may be used as carrier.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a halide by thiocyanate; AgSCN provides SCN⁻ which displaces I⁻ from methyl iodide, precipitating AgI and forming methyl thiocyanate. Conducted in dry ether under reflux or room temperature; AgI removal drives the reaction forward.

Thermal or catalytic cracking – cleaves n‑octane into a smaller alkane (propane) and a terminal olefin (1‑pentene). Purpose is to generate lighter fuels and olefinic building blocks. Key transformation: C–C bond scission between C‑3 and C‑4 with simultaneous hydrogen transfer to give propane and a double bond in the C₅ fragment. Typical conditions: 450–750 °C, short residence time, low pressure; catalytic cracking uses zeolite (e.g., USY, ZSM‑5) at 500–550 °C and often a hydrogen‑free environment. Reaction performed in vapor phase; no solvent.

Acid‑base metathesis and precipitation; oxalic acid reacts with bismuth subnitrate to form insoluble bismuth oxalate precipitate while liberating nitric acid into the solution. This reaction is used when bismuth oxalate is the desired intermediate or for removal of nitrate. Performed in aqueous media, often at room temperature or with slight heating to improve crystal formation. No catalyst; water is the solvent.

Reduction of an amine N‑oxide to the parent amine; NaBH₄ delivers hydride to the N‑oxide, converting N,N‑dimethylbenzylamine N‑oxide back to N,N‑dimethylbenzylamine. Reaction performed in protic or aprotic solvent (methanol, EtOH, THF) at 0 °C to rt, often under inert atmosphere.

Redox (halogen–peroxide) reaction; chlorine oxidizes the peroxide anion in potassium peroxide, yielding molecular oxygen and chloride ions which combine with potassium to give KCl. Typically carried out in aqueous solution at low to moderate temperature; reaction is exothermic and may be initiated by gentle heating.

SN2 O‑alkylation (methylation) of a phenol; the phenoxide of eugenol attacks methyl p‑toluenesulfonate, displacing p‑toluenesulfonic acid and forming methyleugenol. Conducted in aprotic polar solvent (acetone, DMF) with a base (NaH, K₂CO₃) at rt to reflux.

Electrophilic alpha‑halogenation of a ketone; purpose is to install an iodine atom at the α‑position of acetone to give 1‑iodopropan‑2‑one while generating HI. Key transformation: enol formation of acetone followed by attack of I₂ activated by trifluoroacetic acid, yielding the α‑iodoketone and hydrogen iodide. Typical conditions: anhydrous trifluoroacetic acid as solvent, excess I₂, 0 °C to room temperature, reaction monitored under inert atmosphere. No external catalyst needed beyond the strong acid.

Chlorine‑mediated oxidation; industrial route to indigo using bleach.oxyl is oxidized by sodium hypochlorite, dimerizing to indigo while chloride is reduced to NaCl and water forms. Conducted in aqueous alkaline medium (5–10 % NaOCl), temperature 0–25 °C to avoid over‑oxidation; water is the solvent and no extra catalyst is needed.

Metathesis (halide exchange) precipitation; used to synthesize dysprosium(III) fluoride from the chloride; Cl⁻ ions are replaced by F⁻ ions giving solid DyF₃ and soluble KCl; performed in aqueous solution with excess KF, heated under reflux with stirring, then filtered and washed; water as solvent, no catalyst required.

Alkaline hydrolysis (saponification) of an amide; purpose is to convert 2‑hydroxyacetamide into its sodium carboxylate and release ammonia. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of OH⁻ on the carbonyl carbon, formation of a tetrahedral intermediate, collapse to give sodium 2‑hydroxyacetate and NH₃. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH solution (1 equiv), heating at 50–100 °C for 1–3 h. Solvent is water; no additional catalyst required.

Acid–base neutralization (protonation of a carboxylate); the sodium salt is treated with aqueous HCl, converting the carboxylate to the free carboxylic acid and forming NaCl. Usually performed at ambient temperature in water or a water‑organic mixture.

Gas‑phase reduction (hydrogenolysis) reaction; hydrogen reduces TiCl₄ to TiCl₃, generating HCl gas; key transformation: Ti⁴⁺ → Ti³⁺, H₂ → 2 H⁺ + 2 e⁻; carried out in a tubular furnace under a flow of H₂ at high temperature (≈500–650 °C); no solvent; reactor typically stainless steel or quartz; no catalyst required.

Redox dissolution of a metal oxide in acid; purpose is to reduce Mn(III) to Mn(II) while oxidizing chloride to chlorine gas. Key transformation: Mn₂O₃ reacts with concentrated HCl, producing MnCl₂, Cl₂ and water. Typical conditions: excess concentrated HCl, reflux or gentle heating, performed in a glass vessel with a gas‑collection setup. Solvent is aqueous HCl; reaction proceeds without added catalyst.

Metal‑mediated reduction of a lanthanide halide; purpose is to generate the divalent europium compound EuBr₂ from the trivalent EuBr₃. Key transformation: potassium metal donates electrons to Eu³⁺, reducing it to Eu²⁺ and forming KBr as the by‑product. Typical conditions: dry, oxygen‑free THF or diethyl ether, low temperature (−78 °C to 0 °C), inert atmosphere (argon or nitrogen). No catalyst; stoichiometric potassium metal is required.

Periodate oxidation of vicinal diol to quinone; 9,10‑anthracenediol is oxidized by sodium periodate to 9,10‑anthraquinone with concomitant formation of sodium iodate; typically run in a mixture of acetone and water at room temperature, sometimes buffered to pH ≈ 7, with NaIO₄ as the stoichiometric oxidant.

Grignard carboxylation; tert‑butylmagnesium bromide adds to carbon dioxide to form the corresponding magnesium carboxylate, which upon acidic work‑up yields 2,2‑dimethylpropanoic acid; reaction performed in dry ether (diethyl ether or THF) at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen; CO₂ is introduced as a gas; followed by dilute HCl quench.

Oxidation of secondary phosphine to phosphine oxide; diphenylphosphine reacts with molecular oxygen to give diphenylphosphine oxide; can be carried out under an O₂ atmosphere (1 atm) in an inert organic solvent such as toluene or THF at 25–80 °C, often without additional catalyst though trace metal salts may accelerate the reaction.

POCl₃‑promoted condensation/cyclodehydration to synthesize pirfenidone; combines 4‑methylacetophenone with 2‑aminopyridine forming a heterocyclic amide ring; phosphorus oxychloride acts as both dehydrating agent and solvent, facilitating imine formation and intramolecular cyclization; reaction usually refluxed neat POCl₃ at 80‑120 °C under nitrogen; work‑up involves quenching with ice water and neutralization; no additional catalyst required.

Direct synthesis of silicon disulfide (SiS₂) from elemental silicon and sulfur; a high‑temperature combination reaction forming Si–S bonds; silicon powder and sulfur are mixed and heated to 500‑1000 °C in a sealed quartz ampoule or under flowing inert gas; the reaction proceeds without solvent; product is obtained as a solid condensate after cooling.

Redox generation of nitric oxide from nitrous acid and sodium ascorbate; ascorbate reduces HNO₂ yielding NO, water and dehydroascorbic acid; performed in aqueous buffer (pH 4‑6) at room temperature; concentrations typically 0.1‑10 mM; no catalyst needed, though mild stirring and exclusion of oxygen improve yield; common solvents: phosphate‑buffered saline.

Reductive halogenation (hydrogen reduction): molybdenum pentachloride is reduced by hydrogen gas, lowering molybdenum from +5 to +2 to give molybdenum dichloride and hydrogen chloride; conducted at high temperature (≈200‑400 °C) in a sealed tube or flow reactor under inert atmosphere, no additional catalyst.

Thermal decomposition of rhenium pentachloride to rhenium trichloride and chlorine gas; heating ReCl₅ induces reductive elimination of Cl₂, lowering oxidation state of rhenium; carried out at 200‑300 °C under inert atmosphere (argon) to control chlorine release; reaction performed in a sealed tube or flow reactor; no solvent or catalyst required.
