Type: acid dissolution/complexation of a metal oxide; purpose: prepare a soluble gold(III) bromide complex; key transformation: Au2O3 + 6 HBr → 2 HAuBr4 + 3 H2O (formation of tetrabromoauric acid and water); typical conditions: reflux or gentle heating in concentrated hydrobromic acid, aqueous solution; common solvent: water/HBr; no catalyst needed.

Catalytic hydrogenation of 2‑nitrofuran to furan‑2‑amine; selective reduction of the nitro group to an amine while leaving the furan ring intact; uses H₂ gas (1–5 atm) with Pd/C or Raney Ni catalyst in ethanol or methanol at 25‑50 °C.

Acid‑base neutralization with oxidizing acid; calcium methoxide reacts with dilute nitric acid to produce calcium nitrate and methanol; reaction is performed at 0–5 °C in methanol or dilute aqueous medium, acid added slowly to control heat and minimize side oxidation; product isolated by evaporation of methanol.

Halogen displacement (redox) reaction; chlorine gas oxidizes bromide ions to elemental bromine while forming calcium chloride. Used to generate bromine in situ from inexpensive bromide salts. Typically carried out in aqueous solution at room temperature, no special solvent or catalyst required.

Double‑displacement precipitation reaction; aqueous barium chloride reacts with ammonium sulfide to precipitate insoluble barium sulfide and form soluble ammonium chloride. Employed for sulfide generation or removal of barium ions. Performed in water at room temperature with stirring; no catalyst needed.

Acid‑base salt formation; protonates the amine group of 2‑aminoindane with HCl to give the hydrochloride salt; purpose is to isolate a water‑soluble, stable form of the amine; usually performed by adding gaseous or aqueous HCl to a solution of the amine in ether, ethanol or dichloromethane at 0‑25 °C; no catalyst needed

Conversion of a dicarboxylic acid to the corresponding di‑acid chloride using thionyl chloride; propane‑1,3‑dicarboxylic acid is transformed into propanedioyl dichloride with evolution of HCl and SO₂ gases. Standard method for preparing acid chlorides for polymer or acylation chemistry. Typically refluxed in anhydrous dichloromethane or pyridine under inert atmosphere; by‑products are removed by gas venting.

Reductive amination of cyclohexanone with cyclohexylamine using sodium triacetoxyborohydride; the imine formed in situ is reduced to N‑cyclohexyl‑cyclohexylamine, generating acetic acid and sodium acetate as by‑products. Useful for synthesizing secondary amines under mild conditions. Carried out in dry dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to rt, often with a catalytic amount of acetic acid; NaBH(OAc)₃ serves as the mild hyd source.

Acidic decomposition of a ferrocyanide complex. Iron(III) ferrocyanide is treated with concentrated hydrochloric acid, leading to protonation and breakdown of the cyanide ligands, releasing hydrogen cyanide gas, forming iron(III) chloride and water. Conducted in a cold, well‑ventilated fume hood, often at 0–5 °C to control HCN evolution; stoichiometric excess HCl is used, and the reaction is usually performed in aqueous medium without catalyst.

Hydrolysis of thulium trichloride; aqueous TmCl₃ reacts with water, forming insoluble thulium(III) hydroxide precipitate and releasing hydrochloric acid; usually carried out in water with gentle heating to aid precipitation, no catalyst required.

Oxidation of 1,10‑phenanthroline to 1,10‑phenanthroline‑5,6‑dione using Oxone (potassium peroxymonosulfate) in aqueous medium; water acts as solvent and participates in proton transfer. Provides a straightforward route to the dione functional group on the heterocycle. Typically performed at ambient temperature in a mixture of water and an organic co‑solvent (e.g., acetone or MeCN); no additional catalyst is required.

General type: nucleophilic acyl substitution (aminolysis of an ester) with a primary amine. Purpose: synthesize an N‑methyl amide from the ester. Key transformation: methylamine attacks the carbonyl carbon of propyl benzoate, displaces the propoxy group, and forms N‑methylbenzamide while liberating 1‑propanol. Typical conditions: excess methylamine (often as a gas or 2 M solution in ethanol), reflux in a solvent such as ethanol or toluene at 80–120 °C for several hours. Sometimes a catalytic amount of base (e.g., triethylamine) is added to scavenge the released acid. No special catalyst needed.

Acid‑catalyzed transesterification; purpose: exchange the prop of propyl butanoate for a methoxy group, forming methyl butanoate and releasing 1‑propanol. Key transformation: methanol attacks the carbonyl of the ester, forming a tetrahedral intermediate that collapses with loss of the propoxy leaving group. Typical conditions: reflux in methanol with a catalytic amount of acid (e.g., 1–5 % H₂SO₄, p‑TsOH) or a base catalyst (e.g., NaOMe); removal of 1‑propanol by distillation drives the equilibrium. Common solvent: excess methanol itself.

0 Acid‑metal reaction; zinc metal reacts with acetic acid to liberate hydrogen gas and form zinc acetate; typically conducted by adding zinc turnings to glacial acetic acid or aqueous acetic acid and heating under reflux; no catalyst required; solvent is the acetic acid medium itself.

Skeletal isomerization of a branched C8 alkane, shifting the methyl substituent from the 2‑position to the 3‑position via intramolecular hydride or alkyl migration; carried out over solid acidic catalysts such as zeolite H‑ZSM‑5 or Pt/Al₂O₃ at 300–450 °C, often in the gas phase with a hydrogen stream to suppress coke formation; no separate solvent.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction) of 1‑benzylisoquinoline to the fully saturated 1‑benzyl‑1,2,3,4‑tetrahydroisoquinoline; performed with molecular hydrogen (1–5 atm) in the presence of a metal catalyst (Pd/C, PtO₂, Raney Ni) in an alcoholic solvent (ethanol or methanol) at 25–80 °C; purpose is to saturate the heterocyclic ring and remove aromatic character.

Acid‑catalyzed electrophilic addition of ethanol to 2‑methyl‑1‑butene, giving a tertiary alkyl ethyl ether (2‑ethoxy‑2‑methylbutane); carried out with excess ethanol and a strong Brønsted acid such as concentrated H₂SO₄ or H₃PO₄ at 0–30 °C to avoid rearrangements; the alcohol serves both reactant and solvent.

Acid digestion of strontium telluride with hydrochloric acid, producing hydrogen telluride gas and strontium chloride; typically carried out by adding solid SrTe to aqueous HCl at room temperature to gentle reflux, with vigorous stirring; no catalyst; H₂Te gas is collected under an inert atmosphere due to its toxicity.

Double‑replacement (metathesis) reaction between aqueous hydrochloric acid and lanthanum nitrate, yielding lanthanum chloride and nitric acid; performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; often used to exchange the anion of a lanthanide salt; no catalyst required.

Intramolecular phosphoryl‑transfer isomerization catalyzed by phosphoglycerate mutase; purpose is to reposition the phosphate group for subsequent glycolytic steps; key transformation: conversion of 3‑phosphoglycerate to 2‑phosphoglycerate via a phospho‑histidine intermediate; physiological conditions (pH ≈ 7.5, 37 °C) in aqueous buffer; requires 2,3‑bisphosphoglycerate (cofactor) for the cofactor‑dependent isoform or Mg²⁺ for the metal‑dependent isoform.

Lewis‑acid‑catalyzed halogen exchange (nucleophilic substitution) of chloro‑difluoromethane with hydrogen bromide; AlCl₃ activates the carbon center, allowing replacement of chlorine by bromine to form bromodifluoromethane and HCl; carried out under anhydrous conditions in an inert organic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride) at 0–30 °C.

Acid‑base metathesis between ammonium bromate and sulfuric acid; purpose is to produce ammonium hydrogen sulfate and bromic acid in situ; key transformation: proton transfer from H₂SO₄ to NH₄⁺ forming NH₄HSO₄ and generation of HBrO₃; typical conditions: aqueous solution kept cool (0‑25 °C) to avoid further decomposition; solvent: water; no catalyst.

Condensation/complex formation of hydrogen peroxide with urea to give carbamide peroxide (peroxyurea). The reaction proceeds in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, often under neutral to slightly acidic pH; no catalyst is required. The product precipitates on cooling and is isolated by filtration.

Halogen exchange / dealkylation of a trialkylborane. Chlorine gas substitutes for the methyl groups on BMe₃, producing BCl₃ and CH₃Cl. The reaction proceeds by stepwise replacement of B‑Me bonds with B‑Cl, often under UV irradiation or at low temperature (–78 °C to 0 °C) in the gas phase; no solvent or catalyst is needed.

Friedel‑Crafts alkylation (acid‑catalyzed electrophilic aromatic substitution) of phenol with 1‑nonene. Sulfuric acid protonates the alkene to generate a nonyl carbocation which attacks the aromatic ring, giving nonylphenol and water. Conducted at 60–100 °C with excess phenol acting as solvent; strong acid (≥95 % H₂SO₄) is the only catalyst.

Electrophilic aromatic bromination of anthracene to afford 9,10‑dibromoanthracene. bromine (Br₂) adds across the 9‑ and 10‑positions; carbon tetrachloride serves as an inert solvent and may aid radical initiation under light or heat. Typical conditions: reflux or photochemical activation in CCl₄, no additional catalyst required.

Hydrolysis (SN1 nucleophilic substitution) of benzyl iodide to benzyl alcohol with concomitant formation of hydrogen iodide. Conducted in aqueous medium, often heated (50–80 °C) or with a catalytic amount of acid/base; use of a base (e.g., NaOH) is common to trap HI and drive the reaction to completion.

Alkaline hydrolysis (saponification) of a phenyl ester. NaOH attacks the carbonyl carbon, cleaving the C–O bond to give the sodium salt of 2‑methylpropanoic acid and phenolate, which upon acid work‑up yields phenol. Typically performed in aqueous NaOH (1–2 M) at reflux (80‑100 °C) in water or water/ethanol.

Swern oxidation of 2,2‑dimethyl‑1‑propanol to 2,2‑dimethylpropanal. Oxalyl chloride activates dimethyl sulfoxide at –78 °C in anhydrous dichloromethane, forming the chlorosulfonium intermediate; addition of the alcohol followed by triethylamine generates the aldehyde and dimethyl sulfide by‑product. Reaction is performed under inert atmosphere, low temperature, and requires careful quenching.

Transesterification: dimethyl phthalate reacts with excess isopropanol to exchange the methyl ester groups for isopropyl groups, producing diisopropyl phthalate and methanol; typically acid‑catalyzed (e.g., p‑TsOH) or base‑catalyzed (e.g., NaOMe) under reflux, with excess isopropanol as solvent and removal of methanol to drive equilibrium.

Halide exchange (metathesis): palladium(II) chloride is treated with hydrofluoric acid, resulting in palladium(II) fluoride and hydrogen chloride; performed in aqueous HF or HF/acetone at low temperature (0–25 °C) in PTFE‑lined equipment, excess HF pushes the reaction forward.

Fischer esterification of 4‑methylpentanoic acid with ethanol to afford ethyl 4‑methylpentanoate; acid‑catalyzed under reflux in excess ethanol using a catalytic amount of strong acid (H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH); water by‑product is removed (Dean–Stark or azeotropic distillation) to drive the reaction to completion.

Williamson ether synthesis (SN2 O‑alkylation): phenol is deprotonated by a base (NaOH, K2CO₃) to give phenoxide, which attacks allyl iodide to afford allyl phenyl ether and HI; carried out in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetone or DMF at 0–25 °C under inert atmosphere, with the base neutralizing the generated HI.

Single‑electron transfer reductive ring opening. Samarium(II) chloride reduces cyclohexene oxide, opening the epoxide to give cyclohexanol. Carried out in dry THF (often with HMPA) at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; SmCl₂ is the reductant, no additional catalyst.

Reductive amination (single methylation) of dopamine with formaldehyde; purpose is to install a methyl group on the primary amine to afford N‑methyl dopamine; key steps: formation of an imine (or iminium ion) from dopamine and formaldehyde, followed by hydride reduction with sodium cyanoborohydride; typical conditions: methanol or ethanol/water solvent, pH ~7–8 (buffered with acetate), NaBH₃CN added at 0 °C then warmed to rt, reaction time 1–3 h.

Alkaline hydrolysis (saponification) of an amide: 4‑hydroxybutyramide reacts with aqueous sodium hydroxide, cleaving the C–N bond to furnish sodium 4‑hydroxybutyrate and ammonia; heated reflux (80–100 °C) in water, followed by optional acidification to isolate the free acid.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of an α‑bromo ketone: aqueous ammonia displaces bromide from 2‑bromo‑1‑phenylpropan‑1‑one, yielding 2‑amino‑1‑phenylpropan‑1‑one and hydrogen bromide; conducted at 0–5 °C in aqueous or ethanolic ammonia to minimize elimination, with HBr remaining in solution.

Oxidation of aldehyde to carboxylic acid: iodoacetaldehyde is oxidized by hydrogen peroxide to iodoacetic acid, producing water; typically performed in aqueous 30 % H₂O₂ at ambient temperature, optionally buffered (pH ≈ 7) or with a catalytic amount of a transition‑metal catalyst (e.g., Fe²⁺, Ti‑silicalite) to enhance rate.

Acid‑base precipitation (neutralization) forming aluminium molybdate; aqueous double‑replacement reaction where molybdic acid (H2MoO4) reacts with aluminium hydroxide (Al(OH)3) to give Al2(MoO4)3 solid and water; typically carried out in water at ambient to mild heating with stirring; no special catalyst required.

Ozonolysis (oxidative cleavage) of an allylic alkene; cleavage of the C=C bond of allyl alcohol produces glycolaldehyde and formaldehyde. Allyl alcohol is dissolved in a low‑temperature aprotic solvent (e.g., CH₂Cl₂) and bubbled with O₃ at –78 °C, then worked up reductively (e.g., dimethyl sulfide) to afford the aldehydes. This is a standard ozonolysis protocol for generating carbonyl fragments from alkenes.

Redox oxidation of manganese dioxide in strongly alkaline medium (alkaline chlorination); chlorine gas oxidizes Mn(IV) in MnO2 to permanganate (Mn(VII)) while being reduced to chloride; overall yields NaMnO4, NaCl and water; performed in aqueous NaOH solution (≈10 M) with Cl2 bubbled at 0–25 °C, often with cooling to control exotherm; no additional catalyst.

Acid‑catalyzed depolymerisation (hydrolysis) of phenol‑formaldehyde resin; concentrated HCl cleaves the methylene bridges, releasing phenol and formaldehyde; usually conducted in aqueous HCl (1–3 M) under reflux (80–120 °C) for several hours; HCl itself acts as catalyst, no other reagents needed.

Aluminothermic (thermite‑type) reduction of indium oxide; aluminum metal reduces In2O3 to indium metal while being oxidised to Al2O3; a solid‑state redox reaction ignited at high temperature (≈1200 °C) in a dry powder mixture, often under inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation; no solvent or catalyst, heat is the driving force.

Carbamate formation by carboxylation of a primary amine; methylamine reacts with carbon dioxide to afford methylcarbamic acid (methyl carbamate). The process typically uses pressurized CO₂ (1–5 atm) in an aqueous or mixed solvent system at room temperature to mild heating (25‑60 °C). No additional catalyst is required; the amine acts as a nucleophile and base to capture CO₂.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (hydrazinolysis) of succinic anhydride; hydrazine opens the anhydride ring, forming succinic hydrazide and water; usually carried out in refluxing ethanol or methanol (50–80 °C) with excess hydrazine; optional catalytic amount of acid or base can accelerate the reaction, but not essential.

Acid‑catalyzed amide hydrolysis (deacetylation); converts N‑(3‑phenylpropyl)acetamide back to 3‑phenylpropylamine and acetic acid; performed by refluxing the amide in aqueous HCl (conc. 6 M) or in a mixture of HCl/water/organic co‑solvent; the acid provides both protonation of the carbonyl and the driving force for cleavage.

Classical neutralization of a strong sulfonic acid; the vinylsulfonic acid is deprotonated by NaOH, producing sodium vinylsulfonate and water. Reaction is carried out in water or aqueous methanol, typically at 0 °C to room temperature to control exotherm. Stoichiometric NaOH (1 equiv) is sufficient; no catalyst is required.

Redox dissolution of a metal oxide: Concentrated HNO3 oxidizes CeO2, reducing nitrate to NO2 while forming cerium(III) nitrate and water. Purpose is to convert insoluble CeO2 into a soluble nitrate salt. Typical conditions involve heating the mixture under reflux with excess conc. HNO3, generating brown NO2 gas. Reaction performed in aqueous nitric acid; no additional catalyst needed.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an aromatic system: Naphthalene is partially reduced by H2 in the presence of Pd/C to give 1,2,3,4‑tetrahydronaphthalene (tetralin). The reaction serves to saturate one benzene ring while leaving the other aromatic. Conducted under H2 pressure (1–5 atm) at 25–80 °C in a protic solvent such as ethanol or methanol; palladium on carbon acts as the catalyst.

Condensation/cyclization to a carbazole derivative: 2‑Aminobiphenyl reacts with acetaldehyde in an acidic medium, undergoing a cyclodehydration to afford 9‑methylcarbazole with loss of water. The transformation builds the fused heteroaromatic carbazole core and introduces a methyl substituent at the 9‑position. Typical conditions employ polyphosphoric acid or concentrated H2SO4 at 120–180 °C, often using a high‑boiling solvent like diphenyl ether; no external catalyst other than the acid is required.

Oxidative fluorination of a saturated hydrocarbon: Cyclohexane is fluorinated by excess cobalt(III) fluoride, which acts as a powerful fluorine donor and oxidant, replacing all hydrogen atoms with fluorine to give perfluorocyclohexane. The reaction also reduces Co(III) to Co(II) and liberates HF. It is carried out at elevated temperatures (≈200–300 °C) in an inert atmosphere; solid CoF3 serves both as fluorine source and oxidant, no solvent is generally used.

Halogen exchange (metathesis) between chlorine and arsenic tribromide: Molecular chlorine reacts with AsBr3 to produce arsenic trichloride and bromine gas. The process swaps halogens on the arsenic center and is driven by the higher volatility of Br2. Typically performed in a sealed tube or gas‑flow apparatus at room temperature to mild heating; inert solvents such as carbon tetrachloride or dry chloroform can be used to dissolve the reagents, but the reaction proceeds without a catalyst.

Acid-induced formation of chromyl chloride from sodium dichromate; purpose similar to the potassium analogue, generating CrO2Cl2; key transformation is conversion of dichromate to chromyl chloride with formation of NaCl and water; performed with concentrated HCl, gentle heating, under anhydrous conditions, no extra solvent needed.

Methyl ester formation using diazomethane (Diazomethylation): Cyclopentanecarboxylic acid is treated with diazomethane, which transfers a methyl group to the acid, yielding methyl cyclopentanecarboxylate and liberating nitrogen gas. This is a mild, chemoselective esterification often employed for sensitive substrates. The reaction is carried out at 0 °C to rt in anhydrous diethyl ether or benzene under inert atmosphere; no catalyst is required, and excess diazomethane is quenched carefully.

Base‑catalyzed ester saponification. Phenyl 2,2‑dichloroacetate is hydrolyzed with aqueous NaOH, cleaving the ester to give sodium phenoxide and sodium 2,2‑dichloroacetate. Conditions: aqueous NaOH (1–2 equiv), reflux (50–80 °C) until completion, followed by acidification if the phenol is desired. Purpose: conversion of an ester to its corresponding phenoxide salt and carboxylate.

Catalytic dehydrogenation of a saturated cyclic alkane; purpose is to convert ethylcyclohexane into the corresponding olefin (ethylcyclohexene) by removal of H₂. Key transformation: C–H bonds of the alkane are broken and a C=C double bond is formed, releasing molecular hydrogen. Typical conditions: high temperature (300‑450 °C) under inert atmosphere, often gas‑phase or in high‑boiling inert solvent. Common catalysts: supported platinum, palladium, nickel, or bimetallic systems (e.g., Pt‑Sn/Al₂O₃); sometimes a hydrogen acceptor (e.g., propene) is used to drive the equilibrium.

Catalytic hydrocyanation (addition) of 1,3‑butadiene with hydrogen cyanide to afford adiponitrile. The process uses a nickel–phosphine complex (e.g., NiCl₂/PPh₃) as catalyst under high HCN pressure (≈30–60 atm) and moderate temperature (80–120 °C) in an aprotic solvent such as THF or dimethylformamide. The reaction adds two equivalents of HCN across the diene, forming the dinitrile product.

Nucleophilic aromatic substitution (halide metathesis) of 2‑chloropyridine with silverrite; purpose is to install a nitro group onto the pyridine ring. Key transformation: AgNO₂ supplies nitrite/nitro nucleophile that displaces chloride, forming 2‑nitropyridine and precipitating AgCl. Typical conditions: reflux in polar aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile or DMF, often under inert atmosphere; stoichiometric AgNO₂ (or catalytic AgNO₂ with an oxidant). The insoluble AgCl is filtered off after the reaction.

Reduction of a carboxylic acid to a primary alcohol using lithium aluminium hydride; purpose is to convert benzoic acid into benzyl alcohol. Key transformation: the C=O of the carboxyl group is reduced through a hydride delivery sequence, replacing the –CO₂H function with –CH₂OH and generating Al‑containing by‑products. Typical conditions: anhydrous ether (diethyl ether or THF) at 0 °C to reflux under nitrogen or argon; LiAlH₄ is added portionwise, and the reaction is quenched cautiously with water then dilute acid. No additional catalyst is required.

Hydrolysis of an amide to a carboxylic acid and ammonia; purpose is to cleave the 2,2‑difluoroacetamide bond to give 2,2‑difluoroacetic acid and free ammonia. Key transformation: water attacks the carbonyl carbon, leading to tetrahedral intermediate that collapses, expelling NH₃ and forming the acid. Typical conditions: either acidic (e.g., 6 M HCl) or basic (e.g., NaOH) aqueous medium, heated to reflux (80‑100 °C) for several hours. In neutral water the reaction is very slow; catalysis by acid or base is standard.

Acid‑base neutralization/salt formation between sodium hydroxide and ammonium dihydrogen phosphate; purpose is to generate the mixed ammonium‑sodium phosphate salt and water. Key transformation: OH⁻ deprotonates the acidic phosphate proton, converting NH₄⁺H₂PO₄⁻ to NH₄⁺HPO₄²⁻ while Na⁺ replaces the protonated species, yielding NH₄NaHPO₄ and H₂O. Typical conditions: aqueous solution at ambient temperature; stoichiometric amounts (1 equiv NaOH per 1 equiv NH₄H₂PO₄). No special solvent beyond water; reaction proceeds readily with stirring.

Reduction of a long‑chain fatty acid (eicosanoic/arachidic acid) to the corresponding primary alcohol using lithium aluminium hydride; purpose is to obtain eicosanol (C₂₀ alcohol). Key transformation: the carboxyl group is fully reduced to a –CH₂OH group via hydride transfer from LiAlH₄, with formation of aluminium‑based by‑products. Typical conditions: dry ether solvent (THF or diethyl ether), 0 °C to reflux under inert atmosphere, careful quench with water and dilute acid after completion. No additional catalyst is required.

Epoxidation of an alkene using a peracid; peracetic acid transfers an electrophilic oxygen to the C=C double bond of cyclopentene to give cyclopentene oxide. Typical conditions: dilute peracetic acid (often generated in situ) in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform, temperature 0 °C to ambient, reaction proceeds added catalyst.

Halogen displacement/redox solid‑state reaction; iodine oxidizes selenium from –2 in Rb2Se to elemental Se (0) while being reduced to I⁻ forming RbI. Typically performed by grinding the solids together and heating at 200‑300 °C in an inert atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst required.

Selective carbonyl reduction; sodium borohydride delivers hydride to the keto group of chloroacetone, converting it to the secondary alcohol 1‑chloro‑2‑propanol while leaving the α‑chloro substituent intact. Commonly performed in methanol or ethanol at 0 °C to room temperature; work‑up with water or dilute acid yields sodium borate as by‑product.

Acid‑catalyzed amide hydrolysis (decomposition); N,N‑dimethylbutanamide is protonated by aqueous HCl, water attacks the carbonyl, yielding dimethylammonium chloride (as its salt) and butanoic acid; typically refluxed in 5–10 % HCl aqueous solution for several hours; water is the reaction medium.

Acid‑base neutralization and salt formation; hydrogen bromide protonates yttrium carbonate, releasing three equivalents of CO₂ and three equivalents of H₂O while the yttrium cation pairs with bromide to form yttrium(III) bromide (YBr₃). Usually carried out by bubbling HBr gas into an aqueous suspension of the carbonate or by adding aqueous HBr solution, often at reflux to ensure complete gas evolution.

Oxidation of α‑hydroxy acids; chromium(VI) oxide in the presence of concentrated sulfuric acid oxidizes glycolic acid to glyoxylic acid, reducing Cr(VI) to Cr(III) which complexes as chromium(III) sulfate. Reaction is performed in aqueous sulfuric acid, temperature maintained 0–25 °C to control exotherm; the mixture is later quenched and extracted.

Halogen exchange / direct fluorination; elemental fluorine reacts with phosphorus pentachloride, replacing chlorine atoms with fluorine to generate phosphorus pentafluoride and chlorine monofluoride (ClF) as a gaseous by‑product. Conducted in a fluorine‑resistant apparatus, often at elevated temperature (100–200 °C) under anhydrous, inert atmosphere; no solvent is typically used.

Thermal isomerization (rearrangement); solid ammonium thiocyanate, when heated to about 180 °C, undergoes a structural rearrangement to the isomeric ammonium cyanate. Reaction proceeds in the solid state without solvent; the cyanate can subsequently be hydrolyzed or further reacted.

Double displacement (metathesis) reaction; manganese(II) dihydroxide reacts with sodium carbonate to precipitate manganese(II) carbonate while forming sodium hydroxide in solution. Mn(OH)₂(s) + Na₂CO₃(aq) → MnCO₃(s) + 2 NaOH(aq). Carried out in aqueous medium at ambient temperature with stirring; no catalyst required.

Metathesis/transmetalation between cadmium oxide and dimethylzinc; methyl groups transfer from zinc to cadmium forming dimethylcadmium and zinc oxide precipitate; carried out under anhydrous inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar) in dry ether or THF at 0‑25 °C; no catalyst required.

Oxidative hydrolysis of a boronic acid; hydrogen peroxide oxidizes the C–B bond of methylboronic acid to give methanol while the boron is converted to boric acid. This reaction is used to deprotect boronic acids or to generate primary alcohols from organoboranes. It proceeds in aqueous medium, often with a mild base (e.g., NaOH or Na2CO3) to neutralize the formed acid. Typical conditions are ambient temperature to 40 °C, using 30 % H2O2 solution; water or a water‑mixed organic solvent (e.g., THF/H2O) serves as the reaction medium.

Schotten‑Baumann amidation (acyl chloride amidation); benzoyl chloride reacts with the amino group of 4‑aminosalicylic acid under basic aqueous‑organic biphasic conditions to afford the N‑benzoyl amide. The purpose is to derivatize the amine, often for protection or to modify physicochemical properties. The reaction is carried out at 0 °C to room temperature with NaOH (or NaHCO3) as the base, typically using dichloromethane or ethyl acetate as the organic phase. The generated HCl is scavenged by the aqueous base, and the product is isolated after acid–base work‑up.

Enzymatic methyl transfer; protopine is methylated by S‑adenosyl‑L‑methionine (SAM) in the presence of a specific methyltransferase enzyme to give cryptopine and S‑adenosyl‑L‑homocysteine (SAH). This biosynthetic step installs a methyl group on the alkaloid framework, often altering biological activity. Reactions are performed in buffered aqueous media (pH 7–8) at 25–37 °C, sometimes with Mg²⁺ as a cofactor. The enzyme is required for regio‑ and stereospecificity; no organic solvent is normally needed.

Nucleophilic aromatic substitution (S_NAr) on a triazine ring; aqueous ammonia attacks the chlorine‑substituted carbon of 2,4-diamino-6-chlorotriazine, displacing chloride as hydrogen chloride and converting the heterocycle into melamine (1,3,5‑triazine‑2,4,6‑triamine); usually heated to 80–120 °C in aqueous NH₃.

Double‑displacement/precipitation reaction; purpose is to generate insoluble calcium carbonate while forming soluble potassium chloride and evolving CO₂; key transformation: Ca²⁺ from calcium chloride combines with HCO₃⁻ to precipitate CaCO₃, with concurrent formation of CO₂ and H₂O; typical conditions: aqueous solution, ambient temperature, vigorous stirring; water is the only solvent, no catalyst required.

Thermal decomposition of indium(III) phosphate; upon strong heating, the solid indium phosphate breaks down to indium(III) oxide (In₂O₃) and phosphorus pentoxide (P₂O₅). This solid‑state reaction is used for the preparation of high‑purity In₂O₃ or for generating P₂O₅ as a dehydrating agent. It requires temperatures typically above 500 °C in a furnace under air or inert gas. No solvents or catalysts are involved; the reaction proceeds via direct lattice breakdown.

Cross‑aldol (Knoevenagel) condensation of benzaldehyde with 4‑methoxy‑acetophenone; base‑catalyzed (NaOH, KOH) in ethanol/water, reflux; produces the chalcone (E)‑1‑(4‑methoxyphenyl)‑3‑phenylprop‑2‑en‑1‑one and water by dehydration of the β‑hydroxy intermediate.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution (basic hydrolysis); replaces the sulfonate leaving group with hydroxide to give butanol and the sodium salt of methanesulfonic acid. Conducted in aqueous NaOH (1–2 M) often in a water/ethanol mixture, heated to 50‑80 °C; no catalyst needed; solvent: water/ethanol.

Thiazolidine cyclocondensation; the primary amine of cysteine attacks acetaldehyde to form an imine, followed by intramolecular attack of the thiol, yielding 2‑methyl‑1,3‑thiazolidine‑4‑carboxylic acid and water. Performed in water or methanol at ambient temperature, often at neutral to slightly acidic pH; no added catalyst needed.

General type: direct synthesis (interhalogen formation). Purpose: generation of iodine monofluoride, a transient fluorinating species. Key transformation: I2 + F2 → 2 IF, forming I–F bonds. Typical conditions: performed at very low temperature (‑78 °C to ‑30 °C) in a sealed vessel with dry gases; IF is unstable, so the reaction is kept cold and the product is used in situ. No solvent or catalyst required.

Type: base‑catalyzed condensation polymerization. Purpose: synthesis of phenolic resin for adhesives, coatings, foams. Key transformation: phenol reacts with the dialdehyde glyoxal under NaOH to form phenolic methylol intermediates that condense, eliminating water and creating a cross‑linked network. Typical conditions: aqueous or alcoholic medium, NaOH (5–15 % w/w), temperatures 90–120 °C, reaction time 1–4 h. Common solvent/catalyst: water or methanol as solvent; NaOH serves as catalyst.

Type: electrophilic aromatic substitution (halogenation). Purpose: selective bromination of indole at the C‑3 position. Key transformation: pyridinium tribromide delivers Br⁺ which attacks the electron‑rich 3‑position of indole, giving 3‑bromoindole and generating pyridinium bromide as the acid–base by‑product. Typical conditions: room temperature to 0 °C, solvent such as acetonitrile or dichloromethane, inert atmosphere optional. No additional catalyst required.

Type: oxidation (As(III) → As(V)). Purpose: convert the toxic monomethylarsonous acid (CH₃AsO₂⁻) to the less toxic methylarsonic acid (CH₃AsO₃H). Key transformation: H₂O₂ transfers an oxygen atom to the arsenic centre, increasing its oxidation state from +3 to +5. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, pH 4–7, temperature 25–60 °C, stoichiometric or slight excess H₂O₂. No metal catalyst needed; sometimes acidic buffer used to stabilize species.

Double‑displacement/precipitation reaction; thorium tetrafluoride reacts with aqueous ammonium hydroxide to precipitate thorium hydroxide (Th(OH)₄) while forming soluble ammonium fluoride (NH₄F) in solution. Performed in water at room temperature to moderate heat; stirring aids precipitation, no catalyst required.

Type: metal‑hydride reduction of a ketone. Purpose: reduce acetophenone to the corresponding secondary alcohol, 1‑phenylethanol. Key transformation: CaAlH₄ delivers hydride to the carbonyl carbon, forming an alkoxide that after work‑up yields 1‑phenylethanol; calcium and aluminum are converted to their respective hydroxides. Typical conditions: anhydrous ether (THF or diethyl ether), 0 °C to room temperature, inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar). No additional catalyst; reaction quen with dilute acid or water.

Aqueous double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction; ammonium chloride reacts with sodium hexafluorosilicate to give sodium chloride and ammonium hexafluorosilicate; carried out at room temperature in water; no catalyst required; product precipitates upon cooling.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a sulfonyl chloride; ethanol attacks methanesulfonyl chloride to form ethyl methanesulfonate with release of HCl; commonly run in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane with a base (e.g., pyridine or triethylamine) to scavenge HCl, at 0 °C to room temperature.

Acid–base neutralization of tetrafluoroboric acid with cobalt(II) oxide. The basic oxide reacts with aqueous HBF₄, yielding cobalt(II) tetrafluoroborate and water. Typical conditions involve suspending CoO in water, adding HBF₄ dropwise while heating to 60‑80 °C to ensure complete dissolution. The reaction is straightforward and does not require additional solvents beyond water.

Acid‑catalyzed hydration (electrophilic addition, Markovnikov); purpose is to convert hept‑2‑ene into the secondary alcohol 2‑heptanol; key steps are protonation of the alkene to a more stable carbocation followed by attack of water and deprotonation; carried out with dilute H₂SO₄ (or aqueous H₂SO₄) at 0–50 °C, often in aqueous medium; no organic solvent is required, though the reaction may be performed in a water/ether mixture to aid product extraction.

Ester hydrolysis of methyl acetate; under acidic conditions (dilute HCl or H2SO4) or basic saponification (NaOH aqueous), methyl acetate is cleaved to methanol and acetic acid; reflux is used for acid hydrolysis, while base hydrolysis proceeds at room temperature or mild heating followed by acidification; water serves as solvent, sometimes with a co‑solvent such as methanol.

Conversion of a secondary alcohol to the corresponding chloride using thionyl chloride (SOCl₂); purpose is to obtain 1‑phenyl‑2‑chloropropane; key transformation is replacement of the hydroxyl group by chlorine with loss of SO₂ and HCl; usually performed in an inert, aprotic solvent such as CH₂Cl₂ or pyridine at 0 °C to reflux, with pyridine or triethylamine added to scavenge the generated HCl.

Type: nucleophilic substitution (SN2) halide exchange (Finkelstein‑type). Purpose: replace bromine with iodine on acetonitrile substrate. Key transformation: I⁻ from NaI attacks the electrophilic carbon of bromacetonitrile, displacing Br⁻ to form iodoacetonitrile; NaBr precipitates (or remains in solution) as the by‑product. Typical conditions: polar aprotic solvent such as acetone or DMF, reflux (50–80 °C), excess NaI to drive equilibrium. No catalyst required.

Reduction of a nitrile to a primary amine; LiAlH4 serves as a strong hydride donor converting the –C≡N group of 3‑methoxybenzonitrile into a –CH2NH2 group to give 3‑methoxybenzylamine. Typically performed under anhydrous conditions in dry ether (diethyl ether or THF) at 0 °C to reflux, under nitrogen or argon. The reaction is quenched carefully with water or dilute acid after completion.

Reduction of a carboxylic acid to a primary alcohol; LiAlH4 reduces the –CO2H functionality of 4‑methoxybenzoic acid to a –CH2OH group, affording 4‑methoxybenzyl alcohol. Conducted in dry ether (diethyl ether or THF) at 0 °C to reflux under inert atmosphere; excess LiAlH4 is often used. Work‑up involves controlled hydrolysis with aqueous acid or alkali.

N‑alkylation (nucleophilic substitution) of a primary amine with an alkyl bromide to form a secondary amine (dicyclohexylamine) and hydrogen bromide as by‑product. The reaction proceeds via an SN2 pathway where cyclohexylamine attacks cyclohexyl bromide. It is usually carried out neat or in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., DMF, acetonitrile) at elevated temperature (80–120 °C). A base such as triethylamine or excess amine is added to scavenge the HBr and drive the reaction to completion.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) salt exchange between ammonium perchlorate and scandium nitrate in aqueous solution, yielding ammonium nitrate and scandium perchlorate. The reaction is performed by dissolving the two salts in water, stirring at ambient temperature, and allowing the new salts to remain in solution; no special catalyst is required. The products can be isolated by evaporation or crystallization.

Acid‑base neutralization forming a metal formate; two equivalents of formic acid react with solid silver oxide, a basic oxide, to produce water and silver formate (AgCOO). The reaction is carried out in a suspension of Ag2O in water or a mixed aqueous‑organic medium at room temperature, often with gentle stirring. No catalyst is needed; the process proceeds spontaneously due to the acid‑base driving force.

Metathesis/precipitation in aqueous solution; copper(II) sulfate reacts with potassium benzoate, forming copper(II) benzoate (insoluble) and potassium sulfate; usually carried out in water with gentle heating to aid precipitation; no catalyst necessary.

Stille‑type halogen exchange / cross‑coupling between bromoacetylene and phenyltributylstannane; typically Pd(0) (e.g., Pd(PPh3)4) or Cu(I) catalyzed, in THF or DMF, 50–80 °C; yields phenylacetylene and tributylbromostannane as the exchanged halide.

Acid‑base neutralization of a metal oxide; Fe₂O₃ reacts with aqueous hydrochloric acid to form iron(III) chloride solution and water; the oxide is protonated and chloride replaces the oxide ions; usually refluxed in moderate‑strength HCl (1‑6 M) to ensure complete dissolution; no catalyst required.

Base‑mediated decarboxylation of cannabidivarinic acid; sodium bicarbonate neutralizes the acid to its salt, which upon mild heating releases CO₂ and forms cannabidivarin; performed in aqueous or mixed aqueous–organic medium at 50–80 °C; no external catalyst needed.

Salt metesis (double‑displacement) ionic exchange; used to swap the counter‑ions of potassium bromide and ammonium hexafluorophosphate to generate ammonium bromide and potassium hexafluorophosphate (often the latter is desired as a non‑coordinating counter‑ion). The reaction proceeds in solution at ambient temperature, commonly in water or acetonitrile, with complete dissolution of both salts; no additional catalyst is needed.

Hydrogen reduction of a metal nitride; the reaction reduces praseodymium nitride to elemental praseodymium while liberating ammonia. It is a solid‑state high‑temperature process performed under a flow of H₂ gas (3 equiv per nitride) at 500‑800 °C in a tubular furnace. No solvent or catalyst is employed; the driving force is the thermodynamic stability of NH₃ and the metal.

Thermal solid‑state metathesis; heated sodium nitrate exchanges anions with beryllium chloride to produce beryllium nitrate, which sublimes, and solid sodium chloride. Conducted in a dry, inert atmosphere (e.g., nitrogen) at 300‑400 °C in a sealed tube or crucible. No solvent; the volatility of Be(NO₃)₂ allows its separation by condensation, while NaCl remains as a solid residue.

Complete combustion a hydrocarbon; 3‑methyl‑octane reacts with excess O₂ to yield CO₂ and H₂O, releasing heat. The reaction is initiated by ignition at the flash point (~200 °C) and proceeds in the gas phase under atmospheric pressure. No solvent or catalyst; the flame provides the necessary activation energy.

Reductive denitration of o‑nitrophenol using sodium dithionite in alkaline medium; the nitro group is reduced to an amine, forming 2‑aminophenol while dithionite is oxidized to bisulfite. Conducted in aqueous NaOH (pH ≈ 12) at 25‑80 °C, often under nitrogen to prevent oxidation. No metal catalyst is required; sodium dithionite acts as the stoichiometric reducing agent.

A³ (aldehyde‑alkyne‑amine) multicomponent coupling to form propargylamine; ammonia and formaldehyde generate an iminium intermediate that adds to propyne under Cu(I) or Ag(I) catalysis, usually in methanol or ethanol, 25–80 °C; water is the only by‑product.

Base‑catalyzed transesterification of octyl acetate with ethanol to give ethyl acetate and octanol. The ester exchange proceeds via nucleophilic attack of ethanol on the carbonyl, forming a tetrahedral intermediate that collapses to swap the alkoxy groups. Commonly carried out with catalytic NaOEt or K₂CO₃ in excess ethanol, refluxing 2–4 h; acid catalysis (e.g., H₂SO₄) is also possible.

Reductive amination of piperazine with 2,3,4‑trimethoxybenzaldehyde using sodium cyanoborohydride; the aldehyde forms an imine with one nitrogen of piperazine, which is then reduced to the secondary amine, giving trimetazidine. Usually performed in methanol or ethanol with a catalytic amount of acetic acid, 0 °C to ambient temperature.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction between potassium chromate and calcium chloride in aqueous solution, exchanging cations to give soluble potassium chloride and less‑soluble calcium chromate. No special reagents; carried out at room temperature in water.

Complete combustion of 2‑methylheptane in excess oxygen, producing carbon dioxide and water. Requires ignition and a high‑temperature flame; the reaction proceeds rapidly under atmospheric pressure with ample O₂.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration of 3‑methyl‑3‑buten2‑ol to 2‑methyl‑2‑butene, eliminating water. Conducted with concentrated H₂SO₄ under heating (≈130‑150 °C); the reaction follows an E1 mechanism, giving the more substituted alkene.

Thermal decomposition of silver oxalate upon heating, yielding metallic silver, carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide gases. Typically performed by gently warming the solid (≈180‑200 °C) in an inert atmosphere; the process is rapid and exothermic.

Reduction of a carboxylic acid to a primary alcohol using a strong hydride donor; purpose is to convert nonanoic acid into 1‑nonanol. Lithium aluminium hydride supplies H⁻, reducing the –COOH group to –CH₂OH. Typically performed in dry ether (diethyl ether or THF) under inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar) at 0 °C to reflux, followed by aqueous work‑up that generates aluminum hydroxide as by‑product.

Base‑ or acid‑catalyzed transesterification of 2‑phenylethyl propionate with ethanol to produce ethyl propionate and 2‑phenylethanol; typical conditions involve refluxing the ester mixture in excess ethanol with a catalyst such as NaOCH₃, K₂CO₃, or p‑TsOH; ethanol serves as solvent and nucleophile.

Metathesis (double‑displacement) precipitation reaction between oxalic acid and samarium(III) sulfate in aqueous solution; purpose is to isolate insoluble samarium(III) oxalate while producing sulfuric acid in solution. Conducted at ambient temperature with stirring; water serves as the solvent. The samarium oxalate precipitates and is collected by filtration.

Zinc‑mediated reductive dehalogenation of 2‑chloro‑1,1‑dimethoxyethane in acetic acid; zinc dust reduces the α‑chloroacetal, producing zinc chloride and acetaldehyde dimethyl acetal; reflux in glacial acetic acid, no additional catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed Fischer esterification of mandelic acid with methanol to afford methyl mandelate; sulfuric acid acts as a protonic catalyst, activating the carbonyl and promoting nucleophilic attack by methanol, with water formed as the only by‑product. Reaction is carried out by refluxing mandelic acid in excess methanol containing catalytic H₂SO₄, often with azeotropic removal of water (Dean‑Stark) to drive the equilibrium toward ester formation.

Aluminothermic (thermite‑type) redox reduction of antimony(III) oxide by metallic aluminum; aluminum is oxidized to Al₂O₃ while antimony(III) oxide is reduced to elemental antimony. Requires ignition at high temperature (typically >1000 °C) in a dry, inert environment; no solvent is used. The reaction is used to produce metallic antimony.

Reaction type: catalytic hydrogenation (reductive nitro‑to‑amine conversion). Purpose: convert the nitro group of 1‑nitro‑2,5‑dichlorobenzene into an aniline while preserving the chloro substituents. Key transformation: reduction of the nitro group to an amino group using H₂ gas. Typical conditions: 1–5 atm hydrogen pressure, 5 % Pd/C (by weight of substrate), solvent such as ethanol, methanol or ethyl acetate, temperature 25–50 °C, reaction time 1–6 h.

Hydration/precipitation of chromium(III) oxide to form chromium(III) hydroxide; Cr₂O₃ reacts with water (often under mildly acidic or basic conditions) to yield Cr(OH)₃ solid. Typically performed by suspending Cr₂O₃ in aqueous medium and adjusting pH to promote dissolution followed by precipitation of the hydroxide, which is then filtered or washed.

Oxymercuration of an alkene: mercuric acetate adds across the C=C of 2‑methyl‑2‑pentene to form a mercurinium intermediate; water attacks the more substituted carbon (Markovnikov) giving an organomercury alcohol which is then reduced (often with NaBH₄) to yield 2‑methylpentan‑2‑ol. Purpose is hydration of an alkene to a tertiary alcohol without carbocation rearrangement. Typical conditions: aqueous Hg(OAc)₂ in a miscible organic solvent (THF, acetone) at 0 °C to rt, followed by NaBH₄ or Na₂S work‑up. No strong acids or bases required.

Direct combination (halogenation) synthesis; elemental tellurium reacts with iodine to form tellurium tetraiodide (TeI4); heating Te and I2 together in a sealed, evacuated quartz tube or under inert atmosphere at 200‑300 °C yields the molecular solid; used to prepare TeI4 for inorganic chemistry; no solvent or catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution (alkylation of a secondary amine). The lone pair on the nitrogen of nornicotine attacks the methyl carbon of iodomethane in an SN2 process, forming nicotine (a tertiary amine) and releasing hydrogen iodide. Usually performed in an aprotic polar solvent such as acetone, DMF or MeCN with a weak base (e.g., K2CO3 or NaHCO3) to neutralize HI. Reaction is carried out at room temperature to reflux under inert atmosphere.

Metathesis/acid‑base neutralization: magnesium acetate reacts with two equivalents of taurine (2‑aminoethanesulfonic acid) exchanging the acetate for the sulfonate to give magnesium taurate and liberating two equivalents of acetic acid. Purpose is preparation of the magnesium salt of taurine. Conducted in aqueous solution, often under gentle heating (50–80 °C) to promote complete exchange; the mixture can be cooled to precipitate the salt or left in solution.

Acid‑base amidation (ammonolysis) of a carboxylic acid; purpose is to convert 2,2‑difluoroacetic acid into the corresponding amide; key transformation is replacement of the hydroxyl of the acid by an –NH₂ group, producing 2,2‑difluoroacetamide and water; typically performed by refluxing the acid with aqueous or ethanolic ammonium hydroxide (1–2 equiv) and then removing water; solvent often water or ethanol, no catalyst required.

Amide coupling (condensation) of methacrylic acid with aniline: the carboxylic acid is activated (commonly as the acid chloride, mixed anhydride, or via coupling reagents such as DCC/EDC) and then reacted with aniline to give N‑phenylmethacrylamide with loss of water. Purpose is synthesis of an α,β‑unsaturated amide. Typical conditions: dissolve reagents in an aprotic solvent (DCM, THF), add coupling agent (e.g., DCC, 1‑hydroxybenzotriazole), maintain 0 °C to rt, and stir until completion; the by‑product dicyclohexylurea is filtered off. No strong acids are required; a base (triethylamine) scavenges the generated HCl.

Double‑displacement precipitation (metathesis): aqueous silver nitrate reacts with zinc iodate; Ag⁺ exchanges with Zn²⁺ to precipitate two equivalents of sparingly soluble silver iodate (AgIO₃) while zinc nitrate remains in solution. Reaction at ambient temperature in water; stirring ensures complete mixing. Filtration isolates the solid AgIO₃, and the filtrate contains Zn(NO₃)₂. No special catalysts are needed.

Aerobic oxidation; N‑methylnicotinamide is oxidized by molecular oxygen to N‑methyl‑2‑pyridone‑5‑carboxamide with concomitant formation of hydrogen peroxide. The reaction proceeds via metal‑catalyzed activation of O2 (e.g., CuCl₂ or FeSO₄, 1–5 mol %) in aqueous buffer or MeCN/H₂O (1:1) at room temperature or 40‑60 °C under an O₂ atmosphere. No additional reagents besides the catalyst; the H₂O₂ formed may be removed or quenched.

Acid–base double displacement; purpose: convert insoluble copper arsenate into soluble copper sulfate and generate arsenic acid; key transformation: Cu³(AsO₄)₂ + 3 H₂SO₄ → 3 CuSO₄ + 2 H₃AsO₄; typical conditions: aqueous solution, heat to reflux; common solvent: water, no additional catalyst needed.

Catalytic dehydrogenative oxidation of a primary amine to an imine; purpose: synthesize 2‑propanimine from isopropylamine with release of H₂; key transformation: (CH₃)₂CHNH₂ → (CH₃)₂C=NH + H₂ (Pd/C facilitates H₂ removal); typical conditions: Pd/C (5–10 % Pd), inert atmosphere (N₂), temperature 150‑200 °C, solvent such as toluene or xylene; no additional reagents.

Grignard addition to an epoxide (nucleophilic ring opening); purpose is preparation of a secondary alcohol; methylmagnesium bromide attacks the less hindered carbon of propylene oxide forming an alkoxide, which upon acidic work‑up yields 2‑propanol; performed in anhydrous ether (Et₂O or THF) under nitrogen at 0 °C to rt, followed by quench with dilute acid or water; no additional catalyst needed.

Acid‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification) of methyl acrylate; purpose: obtain acrylic acid and methanol; key transformation: CH₂=CHCOOCH₃ + H₂O → CH₂=CHCOOH + CH₃OH (H₂SO₄ acts as proton donor); typical conditions: aqueous 1–2 M H₂SO₄, reflux (80‑100 °C); solvent water; no other catalyst required.

Acid‑base neutralization/precipitation; rhodium(III) nitrate solution is treated with aqueous sodium hydroxide, precipitating rhodium(III) hydroxide while sodium nitrate remains in solution; usually done at room temperature with vigorous stirring; water is the solvent; no catalyst needed.

Halogen exchange (interhalogen formation); purpose: generate iodine monobromide (IBr) from ICl and NaBr; key transformation: ICl + NaBr → IBr + NaCl; typical conditions: polar aprotic solvent (e.g., acetone or acetonitrile), ambient temperature; NaBr is the bromide source, no catalyst needed.

Palladium‑catalyzed Miyaura borylation of bromobenzene to give phenylboronic acid pinacol ester; reaction type: C–B cross‑coupling (borylation); purpose: install a boronate ester onto an aryl ring for later cross‑coupling; key transformations: oxidative addition of Pd(II) to aryl bromide, transmetallation with bis(pinacolato)diboron, reductive elimination to afford the aryl‑Bpin; typical conditions: Pd(OAc)₂ (2‑5 mol %) with tri(o‑tolyl)phosphine (10‑20 mol %), KOAc (2 eq) in 1,4‑dioxane or DMF, heated to 80‑100 °C under N₂; by‑product: KBr and acetic acid.

Acid–base neutralization (double replacement) between a acid and a metal nitrate; purpose: prepare calcium stearate and recover nitric acid; key transformation: Ca(NO₃)₂ + 2 C₁₇H₃₅COOH → Ca(C₁₇H₃₅COO)₂ + 2 HNO₃; typical conditions: melt stearic acid (≈70‑80 °C), add aqueous calcium nitrate solution, stir until complete; common solvent: mixture of water and melted acid; no catalyst required.

Type: thermal decomposition / sulfide formation. Purpose: preparation of rhodium(III) sulfide from rhodium(III) chloride. Key transformation: thiourea serves as a sulfide source, decomposes to carbon dioxide and ammonia; the ammonia is captured as ammonium chloride while sulfide ligands combine with Rh(III) to give Rh₂S₃. Conditions: aqueous solution of RhCl₃ mixed with excess thiourea, heated under reflux (≈150–200 °C) for several hours. Solvent: water or water/ethanol mixture. No catalyst required.

Hydroformylation (oxo process); purpose: extend ethylene by one carbon to give propionaldehyde; key transformation: addition of a formyl (CHO) group and hydrogen across the C=C bond (CH2=CH2 + CO + H2 → CH3CH2CHO); typical conditions: 150‑200 °C, 20‑50 bar CO/H2 (syngas) pressure; catalyst: Rhodium complex such as HRh(CO)(PPh₃)₃ or cobalt carbonyl (Co₂(CO)₈) with phosphine ligands; common solvent: aromatic solvents (toluene, xylene) or tetralin.

Type: double‑displacement precipitation (metathesis). Purpose: synthesis of insoluble chromium(III) sulfide. Key transformation: sulfide ions from Na₂S replace nitrate ligands of Cr(NO₃)₃, forming solid Cr₂S₃ and soluble NaNO₃. Conditions: aqueous solutions combined at ambient temperature with vigorous stirring; mild heating (60–80 °C) may be used to improve precipitation. Solvent: water. No catalyst.

Type: salt metathesis (ion exchange). Purpose: preparation of tetramethylammonium fluoride. Key transformation: chloride anion exchanges with fluoride ion, yielding CsCl and [(CH₃)₄N]F. Conditions: anhydrous polar aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile or DMF, room temperature, often under inert atmosphere to avoid moisture. No catalyst.

Type: acid‑base neutralization (salt formation). Purpose: generation of choline hydrogen tartrate (choline bitartrate). Key transformation: tartaric acid protonates choline hydroxide, producing water and the choline bitartrate salt. Conditions: aqueous solution, ambient temperature, stirring until complete dissolution. Solvent: water. No catalyst.

Type: redox reduction (hydrogen reduction of uranium(V) fluoride). Purpose: conversion of UF₅ to the more stable UF₄. Key transformation: H₂ reduces UF₅, forming hydrogen fluoride gas and solid UF₄. Conditions: solid‑gas reaction at elevated temperature (≈400–600 °C) in a quartz tube or flow reactor under inert gas flow, with continuous removal of HF. No solvent or catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration (E1 elimination) – treats citronellol with concentrated H₂SO₄ to eliminate water and form citronellene; protonation of the hydroxyl followed by loss of water generates a carbocation that loses a proton to give the double bond; performed at 50‑100 °C in neat H₂SO₄ or dilute acidic medium; sulfuric acid acts as catalyst and dehydrating agent.

Type: lithium‑halogen exchange (metal‑halogen exchange). Purpose: generation of vinyllithium reagent. Key transformation: n‑BuLi exchanges its butyl group with the vinyl iodide, producing vinyllithium and butyl iodide. Conditions: anhydrous THF, low temperature (‑78 °C to ‑20 °C), inert atmosphere (argon or nitrogen). Reaction is typically quenched or trapped with an electrophile. No catalyst.

Double displacement (precipitation) reaction where neodymium(III) fluoride reacts with aqueous ammonium hydroxide to form insoluble neodymium(III) hydroxide precipitate and soluble ammonium fluoride; carried out in water at ambient temperature, stirring; no catalyst required.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution; conversion of an acyl chloride to an amide. Ammonia attacks octanoyl chloride, displacing chloride and forming octanamide while releasing HCl. Typically performed at 0 °C to room temperature in an aprotic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane or THF) with a base such as pyridine or triethylamine to scavenge the generated HCl.

Oxidation (hydrogen peroxide oxidation); thioether is oxidized to the corresponding sulfoxide with aqueous or 30 % H₂O₂, often in the presence of a mild acid (e.g., acetic acid) or a metal catalyst such as tungstate to accelerate the reaction; performed at 0 °C to room temperature in methanol or dichloromethane; water is the only by‑product.

Type: alkaline saponification of an ester. Purpose: generate the sodium salt of an α‑chloro carboxylic acid. Key transformation: hydroxide attacks the ester carbonyl, methanol is liberated, forming sodium 2‑chloropropionate. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (1–2 eq), reflux in water/ethanol or methanol for 1–2 h. No additional catalyst needed.

Condensation (dehydration) of two O,O‑diethyl phosphoric acid molecules to give tetraethyl pyrophosphate. Water is eliminated, forming a phospho‑anhydride bond. Usually carried out by heating the diethyl phosphoric acid neat or under reduced pressure (120–150 °C), sometimes with a mild dehydrating agent (e.g., P₂O₅). No solvent is required; the reaction proceeds in the melt.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of ethyl bromide with aqueous ammonia; purpose is to prepare a primary amine. The bromide is displaced by NH3 giving ethylamine, while ammonium bromide forms as a by‑product. Typical conditions: aqueous or ethanolic NH3 solution, reflux or gentle heating, inert atmosphere not required.

Acid‑base deprotonation; generation of a phosphide nucleophile. Methyl lithium abstracts the acidic P–H proton of diphenylphosphine, yielding lithium diphenylphosphide and methane gas. Conducted in dry THF under inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar) at low temperature (‑78 °C to 0 °C) to control exotherm and avoid side reactions.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (amide formation); purpose is preparation of N,N‑diisopropylacetamide; the nitrogen of N,N‑diisopropylamine attacks the carbonyl carbon of ethanoyl chloride, displacing chloride and forming the amide while releasing HCl; typical conditions are dry, inert solvent (dichloromethane or THF) at 0 °C to room temperature, often with excess amine or an added base (e.g., triethylamine) to scavenge HCl.

Redox reduction of a triphenylmethane dye. Ascorbic acid donates electrons to malachite green, reducing the conjugated chromophore to its leuco (colorless) form, leucomalachite green. Performed in aqueous or mixed aqueous‑organic media (e.g., water/ethanol) at ambient temperature, typically at neutral to slightly acidic pH. No additional catalyst is required.

Lewis‑acid mediated alkoxy exchange (formation of a borate ester). Boron tribromide reacts with methanol, each equivalent replacing a Br with an OMe group, ultimately giving trimethyl borate and liberating three equivalents of HBr. Conducted under anhydrous conditions in a non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane or toluene, cooled (0 °C to –20 °C) to control HBr evolution.

Reaction type: nucleophilic addition (carbamoylation) of an aniline to isocyanic acid. Purpose: synthesis of phenylurea. Key transformation: aniline nitrogen attacks the carbonyl carbon of HNCO, forming the phenyl‑urea bond. Typical conditions: mild temperature (0 °C to rt) in a polar solvent such as methanol, ethanol, or THF; optional base (e.g., pyridine) can be used to neutralize the liberated proton. Reaction proceeds without metal catalysts; product isolated by precipitation or extraction.

Metallothermic reduction of a high‑valent metal halide. Magnesium reduces tantalum pentachloride to tantalum trichloride while being oxidized to magnesium chloride. Typically carried out at elevated temperatures (300–400 °C) in a sealed tube or inert‑gas flow, sometimes with a molten salt or inert solid matrix to promote contact. No solvent is used; the reaction is solid‑state.

Acid chloride generation using phosphorus pentachloride; prop‑2‑ynoic acid is treated with PCl₅ (1.2 equiv) in anhydrous dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride at 0 °C to rt under nitrogen. The reaction yields prop‑2‑ynoyl chloride while generating phosphoryl chloride (POCl₃) and hydrogen chloride as by‑products; work‑up involves removal of solvents and neutralization of residual acid.

Base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification); converts methyl isonicotinate to the sodium salt of pyridine‑4‑carboxylic acid and liberates methanol. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (1–2 equiv) heated under reflux (often 60–80 °C) in water or a water/ethanol mixture; the reaction is complete in 1–3 h, then the mixture is acidified to precipitate the acid if desired.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis (reduction of an alcohol to an alkane). Purpose: remove the hydroxyl group from cyclohexanol to give cyclohexane. Key transformation: OH is replaced by H, generating water as the only by‑product. Typical conditions: H₂ gas (1–5 atm) with a metal catalyst such as Pd/C, Raney Ni or PtO₂ in a protic or aprotic solvent (ethanol, THF, acetic acid) at 50–150 °C.

Acetylation (esterification) of propargyl alcohol with acetic anhydride. Purpose: convert the primary alcohol into its acetate protecting group. Key transformation: the OH of propargyl alcohol attacks acetic anhydride, forming propargyl acetate and releasing one equivalent of acetic acid. Typical conditions: use a catalytic amount of pyridine or DMAP as base/activator, solvent such as dichloromethane or THF, temperature 0 °C to room temperature, reaction time 1–2 h.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) salt exchange; purpose is preparation of lithium oxalate from sodium oxalate; sodium oxalate and lithium chloride exchange cations to give sodium chloride and lithium oxalate; typically carried out in aqueous solution vigorous stirring at ambient temperature; solid NaCl can be removed by filtration; no catalyst required.

Acid dissolution/oxidation of mixed‑valence cobalt(II,III) oxide with nitric acid. Purpose: generate soluble cobalt(II) nitrate from the oxide solid. Key transformation: cobalt oxide reacts with HNO₃, yielding Co(NO₃)₂ (often as the tetrahydrate) and water; the metal is reduced to the +2 oxidation state while nitrate acts as both acid and oxidant. Typical conditions: excess concentrated HNO₃, reflux 60–100 °C until the solid dissolves, aqueous medium; safety precautions for nitrogen oxides evolution.

Suzuki–Miyaura cross‑coupling between phenylboronic acid and 2‑iodopyridine. Purpose: construct the C–C bond linking a phenyl ring to a pyridine ring. Key transformation: phenyl‑B(OH)₂ couples with the aryl iodide under palladium catalysis, releasing boric acid and forming 2‑phenylpyridine. Typical conditions: Pd catalyst (Pd(PPh₃)₄ or Pd(OAc)₂ with phosphine ligand), base such as K₂CO₃ or Na₂CO₃, mixed solvent (toluene/ethanol/water or dioxane), temperature 80–100 °C under N₂ or Ar, reaction time 4–12 h.

Mitsunobu ether formation to attach 2‑(hydroxymethyl)pyridine to 1,4,7,10‑tetraazacyclododecane (cyclam), giving Plerixafor (AMD3100). Purpose: synthesize the bicyclam drug by forming N‑CH₂‑pyridyl linkages. Key transformation: the alcohol is activated by triphenylosphine and diethyl azodicarboxylate (DEAD or DIAD), allowing nucleophilic attack by the secondary amine of cyclam; by‑products are triphenylphosphine oxide and diethyl hydrazine dicarboxylate. Typical conditions: dry THF or CH₂Cl₂, 0 °C to rt, inert atmosphere (N₂), stoichiometric PPh₃ and DEAD (or DIAD), reaction 2–12 h, followed by work‑up and purification (e.g., ion‑exchange).

Acid–base neutralization forming a double salt. Ammonia (NH3) reacts with ammonium dihydrogen phosphate ((NH4)H2PO4) in aqueous solution to give diammonium hydrogen phosphate ((NH4)2HPO4). The reaction proceeds at ambient temperature in water; the product precipitates upon cooling or concentration. No catalyst is required.

Thermal decomposition (explosive) of cyclonite (RDX). Upon rapid heating or shock, cyclonite breaks down to gaseous products: carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, nitrogen and water vapor. The reaction occurs at high temperature (>200 °C) and is typically performed in a sealed bomb or calorimetric vessel. No solvent or catalyst is involved; the process is purely thermal.

Sandmeyer halogenation (aryl substitution). Benzenediazonium tetrafluoroborate reacts with copper(I) chloride in an acidic aqueous medium to replace the diazonium group with chlorine, producing chlorobenzene, nitrogen gas, and copper(II) chloride as the oxidized copper species. The reaction is carried out at 0–5 °C to control diazonium stability, then warmed to room temperature; aqueous HBF4 or HCl is the usual medium. Copper(I) chloride functions both as reagent and catalyst.

Oxidation of a sulfoxide to a sulfone. Hydrogen peroxide oxidizes dibenzothiophene sulfoxide to dibenzothiophene sulfone, generating water as the only by‑product. The reaction is typically performed in an organic solvent such as acetonitrile or dichloromethane with a catalytic amount of acid (e.g., trifluoroacetic acid) or base to activate H2O2, at 0 °C to room temperature. No metal catalyst is required.

Double displacement precipitation; carbonate replaces iodide to give insoluble barium carbonate and soluble sodium iodide; employed to precipitate BaCO3 or remove Ba2+; aqueous Na2CO3 added to BaI2 solution at room temperature; water solvent, no catalyst.

Alpha‑halogenation of an aldehyde via enol formation; chlorine electrophilically substitutes the α‑hydrogen of acetaldehyde to give chloroacetaldehyde and HCl. Reaction proceeds through the enol or enolate tautomer under mildly acidic or neutral conditions. Usually carried out at 0–5 °C in a non‑nucleophilic solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane, with gaseous Cl₂ bubbled through the solution.

Pd/Cu‑catalyzed ortho‑hydroxylation (oxidative C–H functionalization). Dimethyl sulfoxide serves as the stoichiometric oxidant, converting 4‑methoxyacetophenone into paeonol (2‑hydroxy‑4‑methoxyacetophenone). Copper(II) acetate and palladium(II) acetate act as co‑catalysts; the reaction is carried out in DMSO as solvent, typically at 80–120 °C under inert atmosphere. By‑products are acetic acid (from acetate ligands) and dimethyl sulfide (from reduction of DMSO).

Metathesis/neutralization leading to precipitation of a metal hydroxide. Two equivalents of sodium hydroxide react with manganese lactate in aqueous solution, exchanging the metal ion to form insoluble manganese hydroxide precipitate and soluble sodium lactate. The reaction proceeds at room temperature with vigorous stirring; no catalyst is required.

Palladium‑catalyzed carbonylative coupling (carbonylative methoxycarbonylation). Purpose: convert an aryl bromide into the corresponding methyl ester using carbon monoxide and methanol. Key transformation: oxidative addition of 3‑bromofuran to Pd(0), insertion of CO, methanolysis to give methyl 3‑furoate and regeneration of Pd(0). Typical conditions: Pd(PPh₃)₄ (5 mol %), CO pressure 10–30 atm, methanol as solvent (often with a base such as triethylamine), temperature 80–120 °C.

N‑acetylation of a primary amine (acylation). Purpose: protect or modify 3‑phenylpropylamine as its acetamide. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of the amine on acetic anhydride, forming N‑acetyl‑3‑phenylpropylamine and releasing one equivalent of acetic acid. Typical conditions: reflux or room temperature in an inert solvent (e.g., dichloromethane, THF, or pyridine); sometimes pyridine acts as both solvent and base to absorb the generated acid.

Acid–base neutralization of arsenic acid. Purpose: generate the mono‑hydrogen arsenate salt. Key transformation: deprotonation of H₃AsO₄ by NaOH to give NaH₂AsO₄ and water. Typical conditions: aqueous solution at ambient temperature, stoichiometric 1 equiv NaOH; stirring until dissolution. No special catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed hydration of a tertiary alkene (Markovnikov addition). Purpose: synthesize 2,3‑dimethyl‑2‑butanol from the corresponding alkene. Key transformation: protonation of the double bond to form the more stable tertiary carbocation, followed by nucleophilic attack of water and deprotonation to give the tertiary alcohol. Typical conditions: dilute H₂SO₄ or H₃O⁺ in water, temperature 25–60 °C; alternatively, oxymercuration‑demercuration (HgSO₄/H₂SO₄, followed by NaBH₄).

β‑Elimination (E2) of a primary alkyl bromide. Purpose: generate a terminal alkene from 1‑bromohexadecane. Key transformation: strong, sterically hindered base (tert‑butoxide) abstracts a β‑hydrogen while the C–Br bond leaves, forming 1‑hexadecene andBr. Typical conditions: potassium tert‑butoxide (1–2 equiv) in dry THF or DMSO, 0 °C to rt, inert atmosphere (N₂), reaction time 1–3 h.

Aldehyde to carboxylic acid oxidation; benzaldehyde is oxidized by trifluoroperacetic acid to benzoic acid, with concomitant formation of trifluoroacetic acid. The oxidation proceeds via a peracid intermediate and is typically performed at 0 °C to 25 °C in dichloromethane or acetonitrile, inert atmosphere, and does not require additional catalysts.

Double displacement (metathesis) reaction where ammonium fluoride exchanges anions with thallium(III) chloride to give ammonium chloride and thallium(III) fluoride; typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; no special catalyst; products may precipitate if TlF3 is insoluble.

Lithium aluminium hydride reduction of an acid chloride to a primary alcohol; converts the carbonyl carbon of 2,4‑dichlorobenzoyl chloride into a CH2OH group yielding 2,4‑dichlorobenzyl alcohol; performed in anhydrous ether (diethyl ether or THF) under inert atmosphere, usually at 0 °C to reflux; LiAlH4 acts as hydride donor, no additional catalyst.

Reaction type: directed metalation (lithiation) via deprotonation. Purpose: produce the 2‑lithio derivative of benzothiazole as a nucleophilic intermediate for subsequent cross‑coupling or addition reactions. Key transformation: n‑butyl lithium abstracts the proton at the C‑2 position of benzothiazole, forming 2‑lithiobenzothiazole and butane as a volatile by‑product. Typical conditions: –78 °C (dry ice/acetone bath) in anhydrous THF under inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar). No additional catalyst; the organolithium reagent itself serves as the base.

Base‑ or acid‑catalyzed transesterification of butyl oleate with methanol producing methyl oleate and n‑butanol; common in biodiesel synthesis; carried out with excess methanol and a catalytic amount of NaOH, KOH, or H2SO4, heated to 60–70 °C (reflux); methanol serves as both reactant and solvent.

Alkaline hydrolysis (saponification) of the amide propanil with aqueous potassium hydroxide; the amide bond is cleaved to give 3,4‑dichloroaniline and potassium propanoate; reaction is performed in water with excess KOH, heated to reflux (80–100 °C); no additional catalyst required.

Oxidation of salicyl alcohol to salicylaldehyde using Dess‑Martin periodinane; primary benzylic alcohol is converted to the corresponding aldehyde under mild conditions; typically run in anhydrous dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen; Dess‑Martin periodinane acts as the oxidant, no catalyst needed.

Oxidation of o‑vanillyl alcohol to o‑vanillin using manganese dioxide; the benzylic alcohol is oxidized to an aldehyde with water as by‑product; usually performed by stirring the alcohol with excess MnO2 in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or acetone at room temperature or gentle reflux; the solid MnO2 is the oxidant and is removed by filtration after completion.

Acid‑base neutralization; reacts Gd(OH)3 with aqueous nitric acid to give gadolinium nitrate and water; typically performed by adding the hydroxide to dilute HNO3 at room temperature with stirring, sometimes with mild heating; the nitrate salt stays dissolved; water is the solvent and no catalyst is required.

Ullmann‑type copper‑catalyzed N‑arylation. Purpose: couple an aryl bromide to the nitrogen of anthranilic acid to give N‑phenylanthranilic acid. Key transformation: formation of a C–N bond via copper(I) iodide/1,10‑phenanthroline catalysis with potassium carbonate as base, bromobenzene serving as aryl donor, and potassium bromide as by‑product. Typical conditions: inert atmosphere, polar aprotic solvent (DMF, DMSO or NMP), 80‑130 °C for several hours. No additional catalyst beyond CuIphenanthroline is required.

Fluorination (acid‑base) synthesis: TeO2 is fluorinated by anhydrous HF, converting the oxide to TeF4 with formation of water. Conducted in excess HF (which also serves as solvent) at 100‑200 °C in a PTFE or nickel reactor; moisture must be excluded.

Friedel‑Crafts acylation of 2‑methoxyphenol (guaiacol) using acetic anhydride and AlCl₃; purpose is introduction of an acetyl group para to the methoxy substituent to afford 4‑hydroxy‑3‑methoxyacetophenone; AlCl₃ generates the acylium ion from acetic anhydride, which undergoes electrophilic aromatic substitution on the phenol ring; acetic acid is formed as by‑product; reaction is run in anhydrous non‑protic solvent (e.g., CH₂Cl₂, CS₂, or nitrobenzene) at 0‑50 °C under inert atmosphere; work‑up with ice water liberates the product.

Type: Radical chlorination/substitution of an ether (photo‑induced). Purpose: Synthesize chloromethyl methyl ether (ClCH2OCH3), an intermediate in chloromethylation reactions. Key transformation: CH3OCH3 + Cl2 → ClCH2OCH3 + HCl (via abstraction of a hydrogen from a methyl group and recombination with chlorine radical). Typical conditions: UV light or thermal initiation, dilute Cl2 in an inert solvent (e.g., carbon tetrachloride or chloroform), temperature 0–25 °C to limit over‑chlorination. Solvent/catalyst: No metal catalyst; radical initiator may be a small amount of benzoyl peroxide if thermal.

Double displacement (precipitation) reaction; used to generate insoluble silver chloride, a classic test for chloride ions; silver acetate reacts with sodium chloride, precipitating AgCl and producing sodium acetate in solution; performed in water at room temperature; no catalyst required.

Salt metathesis (amide exchange); used to prepare the volatile Lewis‑acid Al(NMe2)3 for ALD or organometallic synthesis; AlBr3 is converted to Al(NMe23 while LiBr precipitates; typically performed under inert atmosphere (N2 or Ar) at 0 °C to room temperature in dry ether or THF; stoichiometric LiNMe2 is added dropwise, mixture filtered to isolate LiBr, and Al(NMe2)3 is isolated from the filtrate.

Aqueous double‑displacement/precipitation. Purpose: obtain insoluble gadolinium(III) hydroxide as a solid precursor. Key transformation: reaction of GdBr₃ with excess NH₄OH, forming Gd(OH)₃ precipitate and ammonium bromide in solution. Typical conditions: aqueous medium, addition of NH₄OH at 0‑25 °C with stirring, pH maintained around 9‑10 to ensure complete precipitation filtration and washing of the Gd(OH)₃ solid. No catalyst is needed.

Type: C‑alkylation (SN2) of potassium diethyl malonate with benzyl chloride. Purpose: install a benzyl group at the α‑position of the malonate. Key transformation: malonate carbanion displaces chloride from benzyl chloride, forming diethyl 2‑benzylmalonate and KCl. Typical conditions: polar aprotic solvent (DMF, DMSO) at reflux; sometimes catalytic KI is added to accelerate the SN2 step. No catalyst beyond possible KI additive.

Metal‑acid reduction of nitro groups (tin/HCl reduction). Purpose: convert 2,4‑dinitrotoluene to 2,4‑diaminotoluene, an important intermediate for dyes and polymers. Key transformation: tin metal reduces each nitro group to an amine in the presence of concentrated HCl, producing SnCl₄ and water as by‑products. Typical conditions: excess concentrated HCl (12 equiv), addition of tin powder (3 equiv) to the nitro substrate, reflux at 80‑100 °C for several hours until gas evolution ceases, then filtration to remove tin salts and neutralization or extraction of the diamine product. No additional catalyst is required.

Williamson ether synthesis (SN2 alkylation); sodium butan‑1‑olate (n‑butoxide) attacks dimethyl sulfate, methylating the alkoxide to give methyl butyl ether and sodium methyl sulfate; normally carried out in an aprotic polar solvent such as DMF or DMSO at low to moderate temperature; no catalyst; purpose is to form an ether via methylation.

Type: electrophilic sulfamation of a primary am. Purpose: to install a sulfamic acid functional group on cyclohexylamine, yielding cyclohexylsulfamic acid. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of the amine nitrogen on sulfur trioxide, forming an N‑SO3H linkage. Typical conditions: SO3 gas or fuming sulfuric acid added dropwise to a solution of cyclohexylamine in a non‑protic solvent (e.g., carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane) at 0 °C to ambient temperature under an inert atmosphere; reaction quenched with ice water. No additional catalyst required.

Type: redox (oxidation‑reduction) and double‑replacement reaction. Purpose: conversion of iodide to elemental iodine while reducing Cu(II) to Cu(I) as an insoluble precipitate. Key transformation: I⁻ is oxidized to I₂, Cu² is reduced to Cu⁺ which precipitates as CuI; Na⁺ pairs with nitrate to give NaNO₃. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, stoichiometric amounts of NaI and Cu(NO₃)₂ mixed at room temperature; stirring until a pale yellow CuI precipitate forms. No special solvent beyond water; sometimes gentle heating to improve yield.

Grignard carboxylation; nucleophilic addition of a Grignard reagent to carbon dioxide followed by acidic work‑up. Propylmagnesium bromide attacks CO2 to give the magnesium propionate intermediate, which upon treatment with dilute mineral acid (NH4Cl or HCl) affords propionic acid and precipitates MgBr2. Conducted under anhydrous conditions in dry ethereal solvent (diethyl ether or THF) at 0 °C to room temperature; the reaction is quenched with aqueous acid after completion.

Type: acid‑base neutralization (proton transfer) leading to formation of a more basic phosphate salt. Purpose: to generate ammonium tribasic phosphate from the mono‑basic ammonium hydrogen phosphate. Key transformation: OH⁻ from NH₄OH deprotonates the hydrogen phosphate ion, producing water and converting (NH₄)₂HPO₄ to (NH₄)₃PO₄. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, reactants mixed at ambient temperature with stirring; the product remains in solution or can be crystallized by evaporation. No catalyst required.

Catalytic carboxylation of a terminal alkyne (Reppe‑type reaction); forms propiolic acid by inserting CO2 into the C–H bond of acetylene; copper(I) iodide acts as a homogeneous catalyst, often in the presence of a base (e.g., K2CO3) to generate the acetylide; reaction conducted under elevated CO2 pressure (5–20 bar) at 50–120  in polar aprotic solvents such as DMF or DMSO; yields the alkynoic acid after aqueous work‑up.

Carbonation of cadmium(II) oxide; employed to synthesize cadmium carbonate, often for pigment or precursor production; CO₂ reacts with the oxide to give the carbonate; conducted in an aqueous slurry or supercritical CO₂ environment at 100–200 °C and moderate pressure; water as solvent, no catalyst.

Redox reaction; sodium periodate oxidizes sulfide ion to sulfate and is itself reduced to iodide, affording sodium iodide and sodium sulfate; performed in aqueous solution, often at room temperature to mild heating, sometimes under acidic conditions to keep sulfide soluble.

Reductive amination of phenylacetone with ammonia using sodium cyanoborohydride to afford cathinone (β‑keto‑phenyl‑ethylamine); imine formed in situ is reduced by NaBH₃CN at pH 5‑6 in methanol or ethanol, 0‑25 °C progressing to room temperature, providing the primary amine product.

Type: double‑displacement (metathesis) acid‑base reaction. Purpose: to exchange the sulfate and iodide anions, generating strong acids and soluble thallium iodide.
