Performed in air after drying; no additional solvent after the solution stage.

Acid-catalyzed cleavage of an ether; purpose is ether hydrolysis to alcohols. Sulfuric acid protonates methyl tert-butyl ether, leading to cleavage into methanol and tert-butyl alcohol. Reaction occurs in aqueous sulfuric acid, often heated. No additional catalyst or solvent beyond the acid.

Hydrogenation or reduction reaction; reduces nitro groups to amines in 2,6-dinitrotoluene. Palladium on carbon catalyzes hydrogenation using formic acid as a hydrogen donor. Key transformation: nitro (-NO2) to amine (-NH2). Conducted in protic solvents (e.g., ethanol, water) at ambient or elevated temperature.

Acidic metal–silicide cleavage; concentrated HCl reacts with hafnium silicide, liberating H₂ gas and converting hafnium into solublenium tetrachloride while elemental silicon precipitates. Typically performed with excess 4 M HCl, heating the mixture to 60–100 °C to drive the reaction to completion.

Ester hydrolysis reaction; purpose is ester bond cleavage in aceclidine. Water hydrolyzes aceclidine’s ester linkage, producing acetic acid and 3-quinuclidinol. Reaction often occurs under acidic (e.g., dilute HCl) or basic (e.g., NaOH) conditions. No specific solvent or catalyst mentioned; likely aqueous conditions.

N‑alkylation of an amine (nucleophilic substitution, S_N2). Aniline is deprotonated (often with NaOH, Na₂CO₃, or a weak base) to form the anilide ion, which attacks diethyl sulfate to give N‑ethyl aniline and ethyl hydrogen sulfate. Typical conditions: aqueous alkaline medium, 40‑80 °C, reflux may be employed to improve conversion. Solvent: water or water/ethanol; base acts as catalyst.

Thermal dehydration of arsenous acid (H₃AsO₃) to arsenic trioxide; heating drives off water, giving As₂O₃ solid. Typically performed by gradual heating to 200–300 °C under a stream of inert gas or reduced pressure to remove water; no catalyst is necessary.

Alkaline oxidative cleavage/oxidation of a primary alcohol with potassium permanganate. Purpose: oxidize citronellol to citronellic acid while reducing Mn(VII) to Mn(IV). Key transformation: CH2OH → CO2H, MnO4⁻ → MnO2 (brown precipitate) and K⁺ forms KOH. Typical conditions: aqueous KMnO4 (0.1–0.5 M), pH 8–10, heated gently (30–60 °C) until the purple color disappears, then work‑up. Common solvent: water or water/acetone mixture; MnO2 precipitates and is filtered off.

Reductive dehalogenation of an alpha‑bromo ketone; zinc dust in acetic acid serves as a reducing metal–acid system that removes the bromide from 4‑bromobutan‑2‑one, yielding the unchanged ketone (butan‑2‑one) and forming ZnBr₂; typical conditions are reflux or gentle heating in glacial acetic acid, solid Zn added in excess; no additional catalyst required.

Acid‑metal reaction; cesium metal reacts with acetic acid in a protic solvent (often aqueous or ethanolic) to give cesium acetate and evolve H₂ gas; typically performed at room temperature under inert atmosphere to control vigorous H₂ evolution.

Catalytic nitro‑group reduction (transfer hydrogenation) of 2‑nitropyridine to 2‑aminopyridine; cobalt(II) chloride activates sodium borohydride, generating a cobalt‑hydride species that transfers hydrogen to the nitro group; generally performed in methanol or ethanol at 0 °C to reflux, under an inert atmosphere; no external pressure needed.

Complete combustion (oxidation) of a hydrocarbon. 2‑Methyloctane reacts with excess oxygen under ignition (high temperature) to produce carbon dioxide and water vapor. Typically carried out in an open flame or combustion chamber with atmospheric or enriched O₂; no catalyst is required.

Acid‑base double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation; aqueous sulfuric acid reacts with soluble barium permanganate, exchanging counter‑ions to give insoluble barium sulfate precipitate and aqueous permanganic acid (HMnO₄); carried out at room temperature in water; filtration isolates the BaSO₄ solid.

High‑temperature oxidation of samarium antimonide in oxygen (or air) to yield samarium oxide (typically Sm₂O₃) and antimony oxide (commonly Sb₂O₃ or Sb₂O₅). This combustion‑type reaction is used to obtain the corresponding oxides. The material is heated in a furnace at 600‑800 °C in an oxygen‑rich atmosphere. No solvent or catalyst is needed.

Selenium transfer / phosphine oxidation; triphenylphosphine reduces diphenyl diselenide, forming triphenylphosphine selenide (Ph₃P=Se) and liberating phenylselenol (PhSeH); performed in an aprotic, inert solvent such as dichloromethane or THF at ambient temperature under nitrogen; no additional catalyst needed.

Precipitation double‑displacement (metathesis) of rare‑earth hydroxide; aqueous barium hydroxide reacts with dysprosium chloride to exchange ions, precipitating dysprosium(III) hydroxide (Dy(OH)₃) while forming barium chloride; carried out in water at room temperature with stirring; the solid Dy(OH)₃ is collected by filtration.

SN2 cyanation of a benzyl halide; benzyl chloride reacts with CuCN to afford benzyl cyanide (phenylacetonitrile) and copper(I) chloride. Typical conditions are reflux in DMF or DMSO at 80–100 °C; CuCN provides the nucleophilic cyanide, no extra catalyst is needed.

Esterification (acyl chloride acylation); acetyl chloride acetylates the remaining free hydroxyl of 1,2-diacetylglycerol to give glycerol triacetate, releasing HCl. Typically performed in anhydrous dichloromethane or pyridine at 0 °C to room temperature; a base such as pyridine or triethylamine is used to scavenge the generated HCl.

Oxidative alkaline redox (chlorine oxidation of MnO2). Manganese dioxide reacts with chlorine gas in aqueous sodium hydroxide, oxidizing Mn(IV) to permanganate (NaMnO4) while chlorine is reduced to chloride; water is formed. Typically performed by bubbling Cl2 through a warm (45‑60 °C) NaOH solution with stirring; water is the solvent.

Strong oxidation of a primary alcohol to a carboxylic acid using sodium dichromate/sulfuric acid (Jones‑type oxidation); converts 4‑methyl‑1‑pentanol to 4‑methylpentanoic acid; performed in aqueous sulfuric acid (≈2–3 M) with Na₂Cr₂O₇·2H₂O (≈1.5 eq) at 0 °C then allowed to warm to room temperature or reflux; the mixture is acidic and aqueous, and chromium(VI) is reduced to Cr(III).

Salt metathesis/precipitation; potassium cyanide exchanges anions with copper(II) tetrafluoroborate to precipitate copper(II) cyanide and form soluble potassium tetrafluoroborate. Usually carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; no additional catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed nitrile hydrolysis; water in the presence of acid and heat converts acetonitrile to acetamide. Typical conditions involve refluxing acetonitrile in aqueous mineral acid (e.g., 1–2 M HCl) for several hours, after which the acetamide is isolated after neutralization and removal of excess water.

Radical bromination (benzylic substitution); bromine abstracts a benzylic hydrogen from indane, generating a carbon radical that combines with Br· to give 1‑bromoindane and HBr. Conducted under UV light or heat in an inert, non‑polar solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or chloroform; no catalyst is required.

Aqueous double‑replacement precipitation with ammonium hydroxide; zinc iodide reacts with NH4OH to produce soluble ammonium iodide (NH4I) and insoluble zinc hydroxide (Zn(OH)2) precipitate; conducted in dilute aqueous ammonia at room temperature; no catalyst.

Acid‑catalyzed SN1 substitution (alcohol to alkyl bromide); 1‑methylcyclohexanol is protonated by HBr, water leaves forming a carbocation, which is captured by bromide to yield 1‑bromo‑1‑methylcyclohexane and water. Performed in concentrated aqueous HBr or gaseous HBr, typically refluxed.

Intramolecular base‑induced epoxide formation (dehydrohalogenation); aqueous NaOH deprotonates the alcohol which then attacks the adjacent carbon bearing bromide in an SN2 fashion, yielding propylene oxide, NaBr and water; typically performed in water or water/ethanol at reflux.

Nitrate‑ester hydrolysis; aqueous hydrolysis of 1,2,4‑butanetriol trrate cleaves the nitrate ester groups, yielding 1,2,4‑butanetriol and three equivalents of nitric acid. Performed in water (often warm or reflux) possibly with a mild acid or base to accelerate the reaction; no special catalyst needed.

Double‑displacement precipitation; tribasic sodium phosphate reacts with yttrium(III) nitrate in aqueous solution to form insoluble yttrium phosphate (YPO₄) and soluble sodium nitrate. Carried out at room temperature with vigorous stirring; the precipitate is filtered and washed; no catalyst required.

Type: Metathesis/precipitation acid–base reaction. Purpose: Generate volatile HCN and remove cyanide as insoluble AgCl. Key transformation: Protonation of cyanide to HCN, Ag⁺ combines with Cl⁻ to form AgCl solid. Typical conditions: Aqueous solution, excess HCl, low temperature (0 °C – room temp) to trap HCN gas. Common solvent: water; no catalyst needed.

Type: Condensation/cyclization (Debus‑Radziszewski benzimidazole synthesis). Purpose: Construct a benzimidazole heterocycle. Key transformation: Two equivalents of formaldehyde condense with o‑phenylenediamine, forming a new C–N bond and a fused imidazole ring while eliminating two molecules of water. Typical conditions: Reflux in ethanol or methanol, often with a catalytic amount of acid (e.g., p‑TsOH) or under neutral conditions; reaction time 2–6 h. No metal catalyst required.

Protonolysis of a metal hydride; CsH reacts with aqueous or dilute H2SO4 to give cesium sulfate and liberate H2 gas; a vigorous acid–hydride reaction carried out at 0–25 °C under an inert atmosphere, usually in the absence of solvent or in a minimal amount of THF to keep CsH dispersed; no catalyst required.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution (nitration); dinitrogen tetroxide generates the nitronium electrophile (NO2⁺) which attacks 1,3,5‑trimethylbenzene ortho to a methyl group to install a nitro group, giving 1,3,5‑trimethyl‑2‑nitrobenzene; commonly performed at 0–25 °C in anhydrous, non‑polar solvents such as dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride under inert atmosphere.

Type: Nucleophilic S‑alkylation (SN2). Purpose: Methylate the thiol group of 2‑mercaptobenzothiazole. Key transformation: The sulfur nucleophile attacks methyl iodide, displacing iodide to give 2‑(methylthio)benzothiazole and generating HI. Typical conditions: Anhydrous DMF or acetone, presence of a mild base (K₂CO₃ or NaHCO₃) to scavenge HI, temperature 0 °C to reflux (25 °C‑80 °C). No metal catalyst required.

Hydrolysis (protonolysis) of tert‑butyl lithium; purpose is to quench the organolithium reagent to give tert‑butanol and form lithium hydroxide. Key transformation: t‑BuLi + H2O → t‑BuOH + LiOH. Conditions: addition of dilute water to a solution of t‑BuLi in dry ether or THF at 0 °C to –20 °C under nitrogen; reaction is exothermic.

Type: Imine hydrolysis (reversal of Schiff‑base formation). Purpose: Regenerate the carbonyl compound and the amine. Key transformation: Water adds to the C=N bond, cleaving it to afford benzaldehyde and 4‑methoxyaniline. Typical conditions: Dilute aqueous acid (e.g., 0.1 M HCl) or buffered water, heating under reflux for 1–3 h. Solvent: water/ethanol mixture; no catalyst beyond the acid.

Oxidative combustion/oxidation: MoS2 is oxidized in the presence of carbon monoxide and oxygen to give molybdenum trioxide, carbon dioxide, and sulfur dioxide. Purpose is conversion of sulfide to oxide while simultaneously oxidizing CO. Key transformation: MoS2 + CO + O2 → MoO3 + CO2 + SO2. Typical conditions are a gas‑phase reaction at 500‑800 °C in a flowing mixture of CO and O2 in a furnace; no solvent or catalyst required.

Double displacement (metathesis) reaction; exchanges anions between sodium fluoride and cobalt(II) sulfate in aqueous solution to form cobalt(II) fluoride (sparingly soluble precipitate) and sodium sulfate; typically carried out at ambient temperature in water, no catalyst required.

Type: Nucleophilic aromatic substitution (SNAr) on pyridine. Purpose Install an amino group at the 4‑position. Key transformation: Ammonia displaces bromide on the electron‑deficient pyridine ring, yielding 4‑aminopyridine and releasing Br⁻. Typical conditions: Excess gaseous or liquid NH₃ in a sealed pressure tube or autoclave, solvent such as ethanol, DMSO or water, temperature 100 °C‑150 °C for several hours. No additional catalyst required.

Type: Double‑displacement precipitation (metathesis). Purpose: Separate silver as insoluble chromate and produce soluble rubidium nitrate. Key transformation: Two Ag⁺ ions combine with CrO₄²⁻ to precipitate Ag₂CrO₄ (red solid), while Rb⁺ pairs with NO₃⁻ to remain in solution as RbNO₃. Typical conditions: Aqueous solution at ambient temperature, stirring; precipitate is filtered. No catalyst needed.

Radical hydroxylation of uracil by hydroxyl radical to form uracil glycol; OH· adds across the C5–C6 double bond producing a cis‑diol, generated in aqueous solution by Fenton chemistry (Fe²⁺/H₂O₂) or radiolysis, under neutral pH.

This is an N‑alkylation of a secondary amine (4‑phenylpiperidine) with methyl iodide. Type: nucleophilic substitution (SN2) on a primary halide. Purpose: introduce a methyl group on nitrogen to modify basicity or steric profile. Key transformation: the nitrogen lone pair attacks CH3I, displacing I⁻ and forming N‑methyl‑4‑phenylpiperidine; HI is generated. Typical conditions: dry polar aprotic solvent (DMF, acetonitrile, or acetone) at 0 °C to rt, often with a base such as triethylamine, NaHCO₃, or K₂CO₃ to scavenge the HI. Reaction is performed under nitrogen to avoid moisture.

Nucleophilic substitution/alkylation of cyanogen bromide by phenyl lithium; organolithium attacks the electrophilic carbon of BrCN forming a lithium cyanide intermediate which loses bromide to give benzonitrile; typically performed at –78 °C to 0 °C in dry THF or diethyl ether under nitrogen; no additional catalyst required, work‑up with aqueous NH4Cl quenches excess Li reagent.

Acid‑catalyzed transesterification/ester cleavage; methanol with catalytic H₂SO₄ converts furan‑2‑ylmethyl acetate into methyl acetate while releasing furan‑2‑ylmethanol; performed refluxing methanol with a few drops of concentrated sulfuric acid (1–5 %); after completion, neutralization and separation give the two products.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation in aqueous medium; lead(II) nitrate reacts with potassium thiocyanate, yielding a white precipitate of lead(II) thiocyanate and soluble potassium nitrate; carried out in at room temperature, straightforward mixing, no catalyst needed.

Acylation (esterification) of 2‑methoxy‑1‑propanol with acetic anhydride; the alcohol oxygen attacks the anhydride carbonyl to form the acetate ester (propylene glycol methyl ether acetate) and generates one equivalent of acetic acid; commonly carried out neat or in anhydrous dichloromethane at 0 °C to reflux; catalytic pyridine or DMAP accelerates the reaction and scavenges the released acetic acid; the acid by‑product is removed by simple washing.

Hydrolytic cleavage (ester hydrolysis) of benzyl salicylate with water; under acidic (e.g., 1 M HCl) or basic (NaOH) conditions, the ester bond is cleaved to give salicylic acid and benzyl alcohol; typical procedure refluxes the ester in aqueous acid or base for several hours, then neutralizes and extracts the products; solvent is usually a mixture of water and an organic cosolvent such as ethanol or THF.

Acid-base reaction. Hydrolysis of lithium phenoxide salt to regenerate phenol. Phenoxide ion accepts a proton from water, yielding phenol and lithium hydroxide. Occurs under mild conditions with water at room temperature. No catalyst or solvent required beyond water itself.

Sodium borohydride reduction of prop‑2‑ynal (propargyl aldehyde) to propargyl alcohol; NaBH4 delivers a hydride to the carbonyl carbon, converting the aldehyde to the primary alcohol while generating sodium metaborate asized boron species; performed in methanol, ethanol, or a methanol‑water mixture at 0 °C to room temperature; reaction is with water and the alcohol isolated by extraction.

Multi‑step synthesis of propranolol hydrochloride via nucleophilic ring opening of epichlorohydrin; first, 1n is deproated (often with NaOH) and attacks epichlorydrin, forming a 1‑naphthoxy‑propane epoxide; subsequent SN2 opening of the epoxide by isopropylamine installs the isopropylamino‑propyl side; the final product converted its hydrochloride salt by treatment with HCl; reactions are usually conducted in THF or aqueous dioxane at 0 °C to reflux, with base (NaOH) for deprotonation and acid for salt formation.

Conversion of a primary alcohol to a chloride (nucleophilic substitution); purpose is to obtain 4‑chlorobenzyl chloride. The alcohol reacts with thionyl chloride (SOCl₂) in an anhydrous solvent such as dry dichloromethane or pyridine, typically at 0 °C to reflux. Pyridine can act as a base and catalyst. The reaction releases SO₂ and HCl gases and yields the desired benzyl chloride.

Acid‑base neutralization producing a sodium alkoxide; 2‑(diethylamino)ethanol reacts with stoichiometric NaOH, deprotonating the hydroxyl group to give water sodium 2‑(diethylamino)ethoxide; performed in aqueous or alcoholic solution (e.g., ethanol/water) at ambient temperature; the sodium salt can be isolated by evaporation or used in situ for further alkylation reactions.

Oxidative cleavage of an internal alkene using hot aqueous potassium permanganate; the C=C bond of hex‑3‑ene is broken to give two molecules of propionic acid. Reaction type: oxidative cleavage. Typical conditions: excess KMnO4 in water, heated to 70‑100 °C, followed by acidic work‑up to isolate the carboxylic acids.

Halogen exchange (fluorination) using antimony trifluoride; replaces a bromide with fluorine to give 1‑fluorohexane. Typically performed by heating 1‑hexyl bromide with SbF₃ in a non‑polar solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or chloroform under reflux; the by‑product antimony tribromide precipitates.

Transesterification (alcoholysis) of dimethyl methylphosphonate with ethanol; converts one methoxy group to ethoxy, yielding ethyl methylphosphonate and methanol. Usually carried out with excess ethanol as solvent, catalyzed by a trace acid (e.g., H₂₄) or base (e.g., NaOMe) at reflux; methanol is removed to drive the equilibrium.

The reaction is an intramolecular nucleophilic substitution. Sodium hydroxide deprotonates the hydroxyl group in 2-chloro-2-methylpropan-1-ol, forming an alkoxide that attacks the electrophilic carbon bearing the chloride, expelling Cl⁻ and forming 2,2-dimethyloxirane (epoxide). Conditions: aqueous NaOH at moderate temperature. Purpose: epoxide formation via neighboring-group participation.

Grignard addition to a ketone; methylmagnesium bromide adds to cyclopentanone to form a tertiary alkoxide which upon aqueous work‑up affords 1‑methyl‑cyclopentanol. Reaction is run in anhydrous ether (diethyl ether or THF) at 0 °C to room temperature, followed by acidic quench to protonate the alkoxide; magnesium bromide salts remain in solution.

Acid‑catalyzed hydration of 3‑methylidenepentane to give the tertiary alcohol 3‑methyl‑3‑pentanol (Markovnikov addition); typically performed with concentrated H₂SO₄ or phosphoric acid at 100–150 °C; solvent can be the acid itself or an inert organic solvent like toluene; no external catalyst beyond the acid is required.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of benzyl iodide with sodiumide benzyl az and sodium iodide. Conducted in a polar aprotic such as DMF or DMSO at ambient temperature or mild heating; the reaction proceeds cleanly because the benzyl carbon is primary and unhindered.

Acid‑base salt formation; aqueous or gaseous hydrochlor acid protonates the am adiphenine to give adiphenine·HCl as a crystalline hydrochloride salt. The base is dissolved in a suitable solvent (ethanol, methanol, or ether) and HCl is added at 0 °C to rt; the product precipitates on cooling and is filtered.

Suzuki‑Miyaura cross‑coupling between phenylboronic acid and 4‑(trifluoromethyl)iodobene to afford 1‑phenyl‑4-(trifluoromethyl)benzene. Typical conditions: toluene as solvent, cesium carbonate as base, Pd(OAc)₂ (0.5–2 mol %) with tri‑tert‑butylphosphine ligand, heated to 80–110 °C under nitrogen. The reaction gives the biaryl after aqueous work‑up and chromatographic purification.

Transesterification. Similar to reaction 4 but with ethanol. Heptan-3-yl acetate undergoes ethanolysis in acidic conditions (H+), yielding heptan-3-ol and ethyl acetate. Ethanol solvent, heating with acid catalyst.

Alkylation (SN2) of guanine by methyl fluorosulfonate; methyl group transferred to O6 of guanine forming O6‑methylguanine and fluorosulfonic acid released; typically carried out in anhydrous polar aprotic solvent (e.g., acitrile) at low temperature under inert atmosphere.

Thermal decomposition (or gas‑evolution) of a metal hexafluorosilicate; purpose is to obtain anhydrous magnesium fluoride and volatile silicon tetrafluoride; MgSiF₆ → MgF₂ (solid) + SiF₄ (gas); carried out by heating the solid salt to 300‑500 °C under an inert atmosphere to avoid hydrolysis; no solvent, optional use of a dry, non‑reactive tube.

Williamson‑type O‑alkylation (SN2) of sodium salicylate with ethyl iodide; phenoxide attacks ethyl iodide giving ethyl salicylate and sodium iodide; performed in polar aprotic solvent such as acetone or DMF, often refluxed, sometimes with a phase‑transfer catalyst.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) between potassium carbonate and cadmium oxalate in aqueous solution; carbonate exchanges with oxalate, precipitating sparingly soluble cadmium carbonate while forming soluble potassium oxalate; usually done at ambient temperature with stirring.

Double displacement precipitation; aqueous Ba(OH)2 exchanges anions with Pb(NO3)2, forming insoluble Pb(OH)2 precipitate and soluble Ba(NO3)2; performed at ambient temperature in water; no catalyst required.

Acid‑base neutralization ofodium succinate with hydrochloric acid; the dianion is protonated to succinic acid and sodium chloride forms as the salt; conducted in water at room temperature or with gentle heating.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of methyl iodide by sulfide ion from sodium sulfide; sulfide attacks two equivalents of methyl iodide to produce dimethyl sulfide and sodium iodide; typically carried out in polar aprotic solvent (e.g., DMSO or DMF) at mild temperature, often under inert atmosphere.

Reaction type: transesterification. Purpose: to exchange the propyl alkoxy group for an ethyl group, producing ethyl 2‑hydroxypropanoate (ethyl lactate) and 1‑propanol. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of ethanol on the carbonyl of propyl lactate, forming a tetrahedral intermediate that collapses to release propanol and generate the ethyl ester. Typical conditions: excess ethanol (3–5 equiv) with an acid catalyst (e.g., 1 % H₂SO₄) or a base catalyst (e.g. NaOEt), heat under reflux (60–80 °C) for 2–6 h; removal of the liberated propanol drives the equilibrium forward. Solvent: often solvent‑free, using ethanol as both reactant and medium.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation of sodium chromate with strontium nitrate in water; strontium chromate precipitates as an insoluble solid while sodium nitrate stays in solution; performed at room temperature with stirring.

Electrophilic addition (hydrohalogenation). Markovnikov addition of hydrogen iodide to 1‑butene gives 2‑iodobutane. Purpose: synthesis of alkyl iodide. Key transformation: alkene C=C → C–C single bond with addition of H and I across the double bond, iodide adds to the more substituted carbon. Typical conditions: HI generated in situ with red phosphorus, reflux in anhydrous non‑polar solvent (e.g., diethyl ether or dichloromethane), inert atmosphere.
Double-displacement (metathesis) reaction; forms bismuth(III) bromide and nitric acid; occurs in aqueous solution at ambient temperature.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution with an organolithium reagent. Methyllithium adds to acetyl chloride, displacing chloride and yielding acetone after work‑up. Purpose: preparation of ketones from acid chlorides. Key transformation: R–Li attacks carbonyl carbon, forming a tetrahedral intermediate that collapses to release LiCl and give the ketone. Conditions: low temperature (−78 °C to 0 °C) in dry ether or THF, strictly anhydrous, inert gas (N₂ or Ar). No additional catalyst required.

Carbothermic reduction; solid GeS2 is mixed with carbon and heated strongly, reducing the sulfide to elemental germanium while forming volatile carbon disulfide (CS2). Conducted at >1000 °C in an inert (argon or nitrogen) atmosphere to prevent oxidation; carbon acts as the reducing agent, no additional catalyst required.

High‑temperature fluorination (oxidative halogenation); converts refractory gadolinium oxide to volatile gadolinium fluoride and releases oxygen; key transformation: Gd2O3 + 3 F2 → 2 GdF3 + 3/2 O2; typically carried out with dry F2 gas at 400‑600 °C in an inert atmosphere; no solvent, no catalyst needed.

Redox oxidation combined with neutralization; SeO₂ is further oxidized by O₂ in basic solution to form sodium selenate (Na₂SeO₄) and water. Conducted by bubbling O₂ through a hot aqueous NaOH solution (≈60‑80 °C); no special catalyst, inert atmosphere often used.

Transesterification of phenyl 2,2,2-trichloroacetate to methyl 2,2,2-trichloroacetate using methanol; methoxide catalysis (from trace base) or acidic conditions promote nucleophilic substitution, regenerating phenol and forming the methyl ester.

Neutralization reaction; dinitrogen pentoxide (acidic oxide) reacts with sodium hydroxide to produce sodium nitrate and water; occurs in aqueous solution or at elevated temperatures with solid reagents.

Combustion/redox reaction; chromium(II) sulfide oxidizes to form sulfur dioxide and chromium(III) oxide; requires high temperatures to initiate and sustain the reaction, typically in air or oxygen-rich environment.

Jones oxidation (chromic‑acid oxidation); oxidizes an aldehyde to a carboxylic acid with Cr(VI) reagents. Key transformation: 4‑methylpentanal → 4‑methylpentanoic acid, Cr(VI) reduced to Cr(III) sulfate, water generated. Typical conditions: aqueous sulfuric acid (≈2 M), CrO₃ (or Na₂Cr₂O₇) added at 0 °C then warmed to ambient temperature. No organic solvent required; reaction performed in the aqueous phase.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution; indole 3-functionalization with dimethoxymethane as a formaldehyde precursor to form indole-3-carbinol; sulfuric acid catalyzes regeneration of CH2O from dimethoxymethane; reaction typically proceeds in aqueous organic solvent at moderate temperatures.

Acid–base (salt metathesis) reaction; sulfide ion is protonated by hydrochloric acid producing hydrogen sulfide gas and sodium chloride in solution; carried out at ambient temperature in aqueous medium; H₂S gas evolves and is collected; no catalyst needed.

Oxidation – primary alcohol to carboxylic acid. 2‑Methoxyethanol is oxidized by aqueous potassium permanganate under acidic or neutral conditions, usually heated reflux in water or dilute sulfuric acid. The primary alcohol group is converted first to the aldehyde and then to 2‑methoxyacetic acid; KMnO₄ is reduced to MnO₂ (or Mn²⁺ in acidic medium). Typical solvent: water;: none.

Hydrolysis – ester cleavage. Acephate (O,S‑dimethyl acetylphosphoramidothioate) reacts with water, generally in a mildly acidic or neutral aqueous medium at ambient or slightly elevated temperature. The acetyl ester bond is hydrolyzed yielding acetic acid and the remaining O,S‑dimethyl phosphoramidothioate anion (often isolated as its salt). No catalyst is required; water itself acts as nucleophile.

Gas‑phase partial oxidation (combustion): hydrogen sulfide reacts with oxygen to produce elemental sulfur and water; employed in gas‑cleaning processes at 200–400 °C, usually over metal oxide catalysts such as V2O5 or TiO2.

Redox reduction and ligand substitution. Chloroauric acid (HAuCl₄) is reduced by hydrazine in the presence of dimethyl sulfide (DMS). Hydrazine donates electrons, converting Au(III) to Au(I) while DMS coordinates to the gold center, forming chloro(dimethyl sulfide)gold(I). By‑products are hydrochloric acid, nitrogen gas, and water. The reaction is performed in aqueous acidic solution, typically at room temperature; no external catalyst is needed.

Catalytic hydrogenation – aromatic heterocycle reduction. 3,5‑Dimethylpyridine is hydrogenated over palladium on carbon (Pd/C) under H pressure (1–5 atm) in an alcohol solvent such as ethanol or methanol, at 25–80 °C. The aromatic pyridine ring is fully reduced to give 3,5‑dimethylpiperidine. Pd/C acts as the heterogeneous catalyst; the reaction is conducted in solution under inert atmosphere except for the H₂.

Conversion of (E)-cinnamic acid to (E)-3-phenylprop-2-enoyl chloride using oxalyl chloride; reaction type is formation of an acid chloride; key transformation is activation of the carboxylic acid by replacement of the OH with Cl, releasing CO, CO₂ and HCl; typical conditions use dry dichloromethane at 0 °C to rt with a catalytic amount of DMF or pyridine to scavenge HCl; the reaction is performed under inert atmosphere.

Acid‑base complex formation. Zinc bromide reacts with sodium hydroxide in aqueous solution to give the zincate ion (often written Na₂[Zn(OH)₄] or Na₂ZnO₂ depending on stoichiometry) and sodium bromide. The process is a neutralization/complexation carried out at ambient temperature in water; excess NaOH drives formation of the soluble zincate species.

Electrophilic Markovnikov addition of hydrogen iodide to 2‑methylpropene, yielding tert‑butyl iodide; the proton adds to the less substituted carbon, and iodide adds to the more substituted carbon. Reaction is performed neat or in a non‑protic solvent such as ether at 0 °C to room temperature, often under an inert gas to exclude moisture.

Acidic redox – oxidation of Fe(II) to Fe(III) by permanganate. In strongly acidic medium (sulfuric acid), potassium permanganate oxidizes ferrous citrate to ferric citrate while the permanganate is reduced from Mn(VII) to Mn(II precipitating as manganese(II) sulfate. The overall stoichiometry yields water, potassium sulfate, manganese(II) sulfate, and ferric citrate. Reaction is performed in aqueous solution, typically heated to reflux; no external catalyst is required.

Friedel‑Crafts alkylation; electrophilic aromatic substitution of furan with methyl bromide using anhydrous AlCl₃ to install a methyl group at the 2‑position, yielding 2‑methylfuran; typically performed in an inert, aprotic solvent such as dry CH₂Cl₂ or CS₂ at 0 °C to reflux under nitrogen; AlCl₃ acts as Lewis‑acid catalyst and is removed by aqueous work‑up.

Conjugate (Michael) addition of cyanide to ethyl acrylate; nucleophilic 1,4‑addition of NaCN to the β‑carbon of the α,β‑unsaturated ester producing ethyl 3‑cyanopropionate; usually carried out in aqueous or alcoholic media (e.g., ethanol/water) at 0 °C to room temperature, sometimes with a phase‑transfer catalyst; no additional catalyst required.

Esterification of gallic acid with diazomethane; the carboxylic acid group is methylated by CH₂N₂, releasing N₂ gas and forming methyl gallate; performed in anhydrous ether (diethyl ether or THF) at 0 °C to ambient temperature under inert atmosphere; the reaction is rapid and exothermic, and excess diazomethane is quenched before work‑up.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt formation); the acidic proton of ethoxy(methyl)phosphinic acid is deprotonated by NaOH to give sodium ethoxy(methyl)phosphinate and water; conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no special solvent or catalyst is required beyond the aqueous medium.

Ester hydrolysis (saponification) of methyl perfluorooctanoate; water (often with acid or base catalyst) cleaves the ester bond to afford perfluorooctanoic acid and methanol; typically heated in aqueous acid (e.g., 1 M HCl) or base (e.g., NaOH) at reflux, followed by acidification to isolate the acid; common solvent is a mixture of water and a miscible organic solvent such as methanol.

Reduction of a nitroalkane to a primary amine using lithium aluminium hydride; LAH transfers hydride to the nitro group of 1‑nitrobutane, yielding butan‑1‑amine with concomitant formation of LiOH and Al(OH)₃ upon aqueous quench; performed in dry ether (THF or Et₂O) under nitrogen at 0 °C to reflux; LAH is the stoichiometric reducing agent; work‑up with careful addition of water or dilute acid neutralizes the metal residues.

Halide exchange (Finkelstein‑type) of benzyl chloride with lithium fluoride. Purpose: replace chloride with fluoride to afford benzyl fluoride, a valuable intermediate for fluorination chemistry. Key transformation: SN2 displacement of Cl⁻ by F⁻; LiCl precipitates out. Typical conditions: polar aprotic solvent such as DMF, DMSO, or acetone; temperature 80–120 °C; excess LiF; inert atmosphere optional; no additional catalyst.

Direct fluorination/halogen exchange oxidation where elemental fluorine replaces chlorine ligands on molybdenum pentachloride to give molybdenum pentafluoride and chlorine gas; performed under anhydrous, inert atmosphere at low to moderate temperature (often 0 °C to room temperature) due to the vigorous nature of F₂; no solvent is required, the gases are mixed directly.

Double‑displacement precipitation reaction between sodium sulfide andarium nitrate in aqueous solution; the purpose is to generate insoluble barium sulfide as a precipitate while forming soluble sodium nitrate; typically performed ambient temperature in water with stirring, followed by filtration to isolate BaS.

Acid‑ or base‑catalyzed epoxide ring‑opening (hydrolysis) of propylene oxide to 1,2‑propanediol; water adds across the three‑membered ring to give the vicinal diol; commonly performed with dilute mineral acid (e.g., 1 M H₂SO₄) or NaOH at 50–100 °C; aqueous medium or water/THF mixture is used.

N‑alkylation of p‑phenylenediamine using ethyl iodide in the presence of sodium ethoxide (a strong base); the base deprotonates the amine, enabling SN2 attack of ethyl iodide to give N,N‑diethyl‑p‑phenylenediamine and sodium iodide; conducted in ethanol (or another polar protic solvent) under reflux to ensure complete alkylation.
Single displacement reaction. Purpose: generation of hydrogen gas and ZnBr2. Transformation: Zn replaces hydrogen in HBr. Conditions: aqueous HBr at room temperature; solvent: water; no catalyst.

Acid‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (acidic cleavage) of methyl isovalerate with aqueous hydrochloric acid; the ester bond is protonated and water attacks, yielding methanol and isovaleric acid; usually refluxed in an aqueous HCl solution (1–6 M) until the reaction reaches completion, then the products are separated by extraction.

Acidic decomposition of sodium thiosulfate with hydrochloric acid, a redox reaction that produces sulfur dioxide, elemental cyclooctasulfur (S₈), water, and sodium chloride; performed in aqueous solution at room temperature or with gentle heating; excess HCl ensures full conversion, and the precipitated sulfur is removed by filtration.

Redox oxidation–reduction reaction; dichromate(VI) in strongly acidic aqueous medium oxidizes bromide ions to elemental bromine while Cr(VI) is reduced to Cr(III). Typically carried out by mixing potassium dichromate with excess sulfuric acid and hydrogen bromide, heating the mixture in water; no additional catalyst is required.

Alcoholysis / ligand exchange (transesterification) between niobium(V) ethoxide and acetic acid to afford niobium(V) acetate and ethanol. Each ethoxy ligand is replaced by an acetate group. Reaction is performed by refluxing Nb(OC2H5)5 with excess glacial acetic acid (5–10 equiv) under inert atmosphere; ethanol formed is removed by distillation. Acetic acid serves as both reactant and solvent; no additional catalyst is required.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) alkylation; the thiol group of 2‑mercaptobenzothiazole attacks the electrophilic chloromethyl carbon of chloromethyl thiocyanate, displacing chloride to form a thioether linkage. Conducted in an aprotic polar solvent such as DMF or DMSO, often with a mild base (e.g., potassium carbonate) at room temperature to reflux.

Grignard reagent formation; purpose is to generate cyclopentylmagnesium bromide as a nucleophilic organometallic for further reactions; key transformation is insertion of magnesium into a C‑Br bond of 1,2-dibromocyclopentane giving cyclopentylmagnesium bromide and MgBr₂; typical conditions are anhydrous, inert atmosphere, dry diethyl ether or THF as solvent, freshly activated magnesium turnings, reflux temperature.

Acid‑catalyzed esterification of methacrylic acid with isobutylene to give isobutyl methacrylate; purpose is synthesis of a polymerizable ester monomer; key transformation is protonation of the alkene to a carbocation followed by nucleophilic attack of the carboxylate and loss of water; typically run at 60‑100 °C with catalytic H₂SO₄, water removed (Dean‑Stark) and often performed neat or in an inert solvent such as toluene.

Fischer esterification (condensation) of a carboxylic acid with methanol; purpose is to convert terephthalic acid to methyl terephthalate (mono‑ester) and water; key transformation is nucleophilic attack of methanol on a carbonyl, forming ester linkage and releasing water; typically refluxed in excess methanol with a strong acid catalyst such as sulfuric acid or p‑toluenesulfonic acid; temperature 60–80 °C; methanol serves both reactant and solvent.

Metathesis (double‑displacement) precipitation. Sodium azideions with copper(I) chloride to give insoluble copper(I) azide and NaCl. Conducted in aqueous solution (often cold water) under dark or amber light to avoid photodecomposition of CuN₃; precipitation filtered and washed.

Hydrochlorination/substitution of glycerol with hydrogen chloride to give 3‑chloro‑1,2‑propanediol. Primary hydroxyl is replaced by chloride under reflux in concentrated aqueous HCl (often 6 M) at 100 °C; the reaction proceeds via protonation of the OH and loss of water, forming a carbocation that captures chloride.

Acid–base reaction of a carbonate with hydrochloric acid; purpose is to generate ferrous chloride solution and evolve CO₂; FeCO₃(s) + 2 HCl(aq) → FeCl₂(aq) + CO₂(g) + H₂O(l); performed in water at ambient temperature; no catalyst needed.

Esterification (acylation) of benzyl alcohol with phthalic anhydride to afford monobenzyl phthalate and water. Performed by heating the reagents together, typically in an inert solvent such as toluene or xylene, with removal of water by azeotropic distillation (Dean–Stark trap) and optionally a catalytic amount of p‑toluenesulfonic acid to accelerate the reaction.

Double displacement/crystallization; preparation of potassium alum by mixing aqueous potassium sulfate and aluminum sulfate, dissolving with water, then cooling/evaporating to crystallize KAl(SO4)2·12H2O; typically performed at ambient to moderate temperature, no catalyst, water as solvent.

Decarboxylative elimination of ferulic acid to afford 4‑vinylguaiacol and CO₂; a thermal or metal‑catalyzed decarboxylation; common conditions: heating 150–250 °C in a high‑boiling solvent (toluene) or using solid acid/zeolite or enzymatic ferulic acid decarboxylase at 30 °C, pH≈7; no additional reagents besides catalyst.

Hydrolysis of an isocyanate; water attacks 4‑(trifluoromethyl)phenyl isocyanate forming a carbamic acid intermediate that decomposes to 4‑(trifluoromethyl)aniline and CO2; generally carried out in aqueous medium (often buffered) at room temperature to 50 °C; acid or base can be used as catalyst but not required.

Nucleophilic substitution (S‑alkylation); the thiol group of N‑acetylcysteine attacks benzyl chloride, displacing chloride to give benzyl‑mercapturic acid (N‑acetyl‑S‑benzyl‑cysteine) and HCl; performed in aqueous buffered solution (pH 7–8) or mixed water/acetone, sometimes with a mild base (NaHCO3) to deprotonate the thiol; mild heating (30–40 °C) may be applied.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution of a di‑acid chloride with ethanol to give the di‑ethyl ester and HCl. Performed in anhydrous dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to room temperature in the presence of a base such as pyridine or triethylamine to trap the liberated HCl; the reaction proceeds rapidly to give diethyl 2‑methylpropanedioate.

Redox (oxidation‑reduction) reaction; cerium(IV) sulfate oxidizes hydrogen peroxide to oxygen while being reduced to cerium(III) sulfate; carried out in aqueous acidic solution (often dilute H2SO4) at 0–25 °C to control gas evolution; no external catalyst needed, water is both solvent and product.

Electrophilic nitrosation; N,N‑bis(2‑hydroxypropyl)amine reacts with nitrosyl tetrafluoroborate (NOBF4) to form N‑bis(2‑hydroxypropyl)nitrosamine and tetrafluoroboric acid; performed under anhydrous conditions in a non‑protic solvent such as dry dichloromethane or chloroform at 0 °C to room temperature; the reaction is moisture‑sensitive and does not require additional catalyst.

Aluminothermic reduction of zinc oxide; purpose is to generate zinc metal and aluminum oxide. Aluminum reduces ZnO to Zn; the reaction requires high temperature (≈1000–1300 °C) to volatilize zinc and drive the reduction. Carried out as a solid‑state mixture, often in an inert or reducing atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst needed.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reductive amination) of a nitrile; pentanenitrile is converted to pentan‑1‑amine by hydrogen addition over a metal catalyst (e.g., Raney Ni, Pd/C, or Pt) under high H2 pressure (30–50 bar) and temperatures of 80–120 °C; common solvents include ethanol, methanol, or water; the reaction proceeds via an imine intermediate that is further hydrogenated to the primary amine.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt metathesis) in aqueous solution; purpose is to convert ammonium oxalate to oxalic acid while forming ammonium nitrate; key transformation is proton transfer from nitric acid to oxalate ion producing oxalic acid and exchange of cations to give NH4⁺NO3⁻; typical conditions are room temperature to moderate heating (≤50 °C) in water; no catalyst required.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) between silver azide and silicon tetrabromide to afford silver bromide precipitate and silicon tetraazide; purpose is synthesis of the high‑energy silicon tetraazide; key transformation is exchange of Br⁻ and N₃⁻ ions forming insoluble AgBr and Si(N₃)₄; performed under strictly anhydrous, inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar) at low temperature (0–5 °C) to avoid detonation; dry acetonitrile or THF is common solvent; no catalyst, but careful exclusion of moisture is essential.

Alcoholysis / transesterification of dimethylacetoxysilane with methanol to give dimethylmethoxysilane and acetic acid; purpose is to replace the acetoxy group by a methoxy group on silicon; key transformation is cleavage of the Si–OAc bond and formation of Si–OMe with release of AcOH; typically carried out at mild heating in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or toluene, using a catalytic amount of acid (e.g., pyridine or p‑toluenesulfonic acid) or base to accelerate the exchange; no stoichiometric catalyst required.

Catalytic hydrogenation of a ketone to a secondary alcohol using H₂ and a metal catalyst (e.g., Pd/C, PtO₂, Raney Ni) under H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) at 25–100 °C in an alcohol solvent (EtOH, MeOH). Converts the carbonyl of 2‑methylcyclopentanone to 2‑methylcyclopentan‑1‑ol.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (amidation) of acetyl chloride with aniline in the presence of sodium carbonate; purpose is preparation of acetanilide; key transformation is attack of the aniline nitrogen on the acetyl chloride carbonyl, forming the amide and releasing HCl, which is neutralized by Na₂CO₃ to give CO₂, NaCl, and water; carried out at 0 °C to ambient temperature, often in a biphasic system of water and an organic solvent (e.g., ether or dichloromethane); sodium carbonate serves as base, no additional catalyst needed.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2 hydrolysis); aqueous NaOH attacks cyclopropyl chloride, displacing chloride to form cyclopropanol and NaCl; performed in water or water/ethanol at reflux or ambient temperature.

Transesterification of ethyl anthranilate with methanol to afford methyl anthranilate and ethanol; purpose is production of the methyl ester (flavor/fragrance); key transformation is exchange of the ethoxy group for a methoxy group on the anthranilate carbonyl; reaction is usually performed under reflux in excess methanol with an acid catalyst such as sulfuric acid or p‑toluenesulfonic acid (or a catalytic base like NaOMe); removal of the generated ethanol (e.g., by azeotropic distillation) drives the equilibrium to product; methanol serves as both solvent and reactant.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis of nitroglycerin with sulfuric acid; purpose is decomposition of the energetic nitrate ester to non‑explosive glycerol and nitric acid for safety or analytical work; key transformation is proton‑mediated cleavage of the C–ONO₂ bonds, yielding glycerol, HNO₃, and water; carried out in aqueous medium with dilute H₂SO₄ at 50–80 °C; water is the solvent and sulfuric acid provides the necessary protons; no additional catalyst is required.

Oxidation (peracid oxidation). Peracetic acid oxidizes thiourea, converting the sulfur to the dioxide functionality to give thiourea dioxide while the peracid is reduced to acetic acid. Typically carried out in aqueous solution at 0‑5 °C, often under acidic to neutral pH; water is the solvent and no external catalyst is required.

Acid‑base precipitation (salt formation): erbium(III) hydroxide reacts with phosphoric acid in aqueous solution, neutralizing to give erbium(III) phosphate and water; the mixture is heated gently (≈ 80–100 °C) to promote dissolution and precipitation, then cooled to isolate the insoluble phosphate precipitate; no special catalyst is required.

Acid‑base metathesis (double displacement). Nitric acid protonates the bromate ion and exchanges the cation to form bromic acid and rubidium nitrate. Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; water is the reaction medium and no catalyst is needed.

Oxidation of a thiol to a thione/N‑oxide (formation of pyrithione) using hydrogen peroxide. H2O2 oxidizes the –SH group of 2‑mercaptopyridine, generating the heterocyclic thione (pyrithione) and water as the only by‑product. Usually performed in aqueous or mixed aqueous/organic solvent (e.g., water/acetone) at 20–60 °C, sometimes with a small amount of base to deprotonate the thiol. No metal catalyst is needed; the reaction proceeds via the peroxide’s electrophilic oxygen.

Hydrolysis of silicon tetrachloride; SiCl₄ reacts rapidly with water to form solid silicon dioxide (SiO₂) and gaseous hydrogen chloride; usually achieved by slow addition of SiCl₄ to cold water or dilute acid with vigorous stirring; reaction proceeds at 0 °C to ambient temperature; no catalyst required.

Amide‑forming condensation using a tetramethylformamidinium coupling reagent. Acetic acid is activated by chloro‑N,N,N′,N′‑tetramethylformamidinium hexafluorophosphate, allowing nucleophilic attack by methylamine to afford N‑methylacetamide; the by‑product is tetramethylurea. Usually performed in an aprotic polar solvent such as dichloromethane or acetonitrile, at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst is required.

Chromium(VI) oxidation of a benzylic methyl group. Sodium dichromate in concentrated sulfuric acid oxidizes the methyl substituent of 3,5‑dinitrotoluene to a carboxyl group, yielding 3,5‑dinitrobenzoic acid while the dichromate is reduced to chromium(III) sulfate. Conducted under reflux in a strongly acidic aqueous medium; temperature 80‑120 °C; no external catalyst beyond the dichromate oxidant.

Halogen exchange (fluorination) reaction; used to replace chlorine atoms with fluorine in organic compounds. 1,1,1,2-Tetrachloroethane reacts with hydrogen fluoride to form 1,1-dichloro-2,2-difluoroethane via nucleophilic substitution, releasing hydrogen chloride. Catalysts like antimony pentafluoride may be used. Requires anhydrous HF solvent under controlled conditions.

Direct preparation of methyllithium by metal‑halogen reduction. Methyl chloride reacts with lithium metal to give methyllithium and lithium chloride. Purpose: generation of a strong nucleophilic organolithium reagent. Key transformation: single‑electron transfer from Li to the alkyl halide, forming LiCl and the organolithium species. Conditions: dry ether (diethyl ether or THF), low temperature (−30 to 0 °C), strict exclusion of moisture and air, inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar). No additional catalyst.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt formation). Metaphosphoric acid (HPO₃) reacts with potassium hydroxide to produce potassium metaphosphate (KPO₃) and water. Performed in aqueous solution at room temperature; water is the solvent and no catalyst is required.

Hydrolysis of tetraethyl orthocarbonate; ester (carbonate) cleavage to give ethanol and carbonic acid (which decomposes to CO₂ and H₂O). General type: acid‑ or base‑catalyzed hydrolysis of a carbonate protecting group. Purpose: deprotection, generation of ethanol. Key transformation: C(OR)₄ → 4 ROH + CO₂/H₂O. Typical conditions: aqueous medium, reflux, often with a catalytic amount of HCl or NaOH. Common solvents: water or water/acetone mixtures.

Oxidation of a thioether (diethyl sulfide) to the corresponding sulfoxide (diethyl sulfoxide) using sodium periodate. General type: stoichiometric oxidation of sulfide to sulfoxide. Purpose: selective oxidation without over‑oxidation to sulfone. Key transformation: R₂S → R₂S=O; NaIO₄ reduced to NaIO₃. Typical conditions: aqueous or aqueous‑acetonitrile solution, 0–25 °C, stir under inert atmosphere. No additional catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis (or base‑catalyzed saponification) of menthyl acetate to menthol and acetic acid. General type: ester hydrolysis. Purpose: release the free alcohol from its acetate ester. Key transformation: R‑OCOCH₃ + H₂O → R‑OH + CH₃COOH. Typical conditions: reflux in aqueous H₂SO₄ (or NaOH followed by acid work‑up); temperature 80–100 °C. Solvent often a mixture of water and a water‑immiscible organic (e.g., toluene) to aid phase separation.

Oxidation of primary alcohol (heptanol) to carboxylic acid (heptanoic acid) using chromic acid generated in situ from sodium dichromate and sulfuric acid. General type: strong oxidizing conversion of 1° alcohol to acid. Purpose: functional‑group oxidation to acid. Key transformation: R‑CH₂OH → R‑CO₂H; Na₂Cr₂O₇ + H₂SO₄ → H₂CrO₄ (chromic acid) which is reduced to Cr³⁺; Na₂SO₄ formed asproduct. Typical conditions: aqueous H₂SO₄, reflux 80–100 °C, stoichiometric oxidant. No organic solvent required; aqueous medium suffices.

Oxidation of Albendazole (which contains a thioether) to Albendazole sulfoxide using tert‑butyl hydroperoxide (TBHP) with manganese(III) acetate as catalyst. General type: metal‑mediated radical oxidation of sulfide to sulfoxide. Purpose: generate the pharmacologically active metabolite (sulfoxide). Key transformation: R‑S‑R → R‑S(=O)‑R; Mn(OAc)₃ reduced to Mn(OAc)₂ and acetic acid released. Typical conditions: acetonitrile or acetone as solvent, 0–25 °C to 40 °C, catalytic Mn(OAc)₃ (5–10 mol %), excess TBHP (1.2–2 equiv). Reaction proceeds under nitrogen to avoid over‑oxidation.

Nitration of 2,4‑dinitroaniline to 2,4,6‑trinitroaniline using mixed concentrated nitric and sulfuric acids. General type: electrophilic aromatic substitution (nitration). Purpose: introduce a third nitro group to afford a highly nitrated aromatic compound (explosive precursor). Key transformation: Ar‑H + NO₂⁺ → Ar‑NO₂ + H₂O; H₂SO₄ acts as a proton donor and NO⁺ generator. Typical conditions: chilled mixture (0–5 °C) of conc. H₂SO₄/HNO₃, slow addition of substrate, then stirring at low temperature before quench. Common solvent: none; reaction performed in the acid mixture itself.

Type: conversion of a carboxylic acid to an acid chloride using thionyl chloride. Purpose: activate the acid for subsequent acylation reactions. Key transformation: the -COOH group is replaced by a -COCl group, producing HCl and SO₂ gases as by‑products. Typical conditions: reflux or gentle heating in anhydrous, aprotic solvents such as dichloromethane, chloroform or toluene under nitrogen; a catalytic amount of DMF or pyridine is often added to accelerate the reaction and scavenge HCl. Gases are removed by a vent or inert gas flow.

Type: metathesis/ion‑exchange reaction to generate a nitrosonium salt. Purpose: preparation of nitrosonium tetrafluoroborate (NO⁺ BF₄⁻), a powerful nitrosating agent for aromatic and aliphatic substrates. Key transformation: chloride from NOCl is transferred to silver, forming insoluble AgCl, while the nitrosonium cation pairs with BF₄⁻. Typical conditions: dry, non‑nucleophilic solvent (e.g., acetonitrile, nitromethane) at 0 °C to room temperature under an inert atmosphere; the precipitated AgCl is filtered off. No additional catalyst required.

Type: nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of an alkyl chloride by cyanide. Purpose: synthesis of a nitrile (2‑cyano‑N‑methylacetamide) from the corresponding chloro‑acetamide. Key transformation: the cyanide ion displaces chloride, forming the C≡N bond and producing NaCl as a by‑product. Typical conditions: polar aprotic solvent such as DMF, DMSO, or NMP; temperature 50‑80 °C; stoichiometric NaCN (often used as its aqueous solution) with careful control of pH to avoid hydrolysis. No catalyst required.

Type: alkaline hydrolysis (SN2) of a primary benzylic chloride Purpose: conversion of benzyl chloride to benzyl alcohol. Key transformation: hydroxide ion attacks the benzylic carbon, displacing chloride and forming the primary alcohol; potassium chloride is formed as the inorganic salt. Typical conditions: aqueous KOH (often 10‑20 % w/w) heated under reflux; can be performed in water or a water‑ethanol mixture. Reaction is usually complete within 1‑2 h; product is extracted with an organic solvent (e.g., ether) and purified.

Type: thermal decomposition (calcination) of a heteropoly acid. Purpose: generation of metal oxides (WO₃ and SiO₂) from silicotungstic acid, often as a step in catalyst preparation. Key transformation: the polyoxometallate breaks down, releasing water and forming solid tungsten trioxide and silicon dioxide in a 12:1 ratio. Typical conditions: heating the solid in a furnace at 400‑600 °C under dry air or inert gas; the process may be carried out in a crucible with gradual temperature increase to avoid spattering. No solvent or catalyst is used.

Type: double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction in aqueous solution. Purpose: exchange of cations to produce calcium citrate, which is less soluble and can precipitate, while lithium chloride remains in solution. Key transformation: calcium ions replace lithium ions in the citrate complex, forming Ca₃(C₆H₅O₇)₂ (or Ca‑citrate) and LiCl. Typical conditions: aqueous solutions of lithium citrate and calcium chloride mixed at ambient temperature; stirring for 30‑60 min leads to precipitation of calcium citrate, which is filtered, washed, and dried. No catalyst required.

Esterification (acylation) of sec‑butanol with acetic anhydride to give sec‑butyl acetate and acetic acid; purpose is to protect the alcohol or prepare an ester; key transformation is nucleophilic attack of the alcohol on the anhydride carbonyl with loss of acetate, which is protonated to acetic acid; typical conditions involve mild heating (0‑50 °C) under anhydrous conditions, often with a base catalyst such as pyridine or DMAP, using dichloromethane or no solvent.

Direct combination (halogenation) reaction forming lead(II) chloride. Lead metal reacts chlorine gas, oxidizing to Pb²⁺ while chloride anions are formed, yielding crystalline PbCl₂. Conducted by passing dry Cl₂ over molten lead at 300‑400 °C or by heating solid lead in a chlorine atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst is needed.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) between ammonium hexafluorosilicate and lithium nitrate exchanging counter‑ions to form ammonium nitrate and lithium hexafluorosilicate; purpose may be to obtain a more soluble salt; key transformation is exchange of NH4⁺ with Li⁺; typical conditions are stirring the aqueous salts at ambient temperature or gentle heating until dissolution, no catalyst required, water is the solvent.

Catalytic oxidation of heptane by molecular oxygen producing heptanoic acid and water; purpose is conversion of a hydrocarbon to a carboxylic acid; key transformation involves C–H activation and oxygen insertion forming C=O and O‑H bonds; typical conditions are gas‑phase or liquid‑phase oxidation at 300‑500 °C in the presence of a metal‑oxide catalyst (e.g., V₂O₅, MoO₃, Pt/Al₂O₃) or homogeneous cobalt/bromide systems, with excess O₂ and often an inert carrier gas.

Formation of heptafluorobutyryl chloride from heptafluorobutyric acid using thionyl chloride (SOCl₂); reaction type is acyl‑chloride synthesis (dehydrative chlorination); purpose is to generate a reactive acid chloride for further acylation; key transformation replaces the carboxylic OH with Cl, releasing SO₂ and HCl gases; typical conditions are reflux in anhydrous dichloromethane or chloroform, often with pyridine or triethylamine to scavenge HCl, under nitrogen or argon atmosphere.

Acid‑base neutralization similarly producing ammonia; cesium hydroxide reacts with ammonium nitrate to form cesium nitrate, water, and ammonia gas; carried out in aqueous solution, often with mild heating to remove NH₃; no additional reagents needed.

Salt metathesis/precipitation between silver perchlorate and praseodymium(III) chloride forming insoluble silver chloride and soluble praseodymium(III) perchlorate; purpose is anion exchange to obtain perchlorate salts of lanthanides; key transformation is Ag⁺ pairing with Cl⁻ to give AgCl precipitate; typical conditions involve mixing aqueous or mixed‑solvent solutions at room temperature with vigorous stirring, filtering off AgCl, no catalyst needed.

Hydrolysis of an acyl halide; acetyl iodide reacts with water to regenerate acetic acid while producing hydrogen iodide. Conducted at 0 °C to rt in aqueous medium; the reaction is fast and exothermic. The HI formed can be neutralized with a base (e.g., sodium bicarbonate) during work‑up.

Thermal decomposition; copper(I) azide decomposes upon heating or shock to elemental copper and nitrogen gas; purpose is disposal or generation of N₂; key transformation CuN₃ → Cu(s) + N₂(g); typical conditions: rapid heating to 200–250 °C or mechanical impact; no solvent, often performed in a quartz tube.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of 1‑bromopropane with sodium azide to afford 1‑azidopropane and sodium bromide; purpose is to introduce an azide group for click chemistry or later reduction to amine; key transformation is azide anion attack on the primary carbon displacing bromide; typical conditions use a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO, heating to 50‑80 °C in a sealed tube or under nitrogen, no catalyst required, followed by aqueous work‑up and isolation.

Steglich esterification (DCC‑mediated coupling) to form an ester; purpose is to convert valeric acid and ethanol into ethyl valerate while generating insoluble dicyclohexylurea as by‑product; key transformation is activation of the carboxylic acid by dicyclohexylcarbodiimide followed by nucleophilic attack of ethanol; typically performed in anhydrous dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature, often with catalytic DMAP, and the dicyclohexylurea precipitates out for removal.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a primary alkyl bromide with cyanide ion to give a nitrile. KCN provides CN⁻, which attacks the carbon, expelling Br⁻ and forming butanenitrile; potassium bromide is the by‑product. Commonly carried out in polar aprotic solvents such as DMF, DMSO, or ethanol at 60‑100 °C; a phase‑transfer catalyst may be used to enhance the rate.

Salt metathesis (acid‑base neutralization). Sodium hydroxide exchanges its Na⁺ for the ethacridine cation in ethacridine lactate, liberating the free base ethacridine and forming sodium lactate. Typically performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; no special catalyst required.

Type: reductive dehalogenation; purpose: preparation of tetrafluoroethene; key transformation: zinc reduces 1,2‑dichloro‑1,1,2,2‑tetrafluoroethane, removing two chloride atoms as ZnCl₂ and forming a C=C double bond; typical conditions: Zn dust in dry THF or ether, heated under reflux (80‑120 °C) under inert atmosphere; no external catalyst.

Acylation (acetylation) of a primary aromatic amine using acetic anhydride; purpose is to produce N‑(4‑hydroxyphenyl)acetamide (paracetamol) and acetic acid as a by‑product; key transformation is nucleophilic attack of the amino group on the anhydride carbonyl, forming the amide bond; commonly conducted under reflux in pyridine or a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) with pyridine or triethylamine as a base catalyst to scavenger the generated acetic acid.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of allyl bromide with potassium cyanide yielding allyl cyanide and potassium bromide. Conducted in polar aprotic solvents (e.g., DMF, DMSO) or aqueous/ethanol mixtures, typically at mild temperatures (0–60 °C); potassium cyanide provides the cyanide nucleophile.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) to prepare magnesium gluconate; purpose is to exchange cations between magnesium chloride and sodium gluconate, yielding a chelated magnesium salt and sodium chloride; key transformation is formation of Mg²⁺‑gluconate complexes and precipitation of NaCl in solution; generally performed in aqueous medium at room temperature or slightly warmed to aid solubility, followed by concentration and crystallization of the magnesium gluconate.

Oxidative conversion of dimethylarsine to dimethylarsinic acid using potassium permanganate; purpose is to increase the oxidation state of arsenic from +3 to +5, generating a water‑soluble arsenate; key transformation is KMnO₄‑mediated oxidation of the As–C bonds, producing MnO₂ precipitate and KOH as a base; typically carried out in aqueous alkaline solution (often 0.1–1 M KOH) at moderate temperature (25–80 °C) with stirring until the purple permanganate color fades, then filtration to remove MnO₂.

Acid–base precipitation forming cerium(III) oxalate; purpose is to isolate the sparingly soluble cerium oxalate salt from solution; key transformation is neutralization of cerium(III) hydroxide by oxalic acid, yielding water and cerium(III) oxalate which precipitates; usually performed in aqueous solution at ambient or slightly elevated temperature with stirring; the solid product is filtered, washed, and dried.

Esterification via carbodiimide coupling (Steglich esterification); purpose is to synthesize the local anesthetic Risocaine by forming an ester bond between the carboxyl group of p‑aminobenzoic acid and the hydroxyl of 2‑(diethylamino)ethanol. DCC activates the acid to an O‑acylurea intermediate, which is attacked by the alcohol; dicyclohexylurea precipitates as by‑product. Typical conditions: dichloromethane or THF, 0 °C to room temperature, often with catalytic DMAP, under inert atmosphere.

Base‑induced E2 elimination (dehydrohalogenation); potassium tert‑butoxide abstracts a benzylic hydrogen from phenethyl bromide, generating styrene and tert‑butanol (the latter formed by protonation of the tert‑butoxide). Common conditions: polar aprotic solvent such as DMSO or THF, temperature from 0 °C to reflux, inert atmosphere.

Finkelstein halide exchange (SN2 substitution); sodium iodide in acetone displaces chloride from benzyl chloride to afford benzyl iodide; sodium chloride precipitates out, driving the reaction forward. Typical conditions: refluxing dry acetone, excess NaI, exclusion of moisture, reaction time 1–12 h.

Chlorination of a thiol with thionyl chloride; methanethiol acts as nucleophile toward SOCl₂, yielding methyl chloride while releasing hydrogen chloride and sulfur dioxide gases. Reaction is performed in a dry, non‑nucleophilic solvent (e.g., pyridine or dichloromethane) at 0 °C to room temperature; pyridine scavenges the generated HCl.

Rosenmund‑von Braun cyanation (nucleophilic aromatic substitution with CuCN); copper(I) cyanide reacts with 3‑bromopyridine to replace the bromide with a cyano group, producing 3‑cyanopyridine. Conditions: heating in polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or NMP, often under nitrogen, temperatures 120–150 °C, followed by aqueous work‑up to remove copper salts.

Organolithium addition to an isocyanate, analogous to the Grignard route; phenyl lithium attacks phenyl isocyanate, and after acidic work‑up affords N‑phenylbenzamide; conducted in anhydrous THF, low temperature (–78 °C to 0 °C) under nitrogen; purpose: preparation of amides using a more reactive nucleophile.

Acid‑base neutralization; arsenic acid reacts with ammonium hydroxide to form ammonium arsenate salt and water. Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient or mildly elevated temperature, with stoichiometric amounts to ensure complete neutralization.

Redox reaction (acidic reduction of manganate). Potassium manganate reacts with aqueous hydrochloric acid, reducing Mn(VI) to insoluble MnO2 and oxidizing Cl⁻ to Cl₂ gas while forming KCl and water. Typically performed in dilute HCl at ambient temperature in water.

Oxidation reaction; converts naphthalene to the quinone functional group to afford 1,2‑naphthoquinone. Key transformation is the introduction of two carbonyl groups the 1‑ and 2‑positions of the aromatic ring. Typically performed under aerobic conditions using a metal catalyst (e.g., Co‑acetate, MnO2, Pd/C) at 80‑150 °C in an aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile or toluene; O₂ is supplied at atmospheric or elevated pressure.

Reduction of a nitro group to an amine using tin(II) chloride in hydrochloric acid; 2,4-dichloronitrobenzene is reduced to 2,4-dichloroaniline while water is formed. Classic SnCl₂/HCl reduction conducted under reflux (typically 60‑80 °C) in an ethanol‑water mixture; SnCl₂ serves as the reducing agent, HCl provides acidic medium.

Reaction type: Double displacement. Purpose: Precipitation of barium sulfate to isolate terbium(III) chloride. Key transformation: Sulfate and chloride ions exchange partners. Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient conditions; no catalyst needed.

Acid‑catalyzed nitrile hydrolysis; aqueous hydrochloric acid (≈6 M) and heat (80–120 °C, reflux) convert 2‑(3‑methylphenyl)acetonitrile to 3‑methylphenylacetic acid, with ammonia captured as ammonium chloride.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt formation). Acetic acid donates a proton to tetraethylammonium hydroxide, producing water and the tetraethylammonium acetate salt. Usually carried out at room temperature in aqueous or mixed water‑alcohol media; no additional catalyst is required.

Fischer esterification of a dicarboxylic acid. Ethanol reacts with succinic acid in the presence of catalytic sulfuric acid to form diethyl succinate and water. The reaction proceeds under reflux (≈78 °C) with excess ethanol; removal of water (e.g., Dean‑Stark trap) drives the equilibrium to the ester. Typical solvent is ethanol itself; H₂SO₄ acts as catalyst.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) salt exchange. Copper(II) sulfate reacts with sodium acetate in aqueous solution to give cupric acetate and sodium sulfate. Reaction is performed at ambient temperature with vigorous stirring; both salts remain soluble, so no special conditions or catalysts are required.

Catalytic hydrogenation of a diene. Molecular hydrogen adds across the vinyl double bond and the internal double bond of 4‑vinyl‑1‑cyclohexene, fully saturating the system to produce ethylcyclohexane. Conducted under 1–5 atm H₂ pressure using a heterogeneous metal catalyst such as Pd/C, PtO₂, or Raney Ni in a solvent like ethanol or THF at 25‑80 °C.

Base‑promoted nucleophilic substitution followed by intramolecular ring closure to give an epoxide (allyl glycidyl ether). Allyl alcohol attacks epichlorohydrin under NaOH (aqueous or mixed water/ethanol) at 0 °C to 25 °C, then the mixture is warmed to reflux. Sodium chloride and water are by‑products; no special solvent other than the reaction medium is required.

Acid‑base redox (neutralization/oxidation) reaction; sulfuric acid oxidizes sulfite from sodium metabisulfite to sulfate while generating disulfurous acid; typically performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; water is the solvent and the reaction proceeds without added catalyst.

High‑temperature oxidative combustion; tin phosphide is oxidized by molecular oxygen to give tin(IV) oxide and phosphorus pentoxide; usually carried out in a furnace or flow of O₂ at temperatures above 600 °C; no solvent, solid‑gas contact.

Reaction type: Friedel‑Crafts acylation using an anhydride. Purpose: acetylate toluene to give the same para‑acetyl product while producing acetic acid as the stoichiometric by‑product. Key transformation: acetic anhydride, activated by a Lewis acid (AlCl3, BF3·OEt2), generates an acetyl electrophile that substitutes onto the aromatic ring. Typical conditions: AlCl3 (1.0–1.5 equiv) in anhydrous solvent such as CH2Cl2, CS2 or nitrobenzene, temperature 0 °C to reflux (50‑80 °C) under nitrogen.

SN2 substitution of 3‑(chloromethyl)pyridine with aqueous ammonia; chloride is replaced by an amino group to afford pyridin‑3‑ylmethanamine and HCl. Conducted in water or aqueous ethanol at moderate temperature (≈60‑80 °C) using excess ammonia.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration (elimination) of a benzylic alcohol; concentrated sulfuric acid protonates 1‑phenylethanol, facilitating loss of water to form the alkene styrene; performed at 140–180 °C in neat conc. H₂SO₄ or in a non‑protic solvent such as carbon disulfide; no additional catalyst required.

Direct combination (synthesis): elemental lutetium reacts with fluorine gas to give lutetium(III) fluoride (LuF3). The fluorination requires high temperature (≈400‑600 °C) in a fluorine‑compatible vessel; no solvent is involved.

Carbodiimide‑like coupling (esterification) using carbonyldiimidazole (CDI). CDI activates the carboxyl group of p‑aminobenzoic acid to form an imidazolide intermediate, which then reacts with 2‑(diethylamino)ethanol to afford the ester Risocaine and releases imidazole. Carried out under anhydrous conditions (e.g., dry DMF or DCM) at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen; no additional catalyst needed.

Imide formation via nucleophilic acyl substitution; ammonia attacks glutaric anhydride, ring‑closing to give glutarimide with loss of water; typically reflux in aqueous ammonia or ethanol, often 60‑100 °C, no catalyst needed.

Acid-catalyzed decomposition/gas evolution; used to generate SO₂ gas; bisulfite is protonated by H₂SO₄, releasing SO₂ and H₂O and forming NaHSO₄; performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution/nucleophilic aromatic substitution sequence; 2,4‑dinitrochlorobenzene undergoes substitution by ammonia to give an aniline derivative, followed by further nitration in mixed concentrated nitric and sulfuric acids to afford 2,4,6‑trinitroaniline, with HCl and water as by‑products; reaction carried out at 0–50 °C then warmed to 60–80 °C in a corrosive acid mixture; no additional catalyst beyond the acids.

Acid-base precipitation reaction; aqueous nitric acid protonates sodium stannate generating soluble sodium nitrate and insoluble tin(IV) oxide which precipitates; typically carried out in water with gentle heating to promote complete precipitation, no special catalyst required.

Chromium(VI)-mediated oxidation of a primary alcohol to an aldehyde; sodium dichromate in concentrated sulfuric acid oxidizes benzyl alcohol to benzaldehyde while being reduced to chromium(III) sulfate; performed in aqueous H₂SO₄, often refluxed at 80‑100 °C, water or water–acetone mixtures serve as solvent, no additional catalyst needed.

Nucleophilic substitution followed by hydrolysis (thiourea alkylation); bromoethane reacts with thiourea under basic aqueous conditions to give the ethyl isothiouronium intermediate which on alkaline hydrolysis furnishes ethanethiol, ammonia and urea, while NaBr is formed; conducted in water or aqueous NaOH, reflux for several hours, no catalyst required.

Base‑catalyzed aldol condensation and oxidative cyclization (Baker‑Venkataraman type) to form a flavone; 2,4‑dihydroxyacetophenone condenses with 4‑methoxybenzaldehyde under NaOH in ethanol, then cyclizes (often with I₂ or DDQ) to give acacetin; typical conditions include reflux in ethanol with NaOH, followed by mild oxidant for ring closure, no metal catalyst needed.

Thiophene formation via Lawesson’s reagent (thionation and cyclization); the 1,4‑diketone hexane‑2,5‑dione reacts with Lawesson’s reagent to replace the carbonyl oxygens with sulfur and close the five‑membered ring, yielding 2,5‑dimethylthiophene; usually refluxed in toluene or THF under inert atmosphere for 2‑4 h, Lawesson’s reagent is the sole reagent/catalyst.

Selective reduction of 2‑(4‑methoxyphenyl)acetaldehyde to the primary alcohol 2(4‑methoxyphenyl)ethanol using sodium borohydride; performed methanol (or ethanol/THF) at 0 °C to room temperature, with aqueous quench after completion.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (acylation) forming an amide; acetyl chloride reacts with 3‑nitroaniline to give 3‑nitroacetanilide and HCl; performed in anhydrous solvent such as pyridine or dichloromethane at 0‑5 °C to control exotherm, pyridine or a tertiary amine acts as base/solvent and scavenges HCl.

Precipitation (salt metathesis) reaction; used to exchange the acetate anion for iodide, forming insoluble silver iodide which can be removed by filtration. Key transformation: Ag⁺ pairs with I⁻ to give AgI(s) while acetate becomes acetic acid. Typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no catalyst required; water is the common solvent.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (acid anhydride esterification); converts ethanol into the corresponding ester (ethyl 2,2-dimethylpropanoate) while generating the corresponding carboxylic acid (2,2-dimethylpropanoic acid). Key transformation: the alcohol oxygen attacks one carbonyl of the anhydride, displacing the other acyl group as acid. Conducted in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF, often with a base (triethylamine) or a catalytic amount of DMAP to scavenge the formed acid; mild heating (20‑50 °C) may be applied.

Williamson ether synthesis (SN2 alkylation of a phenoxide); forms benzyl salicylate, an ester/aryl ether, while chloride is displaced as potassium chloride. Key transformation: the phenoxide oxygen of potassium salicylate attacks the benzylic carbon of benzyl chloride, displacing Cl⁻. Conducted in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF, acetone, or DMSO, often with slight heating (50‑80 °C); no catalyst is necessary, though the use of a base (e.g., K₂CO₃) can improve yields.

Fischer esterification of 3‑hydroxybenzoic acid with ethanol; acid‑catalyzed condensation yielding ethyl 3‑hydroxybenzoate and water; carried out with H2SO4 or p‑TsOH under reflux in ethanol, often removing water to favor product formation.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a primary chloride with hydroxide; converts epichlorohydrin to glycidol, preserving the epoxide ring while replacing chlorine with a hydroxyl group, and generates NaCl. Typically performed in aqueous NaOH (1–2 M) at 0‑25 °C, then the mixture may be extracted with an organic solvent; no additional catalyst is required. Reaction may be followed by acidification to isolate glycidol.

Alkaline hydrolysis (nucleophilic aromatic substitution) of an aryl methyl ether. Aqueous NaOH at reflux cleaves the C‑O bond, converting the nitro‑substituted anisole into the corresponding nitrophenol and methanol. No catalyst beyond NaOH; water is the solvent.

Acetylation of ephedrine with acetic anhydride; acylation of the secondary alcohol (and possibly the amine) producing ephedrine acetate and acetic acid; typical conditions: reflux in pyridine or dichloromethane at 50–80 °C; pyridine acts as base and catalyst; removal of generated acetic acid drives the reaction forward.

Fenton‑type oxidative conversion; purpose is to oxidize thymine at the C‑5 position to 5‑formyluracil. In aqueous solution, Fe(II) sulfate reacts with H2O2 to generate hydroxyl radicals that abstract hydrogen and introduce a formyl group. Conditions: aqueous medium, ambient to mild heating, pH neutral to slightly acidic; Fe(II) sulfate acts as catalyst, H2O2 is oxidant.

Enzymatic methyl transfer; trans‑methylation of L‑homocysteine to L‑methionine using betaine (trimethylglycine) as methyl donor. Catalyzed by betaine‑homocysteine S‑methyltransferase (BHMT) in aqueous buffer (pH 7.5–8.0) at 25–37 °C. One methyl group is transferred from betaine to the sulfhydryl of homocysteine, producing L‑methionine and dimethylglycine. The reaction proceeds under physiological conditions; no synthetic catalyst or organic solvent is required.

Chlorination of a carboxylic anhydride using phosphorus pentachloride; purpose is to prepare hexanoyl chloride (acid chloride) from hexanoic anhydride. PCl5 reacts with the anhydride to replace the acyl‑oxygen bridge with two chloride atoms, producing two equivalents of hexanoyl chloride and POCl3 as by‑product. Conditions: anhydrous, inert solvent such as dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride, 0 °C to room temperature; POCl3 is formed in situ, no external catalyst.

Oxidative dissolution of lanthanum metal by concentrated nitric acid; purpose is to generate lanthanum nitrate while reducing nitric acid to nitrogen dioxide. Lanthanum is oxidized to La³⁺, nitrate anion pairs to give La(NO₃)₃, and NO₃⁻ is reduced to NO₂ gas, with water produced. Conditions: concentrated HNO₃, reflux or gentle heating; reaction is exothermic, performed in glass vessel, no added catalyst.

Direct fluorination (synthesis) of rhodium(III) fluoride; purpose is to obtain RhF₃ from elemental rhodium. Gaseous F₂ reacts with rhodium metal, oxidizing Rh⁰ to Rh³⁺ and forming RhF₃ solid. Conditions: flow of dry F₂ gas, elevated temperature (typically 200–400 °C) in a fluorination reactor; inert atmosphere may be used, no solvent.

Simple hydrolysis (ligand exchange) of methylmercury chloride. In water the chloride ligand is replaced by hydroxide, giving methylmercury hydroxide and hydrochloric acid. Typically performed at ambient temperature; no catalyst required.

Double‑displacement precipitation (metathesis). Mixing aqueous sodium oxalate with iron(III) chloride precipitates iron(III) oxalate while sodium chloride stays dissolved. Reaction proceeds at room temperature with stirring in water.

Catalytic transfer hydrogenation of p‑nitroacetanilide. Formic acid serves as a hydrogen donor over palladium on carbon, reducing the nitro group to an amino group to afford 4‑aminoacetanilide; carbon dioxide and water are the only by‑products. Commonly run in ethanol or methanol at 50‑80 °C under atmospheric pressure; Pd/C is the catalyst.

Ester hydrolysis (neutral or acid‑catalyzed). Water attacks the methyl valerate ester, yielding valeric acid and methanol. Typically heated under reflux in aqueous medium; a trace of acid (e.g., HCl) can be added to accelerate the reaction.
